descs.en: The boy next door followed her to university and stayed “unofficial” for years. She loves him. She just doesn’t know how to go from friends to forever.

titles.en: The Boy Next Door Never Left

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
Eliana Lin and Wang Yu Chen grew up next door to each other in the Walled City, with a knee-high wall between their front steps. On the night she finishes school she can't sleep and goes to sit on her step at two in the morning. He comes out with his blanket and sits down beside her, and somewhere before dawn he realises he's in love with her. In the morning he turns down the better medical school in the north and follows her up the hill. He tells everyone it was the course.

She works it out in a fortnight and climbs onto his roof at Mid-Autumn to tell him to stop hovering. He kisses her before she's finished the sentence. After that they're together, in secret, because that's how she wants it. She's the youngest Lin, born the night her mother died, and her father can barely look at her. At night, on five screens, she cleans the family's name out of places it shouldn't be, for Chen Si, and tells nobody. Yu Chen never asks her to stop. He brings tea.

Nobody cheats, and nothing hangs on a misunderstanding. The hard parts are being seen (holding his hand on the hill in daylight), a father who has never once asked her what she wants, and one word she has been afraid of all her life, because people say forever and then they're in a hospital. He's willing to wait, and he won't pretend he isn't.

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
Eliana has been in the corner of every Lin book so far: asleep under a ladder, filming everyone's kisses for the spreadsheet, opening Haozhen's phone in under four minutes. I kept wondering who was waiting for her on the kerb when she got home.

Yu Chen looks like the clean one, and mostly he is. But he reads her food orders every night because they're on his card, he picked his medical school because of her, and he lied once, to his face, to the cousin who raised him. I didn't want the book to tell him off for any of that. What I love most about him is that in seven years he never once asks her to be someone else. He makes more tea.

This is the softest book I've written since The Softest Kind of Love. They're adults the whole way through and they get together early. Their first times are shy and clumsy, with a lot of laughing and starting again, because he researches everything and she wrecks the plan. Her father is hard on her, and there's a death in an emergency department and a bad morning at the flower market. Nobody has a baby. They get a porch, a jar in a wall and two desks facing each other.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
21+ · For adult readers. Mature themes and heated love scenes.

This is a 21+ friends-to-lovers romance, gentle and funny for most of its length, but it has some hard moments:

• Love scenes throughout, heated and detailed but not explicit, from He Researched This Part Too on

• A mother who died giving birth, mentioned, and a father's grief and coldness towards the daughter she had (throughout; most of all Nineteen, and Nobody Says It, The Neighbour and the Cold Gaze, The First Lin Child to Say No to His Face and Elowen Takes Her Side)

• The heroine's secret work for a crime syndicate, and a man's hands broken because of something she found, mentioned (He Already Knew)

• A sister abducted, and human trafficking referred to but not shown (The Fence, The Photograph)

• A nineteen-year-old's death after a road accident, with resuscitation in an emergency department (The Night He Lost One)

• Threatening messages and photographs from strangers (The Boy Next Door, He Always Waits)

• A cyber-attack on the family, a crowd stampede, a crushed leg and heavy bleeding (The Breach, Thirty-Six Hours, Someone Else's Blood)

• An attack with a broken bottle at work, a head injury and stitches (The Ring in the Jar)

• A partner who reads her food orders to know when she hasn't eaten, and a lie told to the police for her, shown without judgement (He Already Knew, The Detective Already Knows)

glossary.title: Names & Terms
glossary.content:
Yu-er — Eliana's family name. Her sisters use it when they want something. Yu Chen uses it all the time, and it's the only time it comes without a favour attached.
The tall house — the Lin family house in the Walled City: old, narrow, too many stairs, a red door, and three front steps under a small tiled roof.
The porch — those three steps, with the crack in the third one, where everything that matters between them happens at two in the morning. From 2026 it runs the width of both houses.
The old Song house — next door to the Lins. Yu Chen's uncle's house, which he bought from Wei Long; later rebuilt with one long room and two desks facing each other.
The persimmon tree — in the Song garden. Its best branch hangs over the Lin side, so by old neighbourly rule its fruit are Lin persimmons. Ripe every October.
The jar — a plum-jam jar of Nainai's, kept behind a loose brick in the garden wall under the persimmon branch. Notes go in it. You don't read one until the writer has gone inside.
The Eraser — what the Syndicate calls Eliana, because she erases the Lin family's footprints. She hates the name.
The fence — what she built in October 2022, after her sister was taken: a watch on the family's names, faces and addresses that wakes her wherever she is. Two short buzzes mean family.
FENCE — her own security firm, from March 2026, in two rooms above a dumpling shop on Terrace Road. For the first month the sign was a sticky note: FENCE. Legal. Mostly.
The Spreadsheet — Eliana's record of every family secret, kept for years. "You're on a spreadsheet" is a warning.
DRAW (OFFICIAL) — Eliana's caption on the video of the paper twins' birthday party at Fig Tree Lane. Raiden contests it every year.
Red egg — a boiled egg dyed red, a traditional birthday gift. One is left at Eliana's door before dawn every 18 February. She thinks for years she knows who leaves it.
Study room 4B — the quiet room at the end of the library's fourth floor, booked to "Wang Y.C." every weekday morning since March 2022. Nobody has ever found out how.
Graduate-entry medicine — a four-year medical degree for students who already have a first degree. Yu Chen's, at the university on the hill, 2021 to 2025.
OSCE — the practical part of medical finals: timed stations with examiners and actors playing patients.
Mid-Autumn — the harvest festival at the full moon of the eighth lunar month: mooncakes, family dinners and lanterns. Every year Yu Chen puts a white rabbit lantern on his roof.
PLAN — Yu Chen's plans, in capitals, on small squares of paper. PLAN, PLAN B, PLAN C. She wrecks every one.
Nainai — grandmother on the father's side. Yu Chen's lives in the north and has had a letter from him every month for years.
The Lins, the Wangs and the Songs — Yu Chen's father was a Wang from the north, the younger brother of Xing Yue's father. His mother was a Song, Wei Long's aunt, which is how he came to live in the old Song house next door to the Lins.

chapters.title: The Boy Next Door Who Never Left
chapters.desc: The night she finishes school, Eliana can’t sleep and goes to sit on her front steps at two in the morning. Yu Chen comes out with his blanket and sits down beside her, and this time he realises he’s in love with her.
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t have to talk. I’ll just sit here. That’s allowed.” — Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
It was too hot to be indoors, so on Friday evening Yu Chen sat on his own front step with his phone and read the same three emails again.

The first was from the medical school in the north. It was the better school. It was an hour on the train from his grandmother, who had wanted him there since he’d first mentioned medicine, and who wrote it at the bottom of every letter in her big sloping hand: The north has better doctors and better weather. The second was from the university on the hill, on the other side of the city. The third was from the polytechnic, where he had sat his last paper two weeks ago. It offered him a master’s, with the fees paid and some money besides.

All three wanted an answer by the end of the month. He hadn’t told anyone about any of them. Not Wei Long. Not Nainai. Not Auntie Dai, who had left at six with her shopping trolley and told him to eat the soup.

He was twenty-one. He had a degree, or would have when they posted it, and a house, and a bicycle, and money from his father’s side that he’d been allowed to touch since January and hadn’t. He had three emails. He could not make himself pick one.

His phone buzzed. The course group chat. Leaving drinks tonight!! Yu Chen you’re coming, no excuses.

He typed Sorry, can’t. Have a good night, and muted it.

The lane had gone orange in the low sun. On the far side of the tall house the old man was singing to his birds.

Then she came round the corner at the bottom of the lane.

She was alone. She had her school bag on one shoulder and her hood down for once, because of the heat, and her hair was coming out of its pencil. She was eating an ice lolly, a green one, and reading something on her phone and frowning at it.

She looked up and saw him, and lifted the lolly at him.

He lifted a hand.

“Finished?” he said.

She stopped at the bottom of her own three steps, which were an arm’s length from his, with the knee-high wall and its iron rail between them. Green juice was running down her wrist. She licked it off. “Chemistry,” she said. “It was fine. I finished early and sat there for forty minutes doing nothing.”

“Well done.”

She looked at him as if he’d said it in another language. Then she said, “Yeah,” and went up her steps, and the red door shut behind her.

No car in the lane. Lin Jian would be at the fishing-net building, or somewhere else; he often was. Ah Sim would have left noodles.

Yu Chen sat on his step until the sun was off the lane. Then he went in and ate the soup, and didn’t answer any of the emails.

✦ ✦ ✦

At two in the morning her light was still on.

He could see it from his desk if he leaned back in his chair: the top window of the tall house, across the two gardens, where her blackout curtains never quite met. A thin white line down the middle.

He had a sheet of paper in front of him with three columns on it, one for each email. It was no help at all. He had written better school under the north, and Nainai, and under the hill he had written nothing, because every reason he could think of for the hill was a reason he didn’t want to look at.

Then he heard the Lins’ front door.

The red door had a bolt that stuck, and in summer, with every window open, the sound of it carried right across. He got up and went to the front window.

She was on her steps. On the third one, against the rail, in a black hoodie, with her knees pulled up inside it and her arms wrapped round them, the way she sat when the tall house got too quiet for her. The step was stone. Even in June it would be cold.

He stood at the window for a minute.

Then he pulled the blanket off his bed, the blue checked one that had been his mother’s, and filled his flask from the pot on his desk, and went down.

He stepped over the low wall by the iron rail. She heard him. She didn’t look round.

He shook out the blanket and sat down on the step beside her, and put half of it round her shoulders, and kept the other half.

She didn’t explain. He didn’t ask.

“You don’t have to talk,” he said. “I’ll just sit here. That’s allowed.”

“I wasn’t going to talk.”

He let that go. She pulled her half of the blanket tighter. Up close she smelled of green-apple shampoo and, still, a little, of the lolly. Her glasses had slid down her nose and she didn’t push them up.

A cat walked along the top of the garden wall and stopped to look at them, and walked on. At the end of the lane the noodle stall had its shutter down.

“I’m not sad,” she said after a while. “If that’s what you’re thinking. I’m just not tired.”

He hadn’t been thinking it. She told him he was doing the face anyway, the one he did at Auntie Dai’s bad knee, as if everybody were a patient, and that he wasn’t even a doctor, so he could stop. He let her say all of it. She was cross with somebody, and he was the one on the step.

She took the flask out of his hand without asking and unscrewed it.

“What’s in it?”

“Chrysanthemum. Pear. Some rock sugar.”

She drank from the lid and made a face. “That’s too sweet.” She drank the rest of the lid and poured another. “That’s the only thing I’ve tasted all week.”

She held the lid in both hands to warm them. Her hands were always cold. “Everybody’s leaving. Did you know that? Half my year are going abroad, and the other half are going north. There was a girl crying in the toilets after the exam because her boyfriend’s going somewhere with snow.”

“You’re not going anywhere.”

“I’m going up the hill.” She didn’t look at him. “Computer science. If my results are all right, which they will be. I looked at who else from my school is going. It’s me and a boy who eats paper.”

He laughed before he could stop it. She looked pleased for half a second, and then she didn’t.

“I’m going to know nobody,” she said. “Not one person. I’ll have to say my name to strangers every day for a month.” She turned the lid round in her fingers. “And nobody in my house said well done, either. Elowen texted. Baba wasn’t back. Ah Sim made noodles, which is the same as well done from Ah Sim, but still.” She shrugged under the blanket. “You said it. On your step. You were the only one.”

He opened his mouth to tell her about the hill.

It was right there. I’ve got a place there too. She would turn and look at him, and she would know the course, because she knew everything, and she would ask why the hill and not the north. And he would need an answer.

He looked at her. She was drinking his tea out of his flask with her hair coming down and his mother’s blanket round her, frowning at the lane as if it had done something to her, and he knew the answer.

It went over in him with no warning, the way you miss a step in the dark.

He was in love with her. He had been for a while. He didn’t know how long. He had only noticed now, on her cold step, because she’d said he was the only one, and he had wanted, more than he’d wanted anything, to be the only one.

It frightened him. He kept still, the way you keep still when there’s a wasp on your arm.

She noticed. She noticed most things. “What?”

“Nothing.” He looked at the lane. “Your hair’s coming down.”

She put a hand up and felt for the pencil, and found it hanging, and didn’t fix it. “Leave it.”

He left it. He kept both his hands on his knees.

She pulled more of the blanket over to her side, which left him with a corner, and pushed her bare feet under his leg on the step. They were freezing.

“Your feet are like ice.”

“So move.”

He didn’t move. After a minute she stopped pretending she’d put them there by accident, and left them, and leaned her shoulder on his arm. Through the hoodie and his shirt he could feel how cold she was all over. He shifted the corner he had left onto her knees, and she let him, and didn’t say thank you.

“You’ll go too,” she said. Her eyes were shut. “You’ve finished your degree. People who finish go.”

He didn’t answer straight away. He didn’t trust what would come out.

He was still trying to find something true that wouldn’t frighten either of them when her head got heavy on his arm, and her breathing changed, and the lid of the flask tipped in her fingers. He took it before it fell. She didn’t wake.

✦ ✦ ✦

He stayed.

The cat came back along the wall. A moped went past on the main road and faded. The stone of the step came up through the seat of his jogging bottoms, and his arm went numb from the shoulder down, and he didn’t move it, because if he moved it she would wake up and go in, and this would be over.

He had no idea what he was going to do. He knew that he wasn’t going to the north.

The sky went grey over the roofs of the Walled City. The first bird started in the persimmon tree behind his house. The noodle man came and rattled his shutter halfway up and looked along the lane at the two of them on the step under one blanket, and went back to his pots without a word.

At five the bolt stuck in the red door behind them.

Elowen came out in jeans, with her car keys in her hand, dressed for the flower market. She’d stayed over in her old room for an early start; he’d seen her car come in after midnight. She stopped on the top step and looked down at her sister, asleep against his shoulder, with her mouth open and her glasses crooked.

“How long has she been out here?”

“Since two.”

Elowen looked at Eliana’s face. She didn’t ask him anything else.

“Thank you, Yu Chen,” she said, and crouched, and shook her sister’s knee.

Eliana woke the way she always woke, all at once and annoyed. She looked at Elowen, and then at him, and then at the sky. She didn’t say anything. She stood up with the blanket still round her shoulders and went inside, half asleep, with one end of it trailing up the steps after her. He watched it go through the red door.

He didn’t ask for it back.

✦ ✦ ✦

He went home over the low wall.

He meant to go upstairs. Instead he sat down on the kitchen floor with his back against the cupboard under the sink, in the grey light, with the empty flask in his lap, and stayed there, because his legs wouldn’t do anything else.

Then he got up and opened his laptop on the kitchen table, and accepted the place on the hill.

He wrote to the north to say thank you, and no. The polytechnic could wait till next week. Nainai would be cross. He would write to her on Sunday, the way he did every month, and this time he would tell her why, and it would be the first time he had written it down anywhere.

Across the garden, the line of light in her window had gone out.

At seven he boiled the kettle and made a fresh pot, chrysanthemum and a pinch of dried pear and a little rock sugar, and let it stand five minutes, and filled the flask. Then he stood in Auntie Dai’s kitchen holding it, with nobody to give it to until she woke up.

chapters.title: Two Gowns, Eventually
chapters.desc: First day on the hill. Eliana starts computer science and would like to be invisible. Yu Chen, three years older, has somehow started graduate-entry medicine at the same university, and swears it’s about the course.
chapters.epigraph: “It’s the best medical course in the country. You being here is a coincidence.” — Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
He was on the kerb when she came out. He had been on the kerb most mornings since June, whether she was going anywhere or not.

Eliana stopped at the top of the three steps with her laptop bag on one shoulder and a second bag, with her portable monitor in it, banging against her knee. It was half past seven on a Monday in September and already warm. The lane smelled of the noodle stall at the end and of somebody’s washing. Her hood was up. She had put it up in her room before she’d even opened the door.

Yu Chen was sitting on the kerb beside his father’s old green bicycle with his elbows on his knees. When the red door shut behind her, he stood up.

He was twenty-one now and taller than anyone needed to be, in a white shirt with the sleeves rolled, and across the basket on the front of the bicycle, folded neatly, there was a white coat.

She looked at the coat.

“They gave them out on Friday,” he said. “There’s a thing at nine where they make us put them on in front of a professor. I’m supposed to bring it.”

“You’re not wearing it on the bus.”

“I’m not getting the bus.”

He never got the bus. He had cycled up the hill on Friday to collect the coat and come back down again in time to eat Ah Sim’s dumplings over the wall, and he would cycle up it again this morning and get there before her, and stand at the gate looking as if he had been there for ages.

She came down the steps.

“There are three medical schools in this city,” she said. “You did your degree at the polytechnic. They’ve got a medical school now. They put up a whole building. I saw it on the news.”

“It’s not as good.”

She had been saving this up since August, when he’d told her, standing on this kerb, as if it were nothing. He’d said it like a thing he had only just decided. But nobody applied to only one place, and he had never once said where else he’d tried. She meant to find out. She hadn’t told him that.

He took the monitor bag off her shoulder before she could stop him and hung it on his handlebars. “It’s the best medical course in the country,” he said. “You being here is a coincidence.”

She looked at him from under the hood. He looked back. He had a face that people trusted. Teachers had trusted it, and the old women at the market, and Baba’s drivers, who called him the Song boy and let him carry things. His ears had gone a little pink at the top. That was the only sign, and she was the only person who knew to look for it.

“Liar,” she said, and went to the bus stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

The bus went up the hill in a long slow zigzag, past the hospital at the bottom with its old grey block and its new glass tower, past the flats and the shrines and the tea shops, and every time it turned a corner she could see him below on the road, riding steadily, with the white coat in the basket and her monitor swinging from the handlebars.

He beat the bus. He always did.

By the time she got off at the top, with forty other people her age pushing past her in a cloud of perfume and loud voices, he was standing just inside the university gates in the coat, with the bicycle locked to a rail and her monitor bag at his feet. A group of students in the same white coats had gathered round him. One of them, a girl with short hair and a lot of rings, was laughing up at him and holding out her phone for a photo.

Eliana stopped by the gatepost.

She watched him smile at the girl, a pleasant, careful smile that didn’t reach anywhere, and say something, and step out of the photo before they took it. The girl’s face fell a little. Two of the others looked at each other. He picked up the monitor bag and came across the stones towards Eliana as if the group behind him had stopped existing.

She hadn’t known that people looked at him like that.

She thought about it, standing by the gatepost. She didn’t like it. She didn’t like that she didn’t like it, either, so she put it away in the part of her head where she kept things to look at later, and pushed her glasses up her nose, and took her bag back.

“Your friends want a picture,” she said.

“I met them on Friday.” He looked down at her. “You’re going to registration first. The computer science building’s the one that looks like a fish tank. The desk’s on the ground floor. I checked.”

“I know where it is. I’ve got a map.”

He held out a folded sheet of paper.

“Now you’ve got a better one,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Registration was a long table with four students behind it in purple T-shirts, and a queue, and a lot of noise.

When she got to the front, the boy behind the table smiled at her and said, “Name?”

Eliana opened her mouth.

Nothing came out. It was always like this with strangers. She could talk to Elowen for an hour and to Yu Chen all night and to anyone at all through a keyboard, but put a stranger’s face in front of her and ask her a question and her voice went somewhere she couldn’t reach it.

“Sorry?” said the boy. “Name?”

She took out her student card and put it on the table and slid it across to him.

He read it. “Lin Yu. Great. Welcome.” He gave her a lanyard and a tote bag full of leaflets and a voucher for a free coffee, and she said thank you so low that she wasn’t sure it had come out at all, and went and stood in a corner by a pillar and breathed.

Then she unfolded his map.

It was the campus, drawn in black pen, neat as a textbook, every building labelled in his small square writing. The fish tank. The library. The noodle stall behind the library, under a tree. The medical school, the anatomy building, the old observatory dome. And all over it, in green pen, little circles.

Toilets on the third floor of the arts block. Nobody uses them.

Bench behind the observatory. Shade after two.

Library, fourth floor, after six. Empty.

Side door of the fish tank. Doesn’t lock till eight. Use it if the front is busy.

There were circles all over it. Every one was a place where nobody would look at her.

She stood by the pillar and looked at the map, and something went tight in her throat, and she was furious with him, because she was about to cry in the computer science building on her first morning.

She folded it up very small and put it in her hoodie pocket.

✦ ✦ ✦

At lunch she went to the bench behind the observatory. It was in shade after two, and it was quarter past one, and she sat in the sun anyway with her laptop on her knees.

He came at half past, without the coat, carrying two boxes of noodles and his flask.

“How was it?”

“Fine.”

“Did you say your name?”

She didn’t answer. He sat down beside her and gave her a box and the flask, and she knew without opening it what would be inside: chrysanthemum and dried pear and a little rock sugar, the tea he had started making her in June, the morning after she’d drunk his whole flask on her front steps. He made it every morning now. She had never asked him to.

“I showed them my card,” she said.

“That’s allowed.”

He’d said that in June, too, on her steps at two in the morning, when she hadn’t wanted to talk and he’d sat down anyway with half his blanket round her. She had thought about it more than she meant to, since. She thought about it now, with the noodles going cold on her knee, and her face got warm, and she was glad of the hood.

A boy ran past chasing a frisbee. Someone threw it too hard. It came spinning out of the sun straight at her head, and before she’d even flinched, Yu Chen’s hand had come up and caught it, without looking, without putting down his noodles.

He tossed it back. The boy shouted sorry.

Eliana sat still.

Two girls on the grass had seen it. One of them said something to the other, and they both looked at him, and then at her, small and hooded beside him with a laptop, as if they were trying to work out what she was to him. Eliana tried to work it out too. She didn’t get far. He had gone back to his noodles as if nothing had happened, with his knee an inch from hers on the bench, and she found she was looking at his hand, the one that had caught the frisbee, resting on his leg with a blue pen mark on the side of the thumb. She couldn’t seem to stop.

She made herself look at the laptop.

“What?” said Yu Chen.

“Nothing.” She opened the noodles. “You were showing off.”

“I was saving your glasses.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The library was five floors of glass and concrete with a staircase up the middle that went round and round like the inside of a shell.

He carried her monitor bag up it. She had told him she could do it herself, and he had said yes, and picked it up anyway. In exchange she carried his flask, which he’d filled again from a hot-water tap on the second floor that he knew about and nobody else seemed to.

She was looking at the fourth floor on his map. She wasn’t looking at the stairs.

Her foot missed the edge of a step. She grabbed the rail, and the flask came out of her hand and went down the gap in the middle of the staircase, and hit the stairs below with a sound like a bell, and went on hitting them, clang, clang, all the way to the bottom.

Everyone in the library looked up.

Eliana stood holding the rail with her face on fire.

He went down and got it. It took him a minute. He came back up with the flask in one hand, and there was a dent in it near the bottom, a deep one, the shape of a step.

“I’m sorry,” she said. “I’ll buy you a new one. I’ll buy you a better one, I’ll—”

He turned it round and looked at the dent. Then he unscrewed the top, and poured some tea into the lid, and drank it.

“Still works,” he said. “I like it better.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She worked on the fourth floor all afternoon, at a long table by the window, and he went to his medical building and came back at four and sat at the other end of the same table with a textbook the size of a paving slab. They didn’t speak. He didn’t look at her. Every hour or so a cup of tea appeared at her elbow.

At six the floor emptied, the way he had said it would.

When they went out, the sun was going down over the harbour and the library steps were orange. She stopped on the top step to put her laptop in her bag, and the pencil holding her hair up slid out and clattered down the steps, and half her hair came down over her face.

He picked up the pencil. He gave it to her. And then, while she was holding it, he reached out and tucked a loose piece of hair back behind her ear.

His fingers were warm. They touched the edge of her glasses and the top of her ear and were gone.

She went completely still.

It was nothing. He had done things like it all summer. Pulled her hood up in the rain. Wiped ink off her chin with his thumb. But she stood on the library steps with the pencil in her hand and couldn’t move at all, and she could see that he’d felt her go still, because he took his hand back as if he’d touched something hot.

“Sorry,” he said. “Was that all right?”

She looked at him. His ears had gone red. Properly red, all the way down.

She thought about the girl with the rings at the gate. She thought about the green circles on the map, and the flask with the dent in it, and about how many times she’d stood in a crowd today and felt him somewhere at the edge of it, not looking at her, and known exactly where he was.

“Don’t ask,” she said. “Just don’t do it where people can see.”

He didn’t say anything. He looked at her as if she had told him something enormous, which she supposed she had. Then he nodded, and put his hands in his pockets, and walked down the steps beside her to unlock the bicycle.

She put her hair up with the pencil on the way down. Her hands weren’t steady. She didn’t let him see.

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten past one in the morning she was at her desk at the top of the tall house with the blackout curtains closed and all five screens lit.

The message had come at midnight, through the channel that only one person used. Qian, Chen Si’s assistant, wrote the way he talked, politely and without wasting anything. A man in the eastern district was offering a buyer a folder of old shipping records with her father’s name on every page. Could she look.

She looked.

It took her an hour. She didn’t feel anything while she did it. That was the part she liked. Her hands knew where to go, and her head was cold and clear, and the man in the eastern district, whoever he was, got smaller and smaller on her screens until he wasn’t anything at all.

Just after two, the buyer opened the folder and found it empty except for one file, which was a photograph of a persimmon.

She sent Qian one line. Done.

Then she sat back and took her glasses off and pressed the heels of her hands into her eyes until she saw colours.

When she opened them, she pulled the edge of the curtain back an inch.

Down in the garden next door, the persimmon tree was black against the paler black of the wall. Across from her window, on the second floor of the old Song house, his light was on.

He had lectures at nine. She knew, because she had his timetable. She’d had it since the week he got it, though she’d never told him.

She let the curtain fall, and turned off the screens one by one, and lay down on the camp bed under the blue checked blanket with the map still folded small in her hoodie pocket, and lay awake until the birds started.

chapters.title: The Flask, the Headphones, the Tea
chapters.desc: Ten days in. He has learned her new timetable, her new silences and the exact brand of headphones she destroys every fortnight. She has learned that she can’t concentrate when he’s reading across the table, which is new and annoying.
chapters.epigraph: “I bought ten pairs. Don’t argue. You go through them like socks.” — Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
Her light went off at ten past four.

Yu Chen saw it because he was awake. He was usually awake at some point between two and four, and when he was, he looked. He didn’t get up to do it. From his bed in the front room on the second floor of the old Song house, if he turned his head on the pillow, he could see past the edge of his own curtain and across the garden to the top window of the tall house, where her blackout curtains never quite met in the middle. A line of white light, thin as a thread. Then nothing.

Ten past four. Lectures at nine. She’d be on the bus at eight with her eyes half shut and her hood up, and she’d fall asleep on the fourth floor of the library by the afternoon.

He turned over and slept until six.

✦ ✦ ✦

If anyone had asked him, he would have said he was organised.

Nobody asked. Wei Long, the one person who might have, had moved out two years ago into a flat near police headquarters, and came round on Sundays to eat Auntie Dai’s food and tell him he was too thin. Auntie Dai came at eight and left at six and asked nothing at all. So there was no one to explain it to, which suited him, because explained out loud it would have sounded worse than it was.

He had a notebook. Her timetable was in the back of it, copied from the computer science department’s website the week it went up, every module and room and the name of every lecturer. He knew she had Programming on Mondays and Thursdays in the big lecture hall in the fish tank. He knew she had a maths tutorial on Wednesday afternoons with a man who wore sandals, and that she hated it, because she had come out of the first one with her mouth in a straight line and not spoken until the bottom of the hill.

He knew she went through a pair of headphones roughly every two weeks. The white wired ones, always the same make, because she said wireless ones could be listened to by anyone who cared to, and she would know because she was usually the one listening. She wound them round her phone, and round her fingers, and round her pencil, and knotted them in her pocket, and pulled at the knots in lectures until something inside the wire gave. In August he had found the shop that sold them and bought ten pairs. The box was in his bag.

And every morning at half past six, before Auntie Dai came, he made her tea.

Chrysanthemum, a pinch of dried pear, a little rock sugar. Boiled water, cooled for a minute. Five minutes, then strained into the flask. He’d started in June, the morning after the steps, because she had drunk his whole flask at two in the morning and said it was the only thing she’d tasted all week. Since then her light had stayed on past three most nights, and she came out in the mornings grey as paper. He had read that chrysanthemum was good for tired eyes. He didn’t know if it was true. She drank it, and that was enough.

The flask had a dent near the bottom now, from the library stairs. He turned it so the dent faced out when he put it in his bag.

He’d known since June.

He had sat on his own front step one evening in early summer and watched her come up the lane from her last exam, alone, with her hood down for once because of the heat and her hair coming out of its pencil, eating an ice lolly and reading something on her phone and frowning at it. She’d looked up and seen him and lifted the lolly at him.

He hadn’t known what it was then. He had found out at two that morning, on her steps, with half his blanket round her and his tea in her hands. It had gone over in him with no warning, the way you miss a step in the dark.

At five he had gone home and sat on the kitchen floor until his legs worked.

Then he had got up and accepted the place on the hill, and written to the north to say no.

✦ ✦ ✦

The mentoring meeting was at eleven, in a corridor on the third floor of the old hospital block, outside a door that said SURGERY — RESIDENTS.

The medical school gave every new student a mentor from the hospital. His was his cousin. He suspected this was not a coincidence either, and that somebody in the north had made a phone call, but nobody had told him and he hadn’t asked.

Wang Xing Yue came out of the door late, at nearly a quarter past, in green scrubs, with a cap in one hand and his glasses pushed up on his forehead. He was twenty-nine, and a surgeon, and he walked as if the corridor belonged to him. He looked at Yu Chen the way he looked at everyone, as if checking whether they were bleeding.

“You,” he said. “Sign this.”

Yu Chen signed it.

“Twice a term. Ten minutes. If you’re failing, sooner. Don’t be failing.” Xing Yue took the form back and looked at it. “Why here?”

“It’s the best course.”

“It’s the third best course. The one in the north is better. Grandmother wanted you in the north.” He folded the form in half. “She told my father you’d gone south because of a girl.”

Yu Chen looked at the wall behind his cousin’s head. There was a poster on it about handwashing.

“Grandmother says a lot of things,” he said.

Xing Yue looked at him over the top of his glasses for a second longer. Then a nurse put her head out of the door and said a name, and he turned without another word and went back in, and Yu Chen walked down the stairs and out into the sun and found his hands were cold.

He liked his cousin. He thought he did. But he hadn’t seen him more than once a year since he was seven, and the man was very hard to talk to, and he was relieved it was over.

In the anatomy lecture after lunch, the girl with all the rings sat down next to him.

She had been at the gate on the first day. She’d asked for a photo. She’d asked since then for his number, his notes from Tuesday, and whether he wanted to come to a thing on Friday that the second years were having. He’d given her the notes, because that cost nothing, and said no to the rest, politely, each time. He thought her name began with a J. He was fairly sure it did.

“You’re always running off,” she said. “Where do you go?”

“Library.”

“Which floor? I’ll come.”

“I’m not very good company,” said Yu Chen. “I don’t talk.” He opened his textbook. “Sorry.”

She laughed as if he’d made a joke, and stayed where she was, and he didn’t mind. He didn’t mind any of it. That was the thing about other people, mostly. He was polite to them and they went past him like weather, and he couldn’t have told anyone afterwards what they’d said.

Then he turned to the page on the bones of the hand and found a yellow sticky note stuck to it.

It was a drawing, in black biro, small. Two people sitting on a step under a little tiled roof, side by side, with one big blanket round both of them. The blanket had checks. The smaller one had a pencil sticking out of her hair and was holding a flask that wasn’t hers. That was all. No words.

He hadn’t seen her touch his bag. He had no idea when she’d done it.

He looked at it for as long as he could stand. Then he looked up at the ceiling of the lecture theatre, which was concrete, with a long crack across it, and kept looking at that until his face had gone back to normal.

“Are you all right?” said the girl beside him.

“Yes,” said Yu Chen. “Thank you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The fourth floor emptied at six, the way it always did.

She was already there when he came up, at the far end of the long table by the window, sitting on her chair with her knees up and her laptop balanced on them, which nobody had ever told her was not how chairs worked. She didn’t look up. He sat down at the other end, with three metres of table between them, and opened his textbook, and put the flask down in the middle of the table where she could reach it.

They didn’t talk. He read, and she typed, and the harbour went from blue to grey to black in the window, and the lights came on along the far shore one by one.

He looked up now and then. He couldn’t help that.

She had her headphones in, and she was frowning at her screen. She frowned when things went well; when things went badly her face went perfectly smooth. Her glasses had slid down her nose and she pushed them up with one knuckle without stopping typing. He watched her and realised that she hadn’t blinked.

He counted. He couldn’t help that either.

At three minutes he got up, walked down the table, unscrewed the flask, poured tea into its lid and put it down by her hand.

“Yu-er,” he said. “You haven’t blinked in three minutes. Drink this.”

She took one earphone out and looked up at him with dry red eyes, and then down at the tea, and opened her mouth to argue, and didn’t. He went back to his chair. After a moment she picked up the lid and drank the tea, all of it, and blinked several times, hard, as if he’d made her, and glared at him over the rim.

Ten minutes later, he turned a page.

Something kicked him under the table.

He looked up. She hadn’t moved. She was typing, eyes on the screen, her face perfectly calm. But her foot, in its grey sock, had come all the way down the length of the table under there and was resting against his shin.

“You turn pages too loud,” she said, without looking at him.

“Sorry.”

“You’ve been turning them too loud since Monday. I can’t think.” She typed something and deleted it. “It’s very annoying.”

He turned the next page as quietly as a page could be turned. Her foot stayed exactly where it was against his leg, warm through his trousers, for the next hour, and neither of them said anything about it.

✦ ✦ ✦

She had disappeared on Tuesday night.

That was how he thought of it, though she hadn’t gone anywhere. Her light had been on at ten, and at midnight, and at two, and at four, and still on when he got up at six. She came out of the red door at eight and looked straight through him as if he were part of the kerb. Her face was grey and her eyes were too bright and she was talking fast, to nobody, under her breath. When he said her name, she jumped.

It had started in June, a week or two after her exams. He didn’t know exactly what she did on those nights. He had a fair idea. He had never once asked, because in July, the first morning he’d seen her come out like this, she had said, If you ask, I’ll have to lie to you, and I don’t want to lie to you, so don’t ask, and he hadn’t.

So on Tuesday he hadn’t asked.

He’d gone home at lunchtime and asked Auntie Dai to make the pork and chive dumplings, the ones that kept, and at seven he’d taken a box of them round to the back gate of the tall house. Ah Sim had opened it. She was a small old woman with a large ladle and she had been taking things from him at that gate all summer: soup when Eliana had a cold in July, a lamp when her desk light broke, a bag of lychees. She took the box without a word and looked at him the way she always did, as if he were a slightly suspicious vegetable, and shut the gate.

On Wednesday the box had come back over the wall, empty and washed, with a sticky note on the lid. A drawing of a dumpling with a smile on it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter past nine, she fell asleep.

He saw it happen. Her typing slowed, and stopped, and her head went down by stages until her cheek was resting on her forearm on the table beside the laptop. Her glasses were crooked. One earphone had fallen out. Her mouth was a little open.

He waited five minutes to be sure.

Then he got up and went down the table. He moved her laptop away from the edge, and saved what she’d been doing, without reading it. He took off his grey jumper and put it round her shoulders. She didn’t wake up. She made a small annoyed noise and pulled the jumper closer with one hand and went on sleeping.

He stood there.

The top of her head was right there. Her hair was coming out of its knot, soft and black, and the pencil had slipped sideways, and she smelled of the green-apple shampoo she always used, and of tea. He could have bent down and put his mouth against her hair. Nobody would have seen. She would never have known.

He thought about it for exactly as long as it took him to notice he was thinking about it. Then he went back to his chair and sat down and got his notebook out of his bag.

He kept the plans at the front. Revision plans, mostly. A list of what he needed for the house. On the page for this week he’d written, in capitals, PLAN, and under it a list of her deadlines and his. Now he turned to a new page and wrote:

Not while she’s asleep. Not until she knows.

He looked at that. Then, underneath, smaller:

Friends. Hers.

Because that was the other thing he had noticed since Monday, and he didn’t like it. She had spoken to nobody but him. Not at registration, not in lectures, not in the queue at the noodle stall. Ten days on the hill and she had a map with green circles on it and a boy at the other end of the table, and nothing else. Part of him liked it. He liked being the only one who knew where she went when the house was too quiet.

He was twenty-one. It frightened him a little, how much of her weight was on him, and how much he liked the weight.

He didn’t know how you gave somebody friends. He’d find out. He’d read something.

He put the notebook away.

At ten the librarian came round to turn off the lights. Eliana woke with a jump, with his jumper half off her shoulders and a red crease down her cheek from her sleeve. She looked at the jumper. She looked at him. He was reading.

“You let me sleep.”

“You needed it.”

“I had a thing due.” She pulled her laptop over. “I’ve lost it. I’ve lost the whole—” She stopped, and scrolled, and looked at him over her glasses.

“I saved it,” he said. “I didn’t read it.”

She didn’t say thank you. She put the laptop in her bag and stood up and pulled his jumper on properly, over her hoodie, so that she looked like a pile of washing with a face, and walked out ahead of him without giving it back.

He followed her down the shell of the staircase. At the bottom she stopped and held out her hand without turning round.

He put the box of headphones in it.

She looked at it. Ten pairs, white, in their plastic.

“What’s this?”

“I bought ten pairs. Don’t argue. You go through them like socks.”

She didn’t say anything. She put the box under her arm, inside his jumper, and walked out into the warm dark towards the bus stop, and he unlocked the bicycle and rode down the hill behind the bus the whole way, the way he always did, where he could see the back window and the shape of a hood against it, leaning on the glass.

chapters.title: Mid-Autumn, on the Roof
chapters.desc: She climbs to his roof to pick a fight: she’s worked out he didn’t follow her to university by accident, and she wants him to admit it and stop hovering. He doesn’t admit it or deny it. He kisses her instead, hand on her jaw, mid-sentence.
chapters.epigraph: “Stop. You’ve been circling me since September. I’m not blind. Say it.” — Eliana Lin
chapters.content:
There were four of them at the long table for Mid-Autumn, and eleven chairs.

Elowen had come in the afternoon with two boxes of mooncakes from the good bakery on Harbour Road and gone again before dark, back to the house on the hill and her husband, who did not come to the Walled City for festivals yet and might never. Raiden had rung to say he was busy and would come at the weekend. He had been busy a lot since the summer, and he never said with what. Elara was on a night placement at the hospital and had sent a photo of herself eating a mooncake in a corridor in scrubs.

So it was Baba at the head of the table, and Evangeline at the far end where she always sat, and Eliana halfway down, and Ah Sim coming in and out of the kitchen with dishes nobody had asked for.

There was a lantern on the porch, a red one, that Ah Sim had hung. Ah Sim hung one every Mid-Autumn, whoever came.

Baba ate his soup. He asked Evangeline whether the orchids on her sill were doing well, and Evangeline nodded. He asked Ah Sim whether the duck was from the usual man. Then he looked at the dish of greens in front of Eliana, which she hadn’t touched, and said to Ah Sim, “Tell her to eat something green. She lives on noodles.”

Ah Sim looked at Eliana. Eliana looked at the greens.

“I’m right here, Baba,” she said.

He didn’t answer. He went back to his soup. Later he asked Evangeline whether she wanted more duck, and Evangeline shook her head, and the clock in the hall ticked, and the lantern moved a little on its hook outside the window.

Eliana ate two pieces of greens, so that Ah Sim would stop looking at her, and asked to be excused, and nobody said no.

✦ ✦ ✦

She had been building the case for a week.

She had done it the way she did everything, with a spreadsheet. Column A, the date. Column B, where she’d been. Column C, where he’d been. It had started as a joke, the night after the library steps, because she couldn’t sleep and couldn’t stop thinking about his hand by her ear. By Friday it was not a joke.

He’d had two offers for graduate-entry medicine. One was in the north, an hour from his grandmother, at the better school. The other was on the hill. He had accepted the hill early on a Saturday morning in June, and she knew which Saturday, because she had woken up in her own bed at noon that day with his blanket still round her and no idea how she’d got upstairs. She had found all of it before her tea went cold.

He had also been offered a master’s at the polytechnic, with money attached. He had turned it down three days later.

He had swapped his anatomy group from Tuesday mornings to Thursday afternoons in the first week, which meant he was in the library on Tuesday mornings, which was when she had her free period. He was on the fourth floor every evening from six. He was at the bench behind the observatory at half past one. He was on the kerb at half past seven. He was at the gate when the bus got to the top.

It was all in the spreadsheet. Every row.

And the flask, and the map, and the headphones. Ten pairs. He knew how often she broke them. She had never told him that.

She had read the spreadsheet three times on Sunday night and felt sick in a way she didn’t understand, and then angry, which she understood much better. Everybody in her life watched her. Baba’s drivers reported where she was. Elowen rang every night to ask if she’d eaten. Ah Sim counted the noodle packets. She had thought Yu Chen was the one person who didn’t. He just sat with her. That was the whole point of him.

She went up to her room and stood at the window.

Across the garden, on the flat roof of the old Song house, beside the water tank, there was one white paper lantern. It was shaped like a rabbit. It was always a rabbit; his mother had bought him one the last Mid-Autumn before the car, and he still bought the same kind.

Someone was sitting beside it.

She put her shoes on.

✦ ✦ ✦

The persimmon tree stood in the corner of the Song garden, by the wall, and its biggest branch came over onto the Lin side and down low enough that if you stood on the edge of Mama’s biggest flowerpot you could reach it.

She’d climbed it for years. Nobody had ever told her it was a stupid thing for a girl in a hoodie and glasses to do in the dark. She went up the branch on her hands and knees, along it over the top of the wall, into the fork of the tree, and then up through the leaves. The persimmons were still green and hard and they hit her in the face. From the top of the tree it was one long step across onto the edge of his roof, if you didn’t look down.

She didn’t look down. She never had.

He was sitting with his back against the water tank and his long legs out in front of him, with the rabbit lantern beside him and a box of mooncakes open on the gravel and his notebook on his knee. He looked up when the leaves shook.

He didn’t look surprised. That made her angrier.

“You’re not wearing a coat,” he said.

“I don’t need a coat.”

“It’s cold up here at night.” He moved the box of mooncakes towards her. “There’s lotus seed. I saved you the one with two yolks.”

She didn’t sit down.

She stood on his roof with the moon coming up behind her over the Walled City, huge and yellow, so bright it threw her shadow across the gravel to his feet, and pushed her glasses up her nose, and said, “Stop.”

He waited.

“You’ve been circling me since September. I’m not blind. Say it.”

The lantern moved in the wind. He put his notebook down on the gravel, closed.

“You had two offers,” she said. “The one in the north was better. You took this one the morning after the steps. Then you turned down money at the polytechnic. You moved your anatomy group so you’d be in the library when I’m in the library. You know how often I break my headphones. I never told you that. You’re at the gate every morning before the bus. You’re at the bench. You’re on the fourth floor. Every single day, Wang Yu Chen. I made a spreadsheet.”

“I know you did,” he said. “You made one in July when the man at the fish stall short-changed Ah Sim, and he gave her back two years of money.”

“Don’t make it a joke.”

“I’m not.”

He wasn’t. She could see that. He was sitting still against the water tank, looking up at her, and he didn’t look caught, or embarrassed. He looked the way he looked when he was listening to a patient in one of the videos he watched for his course: as if what she was saying mattered, and he was going to remember all of it.

“So say it,” she said. “Say it was the course.”

He looked at her for a second. Then he stood up.

It took a while. There was a lot of him. When he was standing, he was a head and a half taller than her, and the lantern was behind him so she couldn’t see his face properly, only the shape of it.

“It wasn’t the course,” said Yu Chen. “You know it wasn’t the course. I came because you came. I’ve never pretended otherwise to you.”

She had expected him to lie.

She had had the whole thing planned. He would say it was the course, and she would show him the spreadsheet on her phone, row by row, and he would go red at the ears and say all right, all right, and she would tell him to stop hovering, and he would stop, and she would go home. That was how it was supposed to go. She had worked it out lying on the camp bed.

He hadn’t lied. He had just said it, plainly, standing on his own roof, as if it were the most obvious thing in the world and she was the strange one for needing it said.

It frightened her much more than a lie would have.

So she kept going.

“You can’t do that,” she said. “You can’t just arrange your whole life round me, that’s insane, people don’t do that. What if I’d gone abroad? What if I fail? What if I decide I hate it and leave at Christmas, and you’re stuck halfway up a hill doing a course that isn’t even the best one, because of me? You don’t get to decide that. You don’t get to follow me round with tea like I’m going to break if you look away. I’m not going to break. I’m not a child. I’ve been fine on my own my whole life, I don’t need anyone standing over me watching me eat, I get enough of that at home, I get it from everyone, I thought you were the one person who didn’t—”

He took her face in his hand.

He didn’t ask. He didn’t say anything. He put one big warm hand along her jaw, with his thumb by her ear and his fingers at the back of her neck under her hair, and bent his head, and kissed her in the middle of the sentence.

The rest of the sentence went somewhere. She never found out where.

His mouth was warm and tasted of lotus seed. His hand on her jaw was steady and he held her face as if it were the only thing on the roof, and for a second she stood there with her arms at her sides and her eyes open and her glasses knocked crooked against his cheek, completely unable to move.

Then she grabbed his collar.

She did it with both hands, without deciding to, the way you put your hands out when you fall. She got two fistfuls of his shirt and pulled him down and kissed him back, hard, up on her toes on the gravel, and he made a small surprised noise against her mouth and his other arm came round her waist and lifted her the rest of the way.

She had thought about it. Of course she had. Since the library steps she had thought about very little else. She had not thought it would be like this. She had not thought her whole body would go hot from the inside out, or that he would kiss her as if he had been waiting all summer to do it and had no intention of hurrying now. She hadn’t thought she would like it this much. She hadn’t thought she would want more of it so badly that it hurt.

That was when she froze.

Because she did want it. She wanted it more than she had ever wanted anything, and he was the only person in her whole life she had never been afraid of losing, because she had never had him in a way that could be lost. He was just next door. He was just there. And now he was holding her face on a roof, and it was real, and if it was real it could end, and everything that could end did.

She let go of his collar. She put both hands flat on his chest and shoved.

He let her. He stepped back at once, and his hand came off her face, and he stood there in the light of the rabbit lantern with his shirt pulled out of shape where she’d grabbed it and his mouth a little open, breathing hard, looking at her.

“Yu-er,” he said.

She went back over the edge of the roof into the tree.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went down faster than she’d ever gone. The green persimmons hit her in the face. A twig went down the neck of her hoodie. She missed the flowerpot at the bottom and landed on her knees on the paving in the Lin garden and scraped one of them through her jeans, and didn’t feel it until later.

She stood up. She was shaking all over.

Above her, on the other side of the wall, the leaves moved. He was standing at the edge of his roof, looking down. She could see the lantern behind him.

“I’m not going anywhere,” he said over the wall. His voice was low and steady. “I live next door.”

She knew he meant it to help. She knew that was how he meant it: you don’t have to run, there’s nowhere I’m going, I’ll be here when you come back. It helped. She also stood in the dark garden with her knee bleeding and heard the other thing in it, underneath, which was that he meant it exactly. He wasn’t going anywhere. He had arranged it, in June, so that he never would.

She didn’t answer. She went inside and up the stairs, all of them, past Baba’s door, past Evangeline’s door open a crack, to the top of the house, and shut her own door and stood with her back against it in the dark.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later she went to the window.

She stood beside it, out of sight, with the curtain held an inch open, and her hand over her mouth. Her mouth still felt hot. Her knee was stinging. She was so angry she could have screamed, and she was smiling, and she couldn’t stop doing either, and she didn’t know which one she was going to be doing when she took her hand away.

He’d kissed her. He hadn’t even asked. He had just decided, in the middle of her telling him off, and done it, as if he’d been sure of her the whole time.

He had been right to be sure of her. That was the worst part.

The rabbit lantern had gone from the roof. Across the garden, in the front room on the second floor of the old Song house, his light was on. His curtain was open. He wasn’t standing at the window. She couldn’t see him at all. Just the light.

She let go of the curtain and turned off her desk lamp. Then the screens, one by one. Then the little light on the extension lead that she normally covered with tape. Then she stood in the complete dark of her room and looked through the gap.

His light stayed on.

One minute. She counted. Then it went off.

She stood there with her hand over her mouth, not smiling now, with her heart going hard and slow.

He had waited for hers to go out.

She lay down on the camp bed in her clothes, with her knee stinging and the blue checked blanket pulled up to her chin, and touched her own mouth with two fingers in the dark, and thought about the spreadsheet, and all the rows she had made, and the one she never had, because the only thing she could have put in it was a night in June, when he had come out at two in the morning with his blanket and sat down on her step, and never asked why.

chapters.title: Not Official, She Says
chapters.desc: The morning after the roof, Eliana arrives with a list of rules: nobody can know, nothing gets a name, and if he agrees she’ll keep kissing him. He agrees to everything except pretending it isn’t real.
chapters.epigraph: “Fine. No name. But I’m not going to lie and say it isn’t the best thing that’s ever happened to me.” — Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
She knocked on his door at seven in the morning with a piece of paper.

She had written it out by hand first, at three in the morning, then decided her handwriting looked frightened and typed it, and printed it with a pillow over the printer so Baba wouldn’t hear. She’d folded it in four. It was in her hoodie pocket and she had her hand on it.

He opened the door in a grey T-shirt and tracksuit bottoms, with his hair standing up on one side and the dented flask in his hand. He’d been making the tea. She could smell the chrysanthemum.

He looked at her. He didn’t say anything about last night. He stood back to let her in.

The old Song house smelled of floor polish and of Auntie Dai’s cooking, even when Auntie Dai wasn’t there, which she wasn’t yet; she came at eight. The kitchen was at the back, looking onto the garden and the persimmon tree and the wall, and over the wall the back of the tall house and Eliana’s own window, high up, with the curtains shut. She had never stood in his kitchen and looked at her own window before. She didn’t like how clearly you could see it.

She put the paper on the table and unfolded it and pushed it across to him.

He sat down and read it.

1. It doesn’t have a name.

2. Nobody knows. Nobody. Not Wei Long. Not my sisters. Not Ah Sim. Not Auntie Dai.

3. No holding hands on the hill.

4. Nothing where people can see. (See previous.)

5. If anyone asks, we’re neighbours. Which we are.

6. You don’t say sorry about last night. You’re not sorry.

He read it twice. She watched him do it. She had her hands in her hoodie pocket so he wouldn’t see what they were doing.

“Number six,” he said.

“You’re not.”

“No.” He looked up. “I’m not.”

She had expected him to argue. That was the whole reason she’d made the list: so that she could stand here and defend each line while he picked at it, and wear him down, and win. She had prepared answers. She had a reason for number three that took nearly a minute to say.

He didn’t argue with any of it.

He got up and found a pen in the drawer by the cooker and sat down again, and at the bottom of her printed list, under number six, in his small square capitals, he wrote:

7. THIS IS REAL. I WON’T SAY IT ISN’T.

He turned the paper round and pushed it back to her.

“Fine,” he said. “No name. But I’m not going to lie and say it isn’t the best thing that’s ever happened to me.”

She looked at the seventh line.

She could have crossed it out. She had a pen in her pocket too. She thought about it. She thought about him on the roof, saying I came because you came in exactly that voice, with no shame in it at all, as if he’d only been waiting for somebody to ask.

She left it.

“If you agree to all of it,” she said, and her voice came out smaller than she wanted, “then I’ll keep—” She stopped. “Then it can keep happening.”

“What can?”

He knew what. He was looking at her across the kitchen table with his ears going red, and he wanted her to say it. She could see that he wanted it very much.

She opened her mouth.

There was a key in the front door. Auntie Dai, twenty minutes early, with her shopping trolley, calling out about the price of pork before she was even in the hall.

Eliana grabbed the list, stuffed it in her pocket and went out through the back door and over the wall by the persimmon branch in about four seconds, and heard behind her, through the kitchen window, Auntie Dai say, “Was that a cat?” and Yu Chen say, “Probably.”

✦ ✦ ✦

So it kept happening.

On Thursday it happened on the library stairs.

They were going up, him a step behind with her bag, and she stopped on the third flight, at the place where she had dropped the flask, and turned round. Standing two steps above him, she was for once exactly as tall as he was. She put her hands on his shoulders and kissed him, fast, while he was still in the middle of saying something about the tea. Then she let go and ran up the rest of the stairs without looking back, and sat on the fourth floor with her face burning for twenty minutes.

He came up eventually. He sat down at the other end of the table. He didn’t look at her once all evening. She could tell, from the back of his neck, what it cost him.

On Friday it happened in study room 4B.

There was a row of small rooms along the side of the fourth floor that you could book for two hours, and she had booked 4B because it was the one at the end with a pillar outside it, so you couldn’t see in from the stairs. She had told him she needed somewhere to practise talking for a presentation. He came in with his textbook. She shut the door and pulled him down by the front of his jumper and kissed him until his textbook fell on the floor.

They sat on the floor behind the pillar afterwards, with their backs against the glass, and she laughed into his shoulder, because his hair was sticking up again and he looked so stunned.

“You booked a room,” he said.

“Under your name,” she said into his shoulder, and felt him start to laugh.

On Saturday it was the back lane, and it was him. She was going out to buy energy drinks from the shop at the end, past the side gate of the Song house, in her slippers, and the gate opened as she went past and a hand came out and caught her wrist. He pulled her into the gap between the wall and Auntie Dai’s bins, where nobody could see from the lane or from either house, and kissed her once, slowly, with his hand still round her wrist and her back against the warm brick. Then he let her go.

“Morning,” he said, and went back in and shut the gate.

She stood there in her slippers with her face hot.

On Sunday it was the kitchen, while Auntie Dai was at the market, and they knocked a bag of rice off the counter and it split, and they spent twenty minutes on their knees sweeping it up with a dustpan, laughing so much that she got hiccups, and he kissed her again in the middle of the hiccups, and she hiccupped into his mouth, and they had to start again.

She didn’t know you could laugh while you were doing this. She’d thought it would be serious. It was serious. It was also the funniest thing that had ever happened to her.

✦ ✦ ✦

She knew why she needed it to be secret. She just didn’t say it, not even to him.

Part of it was Baba. Baba had never trusted the policeman’s house. Wei Long’s father had been a policeman, and had once arrested a man who owed Baba money, and after that Baba had never once said the word Song without his mouth going flat. The policeman was dead now. Wei Long was a policeman too. And Yu Chen was the boy the policeman’s family had raised, and he lived in the policeman’s house, and Baba still called him the Song boy, as if nothing had changed.

If Baba knew, he would look at Yu Chen that way. She couldn’t bear it.

But that wasn’t the real reason, and she knew it.

The real reason was that if nobody saw it, nobody could take it away. Things that people knew about could be talked about and asked about and tidied and ended. Things nobody knew about just went on. She had learned that from her screens. The safest thing in the world was something nobody knew was there.

So she tested him.

She didn’t mean to, the first time. On Tuesday, in the big canteen at the bottom of the arts block, she saw him come in with three people from his course, and she sent him a text from her corner table.

Eliana: sit with them. don’t look at me.

He sat with them. He didn’t look at her.

He didn’t look at her for forty minutes. He ate his rice and listened to a boy with a beard talk about a dissection, and nodded, and said something that made the table laugh, and the girl with all the rings sat down beside him and put her hand on his arm while she talked. He didn’t move his arm, or look across the canteen.

Eliana sat in her corner and stabbed her noodles with her chopsticks until they broke.

She’d asked him to. That was the stupid thing. He was doing it perfectly, and she was furious, and had no right to be. She was jealous of a girl who had touched his sleeve, and she couldn’t say so, because to say so she’d have to say what he was, and he didn’t have a name. That was rule one.

She sent another text.

Eliana: bet you can’t keep a straight face if I look at you

He read it. She watched him read it. Then he looked up, straight across the whole canteen at her, for the first time in forty minutes.

His face was perfectly straight. Polite. Pleasant. The face he gave the girl with the rings. As if he had never seen her before in his life.

She was so annoyed that she looked away first.

When she looked back he’d got up. He was saying something to his table, picking up his tray. He walked past her corner on the way to the tray rack without a glance, and out through the side doors at the back, the ones that led to the corridor by the lifts. It was on his map. Corridor by the lifts. Empty at lunch.

She sat there for one more minute so it wouldn’t look like anything. Then she went after him.

He was waiting round the corner by the lifts, where the corridor turned and there was nothing but a noticeboard and a fire door. He didn’t say anything. He took hold of her by the waist and walked her backwards until her shoulders touched the wall beside the noticeboard, and kissed her.

This one wasn’t slow. He kissed her as if he’d been sitting across a canteen not looking at her for forty minutes and it had nearly killed him, and her hands went into his hair and she pulled him down harder.

“Someone could see,” she said against his mouth.

“I know,” said Yu Chen, and kissed her again.

The lift went past behind the wall, humming. Somebody laughed in the canteen. She held on to the back of his neck and didn’t let go until the lift came back.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Wednesday a boy in her programming lab pulled her hood down.

She didn’t know his name. He was the one with the loud laugh who sat at the back and talked through everything, and he had been looking at her for a week the way some boys looked at a quiet girl in a hood: as if she were a puzzle for him to solve in front of his friends. He came up behind her in the corridor of the fish tank on the way out, and grabbed the top of her hood, and yanked it back.

“There she is,” he said, loud, to the two boys with him. “Lin Yu has a face. Who knew.”

The corridor went cold round her. Her hair had come down. Her glasses had gone crooked. Everyone was looking. She stood there with her arms round her laptop, unable to move or say anything, and felt her face go hot all the way down her neck.

Then Yu Chen was there.

She hadn’t seen him come in. He used the side door. He came and stood beside her, not touching her, and looked at the boy.

“Put it back,” he said.

He said it pleasantly. That was what was strange. It was the same polite voice he used with the girl with the rings, the voice that meant nothing. The boy laughed.

“Who are you, her dad?”

Yu Chen didn’t answer. He took one step forward, so the boy had to tip his head back to look at him, and stood there, and the pleasant thing went out of his face all at once. What was left was so still and cold that the two friends took a step back without meaning to.

“Put her hood back,” said Yu Chen, slowly. “I’m not going to ask again.”

The boy put it back. He did it badly. It caught on her glasses, and he said “sorry” in a voice that had gone up, and then he and his friends were gone round the corner very fast.

Yu Chen turned round.

“Are you all right?”

He was himself again. Ordinary. Worried. Ears a little pink. He reached out and straightened her glasses with one finger, and then remembered where they were, and put his hand in his pocket.

“I’m fine,” she said.

She was. She was shaking, but she was fine, and she had seen something, and she put it away to look at later with the other things.

That night, at the top of the tall house, she looked.

Not at Yu Chen. At the boy with the loud laugh. It took her ten minutes.

By the morning, every email he sent from his university account went out with the same name at the top, where his own name should be. Every post he made on the forum. Every piece of work he uploaded to the lab system. I Pulled A Girl’s Hood Down. The university’s IT people looked at it for six days and couldn’t work out how to change it back.

She showed Yu Chen on Thursday, at the long table on the fourth floor, turning her laptop round.

He looked at the screen. She watched his face, ready for it: the frown, the Yu-er, the little talk about how she shouldn’t. Elowen would have given her the little talk. Elara would have laughed and then given her the little talk.

He put his hand over his mouth and laughed so hard into his tea that he had to put the cup down.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday he tried to introduce her to someone.

She didn’t see it coming. They were at the noodle stall behind the library and a girl came up to the counter, a second year from Eliana’s own department with a short fringe and a laptop covered in stickers, and Yu Chen said, “Oh, hello,” and turned to Eliana. “This is Eliana, she’s in first year. Your brother was on my course at the polytechnic. I thought you two might—”

The girl smiled. “Hi! Are you doing the programming module? It’s a nightmare, isn’t it, the—”

Eliana looked at her shoes.

She tried. She did try. She could feel the words somewhere at the bottom of her throat, yes and it is and what did you get in the first test, and none of them would come up. The girl waited. Eliana pulled her hood forward, and looked at the noodles, and said nothing at all, and after a few seconds the girl said, “Well, nice to meet you,” a bit uncertainly, and took her bowl and went.

Eliana stared at the counter.

“Sorry,” said Yu Chen. “I should’ve asked first.”

She looked up at him to say it didn’t matter.

And she saw it. Only for half a second, before he hid it. When the girl walked away, something in his shoulders had come down, the way they did when he put down something heavy. He had been relieved.

Then he saw her see it, and he looked guilty, and looked away.

She didn’t say anything. She ate her noodles. But she thought about it all the way down the hill on the bus, with her forehead against the window and the green bicycle going steadily below.

He wanted her to have friends. She knew he did. He’d said so, in his way, twice this week.

And some part of him, that he didn’t like, wanted to be the only one.

She found, to her surprise, that it didn’t frighten her. She thought about the corridor by the lifts. She thought about I’m not going to ask again, and the boy’s face going pale, and the seventh line on her list, in capitals.

That night she unfolded the list and pinned it to the wall above her monitors, where she could see it from the camp bed. Seven rules. Six of hers and one of his.

She lay on the camp bed and looked at it until the words went blurry, and for once she was asleep before two.

chapters.title: The Drawing in His Pharmacology Notes
chapters.desc: She can say anything with a keyboard and nothing with her mouth. So she draws him a note she’s too shy to speak, and tells him not to open it until he’s in the library. He opens it in the library and has to leave the room.
chapters.epigraph: “Don’t look at it till you’re in the library. If you look on the bus I’ll know, because you go red on buses.” — Eliana Lin
chapters.content:
It rained on Friday, so she made him take the bus.

Eliana: bus today. it’s pouring. you’ll get pneumonia and then you’ll have to study yourself

He’d been going to cycle anyway. He had a rain cape somewhere. But she’d never once asked him to take the bus with her, so he left the bicycle in the hall and stood at the bus stop at the end of the lane under her umbrella, which was black and had one broken spoke, so that rain ran off it in a stream onto his left shoulder.

On the bus she sat by the window and he sat beside her. It was crowded. His leg was against hers and neither of them moved.

Halfway up the hill she took his pharmacology notes out of her bag.

He’d lent them to her on Wednesday. She’d said she wanted to see how medical people organised things, which he hadn’t believed for a second. She put the folder on his knee, and kept her hand on top of it.

“There’s something in it,” she said, looking out of the window. “Don’t look at it till you’re in the library. If you look on the bus I’ll know, because you go red on buses.”

“I don’t go red on buses.”

“You went red on the number nine in August, because a woman asked if I was your little sister and you said no, and then you couldn’t think what I was.” She took her hand off the folder. “You went red from your collar up. It was like watching a kettle.”

He held the folder on his knee with both hands all the way up the hill, through the wet zigzags, with her shoulder against his arm and the bus steaming up round them. He did not look at it once. He could feel his collar getting hot anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

He waited until he was on the fourth floor. He sat at the long table by the window with the rain running down the glass. The floor was nearly empty, because it was Friday and wet and ten in the morning, and the one other person there was a boy asleep on a beanbag in the corner.

He opened the folder.

It was in the middle, between the pages on how drugs got into the bloodstream and the pages on how they got out again. This time it was a whole page torn from a sketchbook, folded once.

A drawing in black biro, the way she always did them, quick and careful at once. The porch of the tall house, with the little tiled roof and the three steps and the crack across the third one. The red paper charm on the door. The iron rail of the low wall. And on the third step, two people sitting under one blanket with checks on it.

It was the night in June. That was what he saw first. One of them long and folded up, with his knees nearly at his chin. The other small, with a hood and a pencil stuck through the knot of her hair. Her head was on his shoulder, the way it had been when the sky went grey.

Underneath, in her handwriting, which was small and sloped backwards:

don’t go anywhere

He sat and looked at it.

He knew what it cost her. That was the thing. She could write a thousand lines of code without blinking. She could take down a stranger’s whole life before breakfast, he was nearly sure of it, and sleep afterwards. But she couldn’t say a sentence like that out loud to his face. The first thing she ever left him in the jar in the garden wall, in July, was a drawing of a cat in glasses with its ears flat, the day after she’d snapped at him over nothing, because she couldn’t say sorry.

He folded the page along its fold. He put it inside his shirt, against his chest, flat. Then he got up and went down the shell of the stairs and out of the library, and stood under the concrete porch in the rain.

He couldn’t have stayed in there. He’d have done something stupid in front of the boy on the beanbag.

It was cold under the porch and the rain was coming in sideways. He stood with his back to the wall and his hand on the front of his shirt for some time.

Then he got out his phone.
