He thought about what to say, and then sent the true thing.

Yu Chen: Yes.

It took her a few seconds to answer.

Eliana: !!!!!!!

Eliana: STOP

Eliana: i’m in a lecture. i can’t breathe. the man next to me is looking at me

Eliana: you looked on the bus didn’t you

Yu Chen: No. I’m outside the library. I had to leave.

Eliana: why

He looked out at the rain on the steps, the same steps where he’d tucked her hair behind her ear five weeks ago and she’d told him not to do it where people could see.

Yu Chen: Because there were people.

There was a long gap. Then:

Eliana: ok

Eliana: ok that’s fine then

✦ ✦ ✦

In the afternoon he had a small-group case on the second floor of the medical school: eight of them round a table with a tutor and a pretend patient’s notes, working out why a man of sixty had fallen down in a supermarket.

He was good at it. He let the boy with the beard take the credit for a point he’d made first, because the boy with the beard wanted it more. Afterwards, the girl with all the rings asked him to coffee, and he said he had to get home.

He thought about the drawing the whole time. It was still inside his shirt. He could feel the edge of the paper when he moved.

At home, Auntie Dai was making soup and listening to the radio. He went past her and up to his room and got the shoebox out of the cupboard.

Eliana didn’t throw headphones away. She broke them, and then she kept them, in case. In July, clearing her desk for another screen, she had come over the wall with a shoebox that had a skull drawn on the lid and told him to keep it, because she couldn’t throw them out and couldn’t look at them. He’d counted once. There were nearly twenty pairs. Some she’d cut and mended herself, badly, with tape. Some were tied in knots that would have interested a sailor.

He sat on the floor of his room and untangled all of them.

It took two hours. He did it slowly and properly, the way he’d been shown to tie off stitches on a sponge in the skills lab: no pulling, find the end, follow it back. He coiled each pair round three fingers and fastened it with a strip of tape, and on the tape he wrote how long it was now, because the mended ones had all come out different lengths. Full. Full. Missing 10 cm. Missing 22 cm (left side only). Full. He put them back in the box in order, longest to shortest.

When he’d finished he sat back against his bed and thought that this was probably not a normal thing to do for a girl.

It was what he had.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eight the text came.

Eliana: come over

That was all. No question mark. He looked at it, and at the window, and at her window across the garden with the line of light down the middle of the curtains.

He went out of his front door with the shoebox under his arm and stepped over the low wall between the two porches by the iron rail, the way he did most nights now, and went up her three steps. He lifted his hand to knock on the red door.

It opened before his knuckles touched it.

She’d been standing right behind it. She must have been waiting there since she sent the text, in the dark of the hall, with her hand on the bolt. She was in a different hoodie, a big grey one, and he realised after a second that it was his. It had gone missing in the summer.

“Baba’s at a dinner at the office till eleven,” she said, low. “Ah Sim’s gone home. Evangeline’s in her room. Elara’s on nights.”

She took hold of his sleeve and pulled him in.

They went up the stairs in the dark, her first, and on the third flight, when he put his foot down in the middle of a step and it creaked like a shot, she turned round and glared at him and pointed at the edge of the step, where the wood was nailed down tight. He moved his foot to the edge. It was silent. She went up and down these stairs every night without a sound, and she’d never told him how.

Her room at the top was dark except for the screens. It always looked to him like the inside of a ship.

“I’ve got a maths test on Monday,” she said, shutting the door. “I need to revise. I thought you could—” She stopped. “Sit there. Be quiet. Turn pages quietly. I don’t know. I just wanted you to come over.”

He gave her the shoebox.

She opened it on the camp bed and looked at the coils of white wire in their tape, in order, longest to shortest, with his writing on each one. She picked one up. Missing 22 cm (left side only). She turned it over in her fingers.

“You went through my shoebox.”

“You gave it to me. It’s been in my cupboard since July.”

She didn’t say anything. She put the coil back exactly where it had been, and shut the lid, and put the box on her desk next to her keyboard, square to the edge. When she turned round her eyes were bright behind her glasses and she looked annoyed about it.

“You’re so weird,” she said.

“I know.”

“I mean it as a—” She waved her hand. “I don’t know what I mean it as.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The revision didn’t go well, at first.

She sat cross-legged on the floor with her back against the camp bed and a stack of printed problem sheets on her knees, and he sat beside her, and every time she started a problem she looked at him, and every time she looked at him she lost her place.

“I can’t do this with you sitting there,” she said.

“Do you want me to go?”

“No.”

He thought about it. He’d read somewhere that summer, in the long reading on everything from first dates to shyness that he’d have died before admitting to, that small rewards made people work. He’d thought it was rubbish at the time.

“One page,” he said. “One kiss.”

She stared at him. “You can’t even check it. You don’t know discrete maths.”

“I’ll check it looks finished.”

She looked at him with her mouth pressed flat. Then she pulled the first sheet off the stack and put her head down and did it so fast that her pencil tore through the paper at the bottom. She shoved it at him.

It looked finished.

He leaned over and kissed her, once, slowly, with his hand on the side of her face. She made a small sound. When he sat back she was already grabbing the next sheet.

He had meant it to last the evening.

By the fifth page she was doing them with one hand and holding on to the front of his shirt with the other. By the seventh she had stopped pretending to give him time to check. By the ninth she had climbed into his lap with the problem sheet still on her knee and her pencil behind her ear, and was kissing him in the middle of a sum, and he had given up holding his hands still and had them under the hem of the grey hoodie, his hoodie, flat against the warm small of her back. She shivered. She pushed closer. She was laughing into his mouth about something, the pencil maybe, which had fallen down between them, and he was laughing too, and couldn’t stop, and couldn’t stop kissing her either.

“What page is it,” he said, a long way down.

She said she didn’t know, nine, eleven, and when he said she’d skipped ten she said ten was horrible and she wasn’t doing it. He kissed her neck, under her ear, where her hair had come down. She went still and held on to his shoulders.

“Okay,” she said, a bit breathless. “Okay, I’ll do ten.”

She didn’t do ten.

At eleven they heard the car in the lane, and the gate, and the red door, and her father’s heavy feet in the hall. They both froze, with her in his lap on the floor of her room and his hands under her hoodie and the problem sheets everywhere. Her father came up one flight of stairs and then another, slowly, and along the landing two floors below, and his door shut.

Eliana let her breath out against his neck.

“You can’t go out now,” she whispered. “He’ll hear the door.”

“I know.”

“You’ll have to stay till he’s asleep. Properly asleep. He snores, you’ll know.”

“I know,” said Yu Chen, who could hear Lin Jian snore from his own bed when the windows were open. He didn’t say so.

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten past one her phone buzzed on the desk.

Not the normal buzz. A shorter one, twice. She had been half asleep against him on the floor with her test sheets in a heap and his arm round her, and at the sound she came awake all at once, like someone had called her name. She was on her feet before he’d moved. She took the phone out onto the top landing and pulled the door almost shut behind her.

He wasn’t trying to listen. The house carried everything.

“Yes,” she said, on the landing.

It was her voice, but it wasn’t any voice he’d heard her use before. It was low and flat and quick, and there was nothing shy in it anywhere. Nothing small.

“Then he’s lying. No. No, I can see it from here, he’s lying, he moved it on Tuesday. Give me twenty minutes.” A pause. “No. I’ll do it. Not him. He’ll leave a mess and I’ll have to clean it up anyway.” A shorter pause. “Twenty minutes. Tell Qian I said so.”

She came back in.

She went straight to the desk without looking at him and pulled her keyboard towards her. Her face in the glow of the five screens was smooth and white and closed, and her hands were moving before she’d finished sitting down.

He didn’t ask. He had never asked.

He got up from the floor and poured what was left in the flask, lukewarm by now, into the lid. He put it down beside her keyboard, on the side away from her mouse, where she wouldn’t knock it.

She didn’t look round. But her left hand came off the keys for a second and found the lid, and she drank it, and put it back down, and went on typing.

He sat down on the floor again with his back to the camp bed, and picked up the pair she’d tied in a knot on the bus that morning, which she’d dropped beside the shoebox, and started on it.

It took her just over half an hour. He knew because her father’s snoring had started, two floors down, and he timed it against that.

When she finished she sat back in the chair and put both hands over her face.

He waited.

“Done,” she said, from behind her hands, to nobody in particular. Then she took them away and looked at him, sitting on her floor with the headphones half untangled across his knee, and her face came undone a little, the way it only did with him.

“You should go,” she said. “He’s asleep. Keep to the edges.”

She came and knelt down in front of him on the floor and took the half-untangled headphones off his knee and put them on top of the shoebox. Then she kissed him, for no page at all, gently, with her cold hands on his face.

“Thank you for the box,” she said.

He went down the stairs in the dark on the edges of the steps, the way she’d shown him, and every one of them was silent. He let himself out of the red door and stepped over the low wall, and stood on his own porch in the wet for a minute, looking up at her window.

Her light was still on at three. And at four.

At six he filled the flask in Auntie Dai’s empty kitchen and went out and put it on the third step of the tall house, beside the crack, where she’d find it when she opened the door.

chapters.title: He Researched This Part Too
chapters.desc: Their first night together is nothing like his plan and exactly right: shy, clumsy, interrupted by laughing, started over twice. Afterwards, in the dark, he says the thing she’s most afraid of first, so she doesn’t have to.
chapters.epigraph: “I love you. You don’t have to say it back. I just didn’t want to be the only one who knew.” — Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
Auntie Dai had gone to her sister’s for the weekend, and Wei Long was on a case and hadn’t come for Sunday lunch in a fortnight, so on Saturday night the old Song house was empty except for him.

Eliana knew this because he had told her on the bus on Thursday, looking out of the window, in a voice so careful and ordinary that she’d known at once what he wasn’t saying.

She’d said, “Oh,” and nothing else, and then thought about it for two days.

On Saturday at eleven she was at her desk with all five screens lit and a job running. It had come in at nine: a man who had been sending messages to one of the women who worked in Chen Si’s building, the kind of messages that said I know where you live, from accounts he thought nobody could find. It took her nearly two hours to find all of them. Then it took her a few minutes more to make sure that every one of them, and everything else he’d ever said online under any name, had gone in a neat folder to his wife, his boss and the police.

When she pressed the last key she sat back, and her whole body was buzzing.

It was always like that when a job went right. Her hands shook. Her heart went too fast. She couldn’t sit still. She felt about nine feet tall, and as if she could climb anything.

She stood up. She looked at the camp bed. She knew she wasn’t going to sleep.

She looked out of the gap in the curtains. His light was on.

She took the blue checked blanket off the camp bed and put it round her shoulders, over her hoodie, and went downstairs on the edges of the steps.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t knock. There was a key to his back door under the loose brick by the step. She came over the wall by the persimmon branch with the blanket round her like a cape, let herself in through Auntie Dai’s dark kitchen, and went up his stairs, which were newer than hers and didn’t creak at all.

His door was half open. He was lying on his bed in a T-shirt and old jogging bottoms with a textbook on his chest and the lamp on, and he looked up when she came in and nearly dropped the book.

“Yu-er. It’s midnight. Is everything—”

“Everything’s fine.”

She stood in his doorway in the blanket. She was still buzzing. She could feel it in her fingertips.

He sat up slowly. He looked at the blanket. He looked at her face. She saw him understand, and saw his ears go red, all at once, from the top down.

“Oh,” he said.

“Yes,” she said.

Neither of them moved.

His desk was by the door, under the window that looked across at her room. There was a notebook open on it, the one with the plans in. She’d seen it a hundred times. She looked down at it because she couldn’t look at him, and saw, at the top of the open page, in his capitals:

PLAN (IF)

She picked it up.

“Don’t,” said Yu Chen. “Eliana. Don’t read that. Put that down.”

She read it.

1. Ask.

2. Ask again. Make sure.

3. Lamp. Not the big light.

4. Slow.

5. Don’t talk about anatomy.

6. If she laughs it’s fine.

7. If she wants to stop, stop. Immediately. Don’t sulk.

8. Blankets (spare, in cupboard). Water.

There was more. There was a whole other page. She could see the shape of it through the paper.

She turned round with the notebook in her hand and looked at him. He had put both hands over his face. The back of his neck, where she could see it, was the colour of a postbox.

“You made a plan,” she said.

“I make plans for everything.”

“Number five.”

“I panicked,” he said into his hands. “I thought I might talk about anatomy. I talk about anatomy when I’m nervous. I talked about the bones of the foot to Auntie Dai for twenty minutes once because she asked me if I had a girlfriend.”

She started to laugh.

She couldn’t help it. It came up out of her and she couldn’t stop it, standing there in his doorway with the blanket round her and his notebook in her hand. He took his hands away from his face and looked at her laughing, and his mouth went crooked, and then he was laughing too, sitting on the edge of his bed, helplessly, with his face red to the ears.

“I’m going to burn it,” he said.

“You’re not. I’m keeping it.” She put it down on the desk. “Number one. Go on.”

He stopped laughing. He looked at her.

“Do you want to?” he said. “We don’t have to do anything. You can just stay. You can sleep. I’ll sleep on the floor, I don’t—”

She crossed the room and climbed onto the bed and into his lap, blanket and all, and kissed him.

That was the end of the plan.

✦ ✦ ✦

She had thought, the few times she’d let herself think about it, that it would be like the films: smooth, and sure, and somebody knowing what they were doing.

Nobody knew what they were doing.

She kissed him and he kissed her back, at first carefully, with his hands on her waist over the blanket, as if he were following number four. Then she got her hands into his hair and pulled, and he made a sound low in his throat and stopped being careful at all. He pulled her closer by the hips and kissed her harder. The blanket slid off her shoulders onto the floor. Her glasses got in the way and he took them off her face, gently, and reached over to put them on the bedside table, and missed, and they fell on the floor.

“Leave them,” she said.

“You can’t see.”

“I don’t need to see.” She pulled at his T-shirt.

He put his arms up without a word, and she got the T-shirt over his head and it caught on his ears and she had to stop and laugh again, with the T-shirt stuck halfway and him blind inside it, saying “Yu-er” in a muffled voice. When she got it off his hair was everywhere and he was grinning.

Then she looked at him and stopped laughing.

She had seen him without a shirt before, that summer, on his roof in the heat and coming in from the garden with the hose. She had never looked like this. He was thin, and long, and his skin was warm under her hands, and when she put her palm flat in the middle of his chest she could feel his heart going as hard as hers.

“All right?” he said.

“Yes.”

He touched the hem of her hoodie. His. The grey one she’d stolen in the summer. He looked at her, asking. She nodded. He took it off her over her head, slowly, and then the T-shirt she had on underneath, and then he didn’t do anything at all for a second but look, and she felt herself go hot from her face all the way down. She wanted to put her arms over herself. She wanted him to keep looking.

“You’re so beautiful,” he said, as if it hurt to say. “I’m sorry. I know you hate that.”

“I don’t hate it.”

She did, usually. She didn’t now.

He kissed her neck. He kissed her shoulder, where her bra strap was, and moved the strap with one finger and kissed where it had been. His hands were big and careful and a little unsteady, and they went down her back and up again as if he were learning her, every place, slowly, and she arched against him without meaning to and heard herself make a noise she’d never heard herself make before.

He stopped. “Was that—”

“Don’t stop.”

“I’m checking.”

“Stop checking,” she said. “Stop checking, Chen, please, I’m fine, I’m—”

He laughed against her collarbone and didn’t stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

They knocked the lamp over at some point.

She wasn’t sure how. He was pulling the duvet back and she was trying to get her jeans off without getting up, which didn’t work, and one of them kicked the bedside table and the lamp went over and hit the floor and went out. In the sudden dark there was a long silence.

“Number three,” said Yu Chen.

She laughed so hard she had to put her face in the pillow.

He found the lamp by feel and put it back on the table and switched it on, and it still worked, though the shade was crooked now. He looked down at her laughing in his bed with her hair all over his pillow, and his face went soft, and he came back down to her and kissed her until she’d stopped.

Then it was skin, all the way down. His warmth everywhere. His weight coming down onto her slowly, on his elbows, careful even now. The smell of him, soap and tea and the cold air from the open window. The sound of the lane outside, a motorbike going past, far away. His mouth at her throat. Her hands on his back, feeling the long muscles move.

It was strange. It was clumsy. They bumped noses and she laughed and he said sorry and she said stop saying sorry. At one point he went still above her and said her name in a voice she didn’t recognise, low and rough, and asked again, and she wanted to tell him off for asking, and instead she found her eyes were wet and she was nodding, and holding on to him, and saying yes.

And at one point she did need a second. It came on her without warning, a kind of fright, the size of it all, and her hands tightened on his shoulders, and before she’d even said anything he had felt it and stopped. Completely. He didn’t move. He held himself up on his arms over her and waited, and looked at her face in the light of the crooked lamp, and didn’t say anything at all. He just waited.

She looked up at him. She thought: he always waits. He has never once made me hurry.

The fright went.

“Okay,” she said, and pulled him back down. “Okay. I’m okay. Don’t you dare say sorry.”

He didn’t. He kissed her instead, slow and deep, until she forgot what she’d been frightened of, and then they started again, and this time neither of them laughed.

It went on. She lost track of how long. She lost track of everything except him: his breath against her ear, his hand flat on her hip, the way he said Yu-er over and over as if he were checking she was still there. She held on to him and stopped thinking. She hadn’t known she could stop thinking. Her head had never once been quiet in her life. It was quiet now, and full of him, and she arched up into him and held on as hard as she could, and heard him make a sound against her neck like something breaking, and held on harder.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards they lay in the dark.

He’d turned the crooked lamp off. The curtain was open a little and there was a slice of streetlight across the ceiling. She was lying on his arm with her face against his chest, and he had his other hand in her hair, combing it slowly with his fingers, the way he untangled headphones.

Her body felt heavy and warm and strange. She felt like she’d run a long way. She didn’t want to move ever again.

Across the garden, through the gap in his curtain, she could see her own window. The screens were still on behind her curtains. The thin white line down the middle.

“You can see my room from here,” she said.

“Yes.”

She thought about that. She was too tired to think about it properly. She put it away with the other things, for later.

He went quiet. She could feel him thinking. She knew him well enough to know what it felt like when he was getting ready to say something. His chest went still under her cheek.

“Yu-er,” he said.

“Mm.”

“I love you.”

He said it plainly, into the dark, with no build-up, the way he’d said I came because you came on the roof.

“You don’t have to say it back,” he said. “I know you can’t. I know what that word is, for you. I’m not asking for it.” His fingers kept moving in her hair, slowly. “I just didn’t want to be the only one who knew.”

She lay still against his chest.

Her throat had closed. She could feel the words somewhere down at the bottom of it, the same place where the words went at registration and at the noodle stall, where nothing would come up. She tried. She opened her mouth against his skin and tried, and it was like the dream where you try to scream.

Because people said it, and then they went to the hospital. People said it, and then they didn’t come home. That was what the word was. It was a thing you said before you lost something.

She couldn’t.

She felt her eyes go hot. She didn’t let him feel it.

Instead she sat up, a little, and reached down over the side of the bed in the dark, and felt about on the floor until she found it. The blue checked blanket. The one she’d come over the wall in. The one from her steps in June, that he had left round her shoulders and never asked for back.

She pulled it up onto the bed and spread it over both of them, on top of his duvet, and tucked it round his shoulders, and lay back down against his chest under it.

He didn’t say anything. But she felt him breathe in, long and slow, and felt the breath shake a little when it came out. His arm tightened round her. He put his mouth against the top of her head and kept it there.

He’d understood. She knew he had. He always did.

✦ ✦ ✦

She slept.

She didn’t mean to. She never slept, not properly, not in the dark; she lay on the camp bed and listened to the tall house until the birds started. But his bed was warm and he was warm and the blanket smelled of both their houses, and the next thing she knew the slice of streetlight on the ceiling had gone grey.

She half opened her eyes.

He was awake. He was lying on his back with her on his arm, looking at the ceiling, and he was smiling. Not at anything. Just smiling, in the grey light, the way she’d never seen him smile, with his whole face, like a boy.

She watched him for a minute through her eyelashes. He didn’t know she was awake. She could tell from the way his lips were moving slightly that he was counting something. She didn’t know what. She was too tired to ask.

She shut her eyes again and pressed her face into his side, and felt his hand come up at once and settle on her hair, and went back to sleep with him still awake beside her, keeping watch.

chapters.title: He Already Knew
chapters.desc: She comes home from a bad job ready to tell him what she does at night, and finds out he’s known the shape of it since the summer: the nights she doesn’t eat, the light still on at four. She’s furious, and then she isn’t. He never once asks her to stop.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m not going to ask you to stop. I’m going to learn how to keep you fed while you don’t.” — Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
The course dinner was in the back room of a hotpot place at the bottom of the hill, and Yu Chen had said he would go, so he went.

He sat at the end of the long table by the door. Twenty of them from the course, two pots of broth going, a lot of beer. The boy with the beard was telling the cadaver story again. The girl with all the rings had saved him the seat beside her and he had taken the one across from it instead, and she’d laughed at that too.

He ate. He was good at this. You nodded in the right places and passed the beef before anyone asked, and nobody noticed you weren’t really there.

Under the table, he looked at his phone.

He didn’t open his messages. He opened the food app.

It was his account, on his card. She’d made it on his phone in July, on his kitchen floor, because her own cards kept getting frozen by banks that didn’t like the way she spent money at three in the morning, and she’d put his card on it and said she’d pay him back, and never had. She ordered from her own phone, from the top of the tall house. Every order came up on his.

He knew what it said before he looked. He looked anyway.

Wednesday, 12:41. Beef brisket noodles, extra radish. Delivered.

Nothing since.

It was Friday night. Two days, and before that the same order three times in a week, and before that energy drinks and nothing else, delivered at three and four in the morning.

“Yu Chen.” The girl with the rings was leaning across the table. “We’re going on to a bar after. You’re coming. Don’t say you’ve got a thing.”

“I’ve got a thing,” said Yu Chen. “Sorry.”

“You always have a thing.” She said it lightly. Her eyes didn’t. “One day you’ll have to tell us what it is.”

He gave her the pleasant smile, paid for his share and a bit more, and was out on the street with his bicycle before the second pot came.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her light was on when he got home. It was on at midnight. At ten to one his phone went on the desk beside him.

Eliana: are you up

He didn’t answer it. He went.

He went over the low wall by the iron rail and up her three steps and let himself in with the key under the pot, which she had given him in October and which he had hardly ever used. He went up the stairs in the dark on the edges, the way she’d taught him, past her father’s door and Evangeline’s, which was open a crack, as it always was.

Her door at the top was shut. He knocked once with one knuckle.

“Yes,” she said.

She was on the floor.

She was sitting with her back against the wall under the monitors, with her knees up inside her hoodie and her arms round them, the way she’d sat on her step in June. All five screens were on, but there was nothing on any of them, just black, and the lines of light from them came down over the top of her head and her hood and left her face dark. The camp bed was made. She hadn’t been in it.

He shut the door behind him and stood there.

“Sit down,” she said. “You’re making the room small.”

He sat down on the floor across from her, with his back against the camp bed. There were two cans on the carpet by her foot. Both empty.

“I need to tell you something,” she said.

“All right.”

“Don’t say all right like a doctor.” She pulled her sleeves down over her hands. “I need to tell you what I do. At night. When I’m—when you see me in the morning and I look like that. I know you see it. I know I said don’t ask, and you haven’t, and I—” She stopped. “I don’t want you to not know any more. I can’t do it. So I’m going to tell you, and then you can decide if you want to sit there.”

He waited.

She told him, badly, too fast, with her eyes on the carpet. Since June, she said. Since the week after her exams. Chen Si’s people had found out what she could do, from something in the spring she wasn’t going to talk about, and offered her work. She looked after their computers and their messages. She watched for people who wanted to hurt them, and found them first. And she cleaned. That was the main thing. Wherever Baba’s name was, in old shipping records, in files people had kept, in things people wanted to sell, she found it and made it go away. They paid her a great deal. She’d hardly spent any of it. Nobody knew.

“There,” she said. “That’s what I am.”

She looked up at him then, ready.

He didn’t know what she saw in his face. He knew what wasn’t in it. He wasn’t surprised, and he couldn’t make himself pretend to be, and he watched her see that, and watched her face change.

“You knew,” she said.

“Not all of it.”

“How much?”

He thought about lying. It would have been kind, and he’d written on her list in September that he wouldn’t.

“Who for,” he said. “Since the summer, more or less. Not what, exactly. I heard you on the phone, that night in October. Tell Qian I said so. And there’s a car that comes to the end of the lane some nights and doesn’t park, and Chen Si’s assistant gets out of it, and you go down. I’ve seen it from my window.”

She was very still.

“And your light,” he said. “On the nights you work it doesn’t go off before four. The other nights, about two. I can tell which is which.”

“From your bed,” she said.

“Yes.”

She looked at him. He made himself look back.

“What else?” she said.

He could have stopped there. She might have been angry about that much and forgiven it by Monday.

He got his phone out of his pocket, and opened the app, and held it out across the gap between them.

She didn’t take it. She leaned forward and read it where it was, in his hand. He watched her read Wednesday, 12:41, and scroll down with one finger, through the week before, and the one before that, the energy drinks at three in the morning, the noodles, the long gaps. He watched it go through her.

“I forgot,” she said. Her voice was very small. “I forgot it was yours.”

“I didn’t.”

She looked up from the phone to his face, and back down at the little list of her own meals.

“You read this. Every night.”

“Before I sleep.” He put the phone down on the carpet between them, face up. “You haven’t eaten since Wednesday lunchtime. Unless Ah Sim got something into you, and I don’t think she did. She gave me a look at the gate that I’ve only seen her give the fishmonger.”

She got up.

She did it fast, all at once, the way she woke. She stood in the middle of her dark room with her hands in fists inside her sleeves and her face white, and he stayed on the floor because there was nothing to do but stay.

“You’ve been counting me,” she said. “The whole time. You sit next to me in the library and you’re counting my—what I eat, when I sleep, you’re lying in your bed looking at my window, you’re—” She pressed the heels of her hands to her eyes, glasses and all. “I thought you were the one who didn’t. Everyone else does it. Baba’s drivers tell him where I am. Elowen rings every night. Ah Sim counts the noodle packets, she thinks I don’t know. I thought you just sat there. I thought that was the whole point of you.”

“I know.”

“Stop saying you know!”

It came out loud. Two floors down, her father’s snoring stopped. Then it started again.

She took her hands off her face. Her eyes were wet. She looked furious about it.

“Say something,” she said, much lower. “Say why.”

He thought about how to say it so it would be true, and wouldn’t be a speech, because she hated speeches.

“I’ve never told anyone,” he said. “Not Wei Long. Not Nainai. Nobody knows what you do at night but you and me and whoever pays you. I’ve never once used any of it to make you do anything, and I’m not going to. I don’t care what you find. I’m not going to ask you what you find. That’s yours.” He looked at the phone on the carpet. “I just wanted to know when you hadn’t eaten. So I could bring something. That’s all I’ve ever done with it.”

She stood there.

“I’m not going to ask you to stop,” he said. “I’m going to learn how to keep you fed while you don’t.”

The screens hummed.

She sat down again, on the carpet, where she’d been. She didn’t look at him. She pulled her knees up and put her chin on them.

“Something happened tonight,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

There’d been a man, she said. A clerk in a freight office in the eastern district. He’d been selling copies of old records, the kind with Baba’s name on, to someone who wanted them for a court case. Qian had asked her to find out who. She’d found him in an afternoon, last week. She’d sent Qian the name. That was the job. That was always the job. She found the name and sent it and she never asked what happened next, because it wasn’t her part.

Tonight, at eleven, Qian had written to say thank you, the matter was resolved.

“And I looked,” she said. “I never look. I looked. He’s in City Hospital. The one at the bottom of the hill. He went in on Wednesday night. Both his hands.” She held her own hands out in front of her and looked at them. “They broke both his hands. Because I found him. That’s what resolved means.”

Yu Chen didn’t say anything.

“You’re going to be in there,” she said. “On the wards. One night somebody’s going to come in like that, and you’ll stand at the end of the bed being kind to him, and it’ll be because of me.” She swallowed. “What if it’s you who sets the fingers. And you come home and tell me about it, and I have to sit there.”

“Then I’ll set the fingers,” said Yu Chen. “And come home. And you can sit there.”

She looked at him.

“I’m not going to tell you it’s fine,” he said. “I don’t know if it’s fine. You didn’t break his hands. You’re allowed to feel sick about it. You don’t have to decide anything tonight.”

She went on looking at him. Her eyes were red behind her glasses, and her mouth was trembling a little at one corner, and she was angry, still, he could see it. Angry at him, and at Qian, and at the clerk’s hands, and at herself for looking.

Then she got up on her knees and crossed the carpet to him and took his face in both her cold hands and kissed him.

She didn’t kiss him gently. She kissed him as if she was still shouting at him, hard, with her glasses knocking against his cheekbone and her fingers digging into his jaw. He made a sound against her mouth. She pushed him back against the frame of the camp bed and climbed into his lap without letting go of his face, and kissed him harder, as if that would shut it all up, the room and the screens and the hospital at the bottom of the hill, and he let her, and kissed her back, and put his hands on her waist under the hoodie to hold her there.

“I’m still angry,” she said against his mouth.

“I know.” He stopped. “Sorry.”

She bit his lip for that, not hard. He laughed, and she pulled back an inch and looked at him in the light from the screens with her hair coming down and her glasses crooked and her face wet, and her mouth wobbled, and she put her forehead down on his and stayed there, breathing.

When she kissed him again it was different. Slower. Her hands came down off his face to his shoulders and held on. She kissed him as if she were checking he was still the same person, carefully, the corner of his mouth and then the middle, and he held her and didn’t hurry her, and then she made a small cracked sound against his lips and the kiss went wet and salty, because she was crying, without any noise, the way she did.

He held her. He kept kissing her, slowly, wherever he could reach. Her temple. The side of her nose, under the glasses. The wet place on her cheek.

“Don’t stop,” she said.

He didn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

At two he went downstairs on the edges of the steps and found Ah Sim’s kitchen in the dark.

He didn’t turn on the light. There was congee in a pot on the back of the stove, cold, with a plate over it, and he heated it on the lowest flame so it wouldn’t catch, and found a bowl and the jar of pickled radish she liked. Then he made tea in the pot Ah Sim kept on the windowsill, with chrysanthemum from the tin beside it. There had been a tin of it beside the pot since the summer. He had never asked Ah Sim why.

He carried it all up on a tray.

She was where he’d left her, on the floor, with the blue checked blanket round her shoulders. He put the tray down in front of her.

“I’m not hungry.”

“I know,” he said. “Eat it anyway.”

She ate it. She ate the whole bowl, slowly, and then half of the radish out of the jar with her fingers, and drank the tea. He sat beside her with his back against the wall under the screens and watched her do it, and didn’t say anything, and when she’d finished she put the bowl down on the tray and leaned sideways into him, all of her at once, and put her head on his shoulder.

“You’re still weird,” she said.

“Yes.”

“The app is weird. The window’s weird. If anyone else did it, I’d—” She didn’t finish.

“I know,” he said. “I could stop.”

She was quiet.

“Don’t,” she said at last. “I mean. Don’t stop.” Her hand found his on the carpet and held on. “Baba never looked. Not once. Not even to see if I’d eaten. And you’ve been lying in your bed looking at my window every night since June, and I—” She stopped. “It should feel bad. It’s supposed to. I keep waiting for it to.”

He turned his hand over under hers and held it.

“Two rules,” she said. “Mine, this time. You don’t ask what I find. And you don’t go near my computers. Ever. Not even to move a cup.”

“Done.”

“You said that too fast.”

“I’ve been doing both since July,” said Yu Chen. “I’m only agreeing to keep doing them.”

She laughed, a little, wetly, into his shoulder. Then she pulled the blanket off her own shoulders and put it over both of them, and settled against him under it on the floor of her room, with the tea going cold on the tray and the five black screens humming above their heads.

He held her. Some time before four she slept, all at once, the way she had on the step in June, and her hand stayed in his.

At half past five the screens went off by themselves, one at a time. He hadn’t known they did that.

At six he slid out from under her, carefully, and put the blanket back round her, and a cushion off the camp bed under her head. He picked up the tray. He left his phone where it was, on the carpet beside her hand, face up, with the app open.

He thought she should have it for a while.

✦ ✦ ✦

She brought it back at eight, over the wall.

He was on his back step with the flask. She came along the branch of the persimmon tree in her socks and his grey hoodie, and dropped down onto his side by Auntie Dai’s bins, and held the phone out.

He took it.

There was a new order on it, from seven forty. Pork and chive dumplings, two portions. Soy milk, hot. Delivered.

“One’s yours,” she said. “Don’t make a thing of it.”

He didn’t make a thing of it. He moved over on the step, and she sat down beside him, and they ate the dumplings out of the box with their fingers in the cold sun, while Auntie Dai’s radio came on in the kitchen behind them and the noodle man at the end of the lane rattled his shutter up.

chapters.title: The Second Winter
chapters.desc: The heating in the tall house breaks and Eliana is sent to Zhao’s for the weekend. Yu Chen offers his house first, and her father says no to the boy next door. So they keep the weekend in texts, and on Sunday night they find each other at the garden wall.
chapters.epigraph: “He said no to my house. He didn’t say anything about the wall.” — Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
The boiler in the tall house died on Thursday night with a bang that woke the whole lane, and by Friday afternoon you could see your breath in the kitchen.

The boiler man came at two. He lay on his back on the floor of the cupboard under the stairs for an hour with a torch in his mouth, and then he came out and told Baba, in the hall, that the part would have to come from the other side of the harbour and wouldn’t be there till Monday.

Eliana was on the stairs in two hoodies and a scarf. She heard Baba say “Monday” in the voice he used for men who owed him money.

Then she heard Baba go into his study and shut the door, and pick up the phone, and say, after a long pause, “Elowen.”

She went up three more stairs so she could hear better.

He was worse on the phone with Elowen than with anyone, because Elowen had married a man he was frightened of and was now, a little, frightening herself. He said the heating was broken. He said Elara was on nights and would sleep at the hospital, and Evangeline had said she’d be fine with the electric heater, and that he himself would be perfectly all right, he had a coat. He said there was the question of Eliana. Then he stopped. Eliana could hear him breathing.

“Would your husband mind,” said Baba. “Two nights.”

She sat down on the stair.

She knew what that had cost him. She also knew he hadn’t asked her. He’d asked Elowen, and Elowen would ask Zhao, and eventually somebody would tell Eliana where she was sleeping.

✦ ✦ ✦

The boy next door was at the gate when the boiler man left.

She saw him from the front window. He was standing on the pavement in his grey coat, with his bicycle, as if he’d just happened to be coming home, which he had not, because on Fridays he had cases until four. Auntie Dai had told him. Auntie Dai talked to Ah Sim over the back gate about everything, and nothing in the lane stayed secret for more than an hour except the two of them.

Baba came out onto the porch to see the boiler man off, and saw him, and stopped.

“Mr. Lin,” said Yu Chen.

He said it politely. He always did. He stood on the pavement with his ears going pink in the cold and said that Auntie Dai had mentioned the heating, and his house was warm, and there was a spare room at the back that Auntie Dai could make up. For Eliana, or anyone. It was only next door.

Eliana stood behind the curtain with her hand over her mouth.

Baba looked at him for a few seconds.

Then he turned his head and spoke to Uncle Mok, who was standing at the bottom of the steps with the car keys, as if Yu Chen weren’t there at all.

“My daughter will stay with her sister,” said Baba. “Not in the policeman’s old house.”

He went back inside. The red door shut.

Through the glass Eliana watched Yu Chen stand on the pavement. He didn’t move for a second. His hand on the handlebar went tight and then let go, and if she hadn’t been watching his hand she’d never have known.

Then he nodded to Uncle Mok, politely, and wheeled his bicycle the three steps along to his own gate, and went in.

She stood behind the curtain with her face hot.

She’d known it would be no. She hadn’t known he would say the policeman’s old house in that voice, about a house where somebody had come out at two in the morning to sit on her step while her own father slept two floors up. Or that he wouldn’t even look at him.

She went upstairs to pack, and packed one small bag of clothes and one enormous bag of everything else, and then she took the blue checked blanket off the camp bed and stood holding it.

She couldn’t take it to Elowen’s. Elowen would ask.

She went down to the back garden in her socks.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was in his kitchen. She could see him through the window over the wall, standing at the counter with the kettle, not doing anything with it. She climbed onto Mama’s biggest flowerpot and hissed his name, and he came out of the back door at once, as if he’d been waiting.

She held the blanket out over the top of the wall.

“Keep it,” she said. “Elowen will ask.”

He took it. He held it against his chest.

“You’ll be cold,” he said.

“Zhao’s house has heating in the floors. Elowen told me. You can lie on the floor in your socks and it’s warm.” She looked at him. “I’m sorry. About Baba.”

“You don’t have to be.”

“He didn’t even look at you.”

“No.” He was quiet for a second. “I’m used to it.”

That was worse. She stood on the flowerpot with her hands on the cold top of the wall and wanted to climb over it and put her arms round him, and couldn’t, because Baba’s study window looked onto this garden, and Uncle Mok was coming at five.

“Text me,” he said.

“I’ll be bored. I’ll text you all night.”

“Good,” said Yu Chen.

✦ ✦ ✦

Eliana: there’s a camera in the hall pointing at where the door USED to be. he moved the door. nobody noticed for four years

Eliana: i told him. he looked at me like I’d given him a puppy

Yu Chen: Is that good?

Eliana: it’s very good. i asked for the wifi password and he just gave it to me

Eliana: 38 minutes. five holes. one of them is the garage. i could open his garage from the road

Eliana: he is sitting on the floor next to me. he’s sat on the floor for two hours. he says hm

Yu Chen: What does hm mean?

Eliana: everything. it’s the best word anyone has ever invented

Eliana: elowen made fish. he said i had to eat it. i ate it

Yu Chen: All of it?

Eliana: most of it. stop counting

It was half past twelve. She was on the rug in Zhao’s living room with three laptops round her and the floor warm under her, exactly as promised. Elowen had gone up to bed at eleven. Zhao was on the floor beside her with a printed diagram of his own house covered in her red ink, reading it the way other people read letters.

Eliana: what did you have for dinner

Yu Chen: Noodles.

Eliana: what kind

Yu Chen: Your kind.

Eliana: you’re a medical student. you know what’s in them

Yu Chen: Auntie Dai’s off till Monday. I can’t cook.

Eliana: i’m going to tell auntie dai

Yu Chen: She’ll make me eat fish.

She laughed into her sleeve. Zhao looked up from the diagram, looked at her for four seconds, and went back to it.

Eliana: is your light on

Yu Chen: Yes.

Eliana: turn it off and go to sleep. i can’t see it from here anyway

He didn’t answer that. She knew he hadn’t turned it off.

Much later, when the laptops had gone dark, she lay on the warm floor with her hood over her face and tried to feel glad. She was glad. Zhao’s house was a good house. It had locks she liked and a man in it who liked her, and her sister was happy here, which she hadn’t been sure of until tonight. But there was no window across a garden, no thin line of somebody else’s light. It was like falling asleep in a hotel.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday he sent her one message she didn’t answer for an hour.

Yu Chen: Your father came out into the garden at nine tonight. He stood by your mother’s pots.

She was in Zhao’s kitchen with a bowl of congee Elowen had put in front of her. She read it and put the phone face down on the table, and then turned it over again.

Eliana: what did he do

Yu Chen: Nothing. He had his coat on. He stood there. Then he looked up at your window. It was dark, because you weren’t there. He kept looking at it. Then he went in.

Eliana: he was probably checking the gutters

Yu Chen: Maybe.

Eliana: he doesn’t look at me. he looks past me. he’s done it my whole life

Yu Chen: I know. I’m only telling you what I saw.

She didn’t answer. She ate the congee because Elowen was watching, and thought about Baba in his coat by Mama’s empty pots, looking up at the top of the house, and didn’t want to.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday morning, at the top of Zhao’s steps, she hugged him.

She hadn’t planned to. She’d been going to say goodbye and go down the steps to Baba’s car. But Zhao had carried her bag out, and put it down, and told her he’d had the guardhouse box split in two, one on each side of the house, and changed the garage code. She’d already seen the new code, and what it was. So she stepped forward and put her arms round him, as far as they went, which wasn’t far, for one second. Then she let go and picked up her bag.

From the car she sent two messages.

Eliana: the garage code is my birthday backwards. he’s an idiot. i love him

Eliana: i mean zhao. obviously zhao

Yu Chen: I assumed.

Eliana: there’s a blind spot in the hall by the lemon tree. i told him not to fix it. it’s where they stand when they think nobody’s looking

The car went down the hill. Her phone buzzed again.

Yu Chen: Is there one in your house?

She looked at that for the whole of the harbour road.

She didn’t answer it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The heating was still off. The part was still coming on Monday.

They ate supper in their coats, Baba and Evangeline and her, at the long table with Ah Sim’s soup steaming in front of them like three small fires. Baba asked Evangeline if the heater had been warm enough. Evangeline nodded. Baba asked Ah Sim whether the boiler man had rung. He didn’t ask Eliana anything. Halfway through the soup he looked at the end of the table where she was sitting, and his eyes stopped somewhere just beside her left ear, and went back to his bowl.

Her room was freezing. Her breath came out white in the light of the screens, and the camp bed was bare.

At eleven she went down to the garden.

✦ ✦ ✦

There was something on top of the wall.

It was under the persimmon branch, where the wall was in shadow from both houses, a long rolled shape like a sleeping cat. She climbed up on Mama’s flowerpot and put her hand on it.

It was warm.

It was the blue checked blanket, rolled up tight round a hot-water bottle. Somebody had filled the bottle not very long ago; the heat came right through the wool into her cold hands. And beside it, the loose brick had been pulled out of its place in the top of the wall, and the plum-jam jar was sitting in the gap with its lid on and a folded note inside.

She unscrewed the lid and took the note out and read it by the light from his kitchen window.

Hot-water bottle. Filled at ten. I’m up. I’ll refill it.

That was all, in his square capitals.

She stood on the flowerpot holding the warm blanket in both arms.

Then she put it over her shoulders and climbed up onto the top of the wall, by the branch, the way she’d done a hundred times, and sat there with her legs hanging down on his side.

His back door opened before she’d even settled.

He came out in his grey hoodie with his hands in his pockets and stopped below her, under the branch. He’d been waiting at the kitchen window. Of course he had.

“Baba said no,” she said.

“He said no to my house.” He looked up at her. “He didn’t say anything about the wall.”

She laughed, which she hadn’t expected to do tonight. It came out white.

“This bit,” she said. She put her hand flat on the bricks beside her. “Right here. Under the branch. Baba’s cameras can’t see it.”

He didn’t say anything. He waited.

“You asked if there was one,” she said. “In my house. There is. It’s this.” She pulled the blanket tighter. “I did his cameras. The whole house, the gate, the lane, the garden. Raiden was meant to and he gave it to me, and Baba never knew it was me. He thinks some company did it.” She looked down at the top of the persimmon tree, black against the sky. “I did every camera so it could see everything. Then I moved one, a bit. So it couldn’t see this.”

“Why?”

She thought about it, because it was a real question and he was the only person who ever asked her those.

“I needed one place in that house where nobody was watching,” she said. “Even if it was outside. Even if it was a wall.”

He stood below her, looking up. Then he stepped up onto the edge of Auntie Dai’s raised bed, where the winter cabbages were, which put his face nearly level with hers, and his hands on the wall either side of her knees.

“I’m watching,” he said. “I’m sorry. I’m always going to be.”

“I know.” She looked at him. “That’s allowed.”

She took hold of the two strings of his hoodie, one in each hand, and pulled.

He came the last few inches without any fuss, and she kissed him, there on top of the wall with the blanket round her and the hot-water bottle pressing into her stomach, his face cold and his mouth warm. She held on to the strings so he couldn’t go anywhere. He didn’t try to. He made a low sound and his hands came off the bricks and went round her, under the blanket, and pulled her right to the edge of the wall, and then over it.

She went down into his arms with the blanket and the bottle and all. He caught her. He didn’t put her down. He turned and leaned her back against the wall on his side, in the dark under the branch, where no camera of anybody’s could see them, with her feet off the ground and her arms round his neck, and kissed her again, slowly, until she’d stopped shivering and started for a different reason.

“You’re freezing,” he said against her mouth.

“You said you’d refill it.”

“I will.”

He didn’t move to. She didn’t want him to. She pulled him closer by the back of the neck and kissed him until her face was hot and the hot-water bottle had slid down between them onto the cabbages and neither of them went after it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later they sat on his back step with the blanket round both of them and the refilled bottle on her knees, and his flask between them.

“He looked at my window,” she said. “Last night. You said.”

“Yes.”

“I don’t know what to do with that.”

“You don’t have to do anything with it.” He was quiet. “I thought you’d want to know. That’s all. I don’t understand him. I’d like to, one day.”

She looked at the side of his face. I’d like to. About a man who’d talked to his driver as if Yu Chen were a lamppost.

“February’s the worst,” she said.

He waited.

“In our house. February. Because of my birthday.” She held the lid of the flask in both hands. “Everyone knows she died the day I was born. That’s not the bad part. The bad part’s that we go up to the grave at dawn, every year, all of us, and stand there, and then everyone goes to work. Nobody says it. Baba’s never said it. Happy birthday. Not once.” She swallowed. “And every year I think, this year he will. Isn’t that stupid? I’m nearly nineteen. I still think it.”

He didn’t say anything clever. He didn’t say anything at all. He put his arm round her under the blanket and pulled her in against his side and kept her there, and in the end she put her head on his shoulder.

“It’s next month,” he said.

“I know when it is.”

“I know you know.” He put his mouth against her hair. “I’m just telling you I know too.”

She shut her eyes.

Across the wall her own window was dark. Two floors below it, Baba’s light was still on, the only light in the tall house, yellow behind his curtain in the freezing cold. She watched it until it went out, and then a while longer, with the blanket round both of them and the jar back in its place in the wall.

chapters.title: Nineteen, and Nobody Says It
chapters.desc: On her birthday her father takes the family to the grave at dawn and won’t look at her. There’s a boiled red egg at her door, the way there is every year, and she thinks she knows who left it. That night Yu Chen gives her the whole sky, to herself.
chapters.epigraph: “They wouldn’t let me bring a cake in. I asked. So you’ve got the ceiling instead.” — Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
The egg was outside her door at ten to five, the way it was every year.

She nearly stood on it. It was on the landing at the top of the tall house, on a saucer, in the dark: one hen’s egg, boiled hard and dyed red, still a little warm when she picked it up. Nobody else’s door had one. Nobody ever mentioned it.

She took it downstairs in her hoodie pocket.

Ah Sim was in the kitchen in her coat, with the kettle on and the kitchen light off, the way she liked it in the mornings. Eliana stood in the doorway with her hand round the egg.

“Thank you,” she said.

Ah Sim looked at her for a second. Then she turned back to the kettle.

“Eat it,” said Ah Sim. “And wear a proper coat. It’s cold on the hill.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was cold on the hill.

The cemetery was on the slope above the reservoir road, in rows that went up and up like seats in a theatre, and their mother was near the top, where you could see the water. They went up in three cars in the dark. Baba and Evangeline and Elara with Uncle Mok, and Eliana in the back of Raiden’s old car with her knees against the seat in front, and Elowen and Zhao behind them. Zhao didn’t come up to the grave. He never did. He stood by the cars at the gate with his hands in his pockets and watched the road.

The sky was going grey when they got to the top.

Elowen had brought white chrysanthemums from the shop. She knelt and put them in the stone pot and pulled out last year’s dried stems, and Baba lit the incense, three sticks, his big hands cupped round the lighter against the wind. Elara cried, because Elara cried at everything. Evangeline stood at the end in pale blue with her face like a carved thing. Raiden stood with his hands in the pockets of his good coat and, every few minutes, without looking down, felt for his phone.

Eliana knew who was texting him. She’d known since New Year.

He’d left the New Year’s Eve dinner nearly three weeks ago before the dumplings, with a black line of oil under his thumbnail that he kept trying to hide, saying a friend’s car had broken down. On the Sunday after, because she couldn’t sleep and it was easier than thinking, she’d looked. It hadn’t taken long. There was a garage near the Docks, under an old painted sign for a rope and canvas company that had closed before she was born, and it had been bought in December in the name of a woman called Cao Jia, and paid for by Raiden. There were three photos of Cao Jia on the internet. In all of them she was on a motorbike, or under one.

Eliana had put it on the spreadsheet and told nobody. She didn’t know why he was hiding her. She thought she probably did know, and didn’t like it.

She watched him feel for his phone again now, by their mother’s grave, and kept her face still.

Baba stood in front of the stone. He bowed three times with the incense. He said nothing out loud; he never did. Then he stepped back, and the others went up one by one, and Eliana went last, as she always did, and bowed, and put her hand on the cold stone for a second where the name was cut.

When she turned round, Baba was looking at her.

Not at her. Just beside her. At the stone over her shoulder, or the water beyond it. His eyes came close and didn’t land. Then he turned and started down the hill, and the others went after him in a line.

Elowen waited for her. She didn’t say anything either. She took Eliana’s cold hand in her warm one and squeezed it, hard, all the way down the steps to the cars.

That was as close as anyone came. It always was.

At the gate Zhao looked at her for four seconds, which was what he did instead of hello, and then he opened the back door of Raiden’s car for her and shut it after her, carefully, as if she might break.

✦ ✦ ✦

They dropped her at the end of the lane at seven. Everyone else went to work.

Yu Chen was on the kerb.

She’d known he would be. She’d told him in January, on his back step, that nobody said it, and she’d been sorry ever since, because now he knew, and now he would do something about it. That was what he was like. You told him a thing was broken and he went and found the part.

She got out of the car and stood on the pavement in her coat with the egg in her pocket.

He stood up.

“Happy birthday, Yu-er,” he said.

He said it plainly, in his ordinary voice, in the lane, at seven in the morning, where anyone could hear. The noodle man could hear. He was putting his shutter up and he stopped with it halfway and looked at them.

She’d thought she wanted it. She’d thought about it every year. Now somebody had said it, out loud, on the right day, and it went into her like cold water.

“Don’t,” she said.

“All right.”

“I mean it. Don’t do anything. Don’t make a thing.” She heard her own voice going up. “I just came back from the grave. I’ve got a lecture at nine. I’m going to go to the lecture and then I’m going to go to the library and then I’m going to come home and go to bed, and it’s going to be a Friday. That’s all it is. Please.”

He looked at her. She could see him wanting to argue, and deciding not to, and it made her want to cry more than if he had.

“All right,” he said again. He held out the flask. “It’s still a Friday. You still need tea.”

She took it. She went to the bus stop without saying thank you. When she looked out of the back window at the bottom of the hill, he was on his bicycle behind the bus, the way he always was, and she pressed her forehead on the glass and hated herself for the whole zigzag.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t say it again all day.

He was at the bench behind the observatory at half past one with noodles. He was on the fourth floor at six. He didn’t mention it once. He read at the other end of the long table without a sound and put tea by her elbow every hour. By eight o’clock she felt worse than she had in the morning. She had told him not to, and he hadn’t. The day was nearly gone. Nobody had said it but him, and she’d told him to stop.

At half past eight he closed his book.

“I had a plan,” he said.

She looked up.

He got his notebook out of his bag and opened it and turned it round and pushed it down the table to her. It was the page after a lot of revision lists. At the top, in capitals: PLAN (18 FEB). Under it:

1. Restaurant, Harbour Road. Booked 7:00.

2. Museum. 9:00.

3. Say something. (Written. Back page.)

The first line had a neat line through it. He’d cancelled the restaurant. She looked at the time on her laptop. He’d cancelled it at some point today without telling her, sitting at the other end of this table.

“I knew you’d hate the restaurant,” he said. “People singing at other tables. I should have known in January.”

“What’s at the museum?”

“You said not to make a thing.”

“What’s at the museum, Wang Yu Chen?”

He looked at the notebook between them.

“I’d still like to take you,” he said. “If you’ll come. We can not talk about why.”

She looked at number three. Say something. (Written. Back page.) She put her hand flat on the notebook so he couldn’t take it back.

“I’m not reading the back page,” she said.

“Good. I was going to burn it.”

“I’ll come,” she said. “If we get noodles on the way. And you don’t read the back page out either. Ever.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The science museum was down by the harbour, a big white building like a stack of boxes, and it had been shut for two hours. There was a side door round the back by the loading bay, and a man in a lanyard waiting at it with a set of keys, smoking.

“Mr. Wang,” said the man, and put out the cigarette.

“Thank you for staying late,” said Yu Chen. “I’m sorry it’s so late.”

He said it in the voice he used for the girl with the rings, and for professors, and for the boiler man: pleasant, correct, nothing in it. He shook the man’s hand. The man said it was no trouble at all, which, from his face, meant Yu Chen had paid him for the trouble. Then the man looked past him at Eliana, and smiled, and said, “And happy—”

Yu Chen moved half a step, so that he was between them.

“She’d rather not,” he said, pleasantly.

The man stopped. He looked at Yu Chen’s face, and then he nodded and led them in without another word.

Eliana walked behind Yu Chen down a long dark corridor past the dinosaur bones, with her hood up and her hand in the back pocket of his coat, where he couldn’t see it, holding on.

The planetarium was a round room under a dome, with rows of soft seats that tipped back and a console in the middle like the inside of a cockpit, all little lights. The man showed Yu Chen something on the console, two buttons and a dial, and then went up a narrow stair to a booth at the back and shut the door.

There was nobody else. Rows and rows of empty seats in the dark.

“How much did this cost?” she said.

“You said not to talk about it.”

“I said not to talk about why. That’s how much.”

“An hour,” he said. “After closing. I rang on Monday and asked what it would cost to have it to ourselves for an hour, and they told me, and I said yes.” He looked round the dome. “They wouldn’t let me bring a cake in. I asked. So you’ve got the ceiling instead.”

She didn’t sit in the seats.

She walked down the slope to the middle of the room, past the console, and lay down flat on her back on the carpet in her coat with her hood up, in front of everything, and looked up at the blank grey dome.

After a second he came and lay down beside her. He was so long that his feet went under the first row of seats.

“The seats are better,” he said.

“I don’t want the seats.”

He reached up over his head and found the console’s lowest panel by feel, and pressed something.

The dark went darker. Then the sky came on.

✦ ✦ ✦

She had seen the stars before. Of course she had. From his roof, from the bus, out of the window at the top of the house at three in the morning when she couldn’t sleep. You didn’t see many in the city. The harbour lights washed them out.

She had never seen them like this.

They came on all at once, thousands of them, more than she’d known there were, from one edge of the dome to the other and right down to the floor all round, so that there was no edge any more, just the sky, and the two of them lying at the bottom of it. Some were bright and some were barely there. Some were coloured. There was a long pale smear across the middle of everything, like spilt milk, and she knew what it was and had never once seen it.

She didn’t say anything. She couldn’t.

Then he reached up again and turned the dial a little, and the whole sky began to move, slowly, turning round them, the way it really did, the way it had been doing every night above the tall house whether anyone was looking or not.

“There,” said Yu Chen. He pointed. “Low down. Left of the bright one.”

She looked. There was a small star, not bright, on its own. Beside it, in thin white letters, where there were no other words anywhere on the whole sky, somebody had put a label.

LIN YU

“It doesn’t mean anything,” he said. “It’s not official. You can’t buy stars, really. People sell certificates, but they’re nonsense. I asked the man to put a label on the console. That’s all. It’s just for tonight.” He was talking too fast. “I picked a small one. I thought you’d hate a big one.”

She looked at the little star with her name next to it.

This morning she had stood on a hill in the cold and nobody had looked at her, and then everyone had gone to work, and she had told herself that was fair, that was what the day was for. And now there was a star with her name on it turning slowly over her head in the dark, because somebody had rung up on Monday and asked how much.

She started to cry.

She didn’t mean to. It came up from somewhere low down and she couldn’t stop it, lying on her back on the carpet with the tears running sideways out of her eyes into her hood and her ears. She didn’t make any noise. She never did. But her whole chest was shaking with it, and she put her hands over her face.

He didn’t say anything.

He didn’t ask what was wrong, or say it was all right, or tell her not to cry. He turned on his side on the carpet. He took her hands away from her face, one and then the other, gently, and held them. Then he put his hand under her jaw and turned her face up to him, and bent over her, and kissed her.

He kissed her gently at first, on her wet mouth, with the stars going round behind his head. She made a sound she’d never made before, half a sob, and grabbed the front of his coat with both hands, and held on. He kissed her again, harder. She was still crying. She kissed him back anyway, with her mouth open and her face wet and her glasses pushed up crooked, and pulled him down to her by his coat until he was half over her on the carpet and she could feel his heart through all their layers, and the sky went round and round above them both.

She wouldn’t say why. He didn’t ask her to. He kissed the tears off the side of her face, one side and then the other, and then her mouth again, slowly, until she’d stopped shaking and her hands had let go of his coat and gone round his neck instead.

When the hour was nearly up, the man’s voice came down out of the dark, through a speaker somewhere, politely.

“Five minutes, Mr. Wang.”

Eliana laughed. It came out wet and cracked, into Yu Chen’s neck, and she couldn’t stop that either, and he lay on the carpet under the turning stars with her laughing on him and his arm round her, and she felt him smile against her hair.

✦ ✦ ✦

They got the last bus home. He’d left the bicycle at the top of the hill and said he’d fetch it in the morning.

At the end of the lane, under the noodle stall’s dark shutter, she stopped and took the egg out of her pocket. It was cold now. She’d carried it all day.

“Ah Sim leaves it,” she said. “Every year. Outside my door, before we go up to the grave. She’s never said a word about it.”

He looked at it in her hand.

“Every year?”

“Every year.” She cracked it against the edge of the shutter and peeled it, carefully, and the shell came off in red pieces into her palm. Inside it was white and perfect. She broke it in half and held one half out to him.

He took it. He looked at it in the light from the end of the lane, and then at her, as if he were going to ask something. Then he didn’t.

“Happy birthday,” he said.

This time she let him.

chapters.title: She Breaks a System for Fun
chapters.desc: Someone has already been inside the system Eliana built, found her one mistake, fixed it, and sent an invoice. The someone is a stranger called He Si-Mei. Eliana has never been beaten before, and she does not take it well.
chapters.epigraph: “She fixed my mistake and sent a bill. A bill. One day I’m going to beat her.” — Eliana Lin
chapters.content:
She found it at three in the morning on Friday, and at first she thought she’d done it herself.

She’d built the wall over the winter. That was what she called it, though it wasn’t a wall; it was a lot of small careful things stacked up together round the way Chen Si’s people kept their secrets. It had taken her six weeks. Qian had said Mr. Chen was pleased, which from Qian was a great deal. She’d been prouder of it than of anything she’d ever made.

Once a month she went round it in the dark, checking, the way Ah Sim went round the tall house making sure the windows were shut.

This time there was a weak place. She’d missed it over the winter, a small wrong thing she hadn’t known was there.

And someone had already found it, and put it right.

She sat in the light of the five screens with her knees up and her cold hands round a can and looked at it. It had been mended, and not the way she’d have done it. Better than she’d have done it. Neater. Whoever it was had come in, found the one thing she’d got wrong, fixed it, and gone, and left nothing behind at all except a single line in the one place only the person who built the wall would ever think to look.

Fixed. Invoice to client.

She read it four times. Then she put the can down, carefully, on the edge of the desk.

✦ ✦ ✦

At nine Qian’s message came.

Mr. Chen has received the attached and would value your view.

The attached was a report, two pages, plain and short, and correct the whole way through. It didn’t show off anywhere, which was worse than if it had. At the bottom there was a total, in a sum that made Eliana’s eyebrows go up, and a name.

He Si-Mei.

Under it, from Qian: Mr. Chen has taken Ms. He on. He asks that the two of you share anything you find. He also asks me to say that he does not hold this against you.

She read that last line four times too. Then she shut the laptop, and put her hood up, and went to her ten o’clock lecture, and sat in the back row of the hall in the fish tank and did not hear a word of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The tutorial at eleven was eight of them round a table and a postgraduate in a cardigan who liked to go round the room.

“Lin Yu,” he said. “Question three. Walk us through it.”

She had done question three. She’d done all of them, and the ones on the next sheet, at four in the morning when she couldn’t stop thinking about the line in the wall. She knew question three better than the man in the cardigan did.

She opened her mouth and nothing came out.

Seven faces turned towards her. Her neck went hot, and then her ears. The man in the cardigan waited, smiling, the kind smile that made it worse. Somebody’s chair creaked.

She looked down at her laptop and typed it into the shared document on the screen at the front of the room instead, the whole answer, fast, in four lines, with a correction to the question itself in red, because there was a mistake in the question. Then she sat back with her hands in her sleeves.

The man in the cardigan read it on the big screen. He stopped smiling. “Oh,” he said. “Right. Yes. That’s—yes.” He moved on to the next person, and nobody looked at her again.

✦ ✦ ✦

“She sent a bill,” she said at lunch.

She was on the bench behind the observatory with her noodles untouched on her knee, and Yu Chen was beside her with his, listening the way he listened, which was completely.

“Who?”

“A woman. He Si-Mei. I don’t know who she is. Nobody does. I looked, and there’s almost nothing to look at, and that by itself tells you she’s good, because people like that usually leave a trail a mile wide and she hasn’t left one at all.” She stabbed the noodles. “She got into the thing I built. The winter one. The one I was proud of. She found a mistake I didn’t even know I’d made, and she fixed it, and then she sent Chen Si an invoice. For fixing my work. A bill, Chen. With a total on it.”

“Is the total high?”

“Very high.”

“Was she right?”

Eliana chewed a noodle. “Yes,” she said, with her mouth full, bitterly. “She was completely right. It was a good fix. It was a better fix than I’d have done. That’s the worst part. I keep looking at it. I can’t stop looking at it.”

“So she’s good at your job,” said Yu Chen.

“She’s very good at my job.”

She put the noodles down. She hadn’t eaten any of them.

“The thing is,” she said, lower, “I used to think that if there was ever someone better than me out there, I’d want to know. I used to want it. You get tired of being the only one in the room who can see the holes. It’s like reading over everyone’s shoulder all the time. I thought if there was somebody else who saw them too, I’d finally have someone to—” She stopped. “And now there is one, and all I want to do is prove she isn’t better. Which is stupid. She’s probably lovely. She probably likes dogs.”

“You don’t want her to be lovely,” said Yu Chen.

“No. I want her to be lovely and worse than me.” She pulled her hood forward. “I’m a horrible person.”

“You’re a competitive person who hasn’t slept,” he said. “Those aren’t the same thing.”

He thought about it, eating. He didn’t understand most of what she did; he’d told her so, plainly, more than once, and she liked that he didn’t pretend. But he understood this part. He always understood the shape of a thing even when he didn’t understand the inside.

“You’ve never had one before,” he said. “Somebody as good as you.”

She stopped chewing.

Nobody else would have said it like that. Elowen would have told her it didn’t matter and that she shouldn’t stay up all night over a bill. Her father would have told her nothing, because her father didn’t know she did any of it. Yu Chen looked at her over his noodles and said the exact true thing, which was that in her whole life, in the one room where she had never once felt small, somebody had turned out to be standing a little higher up, and she didn’t know what to do with it.

“No,” she said. “I haven’t.”

A girl from his course came along the path then, the one with all the rings, with two others, and saw him and called out something, and waved. He lifted a hand and smiled back, the pleasant smile, the one that didn’t reach anywhere, and said nothing, and they walked on.

“You never talk to them,” Eliana said.

“No. I’m polite to them. That’s not the same thing.” He said it without any weight on it, the plain way he said most things. “There isn’t much of me that’s for people in general. I used it all up on one person.” He looked at her. “You should have more than one, though. That’s different.”

She didn’t like it when he said things like that, not because they weren’t true but because they were, and because he always turned them round at the end so they landed on her and not on him.

“How does it feel?”

She looked at the harbour, down below the hill, grey and flat and crowded with cranes.

“Awful,” she said. Then, after a second: “Amazing.” Then: “Awful.”

He laughed. She hadn’t meant to make him laugh. It came out of him and she looked at him and found she was smiling, horribly, against her will, with her ears still hot.

“I’m going to beat her,” she said. “One day. I don’t know when. I’m going to be ready and I’m going to beat her, and she’s going to have to send me a bill.”

“Of course you are,” said Yu Chen.

He said it as though it had already happened. She looked at him sideways. He wasn’t teasing her. He meant it; he simply believed her, the way he believed the sun came up. It steadied something in her chest that had been rattling since three in the morning.

She ate her noodles.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening the fourth floor emptied at six, and she couldn’t settle.

She tried to work and kept drifting back to the line in the wall. Yu Chen sat at the other end of the long table with his flask and his paving-slab of a book, and turned his pages without a sound, and at half past seven he put the book down.

“I can’t fix the bill,” he said. “I don’t understand the bill. But you’ve read the same page of your own work six times.”

“I’m thinking.”

“You’re sulking.” He said it mildly, which from him was almost a joke. “Here’s a thing you can win tonight.”

She looked up.

“The booking site,” he said. “For the library rooms. You’ve been using it all term under my name, so you can clearly get into it. But you book it a day at a time, and you always cut it close.” He poured tea into the flask lid and pushed it down the table. “If you can book me the end room, the quiet one, for every weekday morning for the rest of term, before I finish this tea—then I’ll take you anywhere you want to go. Right now. Tonight.”

“That’s not a prize. That’s a chore.”

“Anywhere,” he said. “My card. No complaining about the money, because you agreed.”

She looked at the flask, and the tea steaming in the lid, and him sitting there with his hands round his cup, trying to turn her bad night into a game, the way he always did, because he couldn’t do anything about the bill and this was a thing he could do.

She pulled her laptop towards her.

It was a terrible little website, and she didn’t touch anyone’s booking but his. Before the tea had stopped steaming, the end room by the pillar was booked to Wang Y.C., every weekday morning, from now until the last day of term.

“Done,” she said.

He looked at the lid. There was still tea in it.

“That was four minutes,” he said.

“It’s a bad website.” She shut the laptop and stood up and pulled her hood down over her face, where he couldn’t see that she was pleased. “You still owe me anywhere. Finish your tea. We’re going to the roof.”

✦ ✦ ✦
