The roof of the library wasn’t really a roof you were meant to go on. There was a door on the fifth floor that said NO ENTRY, and it opened if you knew which way to lean on it, and behind it a flight of concrete steps went up to a flat space among the air-conditioning units, with a low wall round it, and the whole hill below and the city below that, and the harbour at the bottom with its chain of orange lights.

They went up. It was cold, and clear, and you could even see a few real stars over the dark of the reservoir to the north, washed thin by the city but there.

She leaned on the low wall with his flask and looked out.

“She’s out there somewhere,” she said. “He Si-Mei. Up late. Fixing somebody else’s mistakes and sending them a bill.” She drank the last of the tea. “I can’t decide if I hate her or want to be her friend.”

“Both, probably,” said Yu Chen. “You do that.”

She turned round to tell him she did not do that.

He kissed her before she got the first word out. He didn’t take her face this time. He came up behind her against the wall and turned her round by the shoulders and ducked his head and kissed her, and she dropped the flask lid on the gravel and it rolled, and neither of them went for it. His hands were warm from his cup. The wind came up off the harbour and she didn’t feel it.

“You’re meant to be taking me somewhere,” she said against his mouth.

“This is somewhere.”

She could have argued it. She’d said anywhere, and she could have made him fly her somewhere just to watch him work out the logistics with his ears going red. But the wind was cold and his hands were warm, and she had beaten something tonight, even if it wasn’t the one she wanted to beat.

“Fine,” she said, and pulled him back down by the front of his coat.

He walked her backwards until her shoulders met the side of one of the big air-conditioning units, which hummed and was warm, and kissed her harder. She got her hands inside his coat, and then inside his jumper, and he made a sound into her mouth at how cold they were and didn’t pull away. His mouth went to her jaw, and down her neck under her hair, to the place below her ear that made her knees go, and she held on to his shoulders and pressed the whole length of herself against him and heard herself say his name out loud, on a roof, a flight of stairs above a door that said NO ENTRY.

“Someone’ll come up,” he said, not stopping.

“Nobody comes up. That’s what the sign’s for.” She pulled his face back to hers.

He laughed against her mouth. Then he slid his warm hands under the back of her hoodie, flat on her bare skin, and she shivered for a reason that had nothing to do with the wind, and stopped arguing about anything.

She kissed him until the tea had gone cold in the lid on the gravel and the cold had gone out of both of them, up on the roof of the library with the whole lit city at their feet and one small, bad website somewhere underneath it all, where the end room was his until June.

chapters.title: Yu Chen Asks Raiden for Advice
chapters.desc: Wanting to understand the Lins before he loves one of them out loud, Yu Chen asks Raiden how the family works. It goes wrong in several parts, and ends with the two of them sworn to silence by a girl with a spreadsheet.
chapters.epigraph: “You want to date my sister. I want to go on living. I think we can help each other.” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
He was asked to the birthday lunch as the boy who’d given Eliana a lift.

He hadn’t given her a lift. He didn’t have a car that spring; he had a bicycle, and she had a bus pass, and on the one morning it had rained hard enough to matter he’d put her on the back of the bicycle and she’d shrieked the whole way down the hill and told him afterwards she’d rather have drowned. But Eliana had said, at the table one Sunday, that the Song boy next door could carry the folding tables up from the cellar, because he was tall and polite and did what he was told, and her father had said nothing, which from her father was a yes.

So on Saturday he carried the folding tables up from the cellar.

It was Raiden and Evangeline’s birthday, the ninth of April, which they shared though they weren’t twins by blood; Raiden explained this to Yu Chen twice before noon, both times at length, and Yu Chen already knew it, because Eliana had drawn him the whole family on the back of a lecture handout in October with lines and dates and little notes, and because he listened, and because he had spent eight months learning this family the way he learned anatomy, one careful layer at a time.

He wanted to understand them. That was the truth of why he’d come. Not for the tables.

He had decided, over the winter, that one day he was going to stand in front of Lin Jian and say a true sentence about his daughter, and not be thrown out of the lane for it, and that to do that he needed to understand how the man worked. You did not operate on something you hadn’t read about first. He had read everything he could about the Lins, which was Eliana, who told him things sideways and then told him to forget she’d said them. It wasn’t enough. He needed someone on the inside.

Raiden Lin was on the inside, and Raiden Lin, famously, could not keep anything in.

✦ ✦ ✦

He got Raiden by the cellar steps, where they were stacking the last of the chairs.

“Can I ask you something,” said Yu Chen.

“You can ask me anything.” Raiden set a chair down and sat on it, backwards, with his arms on the back and his chin on his arms, beaming. He had a plaster on his thumb and paint on his wrist. “I’m the easy one. Everyone says so. Elowen’s sharp, Evangeline’s silent, Elara cries, Eliana bites. I’m the one you can ask things.” He tipped his head. “You want to ask me about Eliana.”

Yu Chen said nothing, which was an answer.

“I knew it,” said Raiden, delighted. “I’ve known since the flask. Nobody carries a flask that far for a girl he isn’t—” He stopped, and looked moved. “It’s the sweetest thing. Does she know?”

“She knows.”

“Does your—” Raiden lowered his voice to a stage whisper that carried across the garden. “Does Baba know?”

“No.”

“Oh, good,” said Raiden, relaxing. “Good. Keep it that way. He’ll—” He drew a flat line across his own throat with the thumb that had the plaster on it. “Figuratively. Mostly figuratively. He liked the policeman’s family even less than most policemen, and he didn’t like policemen, and you live in the policeman’s house.” He brightened again. “But you want advice. On how to approach him. Yes? Because you’re a planner. I can tell. You’ve got that look. You’ve written something down.”

Yu Chen had, in fact, written something down. It was in the back of the notebook. PLAN (LIN JIAN), with three points, all of them wrong, as it turned out.

“I want to understand him,” he said. “Before I ever say anything. I don’t want to get it wrong.”

Raiden looked at him with real affection, the way you’d look at someone about to walk into a glass door.

“Right,” he said. “Sit down. This is going to take a while, and most of it is going to be useless, and you’re going to use it anyway, because that’s the kind of person you are. I’ve watched you stack those chairs. You lined them up by height.”

Yu Chen sat down.

“Here’s the first thing,” said Raiden. “You can’t approach him. Nobody approaches him. You can only wait by the thing he loves until he notices you’re always there. That’s how Zhao did it. Zhao stood next to Elowen for three years not saying anything and Baba decided he liked him. Took three years.”

“I don’t have three years.”

“Everyone has three years,” said Raiden, which was the kind of thing Raiden said. “Second thing. Bring something. Not for him. For the house. A fruit. A tool. Something that says I am useful and I will not steal the silver. You’ve already done it; you carried the tables. Keep doing that. Be a thing the house works better with.” He thought. “Third thing—and this is the one nobody will tell you—”

“Raiden,” said a voice.

✦ ✦ ✦

Eliana was standing at the top of the cellar steps with a tray of cold dishes in her hands and an expression Yu Chen had learned to be afraid of.

“What are you doing,” she said. It wasn’t a question.

“Giving advice,” said Raiden. “To your—” He looked between them. “To the Song boy. About carrying tables. We were talking about table-carrying.”

“You were talking about Baba.” She came down two steps. “I could hear you from the kitchen. You did the throat thing. I saw your hand.”

“I was being helpful.”

“You were being you.” She put the tray down on a chair and folded her arms, and looked at the pair of them, sitting on chairs by the cellar steps like two boys outside a headmaster’s office, and Yu Chen watched her do the thing she did, which was to go cold and clear and a little frightening, the face she had on the phone at two in the morning, the one strangers never saw.

“Here’s what’s going to happen,” she said. “Raiden. You’re not going to tell anyone anything. Not that he asked. Not that I—” She stopped, and her ears went red, and she pushed on. “Not anything. And in exchange I’m not going to tell anyone that you bought a garage near the Docks in December, in the name of Cao Jia, who builds motorbikes, and who you have been seeing since last spring, and who you are hiding from this entire family, and whose number is in your phone under ‘Tyres.’”

Raiden’s mouth opened.

“I’ve known since New Year,” said Eliana. “You’re on the spreadsheet. You’ve been on it since February. So has she. So keep your mouth shut about mine, and I’ll keep it shut about yours, and nobody’s throat has to get—” she looked at his hand “—figuratively anything.”

There was a silence by the cellar steps.

“You have a spreadsheet,” said Raiden faintly.

“Everyone’s on the spreadsheet.”

“Am I a column or a row?”

“You’re a row. She’s a row. There’s a tab.” Eliana picked the tray back up. “Lunch is in ten minutes. Wash the paint off. Both of you look guilty and it’s going to be obvious.” She went back up the steps, and at the top she stopped, and without turning round she said, “The third thing, Raiden. The one nobody tells him. What were you going to say?”

Raiden looked at Yu Chen.

“I was going to say,” he said, to his sister’s back, “that Baba’s not angry at the boy next door. Baba’s angry at himself. He’s been angry at himself for nineteen years, and he aims it wherever’s nearest, and lately the nearest thing is you.” He said it gently, for Raiden. “Whoever loves you is going to have to stand in the way of that. That’s the third thing.”

Eliana stood at the top of the steps with the tray.

Then she went in without a word, and the two of them sat there, and after a moment Raiden said, “She’s going to make a frightening wife,” in a voice full of pride, and Yu Chen didn’t correct the word, because he didn’t want to.

✦ ✦ ✦

At lunch he was at the far end of the table, below Uncle Mok, which was where the boy who carried the tables sat.

Nine of them, with Ah Sim coming and going. Lin Jian at the head, grey and enormous, with his hands flat on either side of his bowl. Elowen on his right, in green; Zhao beside her, who looked at Yu Chen once, for four seconds, and then seemed to lose interest, though Yu Chen didn’t believe it. Raiden, scrubbed, opposite, telling a story about a crane. Elara, home from a shift, falling asleep sitting up between courses. Evangeline at the far end by the window, silent, eating very little. Eliana halfway down with her laptop shut beside her bowl, not looking at Yu Chen, which he knew to read as looking at him constantly.

He ate, and said little, and passed dishes before they were asked for, and watched.

He watched the way the whole table talked around Eliana. Elowen asked Ah Sim whether Eliana had eaten properly this week. Ah Sim said she lived on noodles. Raiden said she needed to come out more, she’d gone the colour of a mushroom. They said it over her, pleasantly, the way you talk about a child who’s in the room, and Eliana ate her rice and didn’t look up, and Yu Chen’s hand went still round his chopsticks.

Then Lin Jian spoke.

He didn’t say much. He rarely did. He looked down the table, somewhere past his youngest daughter’s left ear, and said, to Elowen, “Tell her she’s not to be on that computer so late. The neighbours can see her light at four in the morning. It looks like something.”

The table carried on. Elowen started to say something smoothing. Raiden laughed about the crane.

“I can hear you, Baba,” said Eliana, without looking up.

Lin Jian didn’t answer. He reached for the fish.

Yu Chen put his chopsticks down.

He didn’t decide to. It happened the way it had happened in the corridor of the fish tank, with the boy who’d pulled her hood; the pleasant thing he kept on the front of himself slid off, and what was left underneath looked out, cold and steady and older than he was.

“She said she can hear you,” said Yu Chen.

He said it down the length of the table, from the seat below Uncle Mok, without raising his voice. The table had gone silent at the first word, the way a room does when a thing that is always quiet makes a sound.

Lin Jian looked up. He looked down the table at the boy who carried the tables, properly, for the first time all day.

“She’s right there,” said Yu Chen. “You’re talking about her light. You could ask her about it. She’d tell you. She tells me.”

Nobody moved. Zhao had stopped eating. Raiden was looking at his plate as if it were extremely interesting. Elowen’s hand had come off the table. Eliana had gone white.

Lin Jian looked at Yu Chen, and Yu Chen made himself hold it, and felt the cold thing in him look out of his own eyes at the most frightening man in the Walled City and not care in the slightest, because the man had talked about her light as if she weren’t there to hear it.

Then the mask came back. He felt it come; he put it back on, deliberately, the way you’d put a lid on a pot, and his face went pleasant and young and apologetic again.

“Sorry,” he said, to the table. “That wasn’t my place. The fish is good.”

He picked his chopsticks back up.

After a second, Raiden said something about the crane again, too loudly, and Elowen answered it, and the table started up, and the moment closed over. Lin Jian went back to his bowl. But halfway through the next course Yu Chen looked up and found the man looking at him again, from under his heavy brows, with an expression that wasn’t anger. He couldn’t name it. He’d think about it later. It looked almost like recognition.

Across the table, Eliana was staring at him with her mouth open. So was Raiden. Zhao had turned his head and was looking at Yu Chen as if he’d only just walked in.

✦ ✦ ✦

They caught him in the pantry.

He’d gone in to put the empty rice tub back on the high shelf, because he was tall and it saved Ah Sim the stool, and the door opened behind him and shut, and it was her.

“You,” she said, “are an idiot.”

“I know.”

“You said she said she can hear you to Lin Jian. To his face. At his table.” She was backing him into the shelves, into the rice sacks, with one finger in his chest. “Nobody does that. Zhao doesn’t do that, and Zhao once—” she waved the finger “—you don’t say things to Baba. You wait by the thing he loves until he—”

“Raiden already gave me that one.”

“Raiden’s an idiot too.” Her finger was still in his chest. Her ears were red. She was furious, and her eyes were bright, and he had learned to tell her two furies apart, the cold one and this one, and this was not the cold one. “You scared me. You went like you did with the hood boy. Cold. And it’s—”

“Does it frighten you?”

She stopped.

“No,” she said, which surprised her; he watched it surprise her. “That’s the problem. It should. It doesn’t.”

He kissed her.

He didn’t ask. He took her by the waist and turned, so it was her back against the rice sacks and not his, and kissed her in the dark pantry with the smell of dried fish and star anise all round them and thirty feet of family on the other side of the door. She made a small sound and grabbed two fistfuls of his shirt and kissed him back, up on her toes, and he lifted her the last of the way, as he had on the roof, and for a second there was nothing in the whole house but this.

“They’ll hear,” she said against his mouth.

“Then be quiet,” he said, which made her laugh, which was not being quiet, and he had to kiss the laugh out of her, and that didn’t work either.

The pantry door opened.

Ah Sim stood in it with the empty soup pot. She looked at them: the boy next door with his arms round the youngest Lin, both of them holding still now, Eliana with her hand still in his shirt and a bag of rice knocked sideways behind her.

Ah Sim looked at them. She took her time about it.

“The rice,” she said, “goes on the high shelf.”

“Yes,” said Yu Chen.

She put the pot in the sink, and took a jar of pickled radish off the low shelf, and went out, and pulled the door to behind her, not quite shut, and they heard her say, in the kitchen, to nobody, “Tell them the cake’s coming.”

Eliana put her face in his chest and shook with laughing.

“She’s not going to say anything,” she said, when she could. “Ah Sim never says anything. Ah Sim’s the most frightening woman Raiden’s ever met and she leaves me noodles.” She pulled back and looked up at him, and the laughing went out of her face. “You stood up for me. At the table. Nobody’s ever done that. Elowen smooths it. Everyone smooths it. You just—said it.”

“He was talking about you like you weren’t there.”

“I know.” She straightened his shirt where she’d crushed it, with both hands, flat, the way she squared the shoebox to the edge of her desk. “Don’t do it again.”

“I’ll do it again,” said Yu Chen.

She looked up at him. She didn’t argue. He saw her decide not to, and saw her put it away somewhere, the way she put things away, to look at later, and then she got up on her toes and kissed him once more, hard and fast, for no reason at all, and ducked out of the pantry to tell them the cake was coming.

He put the rice on the high shelf. Then he stood in the dark for a second with his hand flat on the shelf and his heart going, and thought that he had come to understand the family, and had instead told the father of it, at his own table, that he was wrong.

It had been the most honest thing he’d done all year. He didn’t regret it. That was the part that would have frightened anyone who thought he was soft.

He went back out to carry the cake.

chapters.title: A Hackathon, Allegedly
chapters.desc: He takes her to the Wang house by the sea for a weekend and tells everyone it’s a coding retreat. Wei Long, who raised him, phones twice with terrible advice. Nobody codes much.
chapters.epigraph: “Bring fruit. Don’t talk about her father. Actually, don’t talk at all — you talk too much when you’re nervous.” — Song Wei Long
chapters.content:
The cover story was a hackathon.

There wasn’t a hackathon. There was a weekend in August, and a house two hours south on the coast road, and Yu Chen had said to Baba, through Eliana, that a group from the university was doing a coding weekend at a friend’s place by the sea, and would Eliana be allowed to go, there’d be four of them, it was for a competition. Baba had said she could go if Elowen said so. Elowen had said so, after looking at Eliana for slightly too long, and Eliana had packed a bag and told no one that the group of four was a group of two, and that the friend’s place was his.

She found out it was his when they came round the last bend of the coast road and he slowed down.

She’d known he had money. She’d known for years, in the abstract way you know a thing about a neighbour: the Song house was his, bought from Wei Long; there was a trust; Auntie Dai came every day. But money in the Walled City was a thing you kept in a drawer. It wasn’t this.

The house stood white on the cliff above a cove, long and low, with a wall of glass facing the sea and a flat roof and steps cut down the rock to a strip of sand that nobody else could reach. There was no other house in sight. The sea went all the way out to a flat line, and there were birds, and nothing else.

“Whose is this,” she said.

“Mine,” he said, pulling in. He looked embarrassed. “My father’s, really. It was his. It’s in the trust. I come about twice a year and open the windows.” He turned the engine off. “Auntie Dai’s cousin keeps it aired. There’s food. I’m sorry. I should have said. I didn’t want you to say no.”

“Why would I say no?”

“Because it’s a lot,” he said, “and you don’t like a lot,” which was true, and she didn’t have an answer to it, so she got out of the car and looked at the sea instead.

✦ ✦ ✦

Wei Long rang at six, while Yu Chen was carrying the bags in.

Eliana knew who it was before Yu Chen said a word, because his face went a little more careful, the way it only did for his cousin. He stood by the glass wall with the phone to his ear and said “yes” and “no” and “it’s fine” several times, and then held the phone away from his ear and looked at it, and she could hear, from across the room, a flat level voice still talking.

“He wants to say something to you,” said Yu Chen, and held the phone out, looking apologetic.

She took it.

“Hello?”

“You’re the Lin girl,” said the voice. Dry. No warmth and no unkindness; just fact, laid down flat. “He’s never taken anyone to that house. He took me once, to open the windows, and I’m the one who raised him, so you can see this is a serious business. I’m not going to ask what your intentions are. I know what his are; he writes them to his grandmother every month. I’m going to ask you one thing, and then you can give him back the phone.”

Eliana, who could talk to no stranger alive, found she could talk to this one, because he wasn’t asking anything that needed charm.

“All right,” she said.

“Are you going to be careful with him,” said Wei Long. “He’s careful with everyone. Nobody’s ever been careful with him back. That’s the whole question. You don’t have to answer out loud. He’s standing right there doing the face.”

She looked at Yu Chen, who was standing by the glass doing the face.

“Yes,” she said.

“Good,” said Wei Long. “Give him back. And tell him to bring fruit when he meets your father, and not to talk about your father, and actually not to talk at all, he talks too much when he’s nervous, he always has. He’ll say he doesn’t. He does.”

She gave the phone back. Yu Chen listened to another minute of it with his ears going red, said “I don’t talk too much when I’m nervous,” listened, said “Goodbye, Wei Long,” and hung up.

“What did he say to you?” said Yu Chen.

“He asked if I liked the house,” said Eliana, and watched him decide whether to believe it, and not quite.

✦ ✦ ✦

They did not code.

She’d brought a laptop, out of habit, and a second one, and it sat zipped in its bag on the long table by the glass for the whole weekend and she never opened it. She didn’t open the first one either. She didn’t take a job. She’d told Qian she’d be away, which she never did, and Qian had written back Understood and nothing else, and for two days nobody needed anything found or cleaned or watched, and the quiet in her head was so strange that for the first few hours she kept checking her phone to see what was wrong.

Nothing was wrong.

She swam. The water in the cove was cold and clear and she swam out past the rocks and lay on her back and looked at the sky, which had more in it out here than it did over the city, and he sat on the sand in his shorts with his trousers rolled and his feet in the water and watched her, and when she swam back in he wrapped her in a towel the size of a tent and rubbed her hair dry roughly, the way you’d dry a dog, until it stood up all over her head.

She slept. That was the strangest part. She slept in the afternoon, on a chair in the sun by the glass, with her mouth open, for two hours, and woke up with a line across her cheek and him sitting beside her reading, not watching her, for once, just there.

“You let me sleep again,” she said.

“You keep doing it,” he said. “I think the sea’s doing it. We should bottle it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He tried to buy her a rig.

He did it badly, which was how she knew it was real. On the Saturday evening he said, over the food his housekeeper’s cousin had left, that he’d been thinking, and that she was always complaining her machine at home was slow, and that he could easily—

“No,” said Eliana.

“I didn’t finish.”

“You don’t have to finish. The answer’s no.”

“It would make your work easier.”

“That’s not the point.” She put her chopsticks down. This was the first time all weekend she’d gone cold, and she felt herself do it, and couldn’t stop it. “I buy my own tools. All of them. With my own money, which I earn, doing the thing you don’t ask me about. You can buy me tea. You can buy ten thousand headphones. You can buy a planetarium, apparently, which I’m still not over. But not the tools. The tools are mine.”

He looked at her for a second.

“All right,” he said.

“That’s it? All right?”

“You’ve drawn a line,” he said, reaching for the rice. “It’s your line. You get to draw it. I’ll buy the tea.” He said it the way he said most things, plainly, with no sulk in it anywhere, and she sat there braced for an argument that didn’t come, and felt the cold go out of her, and felt, underneath it, something she didn’t have a word for, which was that he’d heard her draw a line round herself and had simply moved his chair to the other side of it and gone on sitting with her.

“You’re not allowed to be this reasonable,” she said. “It’s annoying.”

“I know.”

“Buy the tea.”

“I’m going to buy so much tea,” said Yu Chen.

✦ ✦ ✦

He rang Wei Long once himself, on the Saturday night, on the roof.

She wasn’t meant to hear. She’d gone up to the flat roof to look at the stars, which were real up here, not painted, thick across the whole sky with the pale smear right through the middle, and he’d come up after her and his phone had gone, and he’d answered it a little way off along the roof with his back to her.

She heard pieces. No. — It’s not like that. — I know what she does. I’ve always known. — I’m not going to ask her to stop, Wei Long, that’s not— A pause. Because she’d stop being who she is, and I didn’t come down here to make her into someone easier. Another pause, longer. You raised me better than to lie to you. So don’t make me start.

She went very still by the roof wall.

When he came back he put the phone in his pocket and sat down beside her on the warm concrete and didn’t mention it, and she didn’t either, but she moved over and put her head on his shoulder and felt him go still with surprise and then settle, and they looked at the real sky without talking.

“He worries about me,” said Yu Chen, at last. “Wei Long. He’s been worrying about me since I was fifteen. It’s the only way he knows how to—” He stopped. “He thinks you’re dangerous.”

“I am dangerous.”

“I know.” He turned his head. “That’s not why he’s wrong.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was her, on the beach, the last night.

They’d gone down the rock steps in the dark with a torch and a blanket, the blue one, which he’d brought, because of course he had, and spread it on the cold sand above the tide line, and lain on it looking at the sea, which you could hear but barely see, a long pale line of it coming and going in the dark.

He’d been building up to something all evening. She could tell. He got quiet in a particular way when he was building up to something, and he’d been that way since dinner, and there was a shape in his jacket pocket that she’d clocked and said nothing about, and she lay on the blanket in the dark and waited to see what he’d do, with her heart going harder than she let him know.

He didn’t do it.

Whatever it was, he didn’t. She felt him decide not to; she felt the breath go out of him, and felt him put it away, the shape in his pocket, with his hand, pressing it down flat.

“I had a thing I was going to say,” he said. “I’m not going to say it. Not tonight. It’s too soon, and I know what it is for you, the kind of thing it is, and I’d rather say it in ten years than say it too soon and watch you run down a tree.”

She lay there.

She knew what he meant. She knew what the shape in his pocket probably wasn’t, yet, and might be, one day, and she knew that the word for the thing he hadn’t said began with a sound she couldn’t make, the hospital word, the word people said before they didn’t come home.

And he’d known that. He’d carried it down the cliff and decided, lying next to her on his mother’s blanket, not to make her hear it before she could stand it.

“You can be scared of it,” he said. “The whole thing. For as long as you like. You can be scared of it forever and still have tonight. Tonight doesn’t need the other thing. Tonight’s just the beach.”

She turned over on the blanket and climbed half onto him in the dark and kissed him.

She did it first, which she hardly ever did, not like this, not starting it cold with her whole body, and she felt him go still under her with surprise and then his arms came up round her and pulled her the rest of the way on top of him. She kissed him with the sea going in and out behind them and the sand cold under the blanket and his heart going under her hand, and she put everything into it that she couldn’t put into the word, because this she could do, this she had always been able to do, and he could read it, he always could.

“Eliana,” he said, into her hair, when she let him breathe.

“Don’t say the thing.” She kissed him again. “Not tonight.”

So he didn’t say it. He rolled her over onto the blanket instead, slowly, with one hand under her head so it wouldn’t touch the sand, and kissed her as if they had all night, which they did.

It was cold. She didn’t care. She got her hands up under his jumper and he hissed at how cold they were and didn’t make her take them away. He undid her shirt one button at a time and kissed each place he uncovered, her collarbone, the middle of her chest, the soft skin under her ribs that made her laugh and grab his hair, and every time the wind came off the sea he pulled the edge of the blanket up over her again, as if that were his whole job.

“Nobody can see,” she said. It was the first time in her life she’d said it as a reason to keep going.

“Nobody at all,” he said, against her stomach.

After that she stopped keeping track. There was sand in the blanket and in her hair and somewhere down the back of his collar, and she didn’t care about that either. There was his weight, warm against the cold, and his breath at her ear, and the sea going in and out behind them louder than either of them, so that for once she didn’t have to be quiet. She wasn’t. She heard herself, out loud under the open sky, and felt him smile against her throat, and pulled him down by the shoulders until he stopped smiling and said her name into her neck, rough and low, as if it had been dragged out of him.

Afterwards they lay tangled in the blanket with the tide creeping up the sand towards their feet, and she wasn’t scared of anything, up above the dark sea with no other house for a mile, on the blanket from her own front step.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning she found the letter.

She wasn’t snooping. She was looking for the coffee, in a drawer in the long room, and found a letter instead, in his square capitals, addressed to an old address in the north, with the stamp already on, waiting to be posted. It was dated last week. She knew she shouldn’t. She read the first line anyway, because she was who she was.

Dear Nainai. I’m taking Eliana to the house by the sea this weekend, so I’ll write properly when I’m back.

She looked at the next line down, through the fold.

You keep asking when you’ll meet her. Soon, I think. She’s not ready, so don’t send anything, and don’t tell Xing Yue’s father, and don’t put her name in a letter to anyone. But soon.

She put it back where it had been and shut the drawer.

She stood in the long room with the sea all down one wall and her ears hot. You keep asking. His grandmother had been asking. For how long? She did the sum she didn’t want to do, the one that put her name in his letters going back, month after month, further than this weekend, further than the planetarium, back and back.

He came in with wet hair and found her standing by the drawer.

“The coffee’s in the blue tin,” he said, “on the—” He saw her face. “What?”

“Nothing,” said Eliana. “I can’t find the coffee.”

He got the coffee out of the blue tin. She watched his back while he did it, and thought about his grandmother in the north asking when she’d meet the girl, and about how long you’d have to have been writing a person’s name in your letters home for your grandmother to start asking, and she found she wasn’t frightened by it, which frightened her, a little, by itself.

She didn’t tell him she’d read it. She put it on the spreadsheet in her head, in the quiet tab, the one that was only his, the one she never showed anyone, and drank the coffee, and watched the sea, and did not open her laptop once the whole way home.

chapters.title: The Fence
chapters.desc: Her sister vanishes from the flower market and comes back changed, and Eliana — who could find anyone — couldn’t find her in time. She builds a wall of code to watch for the Lin name, and won’t tell even Yu Chen what it’s for.
chapters.epigraph: “I was three days too slow. It won’t happen again. That’s all I can tell you.” — Eliana Lin
chapters.content:
Evangeline went to the orchid stalls at the flower market before six on Tuesday, the way she did on market mornings, and didn’t come back.

Eliana heard about it at nine, when Elowen rang. Elowen’s voice was wrong in a way Eliana had heard only once before. She said Evangeline hadn’t come home, and her phone was dead, and the orchid seller said she’d bought nothing, and nobody had seen her after about twenty to six, and Baba was already at the market with every man he had.

Eliana said she’d look.

She sat down at the five screens with her hood up and her cold hands going and she looked.

She looked for three days.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was good at finding people. It was most of what she did. Give her a name and an afternoon and she could tell you where a man slept and what he was frightened of. She had found a clerk in the eastern district in a few hours once and never forgotten what it cost him. She could find anyone.

She could not find her own sister.

There were no cameras at that end of the market; she knew, because she’d looked at them before, for other reasons, and they pointed the wrong way. There was no phone to follow, because the phone was dead. There was no face to search for, because — and this was the thing that stopped her cold at two in the morning on the first night — there were no photographs of Evangeline anywhere. Not one. Baba had taken her out of every room with a camera in it since before Eliana was born. There was no picture of her sister in the entire world to show a screen and say: find this.

So she made one.

She did it from memory, which she had plenty of, her sister’s carved still face at the end of the long table year after year, and from a drawing. Raiden drew it for her on the second night, sitting on her floor with a pencil and not saying anything for an hour, getting the line of the jaw wrong and rubbing it out and getting it right, and when he’d finished he put the pencil down and put his head in his hands and Eliana had to look away from him and back at the screens.

Then she watched for that face everywhere she watched, in the places where things were sold that couldn’t be bought in shops.

Nothing came back.

She didn’t sleep. She drank the cans and she drank the tea that appeared at her elbow — she didn’t remember Yu Chen coming and going, but the tea kept appearing, and the food, and once a hot-water bottle against her feet under the desk — and she watched the screens, and the screens showed her nothing, and her sister was somewhere she couldn’t reach, and the hours went by.

On Thursday night she fell asleep at the desk, which she never did, and woke at three in the morning on Friday to Elowen ringing.

“They’ve got her,” said Elowen, crying. “She’s at Harbourside General. She’s alive. She walked in. She’s alive, Yu-er.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Baba did not sleep for three days either. Eliana knew, because she watched the house without meaning to, the way she watched everything. His study light stayed on. Uncle Mok’s car came and went at all hours. On the second night she heard him on the stairs, going up and down, a big man moving slowly in the dark, checking doors that were already locked. He didn’t come up to the top of the house. He never did. But once she opened her own door a crack and saw him standing on the landing two floors down, looking up, at the dark above him, where she was; and she shut the door before he could see her see him, and went back to the screens, and found nothing, and hated the screens.

Nobody could tell her how.

That was the part Eliana couldn’t put down, afterwards. Evangeline had walked into the emergency department at Harbourside at three in the morning with four other women, all of them out of a container at West Basin, and she wouldn’t say who had let them out. A man, she said. Tall. That was all anyone could get. A man, tall, who’d driven them and gone.

Eliana went over it for weeks. There was no record of a truck. There was no camera that caught it; she looked, she looked at every camera for miles, and there was nothing. Whoever had found her sister, and got her out, and brought her to the one place she’d be safe, had done it without leaving a mark anywhere Eliana could see, which Eliana would have said was impossible, because nobody moved through the world without leaving a mark. She left marks. He Si-Mei left marks. Everybody did.

He hadn’t. And he’d done in a night the one thing Eliana, who could find anyone, had failed to do in three days.

She didn’t know who he was. She was never going to be allowed to know; she understood that much, later, from the way her sister’s face closed when anyone went near it. She stopped looking, because Evangeline asked her to, with her eyes, across the kitchen, once. But she never got over it. The person who’d saved her sister was better at this than she was, and he was a stranger, and she couldn’t even thank him.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went to the hospital with Elowen at eight on the Friday morning, and saw her sister in a borrowed gown on a trolley, with a girl from the container holding her hand and not letting go, and couldn’t say anything, and Evangeline didn’t need her to. She came home at noon and slept for four hours and woke up and started to build the fence.

She didn’t call it that yet. It didn’t have a name for a few days. It was just a thing she sat down and made, at the five screens, in the dark, the week after the hospital, because she had sat for three days and watched the places where people were sold, and seen nothing, and been too slow, and she was never going to be that slow again.

She built it to watch. Not for anyone’s enemy; for her own family. For the Lin name, wherever it came up. For the address of the tall house. For her sisters’ faces, and when she got to Evangeline’s face she had to use the drawing again, because there was still no photograph, and she sat and looked at Raiden’s pencil line of her sister’s jaw on the screen before she fed it in.

It ran on three of the screens. The other two she kept for ordinary work. If it ever caught any of those things, it would wake her, whatever she was doing, wherever she was.

It took her a week, on and off, between lectures she didn’t go to and a job for Qian she did half-asleep. When it was done she sat back and looked at the three screens, quiet now, watching, and felt the thing she always felt when a thing was built right, except that this time there was no joy in it at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yu Chen came every evening of that week.

He didn’t ask what she was building. He’d said he wouldn’t, and he didn’t, even now, even seeing her grey and shaking and not eating and not sleeping and sitting at those screens till four. He came over the wall after his own day on the hill and let himself in with the key and came up the stairs on the edges, and he brought food and he made tea and he kept her alive while she worked, and he asked her nothing.

Once, on the Tuesday, he reached past her to move a cold cup away from the edge of the desk, and she said “Don’t,” so sharply that they both went still. His hand stopped an inch from the cup. It was her rule: not even to move a cup. He took his hand back and said “Sorry,” and went and stood by the door, and she sat there with her face hot, hating herself, and couldn’t say so. Ten minutes later she moved the cup herself. Then she held her empty hand out behind her without turning round, and after a second he came and put a fresh one in it.

On the Thursday it was finished she was still at the desk at midnight when he came up. She hadn’t moved in hours. She was looking at the three quiet screens, and her hands had stopped, and she was shaking a little, the way you shake when you’ve been cold too long and someone finally puts you by a fire.

“It’s done,” she said, without turning round.

He didn’t ask what was done.

“Will you tell me what it is?” he said. It was the first time he’d ever asked anything close to it, and he asked it carefully, leaving her all the room in the world to say no.

“No,” she said. “I can’t. It’s—” She stopped. “I was three days too slow. Everyone was. Baba had every man he has looking, for three days, and I had every screen I have, and none of us found her, and a stranger did it in one night without trying. This is so that never happens again. That’s all I can tell you. Please don’t ask me the rest.”

“I won’t,” he said.

She turned round in the chair.

He was standing in the middle of her dark room, too tall for it, with a box of dumplings going cold in his hand, and his face was doing the careful thing, the worried thing, the one he did when Auntie Dai’s knee was bad, and for once she didn’t tell him to stop, because she didn’t have anything left to tell anyone anything with.

“I can’t tonight,” she said. “I can’t do—anything. I’m sorry. I just want—”

“I know,” he said. He put the dumplings down. “Come here.”

She got up out of the chair and crossed the room and he caught her, all of her at once, and she put her face in the middle of his chest and stood there, and he put one hand flat on her back and one on the top of her head and held on, and didn’t say anything, and didn’t try to fix anything, because there wasn’t anything to fix.

She didn’t cry at first. Then she did, without any noise, in her hood, against his shirt, the way she always did, and he felt it and didn’t say so. He just stood there in the middle of her room and held her, and let her, and when her knees went he went down with her, onto the floor, with his back against the camp bed and her in his lap under the blue blanket, and stayed there.

“I could find anyone,” she said, into his chest, much later. “That’s the thing. That’s the whole thing I’m for. And I couldn’t find her.”

“You built the thing that means you will, next time,” he said. “That’s not nothing.”

“It shouldn’t have to exist.”

“No. But you made it exist. In a week. Grey and not sleeping.” His hand moved in her hair, slowly, the way he untangled headphones. “I don’t understand what it does. I’m never going to understand what it does. But I understand why you made it. You made it because you couldn’t stand still. That I understand completely.”

She lay against him on the floor with the three screens watching over both their heads.

“You’re scared of me,” she said. “Wei Long thinks I’m dangerous. You built a whole clean life so nobody looks at me too closely. And you sit on my floor at midnight holding me while I build a machine to hunt through the worst part of the world for my own family.” She turned her face up. “Doesn’t that frighten you?”

He thought about it, the way he thought about her real questions.

“It scares me how far you’ll go,” he said. “Not that you go. That you’ll go further than anyone should have to, on your own, in the dark, and not tell a soul, and then come out grey in the morning and get on the bus.” He tightened his arm. “So I’m not going to make you not go. I’m going to make sure you’re not on your own and in the dark. That’s the part I can do. I’ll hold the torch.”

“You can’t even work the torch.”

“I’ll hold it anyway,” said Yu Chen. “I’ll hold it badly. You can point.”

She laughed, a little, wetly, which she hadn’t thought she’d do tonight.

She fell asleep against him on the floor some time before three, under the blanket, with the dumplings cold and the three screens quiet and watching, and he stayed awake, she knew, because every time she half-surfaced his hand was still moving in her hair, slow and steady, keeping count of something she couldn’t hear.

In the morning the fence had a name. She’d dreamed it, or half-dreamed it, slumped against him on the floor: a fence, the kind you put round a thing you were never going to let anyone take again. She wrote it at the top of the three screens where only she would see it, and left it there, and went down to the kitchen where he’d already made her tea, and didn’t tell him, because that was theirs now, the thing he didn’t ask about and she didn’t say, the one wall in her life with a gap in it only he could stand in.

chapters.title: The Detective Already Knows
chapters.desc: Wei Long works out that the Syndicate’s “Eraser” is the girl next door, the one who dates the cousin he raised. He comes to the garden wall, off the record, to decide what kind of uncle he’s going to be — and to ask Yu Chen about a lie.
chapters.epigraph: “I asked you to your face. You looked at me and you lied. I raised you better than that. Or exactly that well.” — Song Wei Long
chapters.content:
Wei Long came on a Saturday evening in July, which was wrong, because Wei Long came on Sundays.

He’d come to Sunday lunch every week since he moved out four years ago, and in all that time Yu Chen could not remember him coming on a Saturday. Sundays were the arrangement. Saturday was a man coming to say something he didn’t want to say over a table.

Yu Chen knew it the moment he opened the door. Wei Long was in his plain dark coat, though it was warm, and he had his hands in his pockets, and he looked at Yu Chen the way he looked at everything, flat, reading the small print, and he said, “Is Auntie Dai still here?”

“She left at six.”

“Good. Come out to the garden. I don’t want to do this in the house.”

They went out to the back, to the wall under the persimmon tree, where the branch hung over onto the Lin side and the fruit was still green and hard. It was nearly dark. Across the wall, up at the top of the tall house, her window had its thin line of light. Yu Chen saw Wei Long see it, and look at it, and then look back at him.

“Sit down,” said Wei Long, and sat on the low garden wall himself, heavily, the way he did everything.

Yu Chen didn’t sit.

✦ ✦ ✦

“There’s a person,” said Wei Long, “that the Syndicate uses. We’ve known about this person for a few years. We’ve never had a name, or a face, or an age, or a country. The person doesn’t exist on paper. They scrub the Lin family out of records, mostly — old shipping files, court papers, anything with the old man’s name on it. They’re good. Better than anyone we have. We call them the Eraser.”

He paused.

“Last October,” he said, “after her sister came out of that container, we were watching the places where women get sold. Somebody else was already in them. Faster than us. Listings that mentioned anyone called Lin went wrong, or vanished. I took a look at that, and at some older things, and I started to see the same hand in all of them. The same way of doing it. The same—” he moved his hand, looking for the word a policeman uses “—signature. Neat. No mess. A photo of a persimmon left in an empty folder, once, as a joke, because whoever it was thought it was funny.” He looked up at the branch over their heads, heavy with green fruit. “Lin persimmons.”

Yu Chen said nothing.

“The Eraser lives in the Walled City,” said Wei Long. “The Eraser is a Lin. The Eraser is twenty years old, and does a computer science degree on the hill, and dates the boy I raised.” He said it without any change in his voice. “I’ve known for a while. I wanted to be sure before I said it to you. I’m sure.”

Yu Chen said nothing.

“That’s the first thing,” said Wei Long. “Here’s the second.”

He took his hands out of his pockets.

“Eight months ago,” he said, “the night after I took her sister’s statement, I came here. To this garden. You made me tea. And I asked you, to your face, whether the girl next door was the one we call the Eraser. I told you I was asking as family and not as police. And you looked at me, and you said no.”

The garden was quiet. Somewhere on the other side of the far wall the old man was putting his birds to bed, a long low whistle and the clack of the cage doors.

“You lied to me,” said Wei Long. “The boy I raised. To my face, in this garden, over tea I made with you. I didn’t know it then. I’d half decided to believe you, because I wanted to, and because you’d never lied to me in your life, not once, not about a broken window, not about anything.” He looked at Yu Chen. “I raised you better than that. Or”—his mouth moved, slightly, which on him was nearly a smile—“exactly that well. I haven’t decided which.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Yu Chen looked at the man who’d raised him.

He thought about lying again, now, and knew at once that he couldn’t, and wouldn’t, because the whole point of the first lie was that it had been the one thing he’d ever decided mattered more than being the kind of person who didn’t lie to Wei Long. You couldn’t protect a thing like that with more lies. You could only own it.

“Yes,” said Yu Chen. “I lied to you.”

Wei Long waited.

“You asked me if she was the Eraser,” said Yu Chen, “and I said no, and it was a lie, and I knew it was a lie when I said it, and I’d say it again tomorrow.” The pleasant thing had gone off the front of him; he felt it go, the way it had gone at the Lin table, the way it had gone with the boy who’d pulled her hood, and what was left was slow and cold and certain, and he was talking to the one man in the world he loved besides her, and it didn’t move him an inch. “You came here as family, you said. So I answered you as family. I kept her out of it. That’s what family does. You taught me that. You kept me out of things for eight years.”

“I kept you out of trouble. Not out of the law.”

“She hasn’t done anything to anyone who didn’t do it first.” His voice stayed level. “She finds names. She cleans the old man’s footprints. She built a thing to watch for her sister’s face because nobody would ever let there be a photograph of her sister to find. That’s what she does at night, while I bring her tea and don’t ask. You can call it what you like. I’m not going to help you put a name on her in a file.”

Wei Long looked at him without blinking.

“You understand what you’re telling me,” he said. “You’re telling a police detective, to his face, that you knowingly lied to shield a person involved with the Syndicate. You’re telling me you’d do it again.”

“Yes.”

“You’re the clean one,” said Wei Long. “You’ve been the clean one your whole life. Top of everything. Never in trouble. The one the old women at the market trust. I used to think it was because you were good. I’m starting to think you keep the whole front of your life polished so that nobody ever looks past you to her.”

Yu Chen didn’t deny it.

“That’s exactly what it is,” he said.

The whistle on the far side of the wall had stopped. The cages were quiet. Up at the top of the tall house the thin line of light moved; she’d got up, crossed the room, sat down again.

Wei Long followed his eyes up to it.

“I’m not here to arrest anyone,” he said, at last, more tired than hard. “I couldn’t, on what I’ve got, and I wouldn’t like myself if I did. I came to decide what kind of uncle I’m going to be. Whether I’m going to pretend I don’t know, which is a thing police don’t get to do, or whether I’m going to do the other thing.”

“What’s the other thing?”

Wei Long stood up off the wall.

“I’m going to give her a number,” he said. “Mine. And I’m going to tell her that one day it may stop being about keeping her family out of the papers and start being about something worse, and that when that day comes, there’s a door she can walk through that isn’t her father’s and isn’t the Syndicate’s. And I’m going to hope she takes it, in a few years, when she’s ready. That’s the other thing. It’s the only thing I’ve got.”

He looked at Yu Chen.

“And you,” he said. “I’m not going to make you choose between her and me. I thought about it on the way over. I’m not going to do it, because you’d choose her, and then I’d have lost you, and I didn’t raise you to lose you over a lie you told the way I’d have told it.” His jaw moved. “But don’t lie to me again. Even for her. Say nothing. You’re allowed to say nothing. You’re not allowed to look at me and lie.”

“All right,” said Yu Chen.

“That’s a promise.”

“It’s a promise.”

Wei Long nodded, once. Then he did a thing he almost never did: he reached out and put his hand on the back of Yu Chen’s neck, briefly, hard, the way he had when Yu Chen was fifteen and newly his, and took it away again.

“Whatever she built last October,” he said, going, “it’s watching the same places we watch, and it’s better at it than anything the city has.” He stopped at the side gate. “The spring just gone, when the arms man — Zhao — went missing for three days, somebody had every camera within five kilometres of the shipyard pulled up inside an hour. I always wondered who. I don’t wonder now.” He opened the gate. “Tell her the number’s coming. She’ll want to check it’s really mine. Tell her it is.”

He went out into the lane, and the gate clicked, and Yu Chen stood in the dark garden under the green persimmons with his heart going hard and slow, and across the wall the line of light at the top of the house went still, as if someone up there had heard the gate too.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was at her window when he came over the wall.

He didn’t go up the stairs. He hissed her name from under the branch, and she opened the window, and then she wasn’t at the window, she was coming down the persimmon tree in her socks faster than he’d ever seen her do it, dropping onto the Lin side and coming straight over the wall into the Song garden, into him, with her hands already in the front of his shirt.

“I heard the gate,” she said. Her face was white in the dark. “That was Wei Long. On a Saturday. What did he—”

“He knows,” said Yu Chen. “About the Eraser. That it’s you.”

She went rigid.

“He’s not going to do anything,” he said, fast, with his hands coming up round her. “He’s not arresting anyone. He can’t, and he wouldn’t. He’s going to give you a number. His own. For one day, later, if you ever need a door that isn’t your father’s. That’s all. That’s the whole thing.”

She was shaking, in the front of his shirt. “He knows. How does he—how long has he—”

“Eight months.” He made himself say the rest, because he’d just promised a man in a garden never to lie again, and that started here. “He asked me, in November. To my face. Whether you were the Eraser. And I told him no. I lied to him. The first time in my life. He worked it out anyway, and he came to tell me he knows I lied, and that I’m not forgiven for it, exactly, and that he’d have done the same.” He held her by the shoulders. “I’d do it again. I want you to know that. I lied to the man who raised me, for you, and I’d do it again tomorrow, and I’m not sorry.”

She looked up at him.

He watched her hear it — the clean boy, the one the market trusted, telling her he’d looked his own uncle in the face and lied — and he watched her be frightened by it, for a second, the size of what he’d do, and then he watched the other thing come, the thing that had come in the pantry and on the roof, which wasn’t shy at all.

She hauled him down by the shirt and kissed him.

She did it hard, shaking, half out of fright, her cold hands in fists against his chest, up on her toes in the dark garden, and he caught her and kissed her back and then took it from her, turned her the half-step so her back was against the garden wall under the branch, in the one place no camera of her father’s could see, and kissed her properly, slow and deep and without a word, until she’d stopped shaking for the first reason and started for the second.

“You lied to the police,” she said against his mouth, breathless. “For me.”

“Yes.”

“You’re not even sorry.”

“No,” said Yu Chen, and kissed her again, and she pulled him closer by the back of the neck and held on, there against the wall where the jar was, with the green persimmons over them and the whole dark tall house behind her.

“Auntie Dai’s gone,” he said.

She looked up at him. Her mouth was red and her glasses had gone crooked and she didn’t fix them.

“I know,” she said, and took his hand, and pulled him across his own garden to his own back door.

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d meant to be careful. He had been careful for two years about everything with her in it, and careful for an hour in the garden with the man who’d raised him, and halfway up the stairs she turned round on the step above him, which put her mouth level with his, and kissed him, and he forgot what careful was for.

They didn’t put the lamp on. There was enough light from her window across the garden to see her by. She pulled his shirt over his head and dropped it on the floor and put both her cold hands flat on his chest, over his heart, and left them there, as if she wanted to feel what a person who’d lie for her was like inside. He let her. Then he picked her up, which made her laugh, and put her down on the bed, and took her hoodie off over her head and her glasses with it, and put the glasses on the desk where they wouldn’t fall.

He kissed every part of her he could reach. He did it slowly, because he wanted her to know he meant each one: her wrists, the inside of her elbow, the place under her ear, the mark on her shoulder where a strap had been. She kept pulling at him to hurry and he kept not hurrying, and in the end she said “Chen,” in the voice that meant she’d stopped arguing, and he stopped making her wait.

Nothing about it was shy any more. She knew where to put her hands, and he knew what made her arch and catch her breath and hold on to the headboard, and he did it again, and again, until she had her face in his neck and was saying things into it he’d never heard her say. He had lied to Wei Long’s face for her and he would do it again. Lying in his own bed with her wrapped round him, he understood that this was what the lie had been for, all of it, the clean front and the polite smile: one place in the world where nobody was looking at her but him. He held on to her as if someone might come over the wall to take her, and she held on back just as hard.

Afterwards she lay on his chest with one leg over his and her hair across his mouth, tracing his collarbone with one finger.

“Your cousin’s going to hate me,” she said.

“He doesn’t hate people. He writes them down.” He moved her hair off his face. “He’s giving you his own number. That’s not hate.”

She was quiet. “I’m still going to check it’s his.”

“He said you would.”

She laughed against his skin, and fell asleep there with her hand over his heart, where she’d put it at the start.

✦ ✦ ✦

Wei Long came to Sunday lunch the next day as if nothing had happened, and ate two bowls of Auntie Dai’s soup, and told Yu Chen he was too thin.

Afterwards he went out to the garden on his own. Yu Chen watched from the kitchen window. Wei Long stood under the persimmon branch and looked up, and after a minute Eliana’s head came over the top of the wall, hood up, glasses on, wary as a cat.

He held a folded piece of paper up to her. She didn’t take it straight away. He said something, short, the way Wei Long’s things always were, and Yu Chen couldn’t hear it through the glass. Then she took the paper and read it and looked down at him again, and nodded once, the way Wei Long nodded, and went back down her side of the wall.

When Wei Long came in, he put his bowl in the sink.

“She checked it in front of me,” he said. “On her phone. Took her under a minute.”

“I told you she would.”

“You did,” said Wei Long, and his mouth moved again, for the second time in two days.

chapters.title: He Held the Ladder
chapters.desc: At Elowen’s flower-shop wedding, Eliana strings a sky of lights and won’t say why. The night before, a lanky boy holds her ladder for hours and slips out before she’s found. The next day, nobody introduces him to anyone.
chapters.epigraph: “I’ll hold it. You do the stars. Don’t look down — you never look down.” — Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
She had worked out the time weeks ago, and she wasn’t going to tell anyone.

Nine forty-one. She’d got it out of the little red book without meaning to, the registry book Elowen kept in the drawer under the till, where the time was printed beside the date three and a half years back: a Tuesday, nine forty-one. Elowen thought nobody remembered the time. Zhao remembered the time. And now Eliana had it, and she’d programmed thousands of tiny lights to come on at exactly that minute, and when Aurelia asked why nine forty-one, and Elowen asked, and even Raiden asked, she said “spreadsheet” and climbed back up the ladder.

She rigged them on the Friday night, after the shop closed.

It took hours. The lights went across the whole ceiling, strung on wire, every run tested and taped and run back to a box under the counter, and she did it alone, on a tall ladder, in her hoodie, with her laptop open on the floor below her and the shop dark except for the street.

Not quite alone.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yu Chen came at nine, because she’d texted him come hold a ladder and nothing else, and he’d come, with a medical textbook under his arm, because he had an exam on Monday and he could read at the bottom of a ladder as well as anywhere.

He held the ladder.

He held it for three hours. He stood at the bottom with one hand on each rail and his book open on the fold-out step, reading the same pages over and over by the light of her laptop, and every so often she said “move it left” and he moved it left, and every so often he said “you’ve been up there two hours, come down and drink something,” and she didn’t.

“Don’t look down,” he said once, when she leaned out too far to reach the last run over the door. “You never look down. Don’t start now.”

“I’m fine.”

“I know you’re fine. I’m holding it anyway.”

By one in the morning the whole ceiling was a sky, dark, waiting. She’d tested it once, all of them on at once, and stood at the top of the ladder in the gold light with her mouth open like everyone else would, and then turned them off and set the time and come halfway down and sat on a rung to check the box on her laptop, and that was the last thing she remembered.

She woke up on the floor of the shop on Saturday morning with her laptop on her chest and a ladder over her and somebody’s jacket over her shoulders.

It was his. Grey, warm, smelling of him. He’d gone. He’d put it over her at some point in the night and taken himself home over the wall before anyone came and found the youngest Lin asleep on the floor of the shop with a boy from next door asleep beside her, because that was a thing that could be talked about, and he knew her rules better than she did.

She sat up with his jacket round her and the empty ladder above her and the dark sky of lights overhead, and heard Elowen come in through the back with the flowers at six, and say, “Yu-er? Why are you on the floor,” and she said, “spreadsheet,” and pulled the jacket round her so Elowen wouldn’t see whose it was.

Elowen looked at her for a second longer than she needed to. Then she went to put the buckets down, and said, over her shoulder, “There’s tea in his flask on the counter. He left it. For when you woke up.” Eliana looked at the counter. The dented flask was there, lid on, exactly square to the edge. She hadn’t seen him bring it. She pulled the grey jacket tighter and didn’t say anything, and Elowen, mercifully, didn’t either.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came to the wedding because she told him to.

She’d said it plainly, on the Thursday: come, stand near me, bring a book so you’ve got something to do with your hands, don’t talk to Baba, don’t let anyone work out what you are. He’d said all right. So on Saturday he stood near her, in the one jacket he owned that wasn’t grey, with a medical textbook under his arm because she’d told him to bring something for his hands and he’d taken her literally, and when people looked at him — and people looked at him, a tall quiet boy nobody knew, standing by the youngest sister — he gave them the pleasant nothing smile and they went back to their tea.

Nobody introduced him. That was the arrangement and it held all night. He was the boy from next door who’d apparently come because Eliana told him to, and that was all anyone was going to get.

She stood beside him by the cooler in her hoodie with her laptop against her chest, watching the shop fill, and a tall woman in a leather jacket got backed into the corner by the fridge and introduced to everyone one at a time, and Eliana went over.

“I’m Eliana, I’m the youngest, I’ve known about you since February 2022, you’re on a spreadsheet,” she said.

She walked off before the woman — Jinx, Raiden’s secret, the garage near the Docks, Cao Jia on the paperwork — could do anything with her face. She felt Yu Chen, behind her, not quite laugh.

✦ ✦ ✦

Across the shop, a tall man in glasses came in off the street, a little out of breath, as if he’d walked fast from somewhere, and went straight to Elara and the cake.

Eliana clocked him at once. She clocked everyone. Dark suit, glasses, serious; he stood close beside Elara without touching her and looked at the cake and said something, and Elara went red. Nobody had been introduced to him either. Two strangers in one shop, each standing close to a Lin sister, each unexplained.

She felt Yu Chen go still beside her.

She looked up. He was looking across the shop at the man in glasses, and the man in glasses had seen him, over the buckets of white roses, and the two of them were looking at each other with the particular blankness of two people who had not expected to find each other in the same room.

They didn’t nod.

That was what she noticed. Two strangers catch each other’s eye and one of them nods; it’s what people do. These two didn’t. They looked at each other for a second, across the whole shop, over the heads and the flowers, and then they both looked away, at the same moment, as if they’d agreed on it, and neither of them had moved a muscle of his face.

“You know him,” said Eliana.

“My cousin,” said Yu Chen, low. “Xing Yue. He’s Elara’s—” He stopped. “I didn’t know it was him. I knew my cousin had someone. I didn’t know it was one of yours.”

“He didn’t nod at you.”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because if we nod,” said Yu Chen, “someone asks how we know each other, and then they ask who I am, and then they ask who he is, and then it’s two Wang cousins and two Lin sisters in one shop, and your father starts counting.” He looked down at her. “Easier to be strangers. He thought of it the same second I did. That’s the thing about him. He always has.”

Later she saw the man in glasses say something to Elara, close, and Elara stare at him with her mouth open, and she thought: he’s just told her. He’s my cousin. Yu Chen. She filed it, in the quiet tab, for the spreadsheet.

✦ ✦ ✦

At nine o’clock, thirty people stood in a flower shop, and Lin Jian walked Elowen down the aisle.

Eliana watched from the back, by the cooler, with her laptop in her arms. She watched her father stop halfway and ask Zhao about the lemon tree, and watched Zhao’s face open like a door, and watched both of them cry, and then everyone. She watched Chen Si say his four sentences. She watched Elowen say the thing about keeping, and Zhao say the thing about the door, and she didn’t hear all of it because she was watching the clock on her laptop, the way she’d watched it in the planetarium, the way she watched every clock.

At nine forty-one she pressed one key, and shut the laptop.

Every one of the lights came on at once, gold and warm, the whole ceiling a sky, and the shop made a sound, and Zhao took Elowen’s face in both his hands and kissed her under them, in front of everyone, and Eliana looked up at her own sky over her sister’s wedding and did not look at the laptop again.

At the very back, in a plain dark coat, Detective Song Wei Long stood with his carved face still and his eyes bright, and did not pretend he wasn’t crying, and did not pretend he was there officially either.

Yu Chen was beside her. He didn’t take her hand; that was the rule, and the room was full. But under the cover of the cooler, where nobody could see, he hooked one finger through one of hers, and held it, while the lights she’d hung came on over her sister, and she let him.

✦ ✦ ✦

They slipped out the back, into the alley, later, when the party was loud enough that two people wouldn’t be missed.

The alley behind the shop was dark and narrow and smelled of flower water and the bins, and the gold light came out of the shop’s back window and lay across the wet ground in a long strip, and the noise of the party came with it, muffled. Across the alley there was an old tea merchant’s building, four storeys, dark, with a ladder up the back. She looked at it once, out of habit, because she looked at everything, and saw nothing, and looked away.

He pulled her into the dark part, out of the strip of light, between the shop wall and a stack of empty buckets.

“You hung a whole sky,” he said. “For a time you weren’t going to tell anyone.”

“I told you it was a spreadsheet.”

“You told everyone it was a spreadsheet.” He had his hands at her waist now, her back against the cool wall of the shop. “You rigged a whole ceiling of lights to a minute out of a book you weren’t supposed to read, so your sister would get her real wedding at the time of her real one, and you won’t take any credit for it. You fell asleep under a ladder.”

“You put your jacket over me and went home,” she said. “Before anyone could see.”

“Your rules,” he said.

She looked up at him in the dark. The gold light caught the edge of his face.

“One day,” he said, “I’m going to hang lights for us. In our own lane. At a time out of a book, that I won’t tell anyone either. And you’re going to fall asleep under the ladder, and I’m going to put my jacket over you, and I’m not going to leave, because by then I’ll be allowed to stay.”

She waited for the fear to come, the way it always came when anyone said a sentence shaped like that one, the sentences that started with a day that hadn’t happened and pointed forward into a thing that could be lost.

It came. But it came smaller than it used to. It came, and she looked at it, and it didn’t send her over a tree or up two flights of stairs or out of a room. She just stood in the dark alley with his hands at her waist and the fear sitting in her chest the size it should be, and let it be there, and let the other thing be bigger.

“One day,” she said. It came out as hardly anything. But she said it, which she’d never once done; she usually just didn’t answer.

He heard it. She felt him hear it.

He kissed her. He took her face in one hand, the way he did, and kissed her against the cool wall of the shop in the dark part of the alley, with her own lights gold in the window behind them and her sister married under them, and she put her arms up round his neck and her laptop pressed between them and kissed him back, and for a while there was no spreadsheet, no rules, no father counting, nothing but the alley and the gold and him.

His hand went from her jaw into her hair and pulled the pencil out, and it dropped somewhere among the buckets, and neither of them looked for it. She got the laptop out from between them and put it down on an upturned bucket without looking, which she had never once done with a laptop in her life, and got both hands inside his jacket. He leaned her back against the wall with the whole length of him and kissed her neck, slowly, all the way down to the edge of her hoodie, and she bit her own lip to keep quiet, and didn’t manage it.

“Someone’ll come out,” she said, breathless.

“The party’s loud.”

“Evangeline’s at the back. She watches the door. She’ll—”

“Then we’ll go,” he said, and didn’t move, and neither did she, not for a long minute, in the dark between the buckets, before they slipped away up the alley and didn’t come back in.

Behind them, much later, long after they’d gone, a door opened at the back of the shop, and a woman in pale blue came out with two slices of cake on a paper plate, and looked up at the dark building across the way, and started to climb.

chapters.title: The Photograph
chapters.desc: At twenty past three in the morning the fence catches the worst thing it was ever built to catch. By ten she’s home, hollow. The boy next door is on the kerb with his bicycle, because he always is.
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t have to be scared on your own. That part’s mine. You can give me that part.” — Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
The fence woke her at nineteen minutes past three.

It did it the way she’d built it to, a short double buzz on the phone by her pillow, the one that cut through anything, and she was awake and across the room and at the screens before she was properly conscious, the way she’d trained herself to be, because the whole point of the fence was speed and she was never going to be slow again.

She read what it had caught. Then she got up and went into the bathroom on the landing and was sick.

She knelt on the cold tiles with her forehead against the edge of the bath. Then she went back and read it again, to be sure it was real and not a dream she was still inside, and it was real: a page on a black site in three languages, and in the middle of it a photograph taken with a flash in the dark, and her sister’s face in the white of it, looking straight down the lens without fear, without anything, and four lines of grey text underneath that she was never going to be able to un-read.

She took it down, and the copies too, the ones she could find, with her hands steady, because her hands were always steady even when nothing else was.

Then she rang Elowen.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t remember much of the morning in order, afterwards.

She remembered Elowen’s car. She remembered the textile building by the harbour, six floors up, and the long room full of light, and a man in it so big that she stopped in the doorway and said “you’re huge” before she could stop herself, because she’d been awake since three and her mouth had come loose. She knew who he was without being told. Evangeline’s man. The one nobody would name. The one who’d found her sister in a night when Eliana couldn’t in three days. She’d stopped looking for him a year ago, because Evangeline had asked her to, and here he was, enormous, talking, holding out congee she couldn’t eat.

She remembered showing them the photograph on the long table and watching Evangeline look at it, and watching her sister’s face not move, and wanting to put her own body between her sister and the screen.

She remembered the name that came up with it. She remembered saying it. She remembered the big man breathing in, once, long and slow, and saying I know him.

And she remembered crying, without any noise, in her hood, with her hands over her mouth, and Elowen’s hand on the back of her neck, and the harbour grey out the window, and thinking: I built the fence so this would never happen, and the fence worked perfectly, and it still happened, it was always going to happen, it had happened a year ago and I only caught the picture.

She’d texted him at four in the morning, before any of it, three words, because her thumb did it without asking the rest of her.

Eliana: home at ten?

✦ ✦ ✦

He was on the kerb at ten.

Elowen’s car came down the lane and stopped, and he was there, on the kerb by his bicycle, in his grey jumper, with a flask. Of course he was. She’d sent him three words at four in the morning and he’d read it and come and sat on the kerb and waited, and he didn’t know what for, because he never asked, and he’d waited anyway.

Elowen looked at him through the windscreen. Then she looked at Eliana.

“That’s the boy next door,” said Elowen. It wasn’t quite a question.

“He holds ladders,” said Eliana, which was the stupidest thing she could have said, and Elowen, to her everlasting credit, let it go, and reached over and squeezed her hand, hard, and said, “Go in. Sleep. I’ll deal with Baba. Ring me tonight.”

Eliana got out of the car.

Yu Chen stood up off the kerb. He looked at her face, grey and wrecked, with the marks of a night’s crying still on it, and he didn’t ask her a single thing. He didn’t say what happened or are you all right or who was that. He put the flask in her hands, because her hands were cold, and he walked up the three steps beside her, close, not touching, and waited while she got the bolt that stuck, and went in after her, and shut the red door on the lane.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t let her near the stairs.

“Not up there,” he said. “Not today. Come and sit.”

So they sat in the front room nobody used, the cold formal one with the stiff chairs, on the floor with their backs against the sofa, because the floor was where she sat when things were bad, and he’d learned that. He made her tea in the kitchen and brought it, and she drank it and didn’t talk, and he didn’t make her, and the house was empty around them, Baba at the office, Evangeline gone, Ah Sim out at the market, the clock in the hall ticking.

Some time in the afternoon she told him a little of it. Not the whole shape; she couldn’t, and he didn’t ask, and it was theirs, the thing he didn’t ask about. She just said, “The thing I built. It caught something today. The thing it was built to catch. And it worked, and I still—” and stopped, and he put his arm round her and pulled her in against his side, and she put her face in his jumper and didn’t finish.

“It worked,” he said. “You said it worked.”

“It was too late. It was a year too late. The thing already happened. I just found the picture of it.”

“But you found the picture. And took it down.” His hand was on her hair. “If you hadn’t built it, it’d still be up. More people would see it. You know that better than I do.” He didn’t make it a speech. He said it the way he said that chrysanthemum was good for tired eyes: plainly, as a fact he believed and couldn’t prove. “You didn’t make the bad thing. You’re the reason there’s a little less of it in the world tonight.”

She didn’t answer. But she stopped shaking.

Later Ah Sim came back from the market and stopped in the doorway of the front room with her bags, and looked at the two of them on the floor: the youngest Lin in her hood, against the side of the boy next door, in the room nobody used. Eliana waited for her to say something. Ah Sim didn’t. She went to the kitchen and came back with a plate of toast cut into fingers, and put it down on the carpet in front of them. On her way out she took off her own cardigan and dropped it over Eliana’s cold feet, and pulled the door to behind her.
