They stayed on the floor of the cold room all afternoon. He got her to eat the toast, eventually, a finger at a time, and she ate it against his side, and slept for an hour, which she never did, and woke to his hand still moving in her hair and the light going gold and then grey in the stiff unused room, and lay there against him and let the day be over.

He went home over the wall at seven, before Baba came, because of the rules, and because she asked him to, and because even today she couldn’t bear her father’s face if he found them. She watched his light come on across the garden. She lay on the camp bed and didn’t sleep, and at midnight her screens were still dark, the fence quiet, watching, and she got up and put the blue blanket round her shoulders and went down.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was already on the step.

She didn’t know how he knew. She came out of the red door at two in the morning in the blanket and he was there, on the third step, in his coat, with the flask, in the exact place he’d been the first time, the June night two years ago when school was over and the house was too quiet and he’d come out with the blanket and sat down and never asked why.

She sat down beside him. He put half the blanket round himself, out of habit, though he had his coat. Across the two gardens the tall house was dark except for Baba’s window, yellow, the only light, the way it always was.

“You can’t sleep,” he said. Not a question.

“No.”

“Is it still—”

“It’s done. For tonight.” She held the flask without opening it. “I keep seeing her face. In the picture. She wasn’t scared. That’s the thing. They took a picture of her to sell her and she looked straight at them and she wasn’t scared of anything, and I thought, I’m the one who’s scared. All the time. Of everything. And she was in a box and she wasn’t.”

He didn’t say anything to that. He let her have it.

“She wasn’t scared,” she said again, lower. “And I’m scared all the time. There’s something wrong with me.”

“There’s nothing wrong with you.” He turned his head. “You’re not her. She goes still. You get scared and you build a fence and you take the thing down at three in the morning with your hands steady because somebody has to. Yours is the kind of brave where you’re frightened the whole time and you do it anyway.” He was quiet a second. “I’d just rather you did it where I can see you. You don’t have to be scared on your own. That part’s mine. You can give me that part.”

She looked at him in the dark, with the yellow window across the garden and the blanket round them both.

And the thing came up out of her that never came up. It came up the way the fright had come up in the planetarium, from somewhere low down, past the place where her voice usually stopped, the place that caught at registration and at the noodle stall and in the dark of his bed two years ago when he’d said it first and she hadn’t been able to say it back.

“I love you,” said Eliana.

She said it fast, and wrong, and too quiet, and then she couldn’t look at him, so she looked at Baba’s yellow window across the garden instead, with her heart going so hard she thought he must be able to hear it through the blanket.

It was the worst day to say it. That was why she could. Today had proved the thing she’d always known, which was that love was a word people said before the hospital, before the box, before the thing got taken; her mother had said it and then she was gone, and here was a photograph of her sister on a black site to prove it all over again, that you loved people and the world came for them. She’d known it her whole life. She said it anyway. Today, of all days, with the proof right there on her screens, she said it, because if she could say it today she could say it any day, and because he’d been sitting on a kerb at ten in the morning waiting for a girl who sent him three words, and had asked her nothing.

He didn’t make it a victory.

That was the thing she’d been most afraid of, without knowing it: that he’d turn and his face would light up and he’d make it a moment, a big one, after two years, and she’d have to be inside the bigness of it on the worst day she’d had in years. He didn’t. He went still beside her, and she felt him go still, and then he put his arm round her under the blanket and pulled her in against his side, the way he had on the first step two years ago, and put his mouth against the top of her head.

“I know,” he said. “I’ve got you.”

That was all. I know. I’ve got you. Not finally, not say it again, not anything that would cost her. He’d understood what the word was for her and taken it the way you take something someone’s handed you with shaking hands: carefully, with both of his, without making a sound.

She turned her face up, then, because she wanted to, and he kissed her, soft, on the cold step with the blanket round them and Baba’s window yellow across the garden, a long slow kiss with nothing hurried in it anywhere, and she held the front of his coat with one hand and kissed him back and didn’t cry, for once, and it was the first thing in the whole long day that hadn’t hurt.

“Say it again?” she said, when she could. “I know you said not to ask you things. I’m asking.”

“I didn’t say not to ask me that.” He pulled the blanket up round her shoulder. “I love you, Yu-er. I’ve got you. Go to sleep. I’ll sit here. That’s allowed.”

She leaned on his arm on the step, the way she had the first time, and this time she wasn’t pretending. She shut her eyes, and the yellow window across the garden went out, Baba going to bed at last, and she fell asleep against him under the blanket on the porch at two in the morning, and he stayed, the way he always stayed, until the sky went grey.

chapters.title: The Night He Lost One
chapters.desc: On a Friday night in the emergency department, Yu Chen does chest compressions on a nineteen-year-old delivery rider, and nothing works. Eliana finds him on the east stairwell at two in the morning and stays until the sun comes up.
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t have to say the right thing. You just don’t leave. I learned that from you.” — Eliana Lin
chapters.content:
The whiteboard by the nurses’ station had the students’ names at the bottom in green pen, under everyone else’s. On Friday night his was the last one. WANG (STUDENT).

He had been in the emergency department for three weeks. He knew where the gloves were kept, and that you didn’t sit in the chair by the window because it belonged to a charge nurse called Bernie, and that students took histories, did bloods, stood where they were put and kept their hands to themselves unless somebody told them otherwise.

Dr. Ada Toh ran the floor on Friday nights. She was small and quick, with grey hair cut short, and a cardigan over her scrubs that she never took off. She called students by their surnames and never got one wrong. People said she was kind at four in the morning. At eight in the evening she was mostly fast.

“Wang,” she said, going past. “Bay six. Fall at home, eighty-one, hip. Get the story before she tells it to someone who doesn’t listen.”

He got the story. The old woman held his hand the whole time and asked if he had a girlfriend, and he said yes, which he didn’t usually say. He was kind to her. He meant it. When the porter wheeled her off to the ward an hour later he’d already forgotten her name before the lift doors closed, and he noticed that he had, and wasn’t proud of it, and couldn’t change it either. There wasn’t much room in him for people in general. Most of it was taken.

At ten he went to wash his hands, and in the corner by the sink he took his phone out and opened the food app.

Friday, 21:38. Beef brisket noodles, extra radish. Lemon tea. Delivered.

She’d eaten. He put the phone away and went back to the floor feeling lighter than he had any reason to.

✦ ✦ ✦

The red phone went at twenty past eleven.

Bernie took it, wrote on the board while she listened, and turned round. “Nineteen-year-old, motorbike against a car in the eastern tunnel. Chest. Not talking. Five minutes.”

“Resus one,” said Dr. Toh. She was already putting on an apron. “Wang. With me. Gloves, apron, stand at the head end by the wall, and when I say compressions, you do compressions. Kenny, you’re after him.”

Kenny was the other student from his year, a boy who talked to fill gaps. Yu Chen put on his gloves and stood by the wall where he’d been put.

They came in at a run, two paramedics and the trolley between them, and the boy on it was wearing the orange jacket. Everybody in the city knew the jacket. It was the delivery app, the one on his own phone, the one she ordered from at three in the morning, and the jacket was torn down one side and dark with wet.

After that it went fast.

Toh’s voice, level, giving jobs. Bernie cutting the jacket off. Two lines going in. Somebody reading out numbers that weren’t good and then were worse. A phone fell out of the jacket pocket onto the floor, face up, and lit, and buzzed against the lino. New order nearby. Accept? Nobody picked it up.

His wallet was in the other pocket. A nurse read the card out for the notes. Fung Ka-lok. Nineteen. He had a cartoon sticker on the back of his phone, a cat.

Then the monitor changed its sound.

“He’s arrested,” said Toh. “Compressions. Wang.”

Yu Chen stepped up onto the little step by the trolley and put the heel of one hand on the boy’s chest and the other over it and locked his elbows and pushed.

He’d done it on the plastic dummies a hundred times. The boy’s chest was warm, and gave under him in a way that was wrong, and on the third push he felt something go under his hands, a soft crack, and kept going, because you kept going. He counted under his breath. Toh was doing things to the chest he’d read about and never seen, quick and sure, and the blood came in from bags squeezed by hand, and he pushed, and counted, and Kenny tapped his shoulder at two minutes and took over and he stood back with his hands up and his arms shaking, and two minutes later he stepped up again.

The phone on the floor buzzed. New order nearby.

He pushed. He watched the boy’s face, which he shouldn’t have done. It was a young face, younger than nineteen, with a bit of a moustache he’d been trying to grow.

They went on for twenty-five minutes.

Then Toh looked at the monitor, and at the clock on the wall, and at the people round the trolley, one by one.

“Has anyone got anything we haven’t done?”

Nobody had.

“Then we’re stopping,” she said, and said the time out loud, and the room went still.

Yu Chen’s hands were still on the boy’s chest.

“Wang,” said Toh, not unkindly. “You can stop now.”

He took his hands away.

Bernie bent down and picked the phone up off the floor and turned it off, with her thumb, and put it in a bag with his wallet and his keys, and wrote his name on the bag.

✦ ✦ ✦

The boy’s mother came at one.

Yu Chen didn’t see her. He was writing up his part of the notes at the desk, in his careful capitals, what he’d done and when, and he heard the doors and then a woman’s voice asking for her son by name, and then Toh’s voice, low, and the door of the relatives’ room shutting. A minute later there was a sound through that door that didn’t have any words in it. It went on. Kenny stopped talking. Bernie put her pen down and looked at the ceiling.

Yu Chen finished his sentence. He signed it. He put the pen back in his coat pocket.

At half past one Toh came out of the relatives’ room and walked down the floor to the desk, and stopped beside him.

“You did it properly,” she said. “Your depth was right and your rate was right and you didn’t stop when the ribs went. I watched.” She looked at him over her glasses. “It doesn’t help. I know it doesn’t help. Go home anyway.”

“Thank you, Dr. Toh,” he said.

He took his coat off the hook, said goodnight to Bernie, and walked out of the department as if nothing were wrong. He was good at that.

He got as far as the east stairwell.

✦ ✦ ✦

The east stairwell ran between the emergency department and the car park. It was concrete and cold and lit too brightly, and it smelled of the porters’ cigarettes. He meant to go up to the car. He sat down on the stairs instead, halfway up the first flight, with his elbows on his knees and his coat still over his arm.

He looked at his hands.

They looked like his hands. There was white powder in the creases from the gloves, and a red mark on the heel of the right one where it had pressed. He could still feel it. The give. The soft crack on the third push.

His phone buzzed in his coat. He took it out.

Eliana: home?

That was from twelve past one. There was another under it from twenty minutes later.

Eliana: chen

He didn’t answer. He’d never not answered her. Without deciding to, he closed her messages and opened the app.

Friday, 21:38. Beef brisket noodles, extra radish. Lemon tea. Delivered.

Somebody had brought that. Somebody in an orange jacket had left it on the third step of the tall house at twenty to ten and gone on to the next one, with the phone buzzing in his pocket. New order nearby. He had read her orders every night for nearly three years, and he had never once thought about who carried them.

He put the phone face down on the step beside him and put his hands over his face, and then he wasn’t holding anything together any more.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t hear the door at the bottom. He heard her feet on the stairs, coming up two at a time, which she never did, and then they stopped.

“Your car’s still here,” said Eliana.

He took his hands away from his face. She was on the step below him in her black hoodie with the hood up and her glasses fogged from the cold outside, and a carrier bag from the all-night noodle place at the bottom of the hill, and she was out of breath.

“Yu-er.” He sat up straight. He wiped his face with the back of his wrist and made his voice right. “You shouldn’t be here. It’s two in the morning. How did you get here?”

“Taxi.”

“On your own? At this time? You can’t just—”

“You’re being polite to me,” she said.

He stopped.

“You never answer late,” she said. “You answer in a minute. Always. You didn’t answer, and you finished at twelve, and your car was still on the top deck, and this is the only door between the department and the car park.” She came up one step. “And now you’re being polite to me. You only get polite when something’s really wrong.”

He couldn’t think of a single thing to say to that.

She came up the last step and sat down beside him, close, her shoulder against his arm, and put the carrier bag on the step above them. She didn’t ask. She didn’t say what happened or are you all right. She pulled her knees up under her hoodie and looked at the concrete wall opposite.

“You don’t have to talk,” she said. “I’ll just sit here.”

It came up out of him as a laugh, and it wasn’t a laugh by the end of it.

She didn’t do anything. She didn’t put her arms round him or tell him it was all right. She sat there against his arm with her knees up and let him, in the bright cold stairwell that smelled of cigarettes, and when a porter came through the door at the top and saw them and went back out again, she didn’t even look round.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later he told her. Not all of it. The jacket. The age. The phone on the floor.

“It kept going off,” he said. “The whole time. On the floor by my feet. New order nearby. Nobody picked it up.” He looked at his hands. “He might have brought yours. Some night. He might have carried your noodles up the lane.”

“He didn’t,” said Eliana. “Mine come from a man with a beard who’s had the lane for a year. He’s about forty. He has a dog in his basket on Sundays.”

He turned his head and looked at her.

“I notice things,” she said, a little defensively.

“Somebody’s did, though,” he said. “Somebody’s noodles. Every night.”

“Yes,” she said. She didn’t argue. “Somebody’s did.”

He held his hands out in front of him, palms up, and looked at them under the bad light.

“I did it right,” he said. “She said I did it right. Depth and rate. I didn’t stop when his ribs went.” His voice wasn’t steady. “I felt them go, Yu-er. On the third one. And I kept going because you keep going, and it didn’t matter, none of it mattered, he was never coming back, probably. Probably he wasn’t. And I did it right.”

She took his hands.

She took them both, the way he took hers when they were cold, and turned them over and looked at them, the powder in the creases and the red mark at the heel. Then she bent her head and kissed his knuckles. One, then the next, then the next, slowly, all along the right hand and then the left, the hands that had pushed and pushed and not been enough, and he sat there and let her and couldn’t breathe properly.

“Eliana,” he said.

She looked up. Then she got up on her knees on the step and put her hands on either side of his face and kissed him.

It was nothing like the knuckles. It was hard, and wet with whatever was on his face, and she didn’t let go of his face while she did it, and he made a sound into her mouth and pulled her in, all of her, off the step and into his lap with her knees on either side of him on the cold concrete. He kissed her the way he hadn’t let himself all night, not carefully at all, his hands in the back of her hoodie and his face in her neck and then her mouth again, holding on to her as if the stairs were moving. She held his head. She kissed his eyes and the wet on his cheeks and his mouth again, and said his name against it, and her hands were cold on his neck, and he didn’t want anything else in the world.

A door banged somewhere above them. Footsteps, a trolley, voices going away.

They stopped, foreheads together, breathing.

“You don’t say the right thing,” she said. “When it’s me. You never say anything. You just don’t leave.” She pushed his hair off his forehead. “So I’m not leaving.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They ate the noodles on the stairs, cold, out of the cartons, sitting side by side. He wasn’t hungry and ate them because she watched him until he did. She talked, which she didn’t usually do, about nothing: a girl in her year who’d cried in a tutorial over a semicolon, Uncle Mok’s new seat covers. Her voice went on, low and steady, filling the stairwell up, and he understood after a while that she was doing it on purpose, the way he sat on her floor when the house was too quiet. She was keeping him company in the only way she knew how to do out loud.

At five she stood up and held out her hand.

“Come on,” she said. “Not home yet. The top deck.”

They went up to the top deck of the car park, where the Volvo was, the dark-green estate he’d bought in September for night placements and drove only for those. The deck was open to the sky. It was cold and empty, and down below the hill the harbour was black, with its chain of lights, and over the far side of it the sky was beginning to go from black to something else.

They sat in the Volvo with the engine running for the heater. She put her feet up on the dashboard in her socks, and he didn’t tell her not to.

He fell asleep. He didn’t mean to. One moment he was looking at the harbour and the next her shoulder was under his cheek and the sky was grey and pink and the first buses were crawling up the hill below them, and she hadn’t moved at all.

“How long?”

“About an hour,” she said. “You snore. A bit. It’s fine.”

He sat up. His neck hurt. His hands, when he looked at them, were only hands.

“I’ll drive us,” he said.

“You’ll drive us slowly.”

He drove them slowly, down the hill, through the empty grey streets, with the radio off and her hand on his leg the whole way, and when they turned into the lane the noodle man was just putting up his shutters and lifted his chin at them through the windscreen, and she lifted hers back.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t let him go to his own room alone.

She made him tea in Auntie Dai’s kitchen, in his flask, with too much rock sugar because she didn’t know how much he used, and brought it up, and made him drink half of it. Then she took his coat, and his shoes, and pushed him down on his bed, and lay down behind him on top of the covers in her hoodie, with her arm round him and her face against his back, and held on.

He was the one who did this. That was the arrangement. He sat on floors and carried tea and stayed until it got light. He didn’t know how to be the one on the bed being held, and he lay there stiff for a minute not knowing what to do with himself.

“Stop it,” she said into his shoulder blade. “You’re thinking. I can hear it. Go to sleep. I’ll be here.”

He went to sleep.

When he woke it was past noon and the sun was on the wall, and Auntie Dai was moving about downstairs, and Eliana was asleep against his back with her arm still over him and her glasses on, crooked, pressed into her cheek. She hadn’t opened her laptop. It was on the floor by the door, in its bag, zipped.

He lay still so as not to wake her, and looked at the light on the wall, and thought about a boy with a cartoon cat on his phone who would never grow the moustache, and let it hurt, because it should.

He was due back at eight on Sunday, and he’d be there on time. Then he put his hand over hers on his chest and held it there, and went back to sleep.

chapters.title: The Criminal Mind
chapters.desc: Eliana goes to a seminar to understand the men she hunts at night, and comes out with friends: a psychology student who won’t stop talking, her two sisters, and a cold profiler who looks at her half a second too long. Outside, Yu Chen breaks one of her rules.
chapters.epigraph: “I went to learn about monsters. I came home with a group chat.” — Eliana Lin
chapters.content:
She went for work.

The poster had been on the psychology board in the library for a week: THE CRIMINAL MIND, an open evening seminar, Wednesday at six, guest speaker Arthur Cheung, criminal profiler. She’d walked past it four times. On the fifth she took a photograph of it.

Finding men was easy. She’d been doing it for Qian for three years. What she couldn’t tell you was what a man would do next. She’d been wrong about that twice in September, and both times somebody else had paid for it, and she was tired of being wrong.

So at ten to six she sat in the back row of the psychology lecture theatre with her hood up and her laptop open on her knees, and the hall filled up round her.

In the front row there was a girl in a pink coat with a great deal of hair who had her phone out, then put it away, then took it out again, and sat on the edge of her seat with her hands clasped as if she were waiting for a concert.

The speaker came in at six exactly.

He was younger than she’d expected, and cold in a way she recognised: not rude, just switched off to anything he didn’t need. Dark suit, no tie, no slides. He put a black notebook on the lectern and didn’t open it once. He talked for an hour, plainly, about how people who hurt other people tend to organise their lives, and how the organising gives them away long before the hurting does. Once he said something dry about a man who’d been caught because he alphabetised his tins, and Eliana snorted, and so did the girl in the pink coat, and nobody else did.

She took notes. She also worked.

Qian had sent her a job at five. A man who sold photographs of women who didn’t know they’d been taken. By the time the profiler got to the difference between a want and a need, she knew who the man was. It took her eleven minutes. She sent it to Qian with one line, Here. He has a daughter, so be careful who sees the photographs, and shut it, and went on writing down what the profiler said about tins.

The boy beside her leaned over and asked, in a whisper, if she had a pen he could borrow.

She went hot to the ears. She found a pen in her pocket and held it out without looking at him, and he said thanks, and she didn’t say anything, and didn’t look at him for the rest of the hour. A man’s whole life had come apart under her hands in eleven minutes and she couldn’t say you’re welcome to a boy who wanted a pen.

Near the end, the profiler looked up at the back row.

It wasn’t long. His eyes went along it the way they’d been going along every row all evening, and they stopped on her. On her hands, on the keyboard. Half a second. She felt it, the way you feel someone reading over your shoulder. Then his eyes moved on, down, all the way to the front row, to the girl in the pink coat, and stayed there a fraction longer than they’d stayed anywhere else, and then he closed the notebook he hadn’t opened and said thank you, and the hall clapped.

✦ ✦ ✦

The girl in the pink coat came up the steps of the lecture theatre two at a time.

“You laughed,” she said. “At the tins. Nobody else laughed. I’m Si-Jie. Who are you? You’re not psychology. I’d know you if you were psychology. I know everyone in psychology.”

Eliana pushed her glasses up her nose.

“Computer science,” she said.

“Oh my God. Even better. Why are you here? No, don’t tell me, you can tell me downstairs. You’re coming to meet my sisters. They’re in the café. They’re always in the café. Bring your laptop.” She had hold of Eliana’s sleeve already. “What’s your name?”

“Eliana.”

“Eliana,” said Si-Jie, as if she’d been given a present. “Come on.”

Eliana had said no to every person who’d ever tried this, mostly by not saying anything until they went away. She opened her mouth to do it now, and Si-Jie looked at her with such open delight, as if Eliana were the best thing that had happened all week, that she shut it again and let herself be towed down the steps by the sleeve.

The café on the ground floor had two people in it at a table by the window.

One of them was wearing sunglasses, inside, at night, and had a face Eliana had seen on the side of a bus that morning. People at the other tables were trying not to look at her. The other one was a girl in a cream coat with her hair cut sharp at the jaw and a cup of black coffee in front of her, sitting straight, with the look of someone who’d been waiting forty minutes and would wait forty more.

“Si-Yuan, Si-Wei,” said Si-Jie. “This is Eliana. She laughed at the tins. She’s computer science. I’m keeping her.”

Si-Yuan took her sunglasses off and smiled, warmly, the smile from the bus. Si-Wei looked at Eliana.

Eliana looked back.

Neither of them said anything. Si-Jie was already talking about the profiler, and whether he’d looked at her, he had, hadn’t he, Si-Yuan, tell her he looked at her. Si-Yuan said he looked at everyone; it was his job.

Si-Wei picked up the teapot on the tray, poured a cup, and pushed it across the table to Eliana without asking whether she wanted it.

“She does this,” said Si-Wei. Her voice was low and dry. “She collects people. You can leave whenever you want. I’ll tell her you were kidnapped.”

Eliana laughed. It came out before she could stop it.

Si-Wei didn’t smile, exactly. But something at the corner of her mouth agreed with something, and she went back to her coffee, and Eliana drank the tea, and the two of them sat there across the little table for twenty minutes while Si-Jie talked for all four of them, and neither made the other say anything. It was the most comfortable twenty minutes Eliana had spent with strangers in her life.

By seven Si-Jie had her number. By ten past, there was a group chat called TRIPLETS + 1, and Eliana’s phone wouldn’t stop buzzing.

✦ ✦ ✦

They came out into the foyer together, the four of them, into the crowd from the seminar still standing about by the doors.

“Lin Yu!”

She knew the voice before she turned. Dominic Ip, from her year, by the noticeboard with three of his friends, grinning. They’d done the second-year group project together, the bus timetable one; he’d been the only one in the group besides her who’d done any work, and she’d almost liked him for it. She’d given him a login to the test server she’d run the project on, so he could work at night, and never thought about it again.

“Stalking psychology now?” He came over, loud, easy, the way he did everything. His friends drifted after him. “Come for a drink. We’re going down the hill.” Then, as if it had just occurred to him and he liked it: “Actually, no. Come out with me. Friday. Properly. Like a date.”

His friends made a noise. Somebody whistled. Half the foyer turned to look.

She couldn’t move.

It was every room she’d ever been in where people looked at her and waited. Her face went hot and then her neck. She could feel Si-Jie beside her vibrating with delight, and Si-Wei on her other side gone still. Every word she had was somewhere at the bottom of her chest and none of them would come up.

“No,” she said.

It came out as almost nothing.

“Is that a maybe?” said Dominic, laughing, and his friends laughed, and she turned round and walked out through the glass doors into the dark, because it was the only thing her legs would do.

He came after her; he thought it was a game. “Lin Yu, come on. One drink. I’m a nice guy. Ask anyone.”

Yu Chen was on the path outside with his bicycle.

He’d been there the whole time. She knew it the second she saw him: he’d come up after his clinic to walk her down, the way he did on Wednesdays, and he’d seen all of it through the glass.

He let go of the handlebars and stepped forward and took her hand.

In front of everyone, on the lit path outside the psychology building, with Dominic and his friends coming out of the doors behind her and half the seminar still looking through the glass. He took her cold hand in his warm one and held it, and turned his head and looked at Dominic.

He didn’t say anything at first. He just looked, and it was the look she’d seen at her father’s table, the pleasant thing gone off the front of him and something under it that didn’t care at all.

“She said no,” said Yu Chen.

Dominic stopped walking.

“Who are you?” he said, not laughing now.

Yu Chen didn’t answer that. He held her hand for perhaps three seconds more, looking at Dominic the whole time, and Dominic looked back, and then looked at the ground, and said, “All right. All right, mate. Sorry,” to nobody in particular, and went back inside to his friends.

Yu Chen let go of her hand.

Behind them, the glass door banged open again.

“Oh my God,” said Si-Jie. “Who is that?”

✦ ✦ ✦

He walked her down the hill with the bicycle between them, and he was polite.

He asked about the seminar. He said her new friends seemed nice, and he was glad she’d gone. He said all of it pleasantly, in the voice he used on the girl with the rings, and Eliana walked beside him with her phone buzzing in her pocket every few seconds, and listened to him be polite, and felt her stomach go tight.

“You held my hand,” she said, at the bottom of the hill.

“I did.”

“That’s rule three. No holding hands on the hill.”

“I know.” He didn’t look at her. “I’m sorry. It won’t happen again.”

That was when she knew how bad it was. He’d never once said sorry about breaking a rule in her favour. He’d stood in her father’s pantry and told her he’d do it again.

Her phone buzzed. She looked at it at the bus stop while he waited. It was Si-Jie. WHO IS HE. IS HE YOUR BOYFRIEND. HE LOOKED AT DOMINIC LIKE HE WAS GOING TO EAT HIM. ELIANA. ELIANA ANSWER ME. Then, from Si-Wei, alone, one line: He was outside the whole time. He watched you through the glass and he didn’t come in until you came out. That’s a good sign.

She put the phone in her pocket.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was washing up when she came over the wall.

Auntie Dai had gone at six. The kitchen was warm and the window over the sink was steamed, and he was standing at it in his grey jumper with his sleeves pushed up, doing one plate at a time, slowly, the way he did when he was thinking about something he didn’t want to think about. He heard the back door. He didn’t turn round.

“There’s soup,” he said. “If you haven’t eaten. I’ll heat it.”

She walked up behind him and hooked two fingers through the belt loops at the back of his jeans and pulled, and turned him round.

His hands came out of the water. He held them up, dripping, away from her hoodie.

“You’re jealous,” she said.

He could have said no. Anyone else would have. He looked down at her with his wet hands in the air and the polite face starting to come apart at the edges, and he didn’t lie to her, because he never had.

“Yes,” he said.

“Of Dominic Ip.”

“Of all of it.” He let his hands drop. Water ran off his fingers onto the floor. “I watched him through the glass and I wanted to put him through it. I didn’t. I held your hand instead and broke your rule. And before that I watched you go in on your own, and come out with three people, and sit at a table with them for twenty minutes laughing, and I stood outside with the bicycle.” He stopped. “I’ve wanted you to have friends for three years. I wanted it more than anything. And I got it, and I stood outside, and I didn’t like it. That’s the whole thing. I’m not proud of it.”

She looked up at him.

“You made a plan,” she said. “For tonight. Didn’t you. Be nice about it. Heat the soup. Ask about the tins.”

His ears went red.

“I’m not having the soup,” said Eliana, and got up on her toes, and kissed him.

He made a sound against her mouth. His wet hands came down on her back, through the hoodie, cold and then warm, and he pulled her in against him and kissed her back hard enough to bend her against the edge of the sink. She didn’t care. She put her hands up into his hair and held on, and kissed him until the polite thing was all the way gone, every bit of it, and the jealous thing was out in the open, and then she kissed that too, because it was hers.

“Come upstairs,” she said against his mouth.

He didn’t argue.

✦ ✦ ✦

His room was dark except for the lamp, the one with the crooked shade. She pushed him down to sit on the edge of the bed and stood between his knees and took his jumper off him, and he let her, with his arms up, watching her face.

She liked this more than she’d ever say out loud: his long body going still under her hands, waiting to see what she’d do. He’d have waited all night. He always did. She didn’t want him to wait tonight.

“You can stop being careful,” she said.

“I wasn’t being—”

“You were. You’ve been careful since the bottom of the hill.” She took her glasses off and put them on the bedside table, and this time they didn’t fall. “So stop.”

He stopped.

He pulled her down onto him and rolled her under him in one movement, so fast she laughed out loud, and then he was kissing her throat, her jaw, the place under her ear that made her arch, and her hoodie went over her head and caught on her hair the way his T-shirt had once caught on his ears, and she was laughing into the fabric while he got her out of it, and he was laughing too, low, against her collarbone. Then he wasn’t. Then it was his mouth and his hands, big and warm and no longer careful at all, learning her again as if three years hadn’t been enough. She held on to his shoulders. She said his name, the one she only used here.

He was different tonight. She felt it. He held her as if somebody might try to take her out of his hands, his arm hard under her back, his mouth at her ear saying things he never said in daylight, plain things, mine and I watched you and I’d have stood out there all night, and she should have minded. She didn’t mind at all. She wrapped herself round him and pulled him closer and told him so, and the old bed creaked like a ship, and the crooked lamp rocked on the table and didn’t fall, and somewhere in the middle of it she started laughing again and couldn’t stop, and he put his forehead against hers and laughed with her and didn’t stop moving, and then neither of them was laughing.

Afterwards she lay on his chest with the lamp still on and his heart going under her ear.

Her phone was buzzing on the floor in her hoodie pocket. It had been buzzing on and off for an hour.

“Si-Jie,” she said. “She wants to know if you’re my boyfriend.”

He didn’t say anything. His hand stopped in her hair.

She reached down over the side of the bed and got the phone out and looked at it. She opened the last one and typed neighbour, and looked at it, and deleted it. Then she didn’t type anything, and put the phone face down on the floor, and lay back down on his chest.

“You held my hand for three seconds,” she said.

“I know. I said I won’t—”

“Next time,” said Eliana, into his skin, “hold it longer.”

He was quiet for a second. Then she felt him start to smile, slowly, under her cheek, and his arm came round her and tightened.

“How much longer?”

“I’ll tell you,” she said. “When I know.”

She fell asleep before he could ask anything else. The last thing she felt was his hand starting to move in her hair again, and the phone buzzing on the floor, and him reaching down without letting go of her to turn it over so the light wouldn’t wake her.

chapters.title: The Boy Next Door, He Always Waits
chapters.desc: A bank wants Eliana quiet, and her family sends Serafina’s husband to drive her to her own talk. Yu Chen is told nothing. He’s on the kerb by half past five anyway, and at two in the morning he stops pretending there’s no name for what they are.
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody. The boy next door. He always waits.” — Eliana Lin
chapters.content:
He saw the man from his kitchen window at ten to eight.

He was making her tea. He did it every morning at the same counter, the chrysanthemum and the dried pear and two pieces of rock sugar, and he looked out of the window while the kettle boiled because the window looked at the lane, and the lane was where she came out. This morning there was a grey estate car at the bottom of the Lin steps, and a man standing beside it in a dark jacket with his hands at his sides, where anyone could see them.

Yu Chen put the kettle down.

The man didn’t look at the house. He looked at the lane, both ends of it, and the roofs, and once, without moving his head much, at the window Yu Chen was standing in. Then away again. Yu Chen stepped back from the glass without deciding to.

At five to eight the red door opened and she came out with her laptop under her arm and a slice of toast in her mouth, in the cat hoodie, and stopped on the top step and looked at the man. They talked. Yu Chen couldn’t hear what they said. She got in the front of the grey car, and the car went down the lane, slowly, and turned at the noodle stall, and was gone.

The tea was still in the flask on the counter. He’d meant to take it out to her on the step.

He picked up his phone.

Yu Chen: Who was that?

It took her a few minutes to answer, which was long for her.

Eliana: Sera’s husband. Elowen sent him. It’s nothing. It’s a lift.

Yu Chen: Why does Elowen send you a lift?

Eliana: because of the talk. the bank. she’s being Elowen. go to your ward

He stood in Auntie Dai’s kitchen and read it twice. The bank. He knew about the bank. She’d found something wrong with a bank in January and told them, and they’d said thank you, and then they’d sent a letter that said something else, and she’d laughed about the letter at the noodle stall and called it “a lawyer having a feeling”. She was giving a talk about it today, at eleven, in the big hall on the hill. He’d known that. He hadn’t known it needed a man in a dark jacket.

He poured the tea back into the pot, because there was no one to take it, and went to his placement.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was eight weeks from his written finals and spending them on a medical ward at City Hospital, on the fourth floor, where the beds looked out over the harbour and most of the patients were old and short of breath. Year Four was supposed to feel like being a doctor. Mostly it felt like being a doctor who wasn’t allowed to sign anything.

The registrar that month was a tired man called Dr. Yiu, who liked him because he wrote neat notes and never needed telling twice. On the ward round at nine Yu Chen presented a man in bed eleven with pneumonia, clearly and in the right order, and Dr. Yiu nodded and moved on, and the man in bed eleven caught Yu Chen’s sleeve as he went and said, “You’re the nice one. The tall one. Will you come back later?”

“Of course,” said Yu Chen, and smiled, and meant it while he was saying it.

He took bloods. He wrote up a discharge. He checked his phone in the sluice at eleven and at a quarter to twelve, and there was nothing on it. He thought about the man in the dark jacket. He thought about why her sister would send a man like that to stand at the bottom of the steps with his hands where people could see them, and the only answer he could find was that someone else had a reason to stand near her too.

He opened the food app. No order since last night. He closed it.

Kenny found him at the nurses’ station at one and asked if he wanted to split the cardiology questions in the library tonight, three hundred of them. Yu Chen said he couldn’t tonight, pleasantly, and Kenny went away and Yu Chen didn’t think about him again.

At ten past one she texted.

Eliana: done. it went fine. a lecturer put his head in his hands. that was the good bit. eating noodles

He breathed out. Then he looked at the word noodles and at the app, which still said nothing, and understood that somebody else had bought them. The man in the dark jacket had bought her lunch.

He didn’t like it. He knew he had no right to dislike it. He disliked it anyway, steadily, through a whole afternoon of a man in bed four who couldn’t remember his own medicines, and at ten past five he went to find Dr. Yiu.

“I need to go,” he said.

Dr. Yiu looked up from a drug chart. In seven months Yu Chen had never left a ward before he was told he could.

“Is it family?”

Yu Chen thought about the truth, which was that it was a girl who would be furious if she knew he’d left early because of her.

“Yes,” he said.

“Go on, then,” said Dr. Yiu, and went back to the chart.

He forgot to take his white coat off. He was on his bicycle and halfway down the hill before he noticed, with the pen still in the pocket, and he didn’t stop to fix it.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was on the kerb at the bottom of her steps at half past five.

She hadn’t told him what time. She hadn’t told him anything, except that it was nothing. He sat on the kerb with the bicycle beside him and his elbows on his knees and watched the end of the lane where the grey car had turned that morning, and the noodle man looked over at him from his stall, and away, and didn’t ask, because the noodle man had seen him sit on that kerb a great many times.

It got dark slowly. The lamp at the end of the lane came on. The old man on the far side was whistling to his birds. Six o’clock came, and the grey car came round the corner by the noodle stall, and stopped at the bottom of the steps, and he stood up.

He could see her through the windscreen. She was looking at him. She said something to the man beside her, short, and then she got out, and stopped, and bent down to the window and talked for a little while longer. He couldn’t hear any of it. He stood by his bicycle and waited.

Then she straightened up and came round the car to the steps, and he went up them beside her.

He didn’t take her hand. The man was still there in the car, watching, and it was the lane, and she had rules. He went up the three steps beside her, very close, not touching, and at the top she stopped and turned round and looked back at the grey car, and lifted one hand, a little, the way you’d wave to someone you weren’t sure you were allowed to like.

Then she pushed the red door, and the bolt stuck the way it always stuck, and they were inside.

✦ ✦ ✦

The hall was dark. Ah Sim had the radio on in the kitchen at the back, and there was a smell of ginger, and the door shut behind them on the lane and the car and the man in the dark jacket, and Eliana turned round to say something to him.

He didn’t let her.

He took her face in his hand, his thumb along her jaw, and kissed her, there in the dark hall with her back against the inside of the red door. He wasn’t careful. He’d been careful since ten to eight that morning. He’d been careful through a ward round and a man who couldn’t remember his medicines and an empty food app and the word noodles, and he’d been careful on the kerb for half an hour, and it all went out of him at once into her mouth. Her laptop hit his chest between them. She made a small surprised sound and then her free hand was in the front of his white coat, holding on, pulling him down, and she kissed him back the way she did when she’d been frightened and hadn’t said so.

He felt it in her. She’d been frightened too.

“You left early,” she said against his mouth. “You’re in your coat.”

“Yes.”

“You never leave early.”

“No,” he said, and kissed her again, and in the kitchen Ah Sim turned the radio up, which was what Ah Sim did instead of coming out.

They stood in the dark with their foreheads together. He could feel her breathing.

“Who was he?” he said.

“I told you. Sera’s husband.”

“Why did your sister send him?”

She looked at him, close, in the dark. He watched her decide how much to say, and watched her decide on less than all of it, and let her. He’d learned to let her.

“Later,” she said. “Baba’s due. Go home. I’ll tell you later.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t come over the wall. He waited until midnight, and then until one, at his desk with the cardiology questions he wasn’t doing, looking across the dark garden at her window. Her light was on. At ten to two it was still on.

At two the red door’s bolt stuck and carried across the lane, the way it had on a night in June nearly four years ago, and he got up and took the blanket from the end of his bed and went out.

She was on the third step in her black hoodie with her knees up. He stepped over the low wall by the iron rail and sat down beside her and put half the blanket round her, and she let him, and leaned on his arm, and neither of them said anything.

“I’ll tell you now,” she said.

She told him. Not the bank, which he half knew, but the rest of it, plainly, looking at the dark lane: that after the letter there had been messages. Since January. From nobody, from numbers that didn’t exist the next day. Nothing in them, mostly. A photograph of the university gates. A photograph of the bus stop at the bottom of the hill, the one she used. Once, in February, a photograph of the third step of the tall house, this step, empty, taken from the lane.

He sat very still.

“I’d have found them,” she said. “I nearly had. By Wednesday I’d have had the whole firm. That’s what I told him, the husband. He said that’s why they sent a man today. Because they knew I’d find them, and they wanted me frightened first.” She pushed her glasses up. “There was a man at the talk. In a grey jacket. He was going to follow me to the toilets and take a picture of me and send it to me tonight with nothing written on it. So I’d know they could. Haozhen sat down next to him and said something and he left. I don’t know what he said. He wouldn’t tell me.”

Yu Chen didn’t say anything for a little while.

He was aware of the cold going down through him from the top, slowly, the way it did. It had happened at her father’s table. It had happened on the path outside the psychology building with a boy called Dominic Ip. It felt like a door shutting somewhere inside him on everything that wasn’t useful. A man in a grey jacket had sat in a hall full of people and waited for her to need the toilet.

“Since January,” he said. “And a photograph of this step. And you didn’t tell me.”

“You’d have done that,” she said. “What you’re doing now. Going quiet like that. You’d have sat on the kerb every day for two months and not slept and not done your questions. You’ve got finals.” She looked at him sideways. “Your hands have gone cold. Stop it.”

He made himself breathe out. He didn’t stop it, exactly. He put it somewhere he could find it again.

“He drove you all day,” he said. “And bought you noodles. And sat next to the man. And I was on the fourth floor taking bloods, and you told me it was a lift.”

“It was a lift.”

“Eliana.”

She looked down at the step.

“He asked who you were,” she said. “When we stopped. He saw you on the kerb and he asked.” She was quiet. “I said nobody. I said you were nobody, the boy next door, and that you always wait.”

It went into him somewhere under the ribs and stayed there.

He didn’t let her see it. He was good at that. But she knew him better than anyone alive, and she heard it anyway, in the way he didn’t move, and she turned and put her face against his shoulder.

“I didn’t mean nobody,” she said into his coat. “I meant—I panicked. He’s Sera’s husband. Everyone tells Sera everything. And then Sera tells Elowen, and Elowen tells Aurelia, and by Sunday Baba—”

“I know,” he said. “I know what you meant.”

He did know. That was the problem. He’d known for three and a half years exactly what she meant every time she said it was nothing, and he’d agreed to it every time, because she needed the secret and he didn’t need anything but her. He’d sat on the kerb today with no information and no right to any, and a stranger had sat beside the man who’d come for her, because the stranger was allowed to, and Yu Chen wasn’t. Nobody was going to ring the boy next door if something happened to her. Nobody would think of it. He wasn’t anybody’s to ring.

He looked at the lane. The lamp at the end of it. The noodle stall shuttered for the night.

“I’m going to say something,” he said. “You don’t have to answer it. Not tonight. Not soon, if you’re not ready. But I’m going to say it, because I’m done not saying it.”

She went still against his shoulder.

“I want to marry you,” said Yu Chen.

He said it plainly, looking at the lane, the way he’d read out a dose. He didn’t have a ring in his pocket. He didn’t have a plan; he’d made eleven over the years and torn them all out. He just said it.

“Not now. Not this year, if you don’t want. But I don’t want to be the boy next door who waits. I want to be the one they ring. I want there to be a word for it that other people have to use. I’ve been unofficial for three and a half years and I’d do another ten if you asked me, but I’m not going to pretend there isn’t a name for it any more. There is. I know what it is. I’ve always known.”

She’d stopped breathing. He could feel it.

Then she was off his shoulder, and off the step, standing on the cracked stone with the blanket fallen off her and her hands at her sides, looking at him as if he’d said something in a language she’d spent her whole life making sure she never had to learn.

“You can’t,” she said.

“I just did.”

“You can’t say that. That’s the word. That’s the—” Her voice went thin. “People say that and then they’re in a hospital. People say that and then they don’t come home. You know that. You know that’s the one thing—”

“I know.”

“Then why would you—”

She stopped. He watched her try to find the rest of it and not find it. She was shaking, not with cold. She looked at him on the step, at the blanket on the stone, at the red door behind her.

He didn’t stand up. He didn’t reach for her. He’d made himself one rule on the kerb that afternoon without knowing it, and he knew it now: he wasn’t going to touch her to make this easier. Not this. If she came back to him it would be because she’d answered it, not because he’d kissed her out of having to.

“I’m not going anywhere,” he said. “You don’t have to say anything. I’ll be here tomorrow.”

She turned round and went up the steps, and pushed the red door, and the bolt stuck, and she got it open, and went in, and shut it.

He heard the bolt go home on the inside.

He sat on the third step until the cold came up through him, with the blanket beside him on the stone where she’d dropped it. Then he folded it and left it on the top step by the door, where she’d find it in the morning, and went back over the low wall to his own house, and sat at his desk in the dark with the cardiology questions, and looked across the garden at her window.

Her light stayed on until it was nearly light.

chapters.title: Nine Days
chapters.desc: She doesn’t answer him. She doesn’t leave, either. For nine days they live on either side of a garden wall and say nothing that matters, until she knocks on his door at two in the morning.
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t know how to promise forever. Nobody in my house ever got to keep one. Teach me how.” — Eliana Lin
chapters.content:
The blanket was on the top step when she opened the door in the morning, folded into a square, with the flask on top of it.

She stood in the doorway in her socks and looked at it. Then she looked across the low wall at his door, which was shut, and at his bicycle, which was gone. He’d left for the ward. He’d made her tea first, at the usual time, and folded the blanket, and gone.

She picked them both up and took them inside and drank the tea standing in the hall, and it was exactly right, and she hated that it was exactly right.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first three days she didn’t go out of the house except for lectures, and she went to those by the back gate.

It was stupid. She was twenty-two and in her last term, creeping out of her own back gate like a burglar to avoid a boy who had done nothing to her except say a sentence. She did it anyway. At seven the flask would be on the third step, and she’d take it in, and go out the back.

He didn’t text. He didn’t come over the wall. She’d thought he might, the first night, and she’d sat at her screens until four with her whole back listening for the back door, and it hadn’t come.

On the Wednesday there was a note in the jar.

She’d seen his back door open at one, from her window, and a tall shape go down the garden to the wall under the persimmon branch and back. She went down at three in her socks and took the loose brick out.

It was one of the small squares he wrote his plans on. In his capitals.

I’M NOT GOING ANYWHERE. EAT SOMETHING.

That was all. She put it in her hoodie pocket and went back up and ordered noodles, at three in the morning, on the account that was on his card, so he’d see that she’d eaten, and then she sat at her desk and didn’t eat them.

✦ ✦ ✦

She worked. That was the only thing she knew how to do with a feeling that size.

The firm that had sent the man in the grey jacket had gone quiet since Monday, which she put down to whatever Haozhen had said and was furious about, because she’d wanted to do it herself. So she took every job Qian had. By Thursday a man who’d been taking money from old people over the phone had nothing left to take it with, and she sent Qian his name at five in the morning with a note that said Fast, please, one of them is ninety, and felt nothing, which was the point.

On the screens she was cold and quick and exact. Nobody on the other end had ever known she was small, or that she couldn’t buy a coffee without practising the words. On the screens she was nobody’s little sister. It was the only place in her life where she never had to answer anyone.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the fourth day she watched him through the library window.

She hadn’t meant to. She’d come round the side of the library on the path to the computer science building, and the window of study room 4B was on the ground floor there, and he was in it.

He was at the table on his own with his books open and the flask beside him. Not reading. He had his pen in his hand and he wasn’t writing anything; he was looking at the door, the room’s own door, the one she always came through at ten past nine with her hood up. It was twenty past. He’d been looking at it, she understood, for ten minutes.

She stood on the path with her laptop against her chest.

She could go in. She’d sit down at her side of the table and say hi, and he’d look up, and his whole face would go the way it went, and then he’d wait for her to say the rest. That was the thing. He’d asked her a question on the step and he wasn’t going to pretend he hadn’t. He’d never once let her lie to him.

He looked down at his book.

His ears were red. Not from anything; from sitting in a room by himself looking at a door. She watched him turn a page he hadn’t read.

She went to the computer science building and sat in the back of a lecture and heard none of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You’re an idiot,” said Si-Wei.

She said it on the sixth day, on a bench outside the business school, in her cream coat, with a black coffee. She didn’t say it unkindly. She said it the way she said most things, as a fact she’d checked.

Eliana hadn’t meant to tell her. Instead she’d said, without looking up, “He asked me something and I didn’t answer and now we’re not talking,” and Si-Wei had waited, and Eliana had told her the rest in about four sentences, and now she was an idiot.

“He asked me to marry him,” said Eliana. “Sort of. He said he wants to. Not now. One day.”

“I know. You said.”

“And I can’t.”

“Why not?”

“Because people say that and then something comes.” It came out flat and ugly and true. “That’s all anyone in my house knows about forever.”

Si-Wei drank her coffee. She took her time about it.

“So you’re scared of losing him,” she said.

“Yes.”

“And you think that means you can’t have him.”

Eliana didn’t say anything.

“It’s the other way round,” said Si-Wei. “You’re only this scared because you’d die if you lost him. People who don’t love someone aren’t scared of anything. They just leave.” She put her cup down on the bench between them. “You’re confusing the fear with the answer. The fear’s just the proof.”

Eliana sat there.

“That’s very annoying,” she said at last.

“I know,” said Si-Wei. “Si-Jie read it in a book. I’ve been waiting to use it on someone.” She picked her coffee up again. “Also he’s been sitting in a library room by himself all week looking at a door. Si-Jie walked past. She’s upset.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Baba said it on the seventh day, at breakfast, to Ah Sim.

He didn’t say it to Eliana. He never said things to Eliana. He sat at the head of the long table with his tea and his paper, a big grey man in a cardigan, and Eliana sat at the far end with her toast, and Ah Sim moved between them, and Baba said to Ah Sim, without looking up:

“Tell her Chen Si speaks well of her.”

Ah Sim stopped with the teapot.

“Tell her,” said Baba, turning a page, “that when she finishes in the summer he’ll want her full time. Properly. A proper position. Tell her she won’t need to go anywhere. She can stay here and do it from upstairs.” He turned another page. “And tell her the policeman’s boy has been sitting on our kerb a great deal. Mok says he was there last Monday for half an hour. In a white coat. I don’t want him on my kerb.”

Ah Sim looked at Eliana down the length of the table. Eliana looked at her toast.

She’d known Baba knew about Chen Si. Chen Si had told him, she was fairly sure, in the first year, between old men, as a courtesy; Baba had never once said a word about it to her, in three and a half years, until now, at breakfast, through the cook. She won’t need to go anywhere. She heard what it was: a door being shut so gently she wouldn’t notice it was a door.

“I heard him,” she said to Ah Sim, and got up, and went upstairs.

She sat on her camp bed in the dark room and thought about staying here forever, upstairs, useful, and her father two floors down never looking up, and she felt something she hadn’t felt in six days, which was clear.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the eighth night she went to the wall.

It was nearly one. His light was on. She stood under the persimmon branch on her side, in the blind spot, and hissed his name the way he’d once hissed hers, and after a minute his back door opened and he came down the garden in his grey jumper and stopped on the other side of the wall.

They looked at each other over it. It came up to her chest and his waist.

“Hi,” she said.

“Hi.”

He looked as if he hadn’t slept in a week, and when he saw her his whole face opened the way she’d known it would, and she couldn’t stand it.

She put both hands on the top of the wall and pulled herself up and kissed him.

She did it badly, half on the wall, with her knee on the bricks, and he caught her by the arms so she wouldn’t fall, and just once he kissed her back. She felt it. His mouth and the breath going out of him and his hands tightening on her arms. Eight days of it in one second.

Then he put her down.

Gently. On her own side. He set her feet back on the paving and let go of her arms, and stepped back from the wall, and stood there in the dark with his hands at his sides, breathing like he’d been running.

“No,” he said.

She stared at him.

“Not like this,” he said. His voice was rough. “I’m not going to do this over a wall so neither of us has to say anything. That’s what you want. I know it’s what you want. You want to kiss me and go back up the tree and have it all be the way it was.” He swallowed. “I can’t. I said a thing and I meant it. If I kiss you now I’m telling you it doesn’t matter whether you answer. And it does. It’s the only thing I’ve ever asked you for.”

“That’s not fair.”

“No. I know.” He didn’t move. “I’m not trying to be fair. I’m trying not to make it easy for you to not answer me. That’s all I’ve got. It’s my rule. It’s not yours. You don’t have to keep it.” His hands closed and opened. “But I’m going to.”

She stood there with her mouth still feeling it.

She was so angry she couldn’t see. She turned round and went back up the persimmon tree in her socks, faster than she’d ever climbed it, and in through her window, and shut it, and sat on the floor under it with her back to the wall and her hand over her mouth.

She didn’t cry. She sat there until her legs went numb, and when she got up and looked out his light was off, and she knew he wasn’t asleep either.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the ninth night she knocked on his door.

Not the back door. The front one. She went out of the red door at two in the morning and along the lane and up his three steps, and knocked with her knuckles, like a visitor, like someone who’d come to say something on purpose.

It took him less than a minute.

He opened it in a T-shirt and old trousers, with his hair standing up on one side, and he’d been asleep after all, or nearly, and his face when he saw her went from asleep to frightened in no time at all.

“What’s wrong? Are you—”

“Nothing’s wrong,” she said. “I came to say something. Let me say it before I stop being able to.”

He stood in the doorway and held on to the frame.

“I don’t know how to do it,” said Eliana. “Forever. I don’t know how. Nobody in my house ever got to keep anything they said forever about. So I don’t know how. I’ve never seen it done. I don’t know what it looks like when it works.” She was shaking. She kept going. “And you said it on the step like it was easy, like it was a dose, and I wanted to say yes so much I couldn’t breathe, and the yes was so big it frightened me more than anything I’ve ever found on a screen. That’s why I couldn’t. Not because I don’t want it. Because I want it so much that if I lose it—”

She stopped. She looked at him.

“Si-Wei says the fear’s the proof,” she said. “She read it in a book. I think she’s right. I hate it.” She pushed her glasses up. “So teach me. I don’t know how. You have to teach me how.”

He let go of the doorframe.

He didn’t kiss her. Not yet. He came down one step, so his face was level with hers under the porch light, and looked at her, and she saw that his eyes had gone wet and he wasn’t doing anything about it.

“I can’t promise I won’t die,” he said. “I’m not going to lie to you. I’m going to be a doctor. I know what happens to people. I could be in a car. Anything.” He took a breath. “But I can promise you I’ll be next door. Every day I’m alive. I’ve been next door every day since you were eighteen and I’m not going to stop. And you don’t have to promise forever. You can’t. Nobody can, really, they just say it. You can promise tomorrow. That’s all. Just tomorrow. And then tomorrow you can promise the next one.”

She looked at him.

“Tomorrow,” she said.

“Yes.”

“That’s it? That’s the answer?”

“That’s an answer,” he said. “It’s enough. Say it every day and it’ll add up.”

She put her hands on his face.

“Tomorrow,” she said. “And the one after. I’ll say it every day. I’m saying it now.”

And that was an answer, and his rule was finished, and he knew it before she’d got the last word out. He made a sound she’d never heard him make and pulled her up the last step into the doorway and into him, and kissed her, and he was crying and so was she and neither of them stopped to do anything about it.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t remember the stairs. She remembered his hands, and the wall of the landing at her back, and his mouth on her neck, and laughing because she’d banged her elbow on the banister and he stopped on the stairs to kiss it.

In his room he put her down on the bed and then just stood there, looking at her, in the light from the lane coming through his curtains.

“Nine days,” he said.

“I know. I’m sorry. I’m sorry—”

“Don’t.” He came down to her. “Don’t be sorry. Just—let me.”

He undressed her as if he’d been thinking about it for nine days, slowly, and then he lost patience with her hoodie and she was laughing into the fabric while it caught on her glasses. She pulled him down by his T-shirt and got it off him and put her hands flat on his chest, on his heart, which was going as hard as hers.

It wasn’t like the other times. They’d been learning each other for three and a half years and she’d thought she knew all of it. She hadn’t known this: what he was like when he’d been without her and got her back. He kissed her as if he were counting something he’d thought he’d lost. He said her name into her skin, over and over, and tomorrow, once, against her throat, like a word he wanted to keep. She held on to him and kept her eyes open because she wanted to see him, all of it, his face over hers in the half-dark, and for once she didn’t hide anything from it. She let him see all of it.

She cried in the middle. Not from anything bad. He felt it and stopped, and she shook her head and pulled him back, and said “don’t stop, it’s not that, it’s not sad,” and he didn’t stop. And then she was laughing, wet, because he’d kissed the tears off her face with enormous seriousness, and then neither of them was laughing, and she held on to him with everything she had and said his name, the one that was only for here, and meant all of it.

Afterwards she lay on his chest and listened to his heart slow down.

“Tomorrow,” she said, into his skin.

“Tomorrow,” said Yu Chen. His hand was in her hair. “I’ll make the tea.”

“You’ll make it at seven.”

“I’ll make it at seven.” He was quiet. “Will you be there? On the step?”

“I’ll be on the step,” said Eliana. “I’ll be there before you.”

She was asleep before he could answer, and the last thing she knew was his breathing going long and slow under her cheek, and that he’d fallen asleep too, for once, at the same time as her.

chapters.title: In Front of Everyone
chapters.desc: After nine days and a knock at two in the morning, Eliana does the bravest thing she can think of. She holds his hand on the hill, in daylight, where the whole university can see. It takes her the entire walk to the gates.
chapters.epigraph: “Don’t make it a thing. I’m just holding your hand. All the way up. In public. Shut up.” — Eliana Lin
chapters.content:
She’d sent him the video before she posted it.

That was the first thing. It was a small thing, and nobody but her would ever know it was a thing at all. On the eighth of April the family had gone up Fig Tree Lane in three cars for the party Evangeline and Raiden had now, two cakes on one table, and they’d blown the candles out at the same moment with everyone counting, and Eliana had filmed it so nobody could argue. Then she’d sat in the back of Uncle Mok’s car on the way down with her phone in her lap and, before she sent it to the family chat, she’d sent it to him.

Eliana: draw. official. raiden will contest it

Yu Chen: He’ll lose.

Eliana: you’re not even in the family chat

Yu Chen: I know. I’m in this one.

She’d looked at that for the rest of the drive. Then she’d posted it to the family with the caption DRAW (OFFICIAL), and Raiden had contested it within four minutes and kept contesting it for a week, and Yu Chen had watched every round of it on her phone over her shoulder on his sofa, with his chin on her head, laughing.

He’d never been in the family jokes before. He’d been next door to them for years. She’d let him in through a window nobody else knew was open, and he’d climbed in without a word.

That was the eighth. By the twenty-sixth she’d decided to do the other thing.

✦ ✦ ✦

His written finals started on the Monday after next. He’d been living in study room 4B since March, and on Saturdays the library opened at nine, and on this Saturday she came out of the red door at half past eight in her cat hoodie with her laptop, and he was on the kerb by his bicycle with the flask.

“You’re coming up?” he said. “On a Saturday?”

“I’ve got my project.”

“You never do your project in the library. You say the chairs are wrong.”

“The chairs are wrong,” said Eliana. “Walk the bike. Don’t ride it. I’m getting the bus.”

He looked at her. She looked at the noodle stall.

“I’ll walk up with you,” he said, slowly. “From the bus.”

“Yes.”

He didn’t ask why. He’d learned, over three and a half years, which questions she could stand on a Saturday morning, and this wasn’t one of them. He put the flask in her hands and walked beside her to the bus stop at the end of the lane, wheeling the bicycle, and she got on the number nine and he cycled behind it the whole way up the main road, which he’d done for years and which she’d always pretended not to see.

✦ ✦ ✦

The bus stopped at the bottom of the hill, by the gates of the lower campus, where the path started.

It was about six hundred metres from there to the main gates at the top. She knew. She’d measured it in the night on a map, at three in the morning, which was the kind of thing she did when she was about to do something frightening. Six hundred metres of path up through the trees, past the medical school and the fish tank and the bench where people ate lunch, past the noodle stall behind the library, and on a Saturday in April with exams coming there’d be people on every bit of it.

She got off the bus. He was there, off the bicycle, holding it by the handlebars.

She walked up to him and took his hand.

His left one. Off the handlebar. She just took it, the way you’d take something off a shelf, and held it, and started walking.

He didn’t move at first. The bicycle nearly went over; he caught it with his other hand. Then he came, because she was pulling, and they were walking up the path side by side with his hand in hers and the bicycle wheeling along clumsily on his other side, ticking.

“Eliana,” he said.

“Don’t.”

“I didn’t say anything.”

“You were going to. Don’t make it a thing. I’m just holding your hand. All the way up. In public.” She could feel her face going. It started at her ears and went down her neck and into her hoodie. “Shut up.”

He shut up.

He didn’t let go, either. His hand closed round hers properly, warm, and she felt him take a breath, and not say anything with it, and she knew without looking that his ears had gone red too.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first people were two girls on the bench by the bus stop with coffees. They looked up. They looked at the hands. Eliana looked at the path.

Then a boy on a scooter who went past, slowed down, looked back. Then three students from the medical school coming down with lab coats over their arms, who all said “Yu Chen!” at once, and then saw, and stopped, and one of them hit another on the arm.

Yu Chen said “Morning,” pleasantly, in the voice he used for everyone, and kept walking.

“You know them,” she said, under her breath.

“I know their names.”

“They’re going to tell everyone.”

“Yes,” he said, and she couldn’t tell from his voice whether that was a warning or something he was looking forward to.

She wanted to let go. She wanted it more than anything. Her hand was sweating and she was sure he could feel it and every face that turned towards them went into her like a needle, and the path was long and steep and there was nowhere to hide on it. She thought about letting go. She thought about saying her hand was cold, or that she needed her phone. Her fingers went loose in his.

He didn’t hold on harder. She noticed that. He didn’t grip her or pull her or make her. He just left his hand where it was, open, warm, so that if she took hers away it would be her who’d done it.

She tightened her fingers again.

✦ ✦ ✦

Halfway up, by the fish tank, they passed Dominic Ip.

He was on the steps of the computer science building with two of his friends, eating something out of a paper bag, and he saw her and started to grin and say Lin Yu, the way he always did, loud, and then he saw the hand. And then he saw who it belonged to.

The grin stayed on a beat too long. Then it went sour.

“So that’s who,” he said, not quite to them.

Yu Chen looked at him.

The look on the path outside the psychology building had been cold. This one had nothing in it at all. He looked at Dominic the way he’d look at a bus timetable, without interest, and said “Morning,” exactly as he’d said it to his friends from medicine, and walked on, with her hand in his, and the bicycle ticking.

Eliana didn’t look back. But she heard Dominic’s friend laugh at him, behind them, and she felt something in her chest she didn’t have a name for, that was a bit like being sick and a bit like wanting to laugh out loud.

“You were rude,” she said.

He didn’t argue.

“You say good morning like a door shutting.” She walked a few steps. “I liked it.”

“I know,” he said. “You’ve gone a different red.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Past the medical school, a lecturer was coming down the path with a briefcase. Professor Ou, her project supervisor, the one who’d put his head in his hands at her talk in March. He saw her. He saw the hand. He raised both eyebrows high above his glasses, and then he smiled, which she’d never seen him do in four years, and said “Miss Lin. Good morning. I’ll expect your draft by Friday,” and went on down the hill.

She nearly sat down on the path.

“He smiled,” she said. “He’s never smiled.”

“Maybe he’s never seen you hold anyone’s hand.”

“Nobody’s ever seen me hold anyone’s hand.”

“I know,” said Yu Chen. He was looking straight ahead up the path. His voice wasn’t quite steady. “I’m the first one.”

She looked up at him then. She hadn’t, the whole way. She’d looked at the path and the trees and people’s shoes. She looked at him now, and he was walking up the hill with his face gone soft and open in a way he never let it go in public, in front of anyone, in daylight, and he wasn’t trying to hide it at all.

She’d done that, with six hundred metres and a hand.

Si-Jie found them by the noodle stall.

Eliana heard her before she saw her. A scream, an actual scream, high and long, from somewhere by the library, and then a pink coat coming at them across the grass at a run with Si-Wei walking behind it at her own pace with a coffee.

“ELIANA. OH MY GOD. ELIANA.”

“Keep walking,” said Eliana, and when he opened his mouth she said it again.

They kept walking. Si-Jie fell in on her other side, talking at a speed Eliana could only half follow, I knew it, I knew it, I’ve known since October, Si-Wei said don’t push, I didn’t push, I’ve been so good, look at your hands, and took a photograph of their hands on her phone while she walked, and then another one. Si-Wei came alongside, drank her coffee, looked at the hands, looked at Eliana’s face, and said, “About time,” and nothing else, and dropped back.

✦ ✦ ✦

The main gates at the top were old stone with the university’s name cut into the arch. There were people under it, people on the steps of the Great Hall opposite, a tour of parents being shown round, a man selling flowers.

Six hundred metres. She’d done it. She stopped under the arch, breathing hard, not from the hill.

“There,” she said. “That’s it. That’s—”

He let go of the bicycle.

It went over on the stones with a crash. He didn’t look at it. He turned towards her, under the arch, in front of the parents and the flower man and Si-Jie and everyone, and he took her face in his hand, his palm along her jaw, the way he had on his roof the first time, and he kissed her.

No warning and no asking. He kissed her in the gateway of the university in front of the whole hill, slowly and on purpose, the way you’d sign something, and she went stiff all over with the shock of it, every eye, every face, and then she didn’t.

She grabbed the front of his jumper with both hands and kissed him back.

She heard Si-Jie make a sound like a kettle. She heard one of the parents say something, and the flower man laugh, and somewhere further off someone clapping, once, sarcastically, which was almost certainly Si-Wei. She didn’t care. She held on to his jumper and kissed him in front of all of it and the sky didn’t fall, and nobody took anything, and when she opened her eyes the world was still there, ordinary, a Saturday in April, a bicycle on its side on the stones.

“You said not where people can see,” he said against her mouth. “I’ve kept it.” He hadn’t let go of her face. “I’m not keeping it any more. Is that all right?”

He’d asked after, when it was already done.

“You’ve already done it,” said Eliana.

“I know. I’m asking anyway.”

She looked up at him under the arch with the whole hill watching and her face burning.

“You asked how much longer,” she said. She pushed her glasses up her nose, because they’d gone crooked. “The whole hill. That’s how much. And next time don’t let go either.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They didn’t do much work in 4B.

He had pharmacology to revise and she had a draft to write for a man who’d smiled at her, and they sat at their two sides of the table for about twenty minutes with their books open, and then she looked up and he was looking at her, not reading, and she said “Stop it,” and he said “Stop what,” and she got up and walked round the table and sat on it, on his notes, in front of him.

“You’re on my notes,” he said. “I’ve got finals in nine days.”

She put her hands on his shoulders, and leaned down, and kissed him.

He made a sound against her mouth and his hands came up to her waist and pulled her off the table into his lap, chair and all, and the chair scraped and his notes slid onto the floor in a heap and neither of them picked them up. She kissed him the way she’d wanted to all the way up the hill, slow and then not slow at all, with her fingers in his hair and his hands under the back of her hoodie, warm on her skin, and the glass door of 4B had a narrow window in it that anyone could have looked through, and for once she didn’t think about the window at all.

“Someone’ll come,” he said, breathless, at her throat.

“It’s booked. It’s always booked. It’s booked to you till the end of time.”

“Who did that?”

“Some girl,” said Eliana. “Years ago. In four minutes.”

He laughed against her neck, and then he kissed it, and she stopped being able to make jokes for a while.

Later, with his notes still on the floor and her head on his shoulder and the afternoon going gold through the window, she got her phone out and looked at the photograph Si-Jie had sent to TRIPLETS + 1 that morning. Two hands on the path under the trees. Hers small and pale, his big, with a blue pen mark on the thumb.

Si-Jie had captioned it in capital letters. Eliana read it, and went red, and didn’t delete it.

She set it as her lock screen instead. It was the first thing she’d ever changed on her own phone for herself.

chapters.title: Two Gowns
