chapters.desc: On the same afternoon, in the same hall, Eliana gets a degree in computer science and Yu Chen gets one in medicine, which was the point of four years of “coincidence”. On the steps afterwards she kisses him in front of both families.
chapters.epigraph: “Four years. One hall. One afternoon. I told you it was the medical programme.” — Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
She was wearing the cat hoodie under her gown.

He saw it in the robing room, where the graduates were queuing for hoods at long tables and the volunteers were pinning caps to people’s hair. The black gown came to her ankles and the sleeves came past her hands, and at the neck, where everyone else had a collar and a tie, there was a cartoon cat’s ear sticking out.

“You can’t wear that,” he said.

“I’m wearing it.”

“It’s the Great Hall. Your father’s in there.”

“That’s why I’m wearing it,” said Eliana, and pushed her glasses up, and let a volunteer put the cap on her head, where it sat on top of the knot of hair and the pencil and looked as if it might leave at any moment.

His own gown was heavier, and his hood was a different colour, because medicine had its own. Two gowns. They’d be in the same hall in an hour, in different rows, called up for different degrees, on the same afternoon. He’d known since a night in June four years ago that this was how it would end, and he’d told everyone, including himself, that it was the programme.

He stood in the robing room and looked at her in a gown too big for her, scowling at a volunteer, and couldn’t stop smiling.

“Stop it,” she said, without looking at him. “You’re doing the face. People are looking.”

“People have been looking since April,” said Yu Chen. “Half the hill’s seen my face.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her half of it had nearly not happened.

On the twelfth of June, at nine minutes past two in the morning, her phone had gone off in his bed.

He’d woken to her sitting up in the dark with the screen lit in her hand and her face white over it. One line on the screen. SMOKE, and the name of Jinx’s shop, and the number of the camera she’d put on its ceiling the November before, the one nobody asked for. She’d made a sound he’d never heard her make. Then she was out of bed and at his desk with her laptop open, and he’d stood behind her and watched a small grey square on her screen that was a picture of a ceiling full of smoke.

Raiden had got there. Jinx had got out. Elowen rang at five to say they were both at City Hospital with smoke in their lungs and Raiden’s hands burned and Jinx’s arm, and they were both alive, and Elara had come down from the wards in her scrubs and said again so the whole corridor heard. Eliana had listened to all of it and said “okay” and put the phone down.

She didn’t go to the hospital. He’d offered to drive her, and she’d shaken her head, and sat on the end of his bed in his T-shirt with her knees up, and said, “I don’t go to hospitals at night. People go in at night,” and he hadn’t said anything, because he knew what she meant and so would anyone in her family.

Then she’d rewired the whole building.

Nine days, at the end of June, on her own. Zhao’s men did the walls and Aurelia’s glazier did the glass and Elara came on her days off for the small jobs, and Eliana sat on the black floor in a hoodie with her laptop open and cables round her like spaghetti and did every wire in the place herself, and put in two more cameras nobody asked for. He brought dinner every night. He wasn’t allowed to touch a wire. He tried once to hand her a reel of something and she took it off him without looking up and said “no,” and he sat on an upturned crate and watched her work and ate his own dinner and hers, when she forgot.

Her final project went in four days late. Professor Ou let it. She’d said, when he asked, “There was a fire,” and Professor Ou had looked at her over his glasses and said “So I heard,” and given her a first.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Great Hall had a hammer-beam roof and pigeons in it somewhere, and it was full.

He found them from the stage steps while the graduates were filing in. The Lins took up most of a row near the middle. Lin Jian, in the black suit he wore to everything formal, which was the suit he’d worn to funerals, sitting straight-backed beside Uncle Mok. Elowen in green, with Zhao beside her in black, looking at the pigeons. Raiden with healed hands, and Jinx with a dressing still on her forearm. Evangeline in pale blue, and beside her Jun Hyuk, who took up a seat and a half and had already made friends with the man on the end.

Nearer the front, Xing Yue, in his dark grey suit, sitting with his back straight, beside Elara. He was there as Yu Chen’s mentor. He’d been asked to come and he’d come. Yu Chen caught his eye across the hall and Xing Yue did nothing with his face at all, which from Xing Yue was warm.

And at the end of the row behind, on his own in his plain dark coat, Wei Long.

Yu Chen sat down in the medicine rows. Eliana was across the aisle and twelve rows back with computer science, and he couldn’t see her without turning round, and he turned round twice anyway, and both times she was looking at him, and both times she glared.

The speeches were long. Somebody important talked about the future. A pigeon flew the length of the hall and everyone watched it instead.

Computer science went before medicine.

When they called Lin Yu she went up the steps to the stage in her too-big gown with the cat’s ear showing at her neck, and her cap nearly came off on the top step and she grabbed it, and the hall laughed, kindly. She shook the hand she was meant to shake. She took the scroll. On her way off she looked out at the hall once, at the middle row, at her father.

Yu Chen looked too.

Lin Jian was looking at her. He sat quite still in his funeral suit, with his big hands on his knees, and he was looking straight at his youngest daughter on the stage, the way Yu Chen had hardly ever seen him look at her, for the two seconds it took her to walk off. Then he looked down at his hands.

She didn’t see it. She’d already turned away.

Twenty minutes later they called Wang Yu Chen and he went up, and shook the hand, and took the scroll, and didn’t hear any of it, because from the stage he could see her in her row with her phone up, filming, the way she filmed everything, and her face over the top of the phone was not the face of someone doing it for a spreadsheet.

Near the front, Xing Yue clapped exactly as hard as everyone else, and his jaw was tight.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the steps of the Great Hall afterwards, in the sun, there were a thousand people in gowns and twice as many families, and pigeons, and a man selling flowers again.

Wei Long found him first. He came down the steps in his plain coat and stood in front of Yu Chen and looked at him in his gown and hood with no expression whatsoever.

“Well,” he said.

From Wei Long that was a speech. Yu Chen said thank you for it, and Wei Long put his hand on the back of Yu Chen’s neck, hard, and took it away. Then he took an envelope out of his coat.

“Nainai,” he said. “She posted it to me. She said I was to read it out on the steps, because she couldn’t come, and she doesn’t trust you to read it out properly. She says you mumble.”

Wei Long looked past him. Eliana had come down the steps from the other side, with her cap in her hand and her scroll under her arm, and stopped a little way off, the way she did, half behind a pillar. “You’d better come here,” said Wei Long to her. “It’s got you in it.”

She went red at once. She came, though.

Wei Long opened the letter and read it out, on the steps of the Great Hall, in his flat detective’s voice that put no feeling into anything, which made it worse.

“Yu Chen. Well done. You’re a doctor. Your mother would have cried and your father would have pretended not to, and I’m going to do both, here, where you can’t see. Don’t work too hard. Write more. Come north at New Year and bring the girl.” He turned the page over. “And to the girl. I know you’re standing there. Well done to you too. I’ve read about you every month for four years. You’re family now, whether you’ve decided or not. Make him eat.”

He folded it up and gave it to Yu Chen.

Yu Chen couldn’t say anything. He held the letter. He looked at Eliana.

She was staring at Wei Long. Then at the letter. Then at him. Her face had gone through red and come out the other side into something else, and she was standing on the steps of the Great Hall in a gown too big for her with her cap in her hand and people all round them and her whole family somewhere on these same steps, and he watched her decide.

She dropped the cap.

She took hold of his hood, the coloured one round his neck and down his back, in both hands, and pulled him down, and kissed him.

In front of everyone. In the sun on the steps, in front of a thousand graduates and the flower man and Wei Long, who said “Ah” and looked at the sky. She held him down by his hood and kissed him with her eyes shut, hard, as if she’d been saving it up for four years and the steps were the place she’d been saving it for. He’d kissed her under the arch in April. This was different. This was hers, on her day, with her degree under her arm, and she’d chosen the most public place on the whole hill to do it.

He put his hand on the back of her head and kissed her back, and forgot where he was.

When she let go of his hood there were people looking. A lot of people. Somebody near the bottom of the steps whistled.

And there was a sound from behind her like someone being stood on, and Elara came through the crowd in a summer dress with her face already crying, and threw her arms round her little sister so hard that Eliana’s cap, which someone had picked up and put back on her head, fell off and rolled down two steps.

Eliana stood in her sister’s arms with her own arms out stiff at her sides.

“Okay,” she said. “Okay. You can stop now.”

Elara didn’t stop. Eliana looked at Yu Chen over her sister’s shoulder with an expression of total despair, and he laughed, out loud, on the steps, and couldn’t make himself stop either.

✦ ✦ ✦

He saw Lin Jian over the crowd.

He was at the top of the steps, by the door of the hall, with Uncle Mok beside him. He’d seen it. Yu Chen knew he had, from the way he was standing, and from his face, which had shut. Not angry. Lin Jian’s face didn’t go angry; it went closed, like a shop at night, every shutter down. He was looking at his youngest daughter in her sister’s arms, and then he looked down the steps at the boy next door, the policeman’s nephew, in a doctor’s hood, with her kiss still on his mouth.

Yu Chen didn’t look away.

He’d looked away from that man for four years. On the porch in January with the boiler broken, on the kerb, across the birthday table. He’d stood behind walls and over walls and on the far side of rules. He stood on the steps now in his gown and looked back at Lin Jian, steadily, without smiling and without anything else, the way you look at a man you’re going to have to deal with, and wait.

Lin Jian turned and said something to Uncle Mok. Uncle Mok nodded. They went down the far side of the steps, away from all of them, through the crowd, and didn’t come back.

Eliana didn’t see. She was still being held by Elara. Yu Chen didn’t tell her. Not today.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xing Yue was standing at the edge of the steps with his hands behind his back, waiting, the way he waited outside operating theatres.

Yu Chen went over with his ears red and shook his cousin’s hand.

“Emergency,” said Xing Yue. “You’ll be good at it. You don’t panic and you don’t like being thanked.”

Yu Chen looked at him.

He hadn’t said anything to Xing Yue about emergency medicine. He hadn’t said it to anyone. He hadn’t, really, said it to himself. He’d only thought it on the stairwell a year and a half ago with his hands on his face, and once in the car park watching the sun come up with her asleep on his shoulder, and Xing Yue had sat across a table from him twice a term for four years and worked it out anyway.

It felt like being handed something heavy and not knowing where to put it down.

“Thank you,” he said.

Xing Yue nodded, once, and let go of his hand. Elara came and put her arm through Xing Yue’s, with her face still wet, and the two of them went off down the steps together, and Yu Chen watched them go and thought that his cousin was the most frightening surgeon in the city and had just told him something nobody else could have.

Eliana came and stood next to him. She’d got her cap back. She was holding it against her chest with her scroll.

“What did he say?”

“He said I’ll be good in emergency.”

She looked up at him. “You will.”

“You don’t know that.”

“I do. I’ve known since February last year. You came out of that department in pieces and went back in on Monday.” She pushed her glasses up. “It’s on the spreadsheet.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They walked home from the bus at the bottom of the hill, in the evening, in their gowns still, because she wouldn’t take hers off. The lane was warm and smelled of the noodle stall. The noodle man saw them coming, two people in black gowns, holding hands, and put down his ladle and clapped, slowly, three times, and went back to his pot.

At the bottom of the Lin steps she stopped.

The tall house was dark except for one window. Her father’s. Yellow, the way it always was.

She looked up at it for a while. He waited.

“He saw, didn’t he,” she said. “On the steps.”

He thought about lying. He didn’t.

“Yes.”

She nodded. She didn’t let go of his hand.

“Okay,” she said. “Good.” She looked at the window a moment longer. Then she looked at him, in his gown, with the coloured hood still crooked where she’d pulled on it. “Come up later. After he’s asleep. I want to show you the wall.”

“The wall?”

“The screens. What I do all night. You’ve never seen it working.” She was going red again. “I want you to see it. Today. I don’t know why today.”

“I’ll come up,” said Yu Chen.

She went up the three steps in her gown and got the red door open, and at the top she turned round and lifted her hand to him, the way she’d lifted it to a grey car once, except that this time she didn’t do it a little. She did it all the way.

chapters.title: The Neighbour and the Cold Gaze
chapters.desc: At the first Sunday lunch after graduation, Lin Jian tells the table, and not his daughter, that she won’t be wasting a Lin future on a policeman’s nephew. Yu Chen, who has never raised his voice in that house, stands up.
chapters.epigraph: “You talk about her as if she isn’t here. She’s always here. You’ve just never looked.” — Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
Elowen invited him. Not Eliana. That was the first thing that went wrong, and Eliana didn’t find out about it until Saturday night.

“I asked him,” said Elowen on the phone, in the voice she used for flower orders. “For tomorrow. One o’clock. He said yes.”

“You can’t just—”

“I can. It’s my lunch. It’s been my rule for years. Everyone comes, and everyone brings who they’re with.” A pause. “You kissed him on the steps of the Great Hall, Yu-er. Elara cried for an hour. Baba saw. It’s not a secret any more, so it’s not going to be a secret at my table either.”

“Baba hasn’t said anything.”

“Baba hasn’t said anything to you,” said Elowen. “He’s said plenty to me. That’s why he’s coming to lunch. So that Baba has to look at him.”

Eliana sat on her camp bed with the phone against her ear and her stomach going.

“What did Baba say to you?”

“It doesn’t matter.”

“Elowen.”

“He said the policeman’s house has wanted something from this family for twenty years,” said Elowen, “and now it’s taken the one thing he couldn’t watch. That’s what he said.” Her voice went softer. “He doesn’t mean the boy, Yu-er. He means himself. But he’ll say it about the boy. So I’m putting the boy at the table, and we’re all going to sit there, and Baba’s going to have to eat his soup.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He came at one in a white shirt, ironed, with a box of pears from the good fruit shop on Harbour Road.

She saw him from the top of the stairs. He came up the three steps of the tall house the proper way, from the lane, and knocked on the red door, and Ah Sim opened it, and looked up at him, and then took the pears and said, “Shoes,” and let him in.

He’d been in the house before. Through the back gate, over the wall, up the stairs on the edges at two in the morning. He’d never come in through the front door to sit at the table as a guest, and she watched him stand in the hall in his socks with his hands at his sides, too tall for it, and look round as if he’d never seen it before.

“Wei Long said bring fruit,” he said, when she came down. “And don’t talk about your father, and don’t talk at all.”

“That’s good advice,” said Eliana. “Take it.”

He looked at her face. Whatever he saw there made his own go careful.

“Do you want me to go?” he said. “I’ll go. I’ll tell Elowen I’m on call.”

“You’re not on call. You don’t start till August.” She pushed her glasses up. “And you don’t lie.”

“I’d lie for this.”

“No,” said Eliana. “I want you here. Sit next to me, and don’t let him make you talk.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The long table had all its chairs out. Baba at the head, in his cardigan. Elowen at his right, then Zhao. Raiden and Jinx, with Jinx’s arm still in its dressing. Evangeline and Jun Hyuk, who had brought an enormous dish of something and was explaining it to Ah Sim, who wasn’t listening. Elara was on call, and so, by a coincidence nobody believed, was her doctor. Eliana at the far end, where she always sat, by the window. Yu Chen beside her.

Baba didn’t look at him. He didn’t look at either of them. He drank his soup.

For twenty minutes it was almost all right. Jun Hyuk talked, the way Jun Hyuk talked, which filled up any room it was in. Raiden told a long story about a client who’d wanted a panic room shaped like a boat. Zhao said “Hm” twice, and once, unexpectedly, passed Yu Chen the rice without being asked, and gave him the four-second look, and went back to his food. Yu Chen said thank you. He said almost nothing else. He ate, and kept his elbows in, and answered Jun Hyuk’s questions about the emergency department in a few plain words, and under the table his knee was against hers, warm, and didn’t move.

She began to think it might be fine.

Then Raiden, who could never leave a silence alone, said, “So Yu Chen starts at City Hospital in August. Real doctor. Proper white coat.”

“He had a white coat before,” said Jinx.

“This one’s got a name on it.”

Baba put his spoon down.

He didn’t put it down hard. He put it down beside his bowl, exactly, the way he put things down at the fishing-net building when a meeting was over. He looked down the table at Elowen.

“Chen Si has a place for your sister,” he said. “When she’s finished. Full time. A proper position.” He picked up his tea. “She’ll have a future. A Lin future. I’m not going to watch her waste it on a policeman’s nephew who carries her shopping.”

The table stopped.

Not all at once. Jun Hyuk stopped in the middle of a word. Raiden looked at his plate. Jinx’s head came up. Evangeline went still, the way she did, all of her at once, like a held breath. Elowen put her chopsticks down and started to say “Baba—”

Eliana didn’t move.

It was what he always did. It was what he’d done her whole life. He said it about her, to the table, over her head, as if she were a piece of furniture at the far end that couldn’t hear. He hadn’t even said her name. Your sister. She sat by the window with her hands in her lap and her face burning and her throat shut, and she felt the old thing happen, the thing that had always happened in this room: she went small. She went somewhere inside the hoodie where none of it could reach. She’d let it go by. She’d always let it go by.

Beside her, Yu Chen stood up.

He did it slowly. He put his napkin on the table beside his bowl, folded once, and pushed his chair back, and stood, and he was taller standing than anyone in the room except Jun Hyuk. He didn’t raise his voice. She’d never once heard him raise it. He went the other way, slower and lower and colder, until the pleasant thing was gone off him entirely and what was left was the thing she’d seen on the path outside the psychology building, and in the garden with Wei Long, and once, for two seconds, at this same table, years ago.

“You talk about her as if she isn’t here,” said Yu Chen.

Baba looked up at him.

“She’s here. She’s always here. She’s at the end of this table every Sunday.” He didn’t look away from Lin Jian’s face. “You don’t look at her. You’ve never looked at her. You talk about her to her sisters and to your cook and to your driver, and she’s sitting there, and she can hear you. She’s always been able to hear you.”

Nobody breathed.

“You can say what you like about me,” said Yu Chen. “I don’t mind. I’m the policeman’s nephew. I carry her shopping. That’s all true. But if you’ve got something to say about her future, you can say it to her. She’s right there. Look at her.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Baba stood up.

He was a big man. He’d been the most frightening man in the Walled City for thirty years, and he still stood like it. He pushed his chair back and came round the head of the table, not fast, one hand on the backs of the chairs, towards the far end, towards the window, towards her.

She didn’t know what he was going to do. She didn’t think he knew either.

Yu Chen moved.

He stepped round behind her chair, so that he was between her and her father, and stopped there, with his back to her and his hands at his sides. He didn’t touch her. He didn’t touch Baba. He just stood there in his ironed white shirt, in the way.

Baba stopped two chairs from him.

They looked at each other. The whole table was watching. Zhao had turned in his chair, and his hand had gone flat on the table, and Jun Hyuk had stopped smiling for the first time since he’d arrived.

“Get out of my house,” said Baba. He said it to Yu Chen.

“I’ll go when she wants to go,” said Yu Chen. “Not before.”

Baba’s face didn’t change.

He looked past Yu Chen’s shoulder, then. For the first time. At her.

It lasted a second, maybe two. But it was at her, her face, not at the table or the window or the space beside her. She saw his eyes on her, the way they almost never were, and in them there was something she couldn’t read at all, something that looked almost like fear, and then he looked away.

“Elowen,” he said. “I’ll be in my study.”

He went out. They heard him on the stairs, slow and heavy. They heard his door shut.

Elowen was half out of her chair. She stayed that way, with her hand on the table. Raiden was still looking at his plate. Evangeline was looking at Eliana. Zhao took his hand off the table.

Yu Chen didn’t move from behind her chair until the study door had been shut for a full minute.

Then he turned round. He looked down at her, and his face had come back. It was his own face again, the one he kept for her, frightened under it, and she understood that he’d been frightened the whole time.

“Do you want to go?” he said.

She stood up.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was angry with him on the steps.

She didn’t expect it. She came out of the red door into the hot white afternoon with him behind her, and the door shut, and she turned round on the top step and her voice came out high and shaking.

“You made it worse.”

He stopped.

“You stood up. In his house. At his table. In front of everyone. Nobody does that. Elowen doesn’t do that, and he’s frightened of Elowen.” She was shaking. “Now he’s in his study and he’s never going to come out, and every Sunday’s going to be like this, and he looked at me, he looked at me, and you don’t know what that—you don’t know what you’ve—”

She stopped, because her voice had gone.

He didn’t argue. He stood on the step below her in the sun with his ironed shirt and his hands at his sides, and let her shout. He’d have let her shout all afternoon. She could see it.

“I’m sorry,” he said. “I couldn’t sit there.”

“I sit there. Every week. I’ve always sat there.”

“I know,” said Yu Chen. “That’s why I couldn’t.”

She looked at him.

It went through her the way the cold went through him. Something she’d been holding for so long, at the end of a table, by a window, small. He’d stood up for it. Nobody had ever stood up for it. Not even her, not once. She’d made it so small nobody could see it, and he’d seen it anyway, from next door, for four years, and today he’d stood up in front of her whole family and the most frightening man in the Walled City and put his body between them.

She came down the one step between them and took his face in both hands and kissed him.

On the front steps of her father’s house. In the middle of the afternoon. Under the window of the study, which looked straight down onto these steps; she knew it did, she’d put the camera on that corner herself. She kissed him there on purpose, with the noodle man watching from his stall and the old man’s birds singing on the far side, and she knew exactly what it was: a flag on a wall.

He made a sound against her mouth and put his arms round her and held her up off the step, all of her, as if he’d been waiting to do it since the soup.

“He’ll see,” he said.

“I want him to.” She kissed him again. “Take me to your house. The front way. Through the front door. In the daylight.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He took her through the front door.

Auntie Dai didn’t come on Sundays. The house was quiet and warm and the hall smelled of the floor polish she used, and he shut the door behind them and she pulled him down the hall by his ironed shirt and up the stairs, not on the edges, on the middle of every step, loud, so that the whole house heard it.

In his room the afternoon came in through the curtains gold and hot. She stood in the middle of it and started undoing his buttons, and her hands were shaking so much that she couldn’t do them, and he put his hands over hers.

“Slow down,” he said.

“I don’t want to.”

“I know. Let me.” He undid them himself, one at a time, with his eyes on her face. “You’re still shaking.”

“So are you.”

“I stood up to your father,” said Yu Chen. His voice wasn’t steady. “I’m allowed to shake.”

She laughed, a little, wet, and he kissed her while she was laughing, and the shirt came off and her hoodie came off, and his hands were on her back, warm, careful, then not careful, and he laid her down on his bed in the gold light from the lane.

The night after the nine days had been finding each other again. This was something else. She’d chosen him in her father’s house, at her father’s table, on her father’s steps, and she wanted him to know it with every part of her, and she didn’t know how to say it, so she said it the only way she’d ever been able to say anything. She pulled him close and didn’t let go. She kissed his shoulder and his throat and the place on his chest where his heart was going too hard. She held his face and made him look at her, in daylight, with her glasses off and nothing between them, and let him see all of it, the shaking and the wanting and the thing under both of them that she’d never had a word for.

He saw it. She watched him see it. He said her name like he was holding something breakable and then he stopped being careful, because she asked him to, and she held on to him in the hot afternoon with the curtains moving and the birds going on the other side of the wall, and somewhere in the middle of it she started crying without any noise, and didn’t stop, and he didn’t stop either, and he kissed her wet face and said I’ve got you into her hair, over and over, until it was only true.

Afterwards she lay against him with her cheek on his chest and the light going orange on the wall.

“He looked at me,” she said. “At the table. Did you see?”

“I saw.”

“He never looks at me.”

“I know,” said Yu Chen. His hand moved in her hair. “He looked frightened.”

“Of you?”

He was quiet for a while.

“No,” he said. “Of you, I think.”

She lay there and thought about it. Across the two gardens, through the gap in his curtains, she could see the back of the tall house and the one window on the second floor that was her father’s study. The blind was down. It had been down all afternoon.

She didn’t know what he was doing in there. She didn’t know whether he’d seen the steps. She thought he had.

“He’s going to do something,” she said. “He’s going to make it so I can’t go anywhere. That’s what the job is. Chen Si. I heard it in March. He thinks if I’m working for him upstairs forever, I’ll never leave.”

“What do you want?” said Yu Chen.

It was the first time anyone had asked her. She lay against his chest in the orange light and didn’t answer, because she didn’t know yet, and he didn’t push. He just kept his hand moving in her hair, and waited, the way he always waited, and she understood for the first time that waiting had never been the same thing as doing nothing.

chapters.title: A Job Offer and a Night Shift
chapters.desc: Her father summons her to the fishing-net building, where Chen Si offers her the Syndicate’s top security post, full time, for life. The same night Yu Chen works his first night as a real doctor, and she takes dinner up to the top of the car park.
chapters.epigraph: “He offered me a corner office so I’d never have to leave. You gave me tea in a car park so I’d know I could.” — Eliana Lin
chapters.content:
The summons came through Uncle Mok, which was how Baba summoned anyone.

“Your father would like you at the office,” said Uncle Mok, at the bottom of the steps on Thursday morning, in his good grey jacket, with the old black Mercedes ticking behind him. “At eleven. Mr. Chen will be there.” He opened the back door. “I’m to drive you.”

She looked at the car. She looked at the window of Yu Chen’s kitchen, where he wasn’t, because he’d gone back to bed at seven to sleep before his first night shift and was, she knew, lying there not sleeping. She looked at Uncle Mok, who had driven her everywhere for years and never once told her what Baba wanted.

“Is it the job?” she said.

Uncle Mok looked at the lane.

“I’m only the driver, Miss Eliana.”

She got in.

✦ ✦ ✦

The fishing-net building stood at the end of the old harbour wall, five storeys of grey stone with the nets still hung along its front from iron hooks, the way they’d been hung when it really was a fishing company, a hundred years ago. Baba’s office was at the top. She’d been in it perhaps four times in her life.

It hadn’t changed. Dark wood, a long desk, the harbour through the window, a smell of old paper and tea. Baba sat behind the desk in his suit. Chen Si sat in a chair by the window with one leg crossed over the other, in a grey suit that probably cost more than the Mercedes, and stood up when she came in, which Baba didn’t. Qian stood by the wall with a folder and a packet of antacids sticking out of his jacket pocket.

“Eliana,” said Chen Si. “Thank you for coming.”

She’d worked for him for four years. She’d met him in person perhaps ten times. He was always the same: quiet, exact, polite in a way that made people afraid. She’d seen him make a man cry once without raising his voice. He was looking at her now the way he looked at everyone, as if he’d already read the whole of her and was being kind enough not to say so.

“Sit down, please,” he said.

She sat in the chair in front of the desk. Baba didn’t look at her. He looked at the papers in front of him.

“Your father and I have been talking,” said Chen Si. “For some time. You’ve finished your degree. With a first, I’m told; congratulations. And you’ve done more for my people in four years than anyone I’ve ever employed, without ever once being in the same room as most of them.” He sat down again by the window. “I’d like you to come and do it properly. Full time. Head of all of it. Everything we have that runs on a screen would be yours, and everyone who looks after it would answer to you. You’d have an office here, in this building. Your father’s offered you the corner on the floor below.” He nodded at Qian. “Qian has the terms.”

Qian came forward and put the folder on the desk in front of her. He opened it to the second page. There was a number on it.

She looked at the number. Qian looked at the ceiling.

It was a year’s pay, and it was more than she’d earned in four years. It was the kind of number that bought houses on the hill.

“You’d never need to go anywhere,” said Baba.

He said it to the papers. Not to her. But he said it in the room with her in it, which was new.

She sat still.

She understood all of it at once, the way she understood a system the moment she saw the shape of it. The corner office on the floor below Baba’s. Uncle Mok driving her here every morning and home every night. The number, so big she’d never need anything from anyone else. Chen Si’s people answering to her, so she’d never have time for anything else. The policeman’s nephew starting at the hospital, nights, while she sat in the fishing-net building, days. Baba upstairs. Her, downstairs. Forever.

It was a beautiful cage. It was the most beautiful thing anyone in her family had ever made for her, and he’d made it out of the only thing he knew how to give, which was a place to be kept.

She closed the folder.

“Thank you,” she said to Chen Si.

Chen Si waited.

“I’m going to think about it.” She heard her own voice, and it was small, the in-person voice, the one that couldn’t order a coffee. She kept going. “Tell my father,” she said, still looking at Chen Si, not at Baba, “that I’ll let him know.”

The room went quiet.

Chen Si’s face didn’t move. But she saw something at the corner of his mouth, faint, that might have been approval, and he looked across the desk at Baba, who had stopped turning the papers over.

“Of course,” said Chen Si. “Take whatever time you need.”

Baba didn’t say anything at all.

She got up and went out, and down the stone stairs past the floor below, past a corner office with its door open and nothing in it yet but a desk and a window full of harbour, and out onto the harbour wall into the wind, and she stood by the nets with her hands in her hoodie pocket and shook for ten minutes, and didn’t know if it was fear or something else.

Uncle Mok drove her home. Neither of them said anything. At the bottom of the steps he got out and opened her door, and as she got out he said, looking at the lane, “Your mother used to make him wait as well,” and got back in the car before she could ask him anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yu Chen’s first night shift started at eight.

He’d been an intern for eleven days. Eleven days of being Dr. Wang on a badge, and signing things, and being the person people turned to when they wanted a doctor and finding out that he was it. He’d done days in the emergency department, with seniors all round him. Tonight there’d be fewer of them. Dr. Toh was the consultant on, which he was glad of and frightened of in equal amounts.

“Wang,” she said, when he came in. She was in her cardigan. She looked at his new badge. “Doctor now.”

“Yes, Dr. Toh.”

“Don’t be frightened of the department,” she said. “Be frightened of not asking. If you don’t know, you ask me. If you think you know and you’re not sure, you ask me. I’d rather be woken up a hundred times than sign one certificate I didn’t need to.”

He wrote it down later. He wrote down most of what she said.

By midnight he’d seen nine patients and knew none of their names. A girl with a sprained wrist. A man who’d been in a fight and wanted it written down that he’d won. A drunk in bay two who called the nurse a word Yu Chen didn’t repeat, and Yu Chen stood at the end of his trolley and said, pleasantly, “You’ll speak to her properly or I’ll ask security to sit with you all night, and they’re very boring,” and the man looked at him and apologised to the nurse, and the nurse looked at Yu Chen afterwards with her eyebrows up.

He didn’t think about it. He went on to the next one.

At ten past one an old man came in with his son, holding his stomach. Indigestion, the son said. Something he’d eaten. He wanted something for it and to go home. The old man was grey and sweating and kept saying he was fine.

Yu Chen looked at him, and didn’t like the grey.

He did the trace of the heart himself, because it was quick and because something in him said to. He looked at it. He looked at it again. Then he walked, not ran, to the desk where Dr. Toh was writing, and put it down in front of her, and said, “I think this is his heart. Not his stomach. I’m not sure. I’m asking.”

She looked at it once.

“You’re right,” she said, and stood up, and after that it went fast, the cardiology team on the phone, and the old man on a trolley going up to the lab with his son running behind, and his grey face going past Yu Chen in the corridor looking frightened and alive.

Toh came back twenty minutes later. She stood beside him at the desk.

“Good,” she said. That was all.

He went to wash his hands, and in the corner by the sink he took his phone out and opened the food app, the way he always did, without thinking.

Nothing since lunch.

There was a message under it instead.

Eliana: top deck. 2am. bring yourself

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d been up there since half past one, sitting on the bonnet of his Volvo with two cartons of noodles from the all-night place at the bottom of the hill going cold in a bag beside her.

The top deck of the car park was open to the sky. It was the only quiet place in the hospital. Below her the hill went down to the harbour, black, with its chain of lights, and above her, because the city was asleep, there were stars. Not many. Not like the house by the sea. But real ones.

He came out of the stairwell door at five past two in blue scrubs with his badge on and his hair standing up. He saw her and stopped.

She’d thought about what to say all the way up in the lift. She didn’t say any of it.

“You saved one,” she said. “Didn’t you. I can see it.”

“How can you see it?”

“You’re walking differently.” She held out the bag. “Eat something. You’ve got twenty minutes. I timed it with the nurse at the desk. She said Dr. Toh says you can have twenty.”

He came across the empty deck and took the bag off her and put it down on the bonnet without looking at it. He looked at her instead.

“Your father,” he said. “Today. Auntie Dai said Ah Sim said Mok took you to the fishing-net building. What happened?”

She hadn’t told him. She’d meant to, and then he’d been asleep, or not asleep, and then he’d been at work, and she’d sat on the bonnet for half an hour trying to decide how to say it.

“He offered me a job,” she said. “Chen Si did. Full time. All of it. An office on the floor below his. A lot of money. A lot.” She looked at the harbour. “So I’d never need to go anywhere.”

He was quiet.

“What did you say?”

“I said I’d think about it.” She looked at him. “I told Chen Si to tell my father I’d let him know. To his face. In his office. Like he does it to me.”

He stared at her.

Then he started to laugh. Not loud. It came up out of him in the empty car park, tired and surprised, and he put his hand over his face and laughed into it, and she sat on the bonnet and watched him and felt her own mouth starting to go.

“You made him wait,” he said, through his hand.

“Uncle Mok said my mother used to make him wait.”

He took his hand away from his face.

He looked at her on the bonnet of his car at two in the morning, in her hoodie, with the stars over her and noodles going cold beside her and her father’s cage folded up somewhere in a drawer, and she saw him decide something.

He didn’t say what. He came the last step and put one hand on the bonnet on either side of her and kissed her.

Nothing about it was careful. This was the top deck of the car park of the hospital he’d worked in for eleven days, with a camera on the lamp post and the stairwell door that anyone could come through, a porter, a nurse, Dr. Toh, and he was always the careful one and he kissed her as if he’d forgotten how. He pulled her off the bonnet into him and turned with her so her back was against the side of the Volvo, against the cool dark-green door, and kissed her with his hands in her hair and her glasses going crooked and the badge on his scrubs digging into her chest, and she grabbed the front of his scrubs and held on and kissed him back, and the stars went round.

When he stopped they were both breathing hard. He kept his forehead on hers.

“Is this all right?” he said. “Here?”

She laughed into his mouth. He’d started asking after, lately, when it was already done. It was the most him thing in the world.

“Yes,” she said. “Yes. Do it again.”

He did it again.

✦ ✦ ✦

He ate the noodles in the end, sitting on the bonnet beside her with the carton on his knee, and she drank his tea out of the flask, because he’d brought it up with him in his pocket, and it was too sweet, and it was exactly right.

“I don’t know what I’m going to say,” she said. “To Baba. I don’t know.”

“You don’t have to know tonight.”

“He’s going to want an answer.”

“Then he can wait,” said Yu Chen. “Your mother made him.” He put the carton down. “I’m not going to tell you what to say. It’s yours. Whatever you say, I’ll be in the car park.”

She looked at him.

“That’s not advice.”

“No. I’m bad at advice. Wei Long says so.” He picked up the flask and put it back in her hands. “It’s tea.”

His pager went. He looked at it, and stood up, and he was a doctor again, in three seconds, his whole face going clear and still.

“Go on,” she said.

He went. At the stairwell door he stopped and looked back at her, sitting on his car under the stars with his flask, and lifted his hand, and went in.

✦ ✦ ✦

He got home at half past nine on Friday morning.

He’d been awake for twenty-six hours. He came down the lane with his bag over his shoulder and his eyes half shut, and he had his key out at the bottom of his own steps, and before he got to the top the door opened from the inside.

She was there. In his T-shirt, barefoot, with her hair down and the pencil in her hand, because she’d let herself in at six with the key under the brick and been waiting for him in his bed ever since.

“You’re not supposed to be here,” he said. “Auntie Dai—”

“Auntie Dai’s gone to the market. She made you congee. It’s on the stove.” She took his bag off his shoulder and dropped it in the hall. “Come here.”

“I haven’t slept. I smell of the hospital.”

“I don’t care,” said Eliana, and took him by the strings of his scrubs, the ones at his waist, and pulled him in, and kissed him in his own doorway, and shut the door behind him with her foot.

It was slow, after that, because he was too tired for it to be anything else, and she didn’t want it to be anything else. She took him upstairs by the hand and took his scrubs off him and pushed him down into the bed she’d made warm, and lay down with him in the morning light coming through the gap in the curtains. He kissed her as if he were half asleep and didn’t want to wake up from it. She held his face. He said her name into her neck, slurred, and she laughed, and he laughed too, and then neither of them was laughing; it was only the two of them in the warm bed in the morning, unhurried, nothing to prove, his hands moving on her slowly as if he’d been thinking about them all night, which he said he had, and she believed him.

He fell asleep afterwards almost at once, with his face in her hair.

She lay awake in his bed with the light moving on the wall, and thought about a corner office, and a number on a page, and a car park with stars over it, and she knew, the way she knew when a thing was built wrong, which one she was going to choose. She just didn’t know how to say it to her father yet.

She held on to Yu Chen and let him sleep.

chapters.title: The Breach
chapters.desc: For the first time in her life, someone gets through Eliana’s walls — a crew called Magpie, let in by an old key she handed out herself in second year. It isn’t just data. It’s the family’s safe-house addresses, and a clock starts.
chapters.epigraph: “Someone’s inside. Not my father’s enemy. Mine. He got in with a door I left open three years ago and forgot about.” — Eliana Lin
chapters.content:
The fence woke her at twenty to four on Friday morning, and it was the wrong alarm.

She’d built two. One was the short double buzz for a threat to the family — the Lin name, the house, her sisters’ faces. The other was quieter and she’d almost never heard it, because it was the one that watched her own walls, the ones that watched everything else. It was a long, low note, three times, and it meant that someone was where no one was ever supposed to be.

She was awake and across the room before the third note finished.

She read what it was telling her. Then she sat down in the chair, slowly, because her legs had gone, and read it again.

Someone was inside.

Not inside a bank, or a market, or a stranger’s phone. Inside hers. Inside the system she’d built for Chen Si’s people over four years, the one that held the things she kept so that the Lin name never came up anywhere it shouldn’t — and, in the oldest, most careful part of it, behind more walls than anything else she’d ever made, the one thing she’d sworn to herself she would never lose: the list. Where the family went when the family had to disappear. Evangeline’s house on the island. Fig Tree Lane. The flat Elowen kept that no one talked about. Addresses nobody was supposed to be able to find, held in the one place she’d been sure no one could reach.

Someone had reached it.

She didn’t know how long they’d been there. That was the thing that made her cold all the way down. The fence had caught them on the way out, not the way in. They’d already been inside. They’d already seen.

She put her hand over her mouth and made herself breathe.

Then she started to work.

✦ ✦ ✦

By six she knew three things, and each one was worse than the last.

The first was that they were real. Not a boy in her year showing off, not a firm’s lawyer with a feeling. A crew, a proper one, who did this for money and were good at it, good enough to have got past things that had never been got past, and quiet enough that she’d nearly missed them.

The second was the way in.

That was the one she sat and stared at without moving, the longest. She’d found the open door they’d walked through, and there was nothing clever about it. It was a key. An old one, that she’d cut herself in her second year and handed to Dominic Ip so he could do his half of a group project at night, and never thought about again. Somewhere in the three years since, Dominic had sold it, or lost it, or had it taken, and it had ended up with people who’d noticed whose key it was.

They hadn’t broken her walls. She’d handed them a door and forgotten to lock it.

The third thing was why. She found that last, and when she found it she put her head down on the desk.

The name under all of it, when she pulled it up, was a firm. Calder Risk Partners. The firm the bank paid to send people who weren’t lawyers. The one that had sent a man in a grey jacket to a lecture hall in March. In the summer the bank had been fined over the door she’d found, the one she’d stood up and told two hundred people about, and the firm had been quiet for six months, and then it hadn’t been quiet any more. They hadn’t come for her this time with a man in a jacket. They’d come for everything she had, and found the one thing worth more than anything, and now they were holding it.

She sat with her head on the desk in the dark room with the screens over her and worked out, slowly, that she’d done this. Her own pride had done it, in March, in front of two hundred people. Her own carelessness had done it, in second year, with a key she handed to a boy and forgot. The thing she’d built her whole life to prevent had happened, and she’d let it in herself, twice.

Then she lifted her head, because her sister’s address was in a stranger’s hands, and there wasn’t time to be sick about it.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t call her father.

She thought about it. For about four seconds, at seven in the morning, with the grey light coming round the blackout curtain, she thought about going down the stairs and across the landing and knocking on his study door and telling him, because he was the most frightening man in the Walled City and he had men who could find anyone and do anything, and if she told him, the people who had the list would stop existing, and so would the problem, and she’d never have to be frightened again.

And then she’d be his. The job she hadn’t answered would answer itself. There’d be no need to think about the corner office, because she’d already have walked into it, because when the family was in danger you went to the man who kept the family safe, and that man was downstairs, and the price of his help was that you belonged to him afterwards.

She didn’t call her father.

She didn’t call Haozhen either, and she wanted to; he’d handled the grey jacket, he’d know what Calder was and how it worked. But Serafina had gone off at the Needle two weeks ago, and Haozhen hadn’t left her side since, and she wasn’t going to take him away from her for this. She’d have cut off her own hand first.

She had a third number. She’d had it for two years, in the quiet tab, where only she could see it. Wei Long’s. He’d given it to her over a garden wall and told her that one day it might stop being about keeping the family out of the papers and start being about something worse, and that there’d be a door that wasn’t her father’s and wasn’t the Syndicate’s, and she could walk through it when she was ready.

She looked at the number, and didn’t call it.

She wasn’t ready. Not yet. She didn’t have enough. You didn’t hand a detective a feeling; you handed him a name and an address and a fact he could use, and she didn’t have those yet, she had the shape of them. First she had to find the crew. Find the people holding the list, before they did anything with it, before they sold it on or sent it to Calder or posted it somewhere the whole dark half of the world could see. Find them, and get it back, and have something solid in her hands.

She had until they decided to use it. She didn’t know how long that was. She gave herself thirty-six hours before she made herself stop guessing, because a number you could see was better than a fear you couldn’t.

Thirty-six hours. By Saturday night she had to have them.

She started.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yu Chen came over the wall at seven, the way he did, with the flask.

He was off that day and had slept a whole night for once, and he’d made her tea, and he let himself in with the key and came up the stairs on the edges and found her at the screens with her hood up and her hands going and a face he hadn’t seen on her before.

He stopped in the doorway.

“What happened,” he said. Not a question. He never asked the question. But he could read her better than her own family, and he read this.

“Someone’s inside,” she said. She didn’t turn round. “Not a bank. Not a stranger. Mine. The thing I built. They got into the thing I built.” Her voice was flat and fast. “It’s got the list in it. Where everyone goes. Where Evangeline is. Fig Tree Lane. All of it. They’ve seen it. They’re holding it.”

He put the flask down on the desk carefully, square to the edge, the way he did when his hands wanted to do something else.

“How did they—”

“Don’t,” she said. “Please. Not now. I can’t tell you how and I can’t explain it and I don’t have the—just don’t ask me the how. I need all of it for this.” She pressed the heels of her hands into her eyes under her glasses. “I did it. That’s all you need. It got in because of something I did. Three years ago. And in March. It’s my fault, it’s completely my fault, and I have to fix it before they do anything, and I don’t know how long I’ve got, and I can’t call Baba and I can’t call Haozhen and I have to do it myself.”

“Why can’t you call your father?”

She took her hands off her eyes and looked at him.

“Because then I’m his,” she said. “Forever. That’s the price. He’d fix it in a day and I’d never leave the fishing-net building again. That’s what the job is. That’s what the job’s always been. If I run to him with this, I’ve taken it. I’ve said yes to all of it.” She turned back to the screens. “I’m not saying yes to it. Not like this. Not scared.”

He was quiet behind her.

She waited for it. She waited for let me call Wei Long or tell your father, it’s your family or this is too much, you can’t do this alone, because any of them would have been reasonable, and any of them would have been the thing anyone else would say. She braced for it the way she’d braced for an argument that time by the sea, and it didn’t come.

What came was his hand on her shoulder, once, and then him taking his coat off.

“What do you need,” he said.

She looked round at him.

“I can’t help with the screens,” he said. “You know that. I don’t understand most of it. So tell me the rest. Do you eat? Do you sleep? When? I’ll do all of that. I’ll keep you alive and I’ll keep the door, and you do the thing you’re for.” He rolled his sleeves up. “However long this takes, I’ve got it too. I’m not going to work tomorrow. I already texted Dr. Toh. I told her a family thing. It’s not a lie.”

She stared at him.

“You can’t just not go to work.”

“I can. I did.” He pulled the second chair over, the one she never used, and sat down by the door, out of her light, with his back to the wall, where he could see her and the door at the same time. “Drink the tea. It’s getting cold. That’s the first thing. Then tell me what time you last ate, so I know when to make you eat again.”

She turned back to the screens because her eyes had gone hot and she wasn’t going to do that now.

“Lunch yesterday,” she said. “Toast.”

“Then you’re eating in an hour whether you’ve found them or not,” said Yu Chen. “That’s the deal. I won’t ask what you find. I won’t touch anything. But you eat when I say, and you drink when I say, and when it’s three in the morning and you’ve been still for too long I’m going to make you stand up and look out of the window at nothing for two minutes, because that’s what Toh makes me do, and it works.” He leaned back in the chair. “That’s my job. That’s the whole of it. Point me at it.”

She drank the tea.

It was too sweet, because he still made it too sweet after all this time, and it was the best thing she’d ever tasted, and she sat in the dark room with her sister’s address in a stranger’s hands and drank it, and started to hunt.

✦ ✦ ✦

The morning went. She didn’t notice it going.

He kept the deal. At eight he put food beside her and she ate it with one hand. At ten he made her stand up and look out of the gap in the curtain at the grey garden for two minutes, and she stood there shaking with her hands in fists and he stood behind her and didn’t touch her and didn’t talk, and she went back to the chair steadier. At one he made tea again. He kept the flask filled. He went down twice to answer the door when a parcel came and once to move Ah Sim’s enquiring head off the bottom of the stairs, and both times he came back up on the edges and sat down again by the door without a word.

He didn’t ask her how. He didn’t ask her what she’d found, or what the list was, or who Calder was, or whether she’d called the police. He’d said he wouldn’t, years ago, and he didn’t, even now, even watching her come apart.

By four in the afternoon she had a thread. Not them, not yet, but a thread; a lazy thing somebody on the crew had done, the kind of small carelessness that she did for a living and that other people did too when they thought no one like her was watching. It was enough to pull on. She pulled on it.

She said, without turning round, “I’ve got a corner of it.”

“Good,” he said, from the chair. “Eat first.”

“I don’t want to stop.”

“I know. Eat first anyway. You’ll see it better.”

She ate first. He was right; she saw it better. He was always right about this, about the body, about the hands, about the way you couldn’t think when you’d forgotten you had a body. He’d read it in a book, probably, the way he read everything, PLAN and PLAN B, how to keep a person alive at a desk. She looked at him in the second chair with his sleeves rolled up, keeping the door of her life open the only way he knew how, and something came up in her that had nothing to do with the breach.

She got up and went over and sat down sideways across his lap in the chair, and put her face in his neck, for one minute, just one.

He went still, and then his arms came round her.

“You’re allowed one minute,” she said into his collar. “Then I have to go back.”

“One minute,” he said.

He didn’t say anything else. He held her in the chair with the screens glowing over both of them and his chin on the top of her head, and she breathed him in, the hospital gone off him now and just him, soap and the cold of the garden, and for one minute she wasn’t the thing people were afraid of or the thing her father wanted to keep or the girl who’d left a door open. She was just a person someone was holding.

Then he turned her face up with one hand under her chin and kissed her, once, slow, on her mouth, and then on her forehead, and said, against it, “Go. I’ve got the door.”

She went back to the chair.

Behind her, he filled the flask again, and sat down, and watched the door, and waited, the way he always waited, except that tonight the waiting had a clock in it, and they could both hear it.

chapters.title: Thirty-Six Hours
chapters.desc: She doesn’t sleep for a day and a half, hunting the crew that holds her family’s addresses. Yu Chen doesn’t leave. When she finds them, the choice is hers: give it to her father, who would make them vanish, or hand it to the law.
chapters.epigraph: “I could give this to my father. They’d disappear. Or I could grow up.” — Eliana Lin
chapters.content:
By midnight on Friday the thread had become a shape, and the shape had a name on it.

She wouldn’t say the name out loud yet, in case saying it made her sure before she was. She sat with it on the screen in front of her: a small crew, the kind that got hired and never signed anything, run by one person who’d been careless in exactly one place and nowhere else. A magpie’s name. That was how they signed the one job she’d ever seen them leave a mark on, years ago, a long way from her: a bird that takes bright things.

She had the crew. She didn’t have them yet. Having the name of a thing and having the thing in your hand were two different hunts, and the second was slower, and the second was the one that mattered, because it was the one that ended with her sister’s address back where no one could reach it.

She kept going.

Yu Chen slept for two hours on the camp bed behind her, because she made him, at one, when he’d started answering her slowly. She put the blue blanket over him and went back to the chair, and worked with the sound of him breathing behind her, which helped, which she’d never have admitted. At three he woke up and took over the door again and made her lie down on the camp bed instead, and she said she wouldn’t sleep, and slept for forty minutes, and woke up furious at herself and went back to the screens.

“You slept,” he said.

“I didn’t mean to.”

“I know. Your brain did it without asking. Toh says that’s the body voting.” He put the flask in her hands. “Drink this. It’s four. The worst hour. It’s always the worst hour. It’ll be lighter soon and it’ll feel different.”

It did. The sky went grey behind the curtain and the worst hour passed and the next one came, and somewhere in it she stopped being frightened and started being something colder and better, the thing she turned into when a hunt got close. Her hands stopped shaking. Her face went still. She forgot she had a body again, and he let her, for a while, before he made her eat.

✦ ✦ ✦

Saturday morning Elowen rang.

Eliana let it go to the phone twice before she answered, because she couldn’t let her sister hear what her voice had turned into. The third time she took it, with her eyes still on the screen.

“You sound terrible,” said Elowen.

“I’m fine. I’m on a thing.”

“What thing?”

“A work thing.” She made her voice ordinary. It cost her. “Elowen. Don’t go to the flat this week. The one you keep. And tell Evangeline to stay home. And don’t ask me why, and don’t tell Baba I said it.”

There was a silence on the line.

“Yu-er,” said Elowen. “What’s happened?”

“Nothing’s happened. I’m making sure nothing happens. That’s my whole job, remember.” She shut her eyes. “Please. Just this week. Stay in. Tell Ev. Don’t tell Baba.”

Another silence. Elowen was not a stupid woman. She had married the most dangerous man in the city and she knew the sound of someone keeping the lid on.

“All right,” she said at last. “I’ll tell her. I won’t tell Baba.” A pause. “Is the boy next door with you?”

Eliana looked across the room at Yu Chen, asleep sitting up in the second chair with his head back against the wall, one hand still on the arm of it, keeping the door even while he slept.

“Yes,” she said.

“Good,” said Elowen, and hung up.

✦ ✦ ✦

She found them at two o’clock on Saturday afternoon.

Not a face. She’d never see the face. But a place — a real one, a flat in the eastern district above a phone-repair shop, with a name on the bill that matched the name on the crew that matched the one careless mark they’d left; and the thread back to Calder, the firm that had paid them, clean and whole and solid, the kind of thing you could put in front of a man who dealt in facts. She had it. She had the crew and the firm and the address and the money that ran between them, and she had the list back, pulled out of their hands and the copies she could find burned behind her, and she sat back in the chair and the room went quiet.

She’d done it. In under thirty-six hours, grey and not sleeping, she’d done the thing she’d built her whole life to be able to do, and this time she hadn’t been too late.

And now she had to choose.

She had it all in one place on the screen. Everything Chen Si would need. Everything Wei Long would need. The same facts, the same names, the same address above the phone-repair shop. The difference was who she sent it to.

If she sent it down two floors to her father, through Qian, it would be over by Monday, and the crew above the phone-repair shop would stop existing, and Calder would get a message that made sure no one ever came near the Lins again, and she’d never have to be frightened. And she’d be his. She’d have run to him with her family in danger, the way you were supposed to, and taken the job without ever saying yes to it, and the cage would shut so gently she’d barely feel it close.

If she sent it to the number in the quiet tab, it would be slower. It would be courts and warrants and a detective with a flat voice, and it might not work, and the crew might get bail, and Calder might find a lawyer, and she’d have to make a statement, maybe, somewhere, as herself, Lin Yu, which terrified her more than the breach had. But it would be hers. It would be the door that wasn’t her father’s and wasn’t the Syndicate’s. It would be the thing Wei Long had held out over a wall two years ago and said she could walk through when she was ready.

She sat and looked at both of them, and the clock went on in the quiet room.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I can’t decide,” she said.

It was the first thing she’d said in an hour. Yu Chen was awake now, by the door, and he’d made tea, and he’d seen her stop, and he’d known not to ask whether she’d found them, and he’d waited.

“I’ve got it,” she said. “All of it. I can send it to Baba and it’s over by Monday and I’m his forever. Or I can send it to Wei Long and it’s slow and legal and it might not even work, and I’ll have to be me, out loud, with my name on it, maybe in a court.” She put her hands over her face. “And the right one is the second one. I know it’s the second one. I’ve known for an hour. And I can’t press the button, because the first one is so much easier and so much safer and nobody I love would ever get hurt.”

He didn’t answer straight away.

He didn’t tell her which one to press. She realised, afterwards, that she’d been half waiting for him to, and that he never did; that in four years he had never once told her which door to walk through, only kept them all open and stood by whichever one she chose.

“What happens to you,” he said, “if you press the first one?”

“I become the Eraser. Properly. All the time. In an office under my father.” She took her hands off her face. “I stop being anything else.”

“And the second one?”

“I stay me. I think. The me that’s not just—” she waved at the screens “—this. The one who holds your hand on a hill.” She swallowed. “But it might not work. And if it doesn’t work, and they come for Evangeline, it’ll be because I chose the slow door when I had the fast one.”

He got up out of the chair and came and crouched down beside her, so his face was level with hers, the way he had on the night of the nine days.

“The clerk in the eastern district,” he said. “His hands. You never look at what happens after, and that one time you looked, and it frightened you.” He looked at her. “The fast door is more of that. For the rest of your life. You press it, and you don’t look, and someone’s hands get broken above a phone shop, and you don’t look, because you can’t, because if you looked you couldn’t keep doing it.” He took her cold hand. “The slow door, you get to look. That’s the whole difference. You get to be a person who can afford to look at what happens after.”

She sat there.

“That’s not advice,” she said. “You said you don’t give advice.”

“It isn’t advice. I’m not telling you which one. I’m telling you what each one costs, because you can see everything on those screens except the thing it does to you, and that’s the one thing I can see better than you can.” He squeezed her hand. “Press whichever one you can live with. I’ll be here for both. If it’s the fast one and you become the Eraser in an office under your father, I’ll bring tea to the office. I mean it. I won’t love you less. I’ll just—bring tea to a different room.”

She looked at him.

Then she turned back to the screens, and she picked up her phone, and she opened the quiet tab, and she called the number Wei Long had given her over a garden wall two years ago.

It rang twice.

“Song,” said the flat voice.

“It’s Eliana Lin,” she said. Her own name. Out loud. To a detective. Her voice was small and it shook and she said it anyway. “You gave me a number. You said one day it might stop being about keeping my family out of the papers. It has. I’ve got something. It’s real. It’s names and an address and the money. I want to give it to you. Not to my father.” She shut her eyes. “I want to do it the right way. The slow way. Will you take it?”

There was a silence on the line, and in it she could hear Wei Long being careful, the way he was careful about everything.

“Yes,” he said. “I’ll take it. Don’t touch anything else. Don’t send it anywhere. I’ll come to you. Is Yu Chen there?”

“Yes.”

“Good,” said Wei Long. “Make him make you eat. I’ll be an hour.” A pause, and then, in the same flat voice, as if it cost him nothing, though she knew by now that it did: “You chose the right door. It’s the harder one. Most people don’t.”

He hung up.

She put the phone down on the desk, and her hand was still shaking, and she looked at the screens with everything on them, and she pressed nothing else. She let it sit. She’d handed it over. It wasn’t hers to do any more. For the first time in her life she’d found a thing in the dark and not kept it, not used it, not become the thing that used it; she’d found it and given it to the law and let it go.

Then the thing she’d been holding up for thirty-six hours let go of her, all at once, and she started to cry.

✦ ✦ ✦

She cried the way she always cried, without any noise, in her hood, and then not in her hood, because he pulled it down.

“Come here,” he said, and she got up out of the chair and he caught her, all of her, the way he had in this same room the night she’d finished the fence three years ago, and she put her face in the middle of his chest and shook, and he held on and didn’t say anything and didn’t try to fix it, because it didn’t need fixing; it had been fixed; this was just the thirty-six hours coming out of her.

“I did it,” she said, into his shirt. “I gave it to Wei Long. I didn’t call Baba. I didn’t—”

“I know. I heard you.”

“I said my name. Out loud. To a policeman.”

“I heard that too.” His hand was in her hair. “Lin Yu.”

She laughed, wetly, into his chest, because he almost never used it.

“Don’t,” she said.

“It’s a good name,” said Yu Chen. “You should use it more.”

He got her onto the camp bed, because her legs had gone again, and lay down with her on the narrow bed under the blue blanket with the screens quiet over them for the first time in a day and a half. She lay against him with her head on his arm and felt the shaking go down slowly, the way the sea had let her sleep once, two hours south on a cliff.

She kissed him, after a while, because she wanted to and because she could, because it was over and she was still herself and he was still next door and the list was back behind its walls and a man with a flat voice was on his way to take her burden off her. She kissed him slowly, exhausted, grateful, and he kissed her back, and it turned, the way it did, into something warmer than either of them had the energy for, and they didn’t do anything about that, not now, not with Wei Long an hour away; she just held on to him and kissed him until she couldn’t keep her eyes open.

“Wei Long’s coming,” she said, against his mouth. “I can’t fall asleep. I have to—”

“I’ll wake you when he knocks,” said Yu Chen. “Forty minutes. Sleep.”

“I can’t.”

“You can. Your brain’s voting. I can feel it.” He pulled the blanket up over her shoulder. “Go to sleep. I’m right here.”

She slept. She slept for forty minutes with her face against his chest and his hand in her hair, and he was awake the whole time, she knew, because every time she half-surfaced his hand was still moving, slow and steady, counting something she couldn’t hear; and when Wei Long’s knock came at the front door downstairs, flat and even, three times, Yu Chen woke her the way he’d said he would, with his mouth against her forehead, and said, “He’s here. You did it. Come on.”

She got up. She pushed her glasses up her nose. She went down to open the door for the detective, as Lin Yu, with the boy next door behind her on the stairs, and gave away the thing she’d found, and kept herself.

Later, much later, Wei Long’s team would knock on a door above a phone-repair shop in the eastern district, and on a glass door in an office tower with CALDER RISK PARTNERS on it, and it would be slow, and it would be legal, and it would work. But that was Thursday. That hadn’t happened yet. On Saturday night it was just a girl and a detective and a boy at a kitchen table in the Walled City, and a folder, and tea nobody drank, and a weight set down at last in the right hands.

chapters.title: Someone Else’s Blood
chapters.desc: The breach turns physical. A man is sent to frighten Eliana at the dawn flower market, the crowd breaks, and a stallholder is crushed under a van. Yu Chen is there, off duty, and Eliana sees for the first time exactly what he chose to do with his life, and what else his hands can do.
chapters.epigraph: “I keep people alive. That’s the whole job. You keep people safe. We’ve been doing the same thing from two sides of a wall.” — Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
Elowen wouldn’t stay home.

“I said I’d keep off the flat,” she said on the phone on Monday night, in the voice she used for late suppliers. “I didn’t say I’d stop working. I’ve bought at that market every morning for ten years, Yu-er. I’m not stopping because a man with a laptop knows my address.”

“He doesn’t know it any more. I took it back.”

“Then there’s nothing to worry about.”

“He’s seen it,” said Eliana. “He knows what time you go.”

Wei Long had everything. He’d said a few days. Elowen had a wedding on Wednesday and two hundred stems of white ranunculus that didn’t come to the house, and in the end she said, meaning it as the end of the argument, “If you’re so worried, come with me.”

Eliana had never been to the market at dawn in her life. She didn’t do mornings or crowds, and the far end of the flower market had almost no cameras; she knew, because she’d once spent three days looking for them and found nothing, and her sister had come back from a container instead.

“Okay,” she said. “I’ll be on your step at a quarter to five.”

She hung up before Elowen could take it back, and climbed down the persimmon tree, and knocked on his back door at midnight in her socks.

“I’m going to the flower market with Elowen at five,” she said. “I’m not asking you to come. I’m telling you so you don’t see me go out in the dark and have a heart attack.”

He had a textbook in his hand and Tuesday off.

“I’ll drive,” he said.

“I said I’m not asking.”

“I heard you.” He stood aside to let her in. “Come and sleep for four hours first. You’ve had about six since Friday.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The flower market ran down the Walled City’s oldest lane towards the water, a long covered street of stalls under tin roofs, and at five in the morning it was the busiest place she’d ever stood in. Vans backed in at the far end. Men carried buckets on their shoulders. The stones were wet and covered in leaves and cut stems, and everything smelled green and cold. There were whole stalls of nothing but orchids, and Eliana walked past those without looking.

Elowen went through it like scissors through paper. She knew everyone. She said “No” to a man with peonies in a way that made him drop his price before she’d taken a step. Eliana walked beside her in her black hoodie with her hands in the pocket, and Yu Chen walked a step behind them both with his arms full of whatever Elowen handed back, watching the crowd over the top of it.

“I’ve had Zhao’s men,” said Elowen, without turning round. “I’ve never had a hoodie and a doctor.”

At the loading end there was a stall of yellow chrysanthemums, big as fists, in tin buckets three deep, and a small round woman in a padded waistcoat behind them, talking to everyone who passed.

“Miss Lin! Early. Who’s this, your sister? She’s tiny. Is she eating?” She pulled a chrysanthemum out of a bucket, shook the water off and held it out across the stall. “For your hair. It’s going everywhere.”

Eliana took it, because there wasn’t a way not to.

“Mrs. Choi,” said Elowen. “She’s been here longer than the roof.”

“Thirty years, and the roof leaks.” Mrs. Choi looked Yu Chen up and down the way old women in the Walled City looked at young men. “Tall,” she said to Eliana, with approval, as if he weren’t there, and Eliana went hot to the ears.

She was still holding the flower when she saw the grey jacket.

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d seen it once before, from a lectern in March: a plain man of forty in the third row, getting up and leaving because a stranger had sat down beside him. A face you’d forget on a bus.

He was by the orchid stall with his phone in his hand, looking at her. Not at Elowen. He’d been told who to look at.

She went cold. Then she went past cold into the other thing, the thing she was at four in the morning when a hunt got close. She’d spent the weekend inside the money that paid men like him. She knew who this one was.

He walked over and stopped a little too close, with people going past on both sides carrying buckets.

“Miss Lin,” he said, pleasantly. “The firm would like you to know that you took something back, and that’s fine. They’d just like you to know they still know what time your sister buys her flowers. That’s all.”

Elowen had gone still beside her.

In March Eliana would have gone small inside her hood and let someone bigger deal with it. She didn’t feel small now. She felt like the screens.

She said his name. His full name, and the street he lived on, above a bakery, and the school his daughter went to, and what Calder had paid into his account the Friday before. She said it in her small in-person voice, clearly, the way she’d have typed it.

“The police have all of that,” she said. “Since Saturday. You can tell the firm what time I know things.”

The pleasant look went off his face as if it had been wiped.

And Yu Chen was already there. She hadn’t seen him put the flowers down. He was between her and the man, half a head taller, with his back to her and his hands empty at his sides.

“Step back,” he said. “I’ll say it once.”

It was the voice from her father’s table. Whatever the man had been told about the boy next door, it hadn’t been this. He stepped back, and back again, and then he turned and went, fast, shouldering towards the loading end. Someone he knocked into dropped a bucket of lilies, someone else shouted, and in the shout there was a word that might have been knife.

There was no knife. It didn’t matter. A word like that goes through a crowd like a crack through ice.

She saw it start at the orchid end and come at them, people turning all at once, buckets going over, water and petals across the stones. Yu Chen pulled her and Elowen back against a pillar with an arm round each and the crowd went past like a river. At the loading end a delivery van that had been backing in lurched forward instead, the driver panicking with fists on his doors, and it went three metres before he found the brake.

Three metres was the chrysanthemum stall.

She heard the tin buckets go, and the table break, and Mrs. Choi make a sound she would hear for weeks.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was moving before he’d decided to.

Two men from the next stall had their shoulders against the van and were rolling it back, and he shouted at them to do it slowly, and they did, and then he was on his knees in the water and the yellow flowers.

Mrs. Choi was on her side against the wall. Her right leg below the knee was wrong. Blood was coming through her trousers too fast, dark and steady, spreading into the wet stones so it looked like more than it was, and then he looked properly and it was exactly as much as it looked.

He put both hands on it, flat, and leaned.

She screamed. He kept leaning.

“Mrs. Choi. I’m a doctor. My name’s Yu Chen. I’m pressing to stop the bleeding. It’ll hurt more for a bit and then less. Stay with me.”

“You’re the tall one,” she said through her teeth.

It wasn’t slowing enough. He looked up and Elowen was crouched beside him in her good coat, calm, with her hands already out.

“Both hands, flat, like mine,” he said. “Lean your whole weight. Don’t let go whatever she says. If it comes through, press harder.”

Elowen leaned. Mrs. Choi swore at her. Elowen didn’t move.

He put his jacket over Mrs. Choi’s chest, felt the pulse at her neck, quick and thin, checked her breathing, found the cut on her head and the wrist that was probably broken. Nothing that would kill her in the next twenty minutes except the leg. He kept talking to her about the roof that leaked, and she answered, and while she was answering she was still there.

“Eliana. Ambulance.”

“I rang them.” Her voice came from behind him, high and fast. “They’re coming. I’m on with Wei Long—”

Then it stopped.

He looked round. The crowd had knocked the man in the grey jacket down by the vans, and he’d got up limping and come back along the wall towards the side lane, and Eliana was standing in the mouth of it with her phone at her ear.
