He didn’t stop for her. He shoved her out of the way with both hands and she went back against a shutter with a bang and her phone skidded across the stones.

Yu Chen got up.

“Don’t let go,” he said to Elowen.

He didn’t remember crossing the street. He remembered the man’s arm in his hand, and turning it, and the man going down on his face among the leaves, and his own knee in the man’s back, and the arm held up behind him at the angle where it would go no further without breaking. He held it there. He didn’t push it the last bit. He knew exactly where the last bit was.

“Lie still,” he said.

The man said something into the stones. Yu Chen didn’t hear it. Everything in him had gone flat and cold and far away, and in the middle of the cold there was only one thing, which was that this man had put his hands on her, and that it would be easy.

Two stallholders came. One sat on the man’s legs. Yu Chen let go and went back to Mrs. Choi without looking at Eliana, because if he looked at her he wouldn’t go back, and put his hands over Elowen’s, which were red to the wrists.

“I’ve got it. Well done. You can let go.”

Elowen sat back on her heels on the wet stones and looked at her hands.

✦ ✦ ✦

The ambulance came down the lane with its lights going. Eliana watched him hand over to the paramedics in about a minute, plain and fast, and watched them nod at him the way people nod at someone who knows what he’s doing. As they carried Mrs. Choi past on the stretcher, with his jacket still over her, she turned her head and found Eliana and said, “Tell him he’s too tall.”

Wei Long came eight minutes later in his plain dark coat. He looked at the broken stall, the blood in the water, the man on the stones with a florist sitting on him. Then he looked at Yu Chen, standing by the pillar, red to the elbows.

“Did you hurt him?”

“No.”

Wei Long looked at his face a second longer. He’d seen that face before, at a garden wall.

“Good,” he said, and his officers got the man up and took him up the lane to the car.

Eliana picked her phone up. The screen had cracked straight across. She went and stood in front of Yu Chen, and he still wouldn’t look at her.

“He pushed you,” he said, without looking up. “Did you hit your head?”

“No. Look at me.”

He looked at her. His face was white, with a smear of someone else’s blood along his jaw where he’d pushed his hair back, and his eyes were still a little far away.

She’d seen two men in ten minutes. One had knelt in the water and kept a stranger alive by leaning on her and talking about a roof, as if he had all day. The other had crossed a street without seeming to touch the ground and put a man on his face and held his arm exactly where it would break. The same hands. She’d known there were two of him. She’d never watched one turn into the other.

“Take me home,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He went straight upstairs to the shower without a word, and she heard the water start.

She stood in his bedroom and understood that he’d gone in there to wash it off before she could look at it properly. Then she went in.

The bathroom was full of steam. He was under the water with his hands flat on the tiles and his head down, and what ran off him was pink, then less pink.

“Go out,” he said. “Please. Give me a minute.”

She got into the shower with him in her clothes.

Hoodie, jeans, socks, glasses, all of it. The water soaked her in a second and her glasses fogged and ran and she didn’t care. She put her hands on his wet jaw where the blood had been and pulled his head down and kissed him under the water.

He went rigid. Then his hands came off the tiles and onto her back, holding her against him through the soaked hoodie, and he kissed her back as if she were the air.

“You saw,” he said against her mouth.

She didn’t pretend she hadn’t.

“I wanted to break it.” His voice was low and rough. “I’m not going to tell you I didn’t. I knew where it would go.”

“You didn’t, though.”

“Because you were watching.”

“Because you’re you.” She pushed her fringe out of her eyes. “You kept her alive and then you put him down and you were back with her before anyone else had moved. I’m not frightened of it. I’m not.”

He looked down at her with the water running off his hair onto her face, and she watched him not quite believe her, and then believe her.

“You said his daughter’s school,” he said. “To his face.”

“I meant it to be frightening.”

He laughed once, helplessly, and put his forehead on hers.

She pulled the wet hoodie off over her head and dropped it with a slap, and put her glasses on the shelf with his soap, and after that she could only see the shape of him in the steam, and it was enough. He undressed the rest of her slowly because everything stuck and his hands were shaking, and her jeans wouldn’t come off her ankles and she laughed at him, and he knelt in the water and did it properly and kissed her knee on the way back up.

He was gentler with her after that than he’d ever been. He kissed her throat and her shoulders and the place on her back where she’d hit the shutter, checking it with his mouth, and she held on to his wet hair and let him. He carried her out in the end, dripping, and didn’t care about the floor. She pulled him down onto his bed because she wanted his weight, all of it, the realness of him after a morning of blood, and he gave it to her, careful and then not, and she kept her eyes open in the grey light and watched the cold go out of his face until it was only his own face again.

Afterwards he lay with his head on her chest.

“I keep people safe,” she said, looking up at the ceiling. “At night. That’s all it’s ever been. I always thought mine was the dirty side and yours was the clean one.”

“It’s the same job,” said Yu Chen into her skin. “You do it from the other side of a wall.”

She thought about a man in a grey jacket going into a police car instead of disappearing, because of a phone call she’d made on Saturday, and a woman in a padded waistcoat going into an ambulance instead of bleeding into her own flowers, because of what he’d chosen to do with his life. Which side of the wall either of them was on didn’t seem to matter as much as it had.

The yellow chrysanthemum was on his bedside table, crushed, where she’d dropped it out of her pocket. She fell asleep looking at it. At nine she half woke to hear him in the corridor on the phone in his doctor’s voice, saying “Thank you. Yes. Thank you,” and then he came back and lay down and put his face in her hair, and she knew without asking that Mrs. Choi was alive.

chapters.title: The First Lin Child to Say No to His Face
chapters.desc: At the Mid-Autumn table, with the whole family watching, Lin Jian announces the job as a thing already decided. Eliana turns it down, and him, out loud and to his face. Nobody in the house has ever done that before.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m not your eraser. I’m your daughter. You’ve had twenty-two years to say it. I’ll wait. But I’m not taking the job.” — Eliana Lin
chapters.content:
Wei Long’s message came on Thursday at twenty past six in the morning, and it was one word.

Wei Long: Done.

Then, a minute later, because he was Wei Long and couldn’t leave a thing half reported:

Wei Long: Both addresses. Both men. The firm’s office too. You’ll get a letter about a statement. Not yet. Eat breakfast.

She read it on the camp bed with the cracked screen in her hand and the grey coming round the curtain, and lay there until the light was white, not thinking anything, just breathing. It had worked. The slow door had worked.

By Saturday her father knew.

She didn’t know how. Chen Si, probably. It had been his system the crew had walked into, and Chen Si knew everything that happened to anything of his, and Chen Si and her father had known each other for thirty years. Nobody told her he knew. She heard it the way she heard everything in the tall house: through the floors. Baba’s voice in his study on the phone, lower than usual, a long time. Baba on the stairs at midnight, stopping on the landing below hers, and standing there, and going down again. Ah Sim at breakfast on Sunday, putting congee in front of her with more care than congee needed.

“Your father says everyone comes tomorrow,” said Ah Sim. “For the moon. Everyone.”

“Everyone always comes for the moon.”

“He said it twice,” said Ah Sim, and went back to the stove.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday morning a woman of about thirty knocked on the red door with a pot of yellow chrysanthemums in her arms, so big she had to look round the side of it.

“My mother said bring it here,” she said to Ah Sim. “For the tall doctor and the small girl. She said you’d know.” She put the pot down on the top step. “They kept the leg. She’ll have a stick. She says she’s going to hit him with it for being too tall.”

Ah Sim carried it in and put it in the middle of the long table, where the mooncakes would go, and stood back and looked at it with her arms folded, and didn’t explain it to anybody.

Eliana took a photograph of it and sent it next door.

Yu Chen: They kept the leg?

Eliana: they kept the leg. she’s going to hit you with a stick

Yu Chen: That seems fair.

Eliana: baba knows. about the police. he’s been on the stairs. tonight’s going to be bad

There was a pause. She watched the dots come and go twice.

Yu Chen: I’m on days. Home by eight. I’ll be on the step.

Eliana: you’re not invited

Yu Chen: I know. I said the step.

She looked at that. Then she went next door at lunchtime, when she knew he’d be gone, and let herself in with the key under the brick, and went up to his room and stood at his window and looked across the gardens at her own, and at the persimmons going orange on the branch between the two houses. She didn’t know what she’d come for. She lay down on his bed with her face in his pillow for ten minutes, and breathed, and went home.

✦ ✦ ✦

They all came.

Baba at the head in his cardigan. Elowen on his right, in green, with Zhao beside her. Raiden and Jinx, with Jinx’s dressing gone now and the new skin on her forearm pink. Evangeline and Jun Hyuk, who had brought lanterns, a lot of lanterns, and hung them in the back garden before anyone could stop him. Elara straight off a shift, hair everywhere, eating a mooncake before the soup. Xing Yue was on call. Ah Sim moved round the table and the yellow chrysanthemums sat in the middle of it like a lamp.

Eliana sat at the far end by the window, where she always sat. The chair beside her was empty.

Nobody mentioned Thursday. Nobody mentioned a flower market, or a van, or why Elowen had come home on Tuesday with blood to the wrists. Elowen had told Zhao, and Zhao had looked at Eliana when he came in tonight and said “Hm,” and that was the whole of it. Jun Hyuk talked about the lanterns. Raiden told a story about a client. Elara laughed at it too loudly. It was all so careful that Eliana could hear the care, the way you can hear a fridge only when it stops.

Baba waited until the fish.

He put his chopsticks down beside his bowl, the way he did, exactly, and spoke to Elowen.

“Chen Si tells me his house was broken into,” he said. “The part your sister looks after. He tells me she found the people who did it in a day and a half, which he says nobody else could have done.” He picked up his tea. “And then she gave them to the police. To the policeman’s son. Not to me. Not to Chen Si. To the police.”

The table went still.

“So she’ll start with Chen Si on the first of next month,” said Baba. “Full time. Upstairs, where she’s safe. He has the room ready. I’ve told him yes.” He drank his tea. “That’s the end of it. She’s not going to be out at markets at five in the morning with men in jackets. She’s not going to be in police stations. She’ll be in this house, where nobody can get at her, and I’ll know where she is.”

He hadn’t looked at her once.

She felt it start. The old thing. Her shoulders coming up, her face going hot, her whole self folding down into the hoodie at the end of the table where none of it could reach. She’d let it go by her whole life. She’d sat at this window and been talked about and gone small and waited for it to be over.

The chair beside her was empty. There was nobody to stand up.

She stood up.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t do it slowly, the way he had. She did it badly, too fast, so the chair scraped and her knee hit the table and the soup bowls jumped. Everyone looked at her. Raiden’s mouth was open. Evangeline’s hand went flat on the cloth.

Baba looked at his tea.

“Baba,” said Eliana.

Her voice came out small. It shook. She made it keep going.

“Look at me.”

He didn’t.

“Please,” she said. “Just for this. Look at me. I’m here. I’m standing up. I’m not going to say it to Elowen and I’m not going to say it to Ah Sim. I’m going to say it to you, and I want you to look at me while I do it, because I’ve never once asked you for anything and I’m asking for this.”

Nobody at the table breathed.

Baba put his cup down. And then, slowly, as if it hurt his neck, he lifted his head and looked down the length of the table at her.

She’d thought it would make her stop. It didn’t. It made her angry, the way it hadn’t been allowed to before, and the anger held her up.

“I’m not taking the job,” she said.

He didn’t move.

“Not on the first. Not upstairs. Not ever. I’m not going to sit in this house in the dark doing Chen Si’s walls so you’ll always know where I am.” Her hands were fists at her sides. “I went to the police because it was mine to go to. I found them. Me. I could have given them to you and they’d have disappeared and I’d never have had to be frightened again, and I’d have been yours forever. I knew that. That’s why I didn’t.”

“Eliana,” said Elowen, low.

“No. Let me.” She didn’t look away from her father. “You think if I’m upstairs I’m safe. You think if I’m useful I’ll stay. I know why. I’ve always known.” Her voice cracked and she pushed through it. “I’m the day she died. That’s what I am to you. You go to her grave on my birthday and you can’t say it to me because it’s not my birthday to you, it’s hers. And I’ve spent my whole life trying to be worth it. Being useful. Fixing the cameras. Doing your alarms. Cleaning our name out of places so nobody can find us. I thought if I did enough of it you’d look at me.”

He was looking at her now. His face was grey.

“I’m not your eraser,” said Eliana. “I’m your daughter. You’ve had twenty-two years to say it. I’ll wait. I’ll wait as long as you want. But I’m not taking the job.”

She sat down.

Her legs had gone. She sat down at the far end of the table by the window with her hands in her lap and her face burning, and the whole table stared at her, and nobody said anything at all.

Baba went on looking at her. She saw his mouth move, as if he were trying to find a word that wasn’t there. Then he stood up, and pushed his chair in, carefully, square to the table, and walked out of the room. They heard him on the stairs. They didn’t hear his study door. He’d gone past it, up, somewhere else.

Raiden let his breath out in a long whistle.

“Well,” he said. “That’s the first time anyone’s—”

“Raiden,” said Elowen, and he stopped.

Evangeline got up out of her chair and came all the way round the table and sat down in the empty one beside Eliana, and took her hand under the cloth, and held it, and didn’t say anything, which from Evangeline was a speech.

Elowen was on her feet. She was looking at the door their father had gone through, and her face had gone the way Eliana had seen it go only once or twice in her life, calm and white, the face of someone deciding something they couldn’t take back.

“Not tonight,” said Zhao.

Elowen looked down at him.

“Not tonight,” he said again. “Let him sit with it.”

Elowen sat down. Her hands were shaking. Eliana had never seen her sister’s hands shake.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went out of the red door at nine with her coat over her hoodie, and he was on the step.

He’d come straight from the hospital. He was still in his work trousers with his lanyard in his pocket, and he’d brought the white rabbit lantern down off his roof, the one he put up every Mid-Autumn, and it was on the step beside him, lit, glowing a little crooked because one ear was bent.

He looked up at her. He didn’t ask.

She sat down on the step beside him. She didn’t say anything either. The lanterns Jun Hyuk had hung in the back garden showed over the wall, red and gold. Somewhere along the lane someone was letting off firecrackers. The moon was up over the noodle stall, full and enormous and yellow as the chrysanthemums.

“I said no,” she said.

“I heard.”

“You can’t have heard. You were at work.”

“Jinx texted me.” He held out his phone. There was one message on it from a number he’d never had before. She stood up. She said no. To his FACE. Your girl. “I don’t know how she got my number.”

“I gave it to her,” said Eliana. “In June. In case of fires.”

She looked at the lantern. Her hands were cold. They were always cold, and tonight they were worse; she couldn’t feel the ends of her fingers.

He didn’t say well done. She’d known he wouldn’t. He reached across and took both her hands in his, the way he’d have taken a patient’s, and held them, and then, because they were so cold, he opened the front of his coat and put them inside it, flat against his chest over his shirt, and closed the coat over them and held it shut.

She could feel his heart under her palms. It was going fast.

“You’re frightened,” she said.

“I’ve been frightened since Jinx texted,” said Yu Chen. “I was halfway through a man’s stitches. I nearly sewed his finger to his thumb.”

She laughed. It came out of her wet and surprised, and she leaned forward, with her hands still inside his coat, and kissed him over the rabbit lantern.

It was the kind of kiss you give someone to stand up straight. Not long. She held on, with her hands on his heart, and kissed him once, hard, on her father’s step with the moon over the noodle stall, and felt him breathe out against her mouth as if he’d been holding it since six o’clock. The lantern’s paper ear caught the string of her hoodie and smoked, and he pulled it away from her with his free hand without looking, and kept kissing her.

“You’ll set yourself on fire,” he said, against her mouth.

“I don’t care.”

“I do. I’ve done enough emergencies today.”

She took her hands out of his coat and put them on his face instead. They were warm now.

“I have to go back in,” she said. “My sisters. Will you stay? Out here?”

He said he would. He’d have said it if she’d asked him to stay till New Year.

She went back up the three steps and stopped at the red door and looked back at him, on the step with the lantern, in his work clothes, waiting the way he’d always waited. She thought of the empty chair beside her at the table.

“Next year,” she said, “you’re coming in.”

✦ ✦ ✦

There was a message from Qian on her cracked phone when she got upstairs, because Chen Si knew everything that happened in any house he cared about.

Qian: Mr. Chen asks if your father’s answer is also yours.

She sat on the camp bed and typed with her thumbs.

Eliana: no. tell mr chen thank you, and no. if the family needs me i’ll be there. not upstairs. not full time. i’ll be at the end of a phone like i always am.

The answer came back in under a minute, and not from Qian. It came from a number she’d only ever seen on the tops of Qian’s messages.

Chen Si: I asked. She answered. Thank you for Thursday.

She read it three times.

Then Elara came up the stairs without knocking, with a plate of mooncakes and her hair everywhere, and sat down on the floor of the dark room, and Evangeline came after her and sat down too, and after a minute Elowen came, still in her good green dress, and stood in the doorway looking at the three of them on the floor among the cables, and then took her shoes off and sat down as well. Nobody turned the big light on. The screens glowed. Elara cut a mooncake into four with a knife from the kitchen and handed it round, and they ate it on the floor with their fingers, and nobody talked about Baba.

Out of the window, across the garden, she could see the rabbit lantern on his step, still lit, and the shape of him beside it.

At one, when her sisters had gone, she heard her father on the stairs. He came up past his study, past the landing where he usually stopped, all the way to the top, and stood outside her door. She sat on the camp bed and didn’t move. He didn’t knock. After a while she heard him go down again, slowly, one stair at a time, and his study door close, and his light stay on.

chapters.title: Elowen Takes Her Side
chapters.desc: The eldest sister comes to the tall house with Zhao a step behind her and says to their father the thing the family has let him avoid for twenty-two years. It doesn’t mend him. But it makes him stop, and that evening, on the roof next door, Eliana says she’s leaving.
chapters.epigraph: “You buried Ma, and you’ve been burying Eliana with her ever since. Stop. She’s the one who lived.” — Elowen Zhao
chapters.content:
Baba didn’t come down to breakfast for six days.

Ah Sim took a tray up every morning and brought it down at noon with most of it still on it. Uncle Mok sat in the Mercedes at the bottom of the steps at eight and waited, and at half past nine went away again. The study light was on when Eliana went to bed and on when she woke, and the house was so quiet that she could hear the old man on the far side singing to his birds through two walls.

She worked. She didn’t know what else to do with it. In the evenings Yu Chen came over the wall with food and sat by her door in the second chair while she did small things for Qian that didn’t matter, and he didn’t ask how she was, because he could see, and on Wednesday he made her stand at the window for two minutes and she cried for one of them and he held her from behind and didn’t say anything.

“He’s going to stay up there forever,” she said, with her face against the curtain.

“He’s not.”

“You don’t know him.”

“I’ve lived next door to him for eighteen years,” said Yu Chen. “He comes out when he’s hungry. Everyone does.”

On Saturday night Elowen rang.

“I’m coming tomorrow,” she said. “For lunch. Early.”

“Don’t.”

“I’m not asking, Yu-er.”

“I know you’re not.” Eliana pulled her knees up on the camp bed. “That’s why I’m saying don’t. I said what I said. I don’t need you to come and say it again louder.”

There was a pause on the line.

“You never ask,” said Elowen. “That’s the trouble with you. You never ask anybody for anything. You’d let him sit up there until you were both dead rather than ask me to help.” Her voice went careful. “So I’m not waiting for you to ask. I’m your sister. I’ll be there at eleven.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She came at eleven, in grey, with no flowers, which was how Eliana knew it was serious. Zhao came up the three steps a pace behind her in black and stopped in the hall with his back to the wall beside the door, the way he stood in rooms he didn’t trust, and gave Eliana his four-second look, and said nothing at all.

Elowen went up the stairs.

Eliana sat down on the bottom step. It was where she sat when there was something in this house she wasn’t meant to hear. She sat there now with her hood up and her arms round her knees and listened to her sister knock on their father’s study door, and not wait, and go in.

She didn’t shut it behind her. Eliana understood afterwards that she’d left it open on purpose.

“Baba,” said Elowen. “Come down. We’re going to talk in the front room.”

A long silence. Then her father’s voice, thick, as if he hadn’t used it in days.

“I’m not coming down.”

“Then I’ll say it here, and Eliana will hear it from the stairs, the way she’s heard everything in this house her whole life. Is that better?”

Another silence. Then the creak of his chair, and his heavy feet, and the two of them coming down the stairs, Elowen first. Eliana stood up off the bottom step to let them past. Her father went by her in his cardigan with his face grey and unshaved and didn’t look at her, and went into the front room nobody used, and Elowen followed him, and this time she did shut the door. Zhao didn’t move from the wall.

Eliana sat back down.

She could hear most of it anyway. The tall house had never kept a secret in its life.

✦ ✦ ✦

“She went to the police,” said Baba. “The policeman’s son. After everything that house has—”

“She went to the police so she wouldn’t have to become you,” said Elowen.

The silence that came after that was the worst one yet.

“Don’t,” said Baba.

“I’m going to. Somebody has to, and it’s always me, so it’s me.” Eliana heard her sister’s heels on the old floor, walking, the way she walked in the shop when she was angry with an order. “You’ve been standing in a hospital corridor for twenty-two years, Baba. You never came out of it.”

“Elowen.”

“You buried Ma. And you’ve been burying Eliana with her ever since.” Her voice didn’t rise. It got harder. “Every birthday, at the grave, at dawn, with her standing there. Every Sunday at the end of the table. You talk to her through Ah Sim. You talk to her through me. You’ve had Mok tell you where she was every day for four years and you never once asked her what she was studying.” The heels stopped. “She can find anyone in the world in a day and a half. Did you know that? Chen Si told you. He told you, and the only thing you heard was the police.”

Her father said something Eliana couldn’t hear.

“Then look at her,” said Elowen, “until you see her instead. That’s all. That’s all anyone’s asking. You learned to ask Raiden. You learned it with Evangeline. You learned it with me, at the end, with Zhao. You never even tried with her. Stop it. She’s the one who lived. Ma didn’t, and Eliana did, and you’ve spent twenty-two years making her pay for the wrong one.”

Eliana put her face down on her knees.

In the hall, by the door, Zhao shifted his weight. She looked up. He was looking at her, not for four seconds this time, for longer. Then he said, so low it barely carried, “She’s been wanting to say that for years.”

Behind the door it had gone quiet. Eliana waited. She heard her father breathing, heavy, the way he breathed on the stairs. She heard him sit down in one of the stiff old chairs nobody sat in. She heard him say something low that might have been her mother’s name, or might have been nothing.

Then she heard him say, quite clearly, “Every time I look at her I’m in that corridor.”

“I know,” said Elowen. Her voice had changed. “I know you are. But she’s not. She was never in it. She was a day old, Baba. She’s twenty-two. Come out of the corridor.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The door opened after twenty minutes.

Elowen came out first, white, with her mouth set, and went straight past Eliana and Zhao and through to the kitchen, and Eliana heard her run the tap and stand at the sink with it running.

Her father came out after her.

He stopped in the hall. Eliana was on the bottom step with her hood up and her knees under her chin. He looked down at her. He didn’t look past her or over her head. He looked at her, the way he had at the table, and she saw it was hard for him, she saw it in his jaw and in the way his hand went to the newel post and held it.

He didn’t say sorry. She hadn’t thought he would.

“The boy next door,” he said.

She waited.

“He’s on my step every night.” He said it to her. Her. Not to Zhao, not to the air. “In the cold. Mok says since the moon.”

“Yes.”

He looked at the red door. He looked back at her. Something worked in his face and didn’t come out.

“Take him some persimmons,” said Baba. “Off our branch. They’re ready.”

Then he went past her, and didn’t go up to his study. He went through to the kitchen, where Ah Sim was, and Eliana heard Ah Sim say “Sit,” and heard him sit, and heard a bowl put down in front of him.

She stayed on the bottom step. She didn’t know what she was feeling. It didn’t have a name she’d been taught.

Zhao came away from the wall and stood over her.

“That,” he said, “was a yes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen found her in the back garden an hour later, under the persimmon branch, with a carrier bag and a long stick for knocking them down.

“You’re doing it wrong,” said Elowen. “You twist them. You don’t hit them.”

“I know how to pick a persimmon.”

“You’ve never picked a persimmon in your life.” Elowen took the stick off her and reached up and twisted one off clean, and dropped it in the bag. Her eyes were red. She’d washed her face. “He’ll be down for lunch. He won’t say anything. You won’t either. That’s fine.”

“I didn’t want you to do that.”

“I know.”

“I wanted to do it myself. I did do it myself. On Monday.”

“You did,” said Elowen. “You stood up at that table and I’ve never been so proud of anyone in my life. And then he went upstairs for six days and you sat in your room and let him, because you’d said your piece and you weren’t going to ask for more. That’s what I mean.” She twisted another persimmon off. “You can do the hard thing on your own. I know you can. You don’t have to. That’s all I came to say. To you, I mean. The rest was for him.”

Eliana looked at her.

“I’ve known about him since the wedding,” said Elowen, not looking down. “My wedding. He left his flask on my counter at six in the morning. The dented one. I’ve seen you drinking out of it on the bus for two years.” She dropped another persimmon in the bag. “I never said. I thought you’d tell me when you wanted.”

“I didn’t want to. In case.”

“In case Baba.” Elowen handed her the stick. “Baba just told you to take him fruit off our tree. I think you can stop worrying about Baba.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She took the persimmons up the tree.

Not the stairs. The tree, the way she’d always gone: Mama’s big flowerpot, the branch, the fork, one step across to the flat roof of the Song house. She did it one-handed with the bag in her other hand and nearly dropped it twice, and when she got to the top he was already there, sitting with his back against the water tank in his grey jumper, because he’d watched her come out into the garden with the bag and known exactly where she was going.

“You’ll drop them,” he said.

“I didn’t.”

“You scraped your knee.”

She looked down. She had. She sat down beside him with her back against the tank, and gave him the bag, and he looked into it, and then at her.

“These are Lin persimmons.”

“Baba said bring you some.”

He went still.

“Your father,” said Yu Chen.

“He said you’re on his step every night in the cold. He said take him some persimmons off our branch.” She pulled her knees up. “That’s the most he’s ever said about you without calling you the policeman’s nephew. I think it’s the most he’s ever said to me, as well.”

He didn’t say anything. He took a persimmon out of the bag and held it in both hands and looked at it, and she saw his ears go red, and then his eyes, and he looked away across the gardens to the tall house.

The sun was going. The windows of the tall house were dark except for the kitchen, and as they watched, the kitchen light went off and the study light came on, yellow, the one window. Her father’s.

“He came down,” said Eliana. “He ate with Ah Sim. He didn’t say anything to me at lunch. He passed me the vinegar.”

“That’s not nothing,” said Yu Chen.

She leaned on his shoulder and watched the window. It was strange to look at it from here. She’d never once looked at it from outside, from where he’d looked at hers.

“I’m going to move out,” she said.

His shoulder went tight under her cheek.

“Not because of today,” she said. “Today’s—I don’t know what today is. Maybe it’s a start. But I’ve lived in that dark room at the top of that house my whole life, waiting for him to come up the stairs, and he came up on Monday night and stood outside my door and didn’t knock, and I sat on the camp bed and didn’t open it. I don’t want to do that any more. I don’t want to wait up there for him.” She took a breath. “I want to live somewhere he can come and knock. Somewhere that’s mine.”

He didn’t answer.

She sat up and looked at him, and he was looking at the persimmon in his hands, not at her, and her stomach dropped.

“I mean here,” she said, too fast. “Next door. With you. If you—I’m not saying you have to. If it’s too soon, or if you think Baba—I know he’s only just said persimmons, I know it’s—”

He put the persimmon down.

Then he stood up, and took her by the waist, and lifted her straight up off the roof.

She shrieked. He’d never picked her up like that, not all the way, not off her feet into the air in front of the whole Walled City, and he did it now and turned round with her on the flat roof beside the water tank, once, all the way round, and her glasses went crooked and the bag of persimmons went over and two of them rolled to the edge and dropped off into the garden, and he didn’t stop. He kissed her up there, holding her above him with her hands on his shoulders and her feet off the roof, and he was laughing into her mouth, and so was she.

“Put me down. We’ll go off the edge like the persimmons.”

“They’re Lin persimmons,” said Yu Chen. “They know the way home.”

He put her down, finally, but didn’t let go of her. He kept his hands on her waist and his forehead on hers, and he was breathing hard.

“Yes,” he said. “Yes. That’s the answer. I didn’t say anything because I couldn’t. I’ve been waiting for you to say that since March.”

“Since March?”

He looked at her. And then, because he never lied to her, he told her.

“There’s a chair,” he said. “Downstairs. In the front room, under a sheet. It’s the same as the one in your room. I bought it after the nine days. I didn’t know when. I didn’t know if. I just wanted it to be there, in case.” His ears were scarlet. “There’s a desk too. It’s in pieces in the cupboard under the stairs. I haven’t put it together. I didn’t want to be the kind of person who put it together.”

She stared at him.

At first it frightened her. A chair under a sheet, waiting in his front room for seven months, for a girl who hadn’t said she’d come. The same chair. He’d have had to look at hers to know which one. He’d have stood in her room some night and read the label on the back of it, and remembered, and gone and found it, and paid for it, and put it under a sheet, and said nothing.

Then she thought of her father on the other side of her door on Monday night, not knocking.

“Is it the right height?” she said.

“I measured yours.”

“When?”

“In April. While you were asleep.” He held her eyes. “I’m not sorry.”

She started to laugh. She couldn’t help it. She put her face in his jumper and laughed until she was crying a little, and he held on to her on the roof with the last of the light going and her father’s window yellow across the yard.

“Put the desk together,” she said into his chest. “Tonight. I want to see you put it together.”

“It’s got about forty screws.”

“Good,” said Eliana. “Then you’ll be busy while I tell Ah Sim.”

Below them, in the Lin garden, someone came out of the back door and stooped and picked up the two persimmons off the paving, and stood with them in one hand looking up at the roof of the house next door. It was too dark to see his face. Then he went back inside, and she heard the bolt.

chapters.title: Two Boxes and a Monitor
chapters.desc: Eliana moves out of the tall house where she’s lived at the top of the stairs in the dark. It takes two boxes, a suitcase of hard drives and one monitor. He carries the monitor. She doesn’t go far, only next door, which was always where she was going.
chapters.epigraph: “I’ll take the monitor. You take the blanket. That’s the whole move.” — Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
It took her four hours to take down what had taken years to put up.

The cables came off the skirting in long strips of coloured tape, red and blue and green, the bundles she’d labelled at three in the morning in a hundred different moods. The two monitors on the wall came down off their brackets and left pale squares behind them on the paint, the only clean squares in the room. The hard drives came off the bed she’d never slept in and went into a suitcase of Raiden’s with a broken wheel, wrapped in her hoodies, one by one, like eggs.

The camp bed she folded flat and leaned against the wall. She didn’t want it. She stood and looked at it, the canvas sagging in the middle where she’d lain on it for so many nights, and then she left it where it was.

By eleven the dark room was a room. She’d never seen it like that. With the blackout curtains open the window let in a square of grey November light and the walls were just walls, a bit dirty, and the floor had dust on it in the shapes of everything that had stood there. It was smaller than she’d thought.

Two boxes. One of clothes, mostly hoodies, and one of everything else: the Spreadsheet’s hard copies, a tin of pencils, the skull shoebox he’d given back to her full of headphones labelled by length, the sticky-note pad, the list of rules with his capitals at the bottom. A suitcase of drives. Three screens on the desk still, which she’d do last.

And the blanket. The blue checked one, folded on top of the second box. She’d had it since a night in June on the step and had never once given it back, and he’d never once asked.

Ah Sim came up the stairs at half past eleven with a carrier bag and stood in the doorway and looked at the room.

“There’s soup,” she said, holding out the bag. “And the radish you like. And dumplings for the freezer. That woman next door can’t make dumplings.”

“Auntie Dai makes good dumplings.”

“She makes dumplings,” said Ah Sim, as if that settled it, and put the bag down on the box, and stood there.

Eliana didn’t know what to do. Ah Sim had fed her every day of her life and never once touched her that she could remember. She was small and eighty and frightening, and she stood in the doorway of the empty room in her apron looking at the pale squares on the wall.

“It’s only next door,” said Eliana.

“I know where it is. I’ve been passing soup over that back gate for four years.” Ah Sim’s mouth went thin. “You come for breakfast. Every day. I’m not cooking for one old man and a ghost.”

“Which ghost?”

“Him,” said Ah Sim, pointing at the floor, which meant the study, which meant Baba. Then she turned and went down the stairs, and on the landing below she stopped and said, without turning round, “Eat the soup tonight. Not tomorrow. Tonight,” and went on.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yu Chen came at twelve, the front way, up the three steps and in through the red door. He’d been in that door twice in his life. He came up the stairs in the middle of each one, not on the edges, so the whole house heard him, and stood in her doorway and looked at the room the way Ah Sim had.

“It’s small,” he said.

“I know. I didn’t know.”

He looked at the two boxes and the suitcase and the three screens, and then at her, sitting on the floor in the middle of it with her knees up.

“I’ll take the monitor,” he said. “You take the blanket. That’s the whole move.”

“There are three monitors.”

“I’ll take the monitors, then.” He picked up the first box instead and put it on his hip. “Are you all right?”

She thought about it.

“No,” she said. “Yes. I don’t know. Take the box.”

He took the box. He took the second one, and the suitcase with its broken wheel, which bumped down every one of the stairs no matter how he held it. He came back for the screens. She unplugged them herself and wouldn’t let him do that part, and he stood back and waited while she did it, and then carried them down one at a time, held flat against his chest in both arms like something alive. She followed him down with the blanket.

Baba was in the hall.

He hadn’t been there when Yu Chen went up. He was there now, standing by the newel post at the bottom of the stairs in his cardigan, with his big hands at his sides. He didn’t move out of the way. He didn’t move into it either. He stood exactly where he’d have to be stepped round.

Yu Chen stopped on the bottom stair with the last monitor in his arms.

Nobody did anything. Eliana stood three stairs up with the blanket against her chest. She watched the two of them look at each other, her father and the boy next door, across a monitor, at the bottom of the stairs of the tall house, and she couldn’t breathe.

“Mr. Lin,” said Yu Chen.

Baba looked at him. Then he stepped back, one step, out of the way.

Yu Chen went past him with the monitor and out of the red door and down the three steps, and Eliana heard him go along the porch to the little wall and step over it, the way he had a thousand times, and then his own door.

She came down the last three stairs.

Her father was looking at the blanket in her arms. She didn’t know if he knew whose it was. She didn’t know what he knew about any of it, really. He’d said take him some persimmons. He’d passed her the vinegar three Sundays running. It wasn’t much, and it was more than she’d ever had.

“The cameras,” he said.

She waited.

“On the house. Will they still—” He stopped. He wasn’t used to asking. “Can you see them from there?”

“I can see them from anywhere, Baba.”

He nodded, slowly. He looked at the stairs going up behind her to the top of the house.

“It’s next door,” she said. “It’s not anywhere. You can see his window from the kitchen.”

He didn’t answer. He went past her to the red door, and the bolt stuck the way it always stuck, and he pulled it back himself with his big hand, hard, and held the door open.

She’d never seen him hold a door for anyone. She stood in the hall with the blanket and looked at him holding it, and he looked at the lane.

She went out.

At the bottom of the three steps she turned round. He was still in the doorway. He lifted his hand, a little, as if he didn’t know what to do with it, and then he shut the door. She heard the bolt go home, and then she heard it come back again, slowly, and stay open.

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d put the desk together the night of the roof. It had taken him three hours and he’d had to start again twice, and there was one screw left over that he swore didn’t belong anywhere and that she kept, in her pocket, all day.

He’d put it in the front room facing his own. Not side by side. Facing. So that when they both sat down they’d be looking across at each other over the tops of their screens, the way they’d sat across a table in 4B for years.

“I didn’t know if you’d want it like that,” he said. “I can turn it.”

“Don’t turn it.”

The chair was the same as hers. Exactly. The same make, the same grey, the right height. She sat down in it and it was like sitting in her own, and it gave her a strange cold feeling in the back of her neck, briefly, that he’d stood in her room in April while she was asleep and read the label. Then she put her feet up on the crossbar the way she always did, and it was hers.

She set the screens up. She didn’t let him help. He sat on the arm of the sofa behind her and watched and passed her the tape when she held her hand out without looking, and when it was done, at four, the front room of the Song house had three monitors glowing on a desk in the corner and cables taped along the skirting in red and blue and green, and it looked like her.

“It looks like you,” he said.

“It looks like a mess.”

“Yes,” said Yu Chen. “That’s what I said.”

She turned round in the chair and looked at him on the arm of the sofa.

“You’ve got a plan for tonight,” she said. “Haven’t you.”

His ears went.

“I’ve got a small plan.”

“Show me.”

He didn’t want to. She held her hand out and kept it there until he took a folded square of paper out of his back pocket and gave it to her. It was a PLAN, in his capitals, the first she’d seen in a long time.

PLAN (FIRST NIGHT). 1. Ah Sim’s soup (she’ll insist). 2. Don’t talk about her father unless she does. 3. The roof if it’s clear. 4. Don’t make it a thing. 5. Let her sleep in the middle.

She read it twice. Then she folded it up and put it in her pocket with the leftover screw.

“Number four’s already gone,” she said.

“I know. I made it a plan.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They ate Ah Sim’s soup on the sofa, because Ah Sim would know if they didn’t, out of the same pot, with the radish. It was dark by six. He’d lit the lamp with the crooked shade and the room was gold and warm and smelled of soup and the new dust off her drives warming up, and she sat sideways on the sofa with her feet in his lap while he talked about the roof and whether it was clear.

She meant to say something back. She remembered starting a sentence about the camp bed.

She didn’t remember finishing it.

✦ ✦ ✦

She woke in the dark, warm, with no idea where she was.

Not the camp bed. A real bed, wide and soft, and a weight of blanket over her, and the blue checked one on top of that, she could feel the wool of it under her hand. The window was in the wrong place. The night light from outside came through curtains that weren’t blackout and lay across the ceiling in a long grey stripe.

His room. She was in his bed. She’d fallen asleep on the sofa and he’d carried her up, and she hadn’t woken, which had never once happened to her in her life.

He wasn’t in the bed.

She turned her head. He was at the window in his T-shirt, with the curtain held back in one hand, looking out. Not at the lane. At the back, across the gardens, at the tall house.

She knew what he was looking at before she sat up.

“Chen,” she said.

He let the curtain go and turned round. In the half-dark his face was startled, and then something else, a little ashamed.

“I woke up at two,” he said. “I always wake up at two. I looked for your light.” He came and sat on the edge of the bed. “It wasn’t on. Your window was dark. And I didn’t—” He stopped. “For a second I thought something had happened. Then I remembered you were here.”

She looked at him.

“Every night?” she said. “You look every night?”

“Every night,” said Yu Chen. “Since that June. I don’t know how to stop.”

She thought about that. A man waking at two every night for years to check whether a window was lit, and lying back down only when it was. She should mind. Some part of her did, a little, the same cold little feeling as the chair. And then the rest of her thought of the dark room at the top of the tall house, and the camp bed, and every night she’d sat under that light thinking nobody in the world knew whether it was on.

“Don’t stop,” she said.

She reached out and took her glasses off the bedside table, where he’d put them, folded, and put them on his face.

He blinked. They were far too strong for him. She watched his eyes go huge and helpless behind them.

“I can’t see anything,” he said.

“Now you know what it’s like. Every morning. Before you give me the tea.” She was starting to laugh. “Look at my window now. Go on.”

“I can’t see the window. I can’t see you.”

“I’m here,” said Eliana, and kissed him, with her glasses crooked on his face, and the frames clicked against her cheekbone, and he laughed into her mouth, blind, and took them off with one hand and put them down somewhere on the floor and pulled her down into the bed.

None of it was like the careful PLAN. She was the one who’d woken up, so she was the one who decided, and she decided fast: she climbed over him and pinned his wrists to the pillow, laughing, and he let her, and lay there looking up at her in the stripe of grey light with his face gone open and soft.

“This wasn’t on the list,” he said.

“I’ve got the list in my pocket. I’ll add it.”

He laughed so hard she nearly fell off.

Then neither of them was laughing. She let go of his wrists and his hands came up to her face, and she kissed him slowly, then not slowly, in his bed, which was hers now too. She pulled his T-shirt off and he pulled the old hoodie she’d slept in over her head, and it caught on her ears and they both started again. She’d been in this bed a hundred times. She’d never been in it like this, knowing she’d wake up in it tomorrow and the next day, knowing that the soup in the fridge downstairs and the screens in the front room and the blanket at the bottom of the bed were all here and weren’t going back over the wall. It made her bold. It made her shy, too, all at once, in a way she hadn’t been since the first time, and he felt it and slowed down and held her face and looked at her until it passed.

“You live here,” he said, as if he were only now finding it out.

It went through her like heat, and she pulled him to her and didn’t let him go until the grey stripe on the ceiling had turned white.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards she lay on his chest and couldn’t sleep, for once, for happiness, which she’d never had happen before.

The window was behind his head. She could see it over his shoulder, the curtain not quite shut, and through the gap the back of the tall house, and her own old window, high up, at the top of the stairs.

It was lit.

She went still. He felt it.

“What?”

“My room,” she said. “The light’s on.”

He turned his head and looked.

It was the small lamp, not the big light. She’d left the lamp; it was the one thing she hadn’t taken. Someone had gone up the stairs in the dark and turned it on, and through the window she could see the shape of the room, the pale squares on the wall, the folded camp bed leaning against it.

And a shape in the chair by the desk. Big. Still. Sitting in the empty room at the top of the house in the light of the lamp she’d left, with his hands on his knees.

Neither of them said anything.

They lay in his bed and watched her father sit in her empty room, not doing anything, not looking at anything, just sitting there, until the sky began to go grey behind the tall house and the lamp looked thin against it, and then the light went off, and he was gone.

chapters.title: The Red Egg
chapters.desc: The first February she wakes up next door, there’s still a red egg on the step, and this time she catches who leaves it. At the grave at dawn her father turns to her and says the words. That night she writes one word on a sticky note and puts it in Yu Chen’s textbook.
chapters.epigraph: “I boiled you an egg every year and left it where you’d find it. I couldn’t do the rest. I’m sorry. Happy birthday, Yu-er.” — Lin Jian
chapters.content:
She asked her father on the Sunday before New Year, at lunch, in front of everyone, because that was the only way she’d make herself do it.

“Can Yu Chen come on Monday night? For the dinner.”

The table went quiet. It always went quiet now when she spoke to him directly; four months in, nobody had got used to it, including her. Baba put his chopsticks down.

He’d changed since November. Not much. He came to breakfast. He passed her things. Some Sundays he asked her a question, short, about nothing, and waited for the answer, and she could see what it cost him every time. In November a man had come to the red door with a knife, and Elara had been hurt; for three weeks after it Eliana had sent her one word every night, here, and got nothing back. Something had gone out of Baba since then and not come back, and Elara still didn’t come to the house, and nobody at the table said why. Eliana knew more than she said. She always did.

“Not this year,” said Baba.

She’d known he’d say it. It still went in.

“Next year,” he said, looking at his bowl. Then he looked up, at her, the way he’d learned to, for about a second. “Next year. Tell him.”

It wasn’t yes. She went next door that night and told Yu Chen anyway, in the front room, across the two desks, and he went red and pretended to read and turned two pages at once.

“I’m on nights on Monday,” he said. “I’d have had to say no.”

“That’s not the point.”

“I know it’s not,” said Yu Chen. “Next year.”

✦ ✦ ✦

New Year’s Eve at the tall house was loud and red and too hot, and her chair at the far end by the window was still hers, and the chair beside it was empty, and the one halfway down where Elara should have been was empty too, and nobody moved either of them.

Jun Hyuk talked, which helped. He’d made dumplings that afternoon, he said, two hundred of them, and left most of them somewhere else, and wouldn’t say where, and Evangeline beside him looked at her plate and said nothing, which meant she knew where. Raiden wore a red waistcoat. Zhao said “Hm” to the fish. At midnight they went out onto the steps for the firecrackers and the whole lane was smoke and noise and red paper, and Eliana stood on the third step with her hands over her ears and looked across the little wall at the dark windows of the Song house and thought about a boy at a hospital, on nights, with a flask of the wrong tea.

She went home over the wall at one with a box of dumplings and a red packet from Baba that she didn’t open, and sat at her desk facing his empty one, and worked, and ate the dumplings cold, and texted him a photograph of the box.

Yu Chen: Did he say anything?

Eliana: he gave me a red packet. he looked at me when he did it. two whole seconds

Yu Chen: That’s two more than last year.

Eliana: you’re supposed to be saving lives

Yu Chen: A man in bed nine has had eleven dumplings and I’m watching his sugar. It’s the same thing.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the morning of her birthday he was home.

She’d asked him in January not to mark it, the way she asked every year, and he’d said all right, the way he said it every year, and this time she’d stopped in the doorway of the front room and said, “No. Wait. You can say it. This year. If you want,” and gone out before he could answer, and sat on the stairs with her face hot.

So he’d swapped a shift. She’d found out by accident, from the rota she wasn’t supposed to be able to see. He’d come home from his last night at eight on the Tuesday and slept all day so he could be awake for the dawn, and now he was in bed beside her, and she was asleep, properly asleep, the way she slept now in this house and never had in the other one.

He woke her at a quarter to five with his hand on her shoulder.

“Yu-er.”

She opened her eyes. It was black outside. He was up on one elbow, looking at the door.

“Your father’s on our step,” he said.

She sat up so fast her head swam.

“What?”

“I heard the rail on the little wall. He’s on our step. He’s got the egg.” He looked at her in the dark. “Go down. Quickly, or you’ll miss him.”

She was halfway out of bed before the last part reached her. She stopped with one foot on the floor.

“How do you know about the egg?”

He didn’t answer straight away. And she knew, then, from the way he didn’t, before he said anything at all.

“There’s a light in your kitchen at four,” said Yu Chen. “Every year. On this morning. I can see it from the bathroom window. And a shape at the stove. Big. It isn’t Ah Sim.” He held her eyes. “Then Ah Sim takes something up the back stairs at a quarter to five. I’ve seen it four years.”

“You knew.”

“Yes.”

“Four years. I thanked Ah Sim. Every year. You let me thank Ah Sim.”

“It was his to tell you,” he said. “Not mine. I don’t go near what’s his to tell you. I’ve never told you anything I watched that was somebody else’s.” He didn’t look away. “Go down. He’s leaving.”

She stood there with one foot on the cold floor and her whole chest hot and angry and something else under the anger that she didn’t have time for. He’d known. He’d watched her father at a stove at four in the morning four Februaries running and never said a word, because it was her father’s to say. It was exactly the kind of thing he would do. It was exactly the kind of thing she’d have wanted him to do, if anyone had asked her, which nobody had.

She went down the stairs in his T-shirt and her socks and opened the front door.

Baba was at the bottom of the three steps, going.

He’d put it on the top step, where she’d find it when she came out. A red egg in a white saucer, still warm; she could see it steaming a little in the cold. He’d turned to go back along the porch to the little wall and step over it, a big old man in a coat in the dark, and he heard the door and stopped with his back to her.

Neither of them said anything.

Then he turned round. He looked up at her in the doorway of the policeman’s old house, in a boy’s T-shirt, barefoot nearly, on her birthday. In the light from the hall she saw his face, and it was terrible, it was the face of a man caught doing the one thing he’d never let anyone catch him at.

“Ah Sim’s knees,” he said. “The step’s too high for her this side.”

She looked at the egg.

“Baba,” she said.

He stood there. She watched him try to keep the lie and not be able to.

“It was always me,” said her father. “Every year.”

Then he went back along the porch and stepped over the little wall, slowly, holding the iron rail, and went in at the red door, and she stood with the warm saucer in her hands and the cold coming in round her ankles and didn’t know what to do with any of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the grave it was grey and cold and the wind came up off the reservoir the way it always did.

They went up the path in the dark, the way they always had: Baba first, then Elowen, then Raiden with his hands in his pockets, then Evangeline in pale blue with Jun Hyuk a step behind her carrying the flowers. Zhao waited at the gate, the way he always waited, and so did Yu Chen this year, beside him, in his dark coat, with his hands in his pockets. The two of them stood together at the bottom of the hill and didn’t speak, and Eliana thought it was the longest Zhao had ever stood next to anyone without leaving.

Elara wasn’t there. Nobody said anything about it.

Eliana came last, as she always did. She’d peeled the egg in the kitchen of the Song house and eaten half of it standing at the counter and put the other half in her pocket in a twist of paper. She didn’t know why.

Elowen knelt and put the white chrysanthemums in the stone pot. Baba lit the incense, three sticks, his big hands round the lighter. They stood in a row and nobody spoke, and the incense went sideways in the wind, and the sky started to come up white over the reservoir.

She stood at the end and waited for it to be over.

Baba turned round.

He didn’t turn to Elowen, or to the stone. He turned to the end of the row, where she was, and looked at her, and the others saw it, and went still.

“Yu-er,” he said.

She couldn’t move.

“I boiled you an egg,” said her father. “Every year. And left it where you’d find it. I couldn’t do the rest.” His voice was rough, the voice from the front room with the door shut. “I couldn’t come up the stairs. I couldn’t say it at the table. I stood at your door. I couldn’t knock. I’m sorry.” He stopped. His jaw worked. “Happy birthday, Yu-er.”

The wind came up off the water. Somebody in the row made a sound, Elowen, she thought, or Raiden. Nobody moved.

She’d waited her whole life for him to say it, and now that he had she found she didn’t know what you did next. Nobody had ever shown her. She stood at the end of the row in the cold and looked at her father, and he looked back, and didn’t look away, and his eyes were wet and he didn’t do anything about it.

“Thank you, Baba,” she said. It was all she had.

She took the half egg out of her pocket in its twist of paper and held it out to him.

He looked at it. Then he took it, carefully, in his big hand, and stood there holding it, and she saw his mouth go, and he turned back to the stone.

At the bottom of the hill, on the way out, he stopped by the gate where Zhao and Yu Chen were waiting. He didn’t look at Zhao. He looked at Yu Chen, and Yu Chen took his hands out of his pockets.

“Sunday,” said Baba. “Lunch. You’ll come.” He paused, and Eliana watched him make himself do the next part. “Will you?”

“Yes,” said Yu Chen. “Thank you.”

Baba nodded once, and went down to the car, and Uncle Mok opened the door for him, and as he got in Eliana saw that he still had the egg in his hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past eleven, at her desk in the front room, her phone buzzed with a voice message from Elara.

It was six minutes long. She sat with it in her lap and looked at the number before she pressed it. Then she put her headphones in and listened to her sister talk, from a car somewhere, with the engine off, for six minutes: about nothing, about the grave, about the wind, about a bird on the wall, about a stupid thing Raiden had done at Christmas, laughing, then not laughing, then saying happy birthday, Yu-er, I’m sorry I haven’t, then stopping, then going on about something else. It was the first time she’d heard Elara’s voice since November. She listened to it twice. Then she sat with her headphones in and her hands over her face and didn’t play it again, because she wanted to keep some for later.

Across the two desks, Yu Chen didn’t say anything. He got up and made tea, and put it down by her elbow, and went back to his chair.

✦ ✦ ✦

She did it at ten that night, while he was in the shower.

She’d thought about it all day. She’d thought about it at the grave, with the half egg in her pocket, and in the car, and through six minutes of her sister’s voice. She’d thought about it for longer than that, if she was honest. Since the hill. Since the steps of the Great Hall. Since a night in March last year when he’d said a word on the porch and she’d run inside and bolted the door.

His textbook was on his desk. A big one, on emergency medicine, that he wasn’t supposed to need until August and had been reading every night since Christmas. She took a sticky note off her pad, yellow, and wrote on it in pencil in her small square handwriting. She didn’t draw anything. For once she didn’t draw a single thing.

Official. — Yu-er

She opened the book to the page his bookmark was on, and stuck the note in the middle of it, and shut it, and went and sat on the sofa with her knees up and a laptop she wasn’t looking at.

He came down at twenty past with his hair wet. He sat at his desk. He opened the book.

She watched him over the top of the laptop.

He didn’t say anything. He sat and looked at the page for long enough that she started to think he hadn’t seen it, or that he’d seen it and didn’t know what it meant, and her face started to burn. Then he peeled it off the page, carefully, by one corner, and sat holding it on the end of his finger.

Then he stood up and came round the two desks and across the room to the sofa, with the note on his finger, and she couldn’t look at him and couldn’t look away.

He stuck it on her forehead.

She went cross-eyed trying to see it. He looked at it there, at her, with the yellow square stuck to the middle of her forehead and her glasses pushed up under it, and his whole face went, all at once, the way it never went in front of anyone else.

“Official,” he said. “In your handwriting.”

She told him she was aware it was in her handwriting, and her voice came out wrong, and he heard it.

He peeled it off her forehead, slowly, and kissed the place where it had been. Then he kissed her mouth. He knelt on the floor in front of the sofa and took the laptop off her knees and put it on the floor and kissed her with both hands holding her face, and she slid down off the sofa into him because she couldn’t stay up, and he held her there on the floor of the front room and kissed her until she was dizzy and breathless and laughing, with the note stuck to the end of his thumb behind her ear.

“I’ve got a drawer,” he said, against her mouth. “Upstairs. Every one you ever gave me. In order.”

“I know. I’ve seen it. I looked.”

He pulled back far enough to stare at her.

“I’m me,” said Eliana. “Of course I looked.”

He laughed, and kissed her again, and when he got up, eventually, he went upstairs and put the note in the drawer, at the front, on top of all the others, and came back down, and didn’t say anything else about it. He couldn’t stop smiling.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went to bed at midnight.

She didn’t wake at two. She didn’t wake at four. Nobody put an egg on the step, because nobody needed to any more. She slept with her face against his back and the blue blanket on top of everything, and she slept the whole night through, on her birthday, for the first time in her life, and when she woke the sun was already on the wall and he was still there, awake, watching her, with the tea gone cold on the bedside table because he hadn’t wanted to get up.

chapters.title: Legal, Mostly
chapters.desc: Eliana opens her own security firm in two rooms above a dumpling shop, with a sticky note for a sign. Si-Wei writes the business plan. Yu Chen bought the building a week ago and mentions it on opening night, which goes about as well as he expected.
chapters.epigraph: “The sign’s a sticky note. I’ll get a real one when we can afford it.” / “We own the building, Yu-er.” / “You did WHAT.” — Eliana Lin and Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
The sign was a sticky note.

Yellow, the big square kind, stuck to the inside of the front window of the first floor at eye level for anyone standing on the opposite pavement of Terrace Road and looking up past the steam from the dumpling shop. It said FENCE in her small square capitals, and underneath, smaller, Legal. Mostly.

“You can’t put mostly,” said Si-Wei. “Clients will read it.”

“Good clients will laugh,” said Eliana. “Bad clients won’t come up the stairs. That’s a filter.”

Si-Wei looked at the sticky note through the glass with her black coffee in her hand and her cream coat buttoned to the throat. Then she looked at Eliana, sitting on the floor of the empty front room in a paint-spattered hoodie with her laptop on her knees, and something happened at the corner of her mouth that in anyone else would have been a smile.

“Fine,” she said. “It’s a filter. I’ll put it in the plan.”

The plan was forty pages long. Si-Wei had written it in three weeks in the evenings at her kitchen table, and it had charts in it, and a section called RISKS that was mostly about Eliana, and a page near the back that said S-W. Yen: 15% in small type that Eliana had found on the second read and not mentioned. Si-Wei hadn’t asked for it. She’d just written herself in, the way she’d written herself into Eliana’s life over a cup of tea she’d poured unasked, a year and a half ago.

“Fifteen percent,” said Eliana now, not looking up.

“I’m worth it,” said Si-Wei, and sat down on the dust sheet beside her with her coffee, carefully, in her good coat. “Who’s coming today?”

“Nobody. It’s the first day. Nobody comes on the first day.”

“Then what’s on your screen?”

Eliana turned the laptop round. There were nine emails. Three were from people who wanted to know if she was the one who’d done the bank talk last March. Two were from companies that wanted someone to test their walls before somebody else did. One was from a man at Chen Si’s that just said Good luck. Q. One was from Professor Ou, and was four words long, and the four words were I knew you would. Two were spam, and she’d already found out who’d sent them.

Si-Wei read them all, slowly.

“Nobody,” she said.

“Nobody important.”

“You’re impossible,” said Si-Wei, and drank her coffee.

✦ ✦ ✦

The rooms were two, over the dumpling shop, up a narrow staircase with a turn in it. The front room had the window and the sticky note and the view of the street going down the hill. The back room had a door that locked properly, which was the only thing Eliana had asked for when she saw it, and a smaller window onto the fire escape and the yard behind. It had been an accountant’s office for twenty years and then empty for two, and it smelled of old paper and pork and ginger, and she loved it the moment she walked in.

She was going to do it properly. That was the whole point. People paid her to find the holes in their walls before someone else did, and she found them, and wrote them up, and showed them how to close them, and sent an invoice that a lawyer had read. Nobody’s hands got broken. Nobody disappeared. She’d stood up last March in front of two hundred people and told a bank its door was open, and they’d fined the bank, and then a firm had come after her family. She was never going to do it like that again. She was going to do it in writing, with contracts, above a dumpling shop.

The family’s work she still did. She’d told Si-Wei and she’d told Yu Chen, plainly, at the start: if Baba rang, or Chen Si, or one of her sisters, she’d go. None of it was on any page of the plan. It lived in a separate place, on a separate machine in the back room, behind the door that locked, and it was hers, and it was small now, and she didn’t do it upstairs at four in the morning any more.

“You’ll keep the two apart,” Si-Wei had said, reading the plan back.

“I’ve kept everything apart my whole life.”

“I know,” said Si-Wei. “I meant it as a compliment.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Yu Chen came at seven, straight from the hospital, with a carrier bag of paint and a box of dumplings from downstairs.

“The woman downstairs says you owe her for the sign,” he said, coming up the narrow stairs sideways because he didn’t fit them any other way. “She says it’s on her window, and the steam makes it curl.”

“It does curl,” said Eliana. “That’s character.”

He put the paint down. He looked round the front room, at the dust sheets, the laptop, Si-Wei’s coffee cup on the windowsill, the sticky note curling in the steam. He was pleased and trying not to show it, which with him meant showing it completely.

“It’s good,” he said.

“It’s two rooms over a dumpling shop.”

“It’s yours,” said Yu Chen. “That’s what’s good about it.”

They painted. The front room, first: plain white, because she didn’t care about colour and he did, a bit, and had brought three sample pots she sent back down the stairs without opening. He did the ceiling, because he could reach it. She did the walls, badly, in long uneven streaks with her tongue between her teeth, and got it in her hair and on her glasses and down the front of the hoodie, and he came behind her with the roller and fixed it without saying anything and she pretended not to notice.

At nine they sat on the floor on the dust sheet and ate the dumplings out of the box with their fingers, and the street outside had gone dark except for the shop lights and the steam.

“I’ll get a real sign,” she said, with her mouth full. “When we can afford it. When there’s a client. A proper one, metal, with a light.”

He didn’t say anything.

She looked at him. He was looking at a dumpling.

“What?”

“We don’t need to afford it,” said Yu Chen.

“Of course we need to afford it. It’s a business. Si-Wei’s got a whole page on cash flow.”

“I know. I read it. It’s a good page.” He put the dumpling down in the box. He looked at her, and his ears had started to go, and she felt her stomach start to go with them. “Yu-er. We own the building.”

She stared at him.

“You did what.”

“Last week. Tuesday. The accountant who had it before wanted to sell, and the agent was going to let it to you on a two-year lease, and in two years he could have put the rent up or sold it to someone who’d want you out, and I didn’t—” He stopped. “So I bought it. The whole building. The dumpling shop’s on a long lease now. Nobody can ever put you out of here.”

She got up off the dust sheet.

She didn’t know she was going to until she was standing. Her face was hot. Her hands had paint on them and she didn’t know what to do with them.

“You bought it,” she said. “Without asking. Last week.”

“I was going to tell you on Friday. Then on Sunday. Then you were so happy this morning—”

“So you told me now. On the first night. On the floor.”

“Yes.”

“That’s what Baba does,” said Eliana. Her voice had gone high. “That’s exactly what he does. He buys the room. He buys the corner office on the floor below and the number on the page and the driver, so you never need anything, so you never go anywhere. I said no to him at a table in front of everyone. I said no to Chen Si. I came here to do something that was mine, that nobody bought for me, and you—”

She couldn’t finish. She went past him into the back room and pushed the window up and climbed out onto the fire escape into the cold, because it was the only door in the place she could go through that wasn’t the stairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

The fire escape was iron and rusted and looked down into the yard behind the dumpling shop, where the dumpling woman’s son was sitting on an upturned crate with a cigarette. Past the roofs she could see the lights of the street going down the hill, and past them, the harbour.

She stood with her paint-covered hands on the rail and breathed.

She heard him climb out behind her. He was too big for the window and banged his head, and swore, which he never did, and then he stood on the iron grating beside her, not touching her, with his hands in his pockets.

He didn’t say sorry. She waited for it and he didn’t.

“He bought a room to keep you in,” said Yu Chen. “I bought a building so nobody can ever make you leave this one. That’s not the same thing. I know it feels the same. It’s not.” He looked at the harbour. “You can hate it. You can be angry for a week. I’d still do it. I’m not going to pretend I wouldn’t.”

She turned and looked at him.

He was standing on a rusty fire escape in the cold in a shirt with white paint down one sleeve and a dumpling crumb on his collar, looking at the harbour with his ears scarlet and his jaw set, and he’d bought her a building because he couldn’t stand the thought of her being moved out of a room she liked. Not to keep her in it. So that it was hers whether he was there or not.

She was still angry. She was so angry. She took hold of his paint-spattered collar in both fists and pulled him down and kissed him anyway.

It wasn’t gentle. She didn’t want it to be. She kissed him furious, on the fire escape, with paint on her hands going onto his neck and her glasses pushed crooked against his cheek, and he made a sound into her mouth and his hands came out of his pockets and onto her back and held on.

“I’m still angry,” she said against his mouth. “I’m going to be angry for a week.”

“Take two,” said Yu Chen, and kissed her back.

From the yard below, the dumpling woman’s son whistled.

She went to pull away. She’d have pulled away a year ago, she’d have gone scarlet and climbed back through the window and hidden in the back room. She felt herself start to do it now, out of habit, and then he caught her face in his hands, paint and all, and kissed her again, on purpose, slowly, out on the fire escape over Terrace Road with the whole yard and half the street looking up, and she stopped trying to go anywhere.

Below them a window banged open and the dumpling woman herself leaned out.

“You two! Up there! Is that the landlord?”

“Yes,” said Yu Chen, without letting go of her.

“Then tell him the drain’s blocked!”

Eliana put her face in his chest and laughed until she couldn’t stand up.

✦ ✦ ✦

They didn’t finish the painting.

She made him put it in writing first. She sat on the dust sheet in the half-painted front room and wrote it on the back of one of Si-Wei’s spare pages, a lease, a proper one, with a rent in it, the real rent the agent would have charged her, to be paid into an account in his name on the first of every month by FENCE, which was her.

“You don’t have to pay me anything,” he said.

“I’m paying you rent. It’s a business. Si-Wei will kill me if I don’t.”

“Then I’ll put it back in your account.”

“Then I’ll stop paying it in money and pay it in dumplings,” said Eliana, “and you’ll have to eat them, every month, a whole box, in front of me, so I know.” She signed it. She held the pen out. “Sign. Landlord.”

He signed it. He signed it with his whole name, carefully, the way he wrote on drug charts, and then sat looking at the two names on the page side by side.

“That’s the first thing we’ve ever signed,” he said.

“It’s a lease.”

“I know what it is.”

She looked at him across the page, and saw his face, and took the pen out of his hand.

The dust sheet was big enough. Just. It smelled of new paint and the dumplings and the old paper of the accountant’s twenty years, and the floor under it was hard, and neither of them cared. She pulled his shirt off over his head and it left a long white streak of wet paint across his chest from her sleeve, and she laughed at it, and he looked down at himself.

“That’s not coming off,” he said.

“Good,” said Eliana, and pushed him down on the sheet.

He let her. He lay on the floor of her office with white paint on his chest and in his hair and looked up at her with his face gone open and soft, the way it went only for her, and put his hands on her waist under the paint-stiff hoodie.

“Someone could come up the stairs,” he said.

“It’s locked. I locked it. I own the lock.”

He pointed out, reasonably, that he owned the lock. She told him he owned the door and she rented the lock, and he laughed so hard he couldn’t kiss her, and she kissed him anyway, on the laughing mouth, until he stopped. Then it was slow. The street went on outside, the steam and the shop lights and somebody’s radio, and inside it was only the two of them on a dust sheet in the half-white room, with paint on their hands and the sticky note curling in the window. He was careful with her on the hard floor, and then less careful because she asked him not to be, and she held his face and kissed him and didn’t hide anything, not in her own rooms, not in a place that was hers and that nobody could take. She felt, holding on to him on the floor of FENCE with her hair full of paint, more like herself than she’d ever felt anywhere, and she didn’t know how to say that, so she just said his name, the one for here, over and over, until it said it for her.

Afterwards they lay on the sheet with his coat over them and looked at the ceiling he’d painted, which had a bare patch in the corner where he’d missed.

“You missed a bit,” she said.

“I’ll do it on Friday. When I come for the rent.”

Her laptop, on the floor by the window, made the small sound it made for a new email. She reached out with one arm and turned it round without getting up.

It was from a man she’d never heard of. The subject line was in capitals. The signature had three phone numbers in it, and a firm’s name she’d heard of, a big one, and under the three phone numbers, where a person would put kind regards, it said I love you already. I’m abroad till April. Can we meet when I’m back? I’ll bring my own chair.

She read it twice.

“Who is it?” said Yu Chen, into her hair.

“I think,” said Eliana slowly, “it’s a client.”

chapters.title: The First Client Is Very Loud
chapters.desc: FENCE’s first real client is Ren Hao, who hires Eliana at top volume, hugs everyone in the building and says “I love you” to the dumpling woman. Two weeks later, at Serafina’s wedding, Eliana leaves early with cake, because Yu Chen is on nights.
chapters.epigraph: “I pay triple and I hug. Those are my terms. Fix my firm and come to my parties.” — Ren Hao
chapters.content:
She heard him before she saw him.

Everyone on Terrace Road heard him. At ten o’clock on Monday morning a voice came up from the street, through the window, past the sticky note, saying “THAT’S IT, that’s the one, the yellow one, I love it, look at it, it says mostly,” and then the street door banged, and then the dumpling woman was shouting something, and the voice shouted back “I LOVE YOU TOO, I’ll have twelve on the way out,” and then there were feet on the narrow stairs, a lot of feet for one person, and Si-Wei, at the desk by the window, put her coffee down and closed her eyes.

“Oh no,” she said.

“Do you know him?”

“Everyone knows him,” said Si-Wei.

The man who came through the door had to turn sideways at the top of the stairs, not because he was tall but because he was wide, in a three-piece suit the colour of strong tea, with a watch chain and a pocket square and a face that was already smiling before it had seen anyone to smile at.
