He looked round the half-painted front room, at the dust sheets and the two desks and the laptop and the box of dumplings on the windowsill, and spread his arms.

“Perfect,” he said. “It’s perfect. It’s exactly what I wanted. No marble. No lobby. A girl with a laptop over a dumpling shop. Which one of you is the Eraser?”

Eliana went cold all over.

“Nobody here’s called that,” she said.

“Ah.” He looked at her properly then, at her face, and his own face changed, not much, just enough. “Sorry. That’s what they call you in the business. My business. The people who are frightened of you. I didn’t mean it rudely.” He held out his hand. “Ren Hao. I love the sign.”

She looked at the hand. She didn’t take it. She didn’t take anyone’s hand if she could help it.

He didn’t seem to mind. He turned and held it out to Si-Wei instead, and Si-Wei looked at it as if it were a fish, and then, slowly, took it, and he shook it and then pulled her in and hugged her, all at once, enormous, in her cream coat.

“Si-Wei Yen,” he said into her hair. “I haven’t seen you since your sister’s premiere. You’ve got so tall.”

“I haven’t grown since I was fourteen,” said Si-Wei, muffled.

“You’ve got taller in spirit,” said Ren Hao, and let her go, and turned back to Eliana, and she saw him decide not to hug her, which was the first thing about him she liked.

✦ ✦ ✦

He sat in the second chair with his legs crossed and explained it at the top of his voice.

His firm looked after risk. Big companies paid it to tell them what might go wrong in the places they did business: who was dangerous, who could be bought, what the roads were like, which governments were about to fall. He had offices in more cities than Eliana could keep in her head as he listed them. He said “I love you” to Si-Wei twice in the first ten minutes, once when she brought him water and once when she corrected his figures, and both times it sounded exactly like thank you.

“Risk,” said Eliana.

She’d gone stiff. He noticed.

“I know,” said Ren Hao. “Calder. Hsieh Kai-yan. I know exactly who he was and what he sent to your market.” His voice came down, for the first time, from the top of the room to somewhere ordinary. “He used to do work for some of my clients. Before. We’re not the same. They’re what I’m afraid of. People like him, and people like the crew he hired. That’s why I’m here.” He uncrossed his legs. “Somebody good got into his people in thirty-six hours. I want that somebody to get into mine, and tell me how, before somebody worse does.”

She looked at him.

“I’ll find things you won’t like,” she said.

“I should hope so.”

“I’ll write them up in plain words. I won’t make them sound nicer than they are.”

“Good.”

“And if I find something that isn’t about your walls,” said Eliana, “something one of your own people is doing that they shouldn’t, I’m not going to keep it quiet for you because you’re paying me.”

He looked at her without smiling. Then he smiled so wide it went up into his ears.

“I love you,” said Ren Hao.

“Don’t.”

“I can’t help it. I say it to everyone. I said it to your dumpling lady. My sister says it’s a medical condition. She’s in the foreign service, she thinks everything’s a medical condition.” He took an envelope out of his inside pocket and put it on her desk. “That’s what I’ll pay. If you think it’s too low I’ll triple it. Those are my terms. I pay triple and I hug.”

Si-Wei picked up the envelope, opened it, read the number, and put it down again, carefully.

“It’s not too low,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

By Thursday Eliana had found four things he wasn’t going to like, and one he was going to hate.

She did it in the back room, behind the locked door, with the window open onto the fire escape and the smell of pork coming up. It was the first job she’d ever done with a contract, and it was the cleanest work she’d ever done in her life. Nobody had to be found afterwards. Nobody’s name went to Qian. She opened doors that a man had asked her to open, and wrote down which ones and how wide, and at the end of it she had a report on Si-Wei’s desk in plain words, and on the last page the fifth thing: that a senior man in his overseas office had been copying client files home for a year.

Ren Hao read it in the second chair on Friday afternoon, with his legs crossed. He read every page without saying anything, which Si-Wei said afterwards was the longest she’d ever known him be silent. On the last page he stopped.

“Ah,” he said. His face had gone grey. “Ah. Him. He’s been to my house for New Year.”

“I’m sorry,” said Eliana.

“No. Don’t be. That’s what I paid for.” He closed the report and sat with it on his knee. “You said you wouldn’t keep it quiet. You didn’t.” He looked up at her. “I’m going to ring him now, from your stairs, and then I’m going to be sad for a week, and then I’m going to send you every client I have.”

He went out to the landing and rang him. They heard his voice through the door, and it wasn’t loud at all.

At five Yu Chen came up the narrow stairs with a box of dumplings, because it was Friday and the rent was due.

Ren Hao was still on the landing. He looked at Yu Chen, at the lanyard he’d forgotten to take off and the box in his hands, and his whole face came back on again, all at once, like a shop with its shutters going up.

“You’re the landlord!” he said. “The dumpling lady told me. The tall doctor who owns the building and pays his rent in dumplings to himself. I love it. I love you.” And he hugged him.

Yu Chen stood in the middle of it with the dumpling box held out to one side and his face perfectly polite and perfectly empty, the face he used for everyone who wasn’t her, the one that said good morning like a door shutting. He bore it. He waited for it to be over.

“Thank you,” he said, when Ren Hao let go.

“He’s lovely,” said Ren Hao to Eliana, through the door. “He’s terrifying. I love you both.”

When he’d gone, at last, down the stairs and out and away up Terrace Road with twelve dumplings in a bag, still talking, Yu Chen put the rent on her desk and stood there.

“He said he loves you,” he said.

“He says it to everybody. He said it to the dumpling lady.”

“I heard.” He didn’t look at her. “I didn’t like it.”

She looked at him, standing by her desk in his lanyard with his ears going, not liking it, and not pretending he liked it, and not asking her to do anything about it either.

“You’re jealous of a man who hugged you.”

“I’m jealous of a man who’s allowed to say it to you in a voice like that. Out loud. Like it’s nothing.” His ears were scarlet now. “I can’t say it like it’s nothing. I’ve never been able to.”

She got up and went round the desk and stood in front of him, and put her hand flat on his chest, over the lanyard.

“I know,” she said. “That’s why I believe you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Serafina married Haozhen on the twenty-fifth of April, in the morning at the registry and in the evening in a garage under a railway bridge, and Yu Chen was on nights.

“Bring me cake,” he said, on the Saturday morning, in the doorway, already in his coat. He was on surgery now, the third part of his intern year, ward nights, and he looked tired the way he only looked in April. “Any cake. And tell me what she wore.”

“You don’t care what she wore.”

“I care that you’ll tell me,” said Yu Chen, and kissed her forehead, and went.

The garage had lights along every girder of the railway bridge, thousands of them, warm white, and nine round tables with red cloths, and two cars, one at each end, and two hundred people, and a sign over the kettle that said what you couldn’t do in the garage and then, in fresh paint, EXCEPT TODAY. Eliana sat at table three with her family. Baba, grey and quiet and enormous, in his funeral suit. Elowen in green with a camellia in her hair. Raiden drawing on a napkin. Jinx with new beads round her wrist. Evangeline, who said nothing at all and beat Aurelia at a game with toast glasses in four minutes and then said nothing about that either. Zhao at the next table with his back to Elowen’s chair, facing the alley door.

Eliana had her phone under the table.

She’d got into Haozhen’s phone the year before, in a car, in under four minutes. She got into it again now, under a red tablecloth, between the scallops and the chicken, in rather less, because some things you didn’t forget. She changed his wallpaper to a photograph she’d taken that afternoon outside the registry, of a short white dress and a pair of black boots with the heels worn down on the outside, and across the bottom of it in white capitals, SHE DRIVES.

She put the phone away. Nobody had seen. Except Baba, beside her, who’d watched her thumbs with a face she couldn’t read, and then nearly smiled, and looked at his soup.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ren Hao was there. Of course he was; he knew everyone. He came round the tables with a glass in his hand hugging people who didn’t want to be hugged, and when he got to table three he stopped behind her chair and put his hands on her shoulders.

“My Eraser,” he said. “I’ve sent you two clients. Did they ring?”

They had, on Wednesday. He said he loved her and leaned down and asked where the landlord was, and she said at work.

“On a night like this? Doctors.” He shook his head at the girders. “So. When’s yours? Your wedding. I want to come. I want to be the loudest one there.”

Table three went quiet.

Elowen’s head came up. Raiden stopped drawing. Evangeline, across the table, didn’t move at all, which meant she was listening harder than anyone. Baba, beside her, put his spoon down.

A year ago she’d have gone under the table. Two years ago she’d have left. She felt the heat start in her ears, and she let it, and she didn’t do anything about it.

“When I’m ready,” said Eliana. “You’ll be the loudest. I promise.”

Ren Hao beamed and kissed the top of her head and went off to the next table. Nobody at table three said anything. Elowen picked her chopsticks up again. And Baba, beside her, without looking at her, moved the dish of scallops a little nearer her bowl.

✦ ✦ ✦

She left at a quarter to midnight, before the rice and the sparklers, with two slices of wedding cake in a napkin in a takeaway box that Mr. Kwok had given her without being asked.

The taxi took her down to City Hospital. She went up in the lift to the top deck of the car park, where the Volvo was, and sat on the bonnet in her good dress with her hoodie over it, because she’d brought the hoodie in her bag, and texted him one word.

Eliana: cake

He came out of the stairwell door at ten past two in blue scrubs, at a run, which made her laugh.

“Twenty minutes,” he said. “The registrar said twenty. There’s a man on the ward who thinks it’s 1987.”

“Is it bad?”

“He’s very happy,” said Yu Chen. “It’s a good year for him.” He sat down on the bonnet beside her. “What did she wear?”

She told him. The short white dress, the boots, the way Haozhen had looked at the end of the aisle that wasn’t an aisle. The lights on the girders. Nonna and Gilded. The sign over the kettle. She told him about the wallpaper and he laughed so hard he had to put his face in his hands.

She opened the box. The cake was a bit squashed from the taxi. She hadn’t brought forks; she hadn’t thought.

“No forks,” she said.

“I’ve got hands.” He saw her face. “I washed them,” said Yu Chen. “Twice. It’s a hospital.”

She broke a piece off with her fingers instead and held it out to him, and he looked at her and leaned in and ate it off her fingers, and then didn’t move away. He held her wrist. He kissed the icing off the ends of her fingers, slowly, one by one, with his eyes on hers in the dark, and she forgot about the cake.

“There’s more on your thumb,” he said.

“There isn’t.”

“There is now,” said Yu Chen, and kissed it, and then her palm, and then the inside of her wrist where his hand was, and then her mouth, which tasted of icing too.

He kissed her slowly on the bonnet of his car on the top deck of the car park at two in the morning, with the city below them all the way down to the harbour and the sky over them with a few real stars in it, and he hadn’t planned anything, and she’d brought squashed cake in a takeaway box, and it was the best kiss she’d had in months. She put her hands in his hair. He made a small sound and pulled her closer by the hoodie, and the box slid off the bonnet onto the concrete and neither of them looked.

“Ren Hao asked when ours was,” she said, when she could.

He went still against her.

“At the table,” she said. “In front of everyone. In front of Baba.”

“What did you say?”

“I said when I’m ready, he’ll be the loudest.” She looked at him. “I didn’t go under the table. I didn’t leave.”

He looked at her in the dark. She could see him not say anything. She could see him want to and hold it, the way he held everything, because he’d said it once on a step and he wasn’t going to push her with it twice.

“Baba moved the scallops,” she said. “After. Closer to my bowl.”

“That’s a lot, from him.”

“I know,” said Eliana. “I thought so too.”

His pager went. He looked at it and stood up, and became a doctor again, all at once, the way he did. He picked the cake box up off the concrete and put the last squashed slice in her hands.

“Eat that,” he said. “Then go home and sleep.”

“I’ll wait. You finish at eight.”

“You’ll fall asleep on the bonnet.”

“Then you’ll find me here,” said Eliana, and he looked at her, and didn’t argue, and went in through the stairwell door; and at eight o’clock, when he came out into the white morning with his eyes half shut, she was asleep in the passenger seat, let in with the spare key he’d given her when he bought the car, with her hoodie over her face and the empty cake box in her lap, and he drove her home without waking her.

chapters.title: He Matches to Emergency Medicine
chapters.desc: Yu Chen is offered emergency medicine training at City Hospital, the first thing in years he has chosen entirely for himself. He doesn’t know how to say it out loud. Eliana throws him the loudest party a quiet person can stand.
chapters.epigraph: “I didn’t pick it because of you. I picked it because it’s mine. That’s new for me.” — Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
The email came at twenty to eleven on a Friday morning, and he read it in the sluice.

He was on surgery, the last part of his intern year, on a general ward on the seventh floor, and the sluice was the only room on the ward with a door that shut. He’d gone in to empty something and his phone had buzzed in his pocket and he’d known what it was before he took it out, the way you know a voice on the stairs. He stood between the macerator and the rack of bedpans and read it twice.

We are pleased to offer you a post in Emergency Medicine training at City Hospital, commencing Monday 3 August 2026.

He read it a third time. Then he put the phone back in his pocket and emptied what he’d come in to empty, and washed his hands, carefully, the full way, all the steps, and went back out onto the ward and finished the drug chart he’d been writing up.

He didn’t know what else to do with it.

The registrar, a cheerful woman called Dr. Sze who’d been nice to him for five weeks because he never made her ask twice, found him at the nurses’ station at lunch.

“You’ve heard,” she said. “I can see it on you. Emergency? City?”

He said yes to both.

“Brilliant. Drinks tonight. The whole team. I’ll book somewhere.”

“That’s kind,” said Yu Chen, pleasantly, and smiled, and meant to say yes, and heard himself say instead, “I can’t tonight, I’m sorry,” and watched her face go a little flat, and felt nothing about it at all. He liked Dr. Sze. He’d forget her name in a year. There was only one person he wanted to tell, and he hadn’t told her yet, and he didn’t know why.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xing Yue came down to the ward at four.

He was a consultant now, had been for nearly a year, and consultants from the trauma team didn’t come to general surgery wards at four on a Friday unless something was wrong, and the nurses all straightened up as he came through the doors in his dark suit and his glasses. He didn’t look at any of them. He found Yu Chen by bed twelve and stood in front of him.

“You accepted,” he said.

“Not yet.”

Xing Yue looked at him over his glasses.

“Why not?”

Yu Chen didn’t answer. He looked at the man in bed twelve, who was asleep, and at the drip, and at the chart, and at anything that wasn’t his cousin’s face.

“I said you’d be good at it,” said Xing Yue. “I don’t say things to be kind. Accept it. Today.”

“I will.” He made himself look up. “I haven’t told her.”

Xing Yue didn’t say anything. He was the only person in the hospital, perhaps the only person in the city, who’d watched Yu Chen arrange his whole life round one girl from across a table twice a term for five years and never said a word about it. He looked at him now with his cold clever face, and Yu Chen saw him understand, and not say that either.

“It’s yours,” said Xing Yue. “That’s why you haven’t told her. Because it’s the first thing that is.” He took his glasses off and cleaned them on his tie, which he did when he was going to say something he didn’t like saying. “She’ll be glad. Go home and tell her. Then accept it. In that order.”

He put his glasses back on and went, and the nurses all breathed out.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was at her desk when he came in, in the front room, facing his, with her hood up and three screens going and the flask he’d left her at seven empty beside the keyboard.

“You’re early,” she said, without looking up. “You’re never early.”

He didn’t say anything. He took his phone out and opened the email and put the phone down on her keyboard, on top of whatever she was doing, which he’d never once done in five years.

She looked at the phone. Then at him. Then she read it.

He watched her read it. He saw her get to the end and go back to the beginning. He saw her mouth open.

Then she screamed.

He’d never heard her scream. Not like that, high and long and with her whole body, the way Si-Jie screamed. She came up out of the chair so fast it went over backwards with a crash, and she was round the desks and on him before he could do anything, her arms round his neck and her feet off the floor, and he caught her and staggered back against his own desk and the lamp with the crooked shade went over.

“You got it,” she said, into his neck. “You got it. You got it, you got it. City. Emergency. Chen. When did it come?”

“This morning.”

She pulled back and looked at him.

“And you came home at six. And didn’t ring me.” Her face went from shining to something sharper. “You had it all day and you didn’t ring me.”

“I didn’t know how to say it.”

“You say I got it. That’s how you say it.” She was still in his arms, still off the floor, glaring at him from close up. “Why didn’t you ring me?”

He put her down. He kept his hands on her waist. He made himself say it, because he’d made himself a promise once on a step that he’d never pretend there wasn’t a name for things.

“Because it’s the first thing I’ve picked that isn’t you,” said Yu Chen.

She went still.

“Everything else,” he said. “The course. The hill. The library. This house, when I bought it off Wei Long. The car, for nights, so I could get home to the lane faster. I chose all of it because of you. I’ve never minded. I’d do it all again. But this—” He stopped. “I didn’t pick it because of you. I picked it because it’s mine. Because of a boy on a trolley, and Toh, and a man with indigestion who wasn’t. That’s new for me. I didn’t know if you’d—”

“If I’d what?”

“If you’d think it meant I was going somewhere,” he said. “Away from you. A bit.”

She looked up at him. He could see her decide what to feel, and see it come out of her not the way he’d been afraid of.

“You’re an idiot,” said Eliana.

“Si-Wei says that to you.”

“She’s right about me and I’m right about you.” She put her hands flat on his chest. “You picked something for yourself. You. On purpose. For the first time since I’ve known you.” Her eyes had gone wet. “Do you know how long I’ve wanted you to do that? I thought you never would. I thought you’d stand next to me for the rest of your life and never want anything you couldn’t hand me.” She pushed him, not hard. “And you hid it all day because you thought I’d mind?”

“I didn’t know.”

“Now you know,” said Eliana. “Ring them. Now. Accept it. While I watch.”

He rang them. She stood in front of him with her arms folded the whole time and watched him say yes to the woman at the training office, and when he put the phone down she took it off him and put it face down on the desk and pulled his head down by both ears and kissed him, hard, with the lamp on its side on the floor throwing light across the ceiling.

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d already done things. He found out over the next week, one at a time.

She’d built a thing on her phone and his that showed his rota as a coloured bar, his shifts in green and his nights in blue, and it had his new rota in it already, August onwards, which nobody had sent him yet and which she said she’d “estimated”. She’d put a camera on his bicycle, small, on the back of the seat, that nobody had asked for. She’d found out the name of the consultant who ran the emergency training programme and what he liked to read and left a list of it on his desk, under his flask, in her square handwriting, with don’t tell him I did this at the bottom.

He didn’t ask how. He never asked how. He read the list and put it in the drawer with the sticky notes.

“And there’s going to be a party,” she said, on the Sunday. “On the thirtieth. Here.”

“You hate parties.”

“I know. This one’s for you, so I’ll survive it.” She was sitting on his desk with her feet on his chair. “It’s small. I’ve done a list. Don’t look at the list.”

He looked at the list. It was eleven names, counting both of them, and the last one was Auntie Dai (she says she’s coming whether or not).

✦ ✦ ✦

They came on the Saturday evening into the front room of the old Song house, which wasn’t big enough for eleven people, and somehow was.

The triplets came first, together, in a noise like a flock of birds. Si-Jie in pink, already crying, who hugged him round the middle and said she’d always known he’d be in emergency because he had emergency hands. Si-Yuan in sunglasses she took off indoors only because Auntie Dai told her to. Si-Wei in her cream coat, who gave him a bottle of something old and expensive without a word and went and sat by Eliana. Ren Hao, in a suit the colour of plums, who hugged him so hard his feet left the floor, and said “I love you, Doctor,” and then said it to Auntie Dai, who hit him with a dishcloth. Kenny, from his year, who’d matched to medicine somewhere across the harbour and talked for the first twenty minutes without stopping. Wei Long in his plain dark coat, with fruit, because Wei Long always brought fruit. Elara, who cried, because she cried at everything, and Xing Yue beside her, who said “Accepted?” in the doorway, and when Yu Chen said yes, nodded once and didn’t say anything else all evening.

Yu Chen stood in the middle of all of them and was polite. He was good at it. He thanked everybody and poured drinks and said the right small things to Kenny and Ren Hao and the triplets. He liked most of them well enough. If he was honest, and he was always honest with himself about this one thing, he’d have been just as happy if every one of them had gone home and left him on the sofa with her and the cake.

But she’d done this. She’d done this for him, a girl who couldn’t order a coffee without practising, and she’d done it with her hands shaking, and he’d have stood in that room till morning for that.

At nine, Si-Jie banged a spoon on a glass.

“Toast!” she said. “Eliana’s doing a toast!”

“I’m not doing a toast.”

“You said you would! You said in the chat!”

Every face in the room turned to Eliana, at the end of the sofa, with her knees up and her hood half up. He saw her go white, and then red, from the neck. He saw her look at the door.

Then she stood up.

She didn’t hold a glass. She stood in front of the sofa with her hands at her sides and looked at a point on the wall above everybody’s heads, and said it fast, all in one breath, the way she’d once said her own name to a detective.

“He’s the best person I know. He’s never once in his life chosen anything for himself and this time he did. He’s going to be so good at it that everybody in that hospital is going to be frightened of him. And he’s mine, and I’m so proud of him I can’t stand up.”

Then she sat down, hard, and put her face in her hands.

The room went quiet. Then Si-Jie burst into tears again. Ren Hao said “I LOVE that,” at the top of his voice. Elara was crying too. Wei Long looked at the ceiling.

From the kitchen doorway Auntie Dai said, “Four sentences. She’s been practising in my kitchen since Tuesday.”

Yu Chen put his glass down.

He went across the room to the sofa and knelt down on the floor in front of her. She still had her face in her hands. He took her wrists, gently, and drew her hands away from her face, and she let him, and looked at him with her face scarlet and wet and her glasses steamed, and he kissed her.

In front of all of them. On his knees on the floor of his own front room with eleven people watching. He kissed her slowly, holding her wrists, and felt her stop breathing and then breathe again against his mouth, and her hands turned in his and held on. Si-Jie made a sound like a kettle. Somebody, probably Si-Wei, said “Oh, for heaven’s sake.” He didn’t stop. He’d stopped caring who saw on a hill a year ago.

“You can’t stand up,” he said against her mouth. “You said.”

“I can’t.”

“Then I’ll have to carry you,” said Yu Chen.

✦ ✦ ✦

He carried her up the stairs when they’d gone, all the way to the top, and out through the door onto the flat roof, because she couldn’t stand up and he’d said he would.

She laughed the whole way. She told him he’d drop her on the stairs and he didn’t. She told him he’d hit her head on the roof door and he nearly did. He set her down on the roof beside the water tank, where she’d first come up the persimmon tree to shout at him on a Mid-Autumn night nearly five years ago, and she pulled him down beside her, and they lay on their backs on the warm concrete with the city round them and the stars over them, as many as there ever were over the Walled City, which wasn’t many, and real.

“You’ll be good,” she said. “I mean it. I’ve got it on the spreadsheet.”

“You’ve got everything on the spreadsheet.”

“Not everything,” said Eliana. “I keep some things off.”

He turned his head and looked at her. She was looking at the sky with her glasses pushed up into her hair.

He hadn’t meant to say anything. It was her party for him and he’d had more wine than he usually did and her hand was in his on the concrete, and the thing he’d said once on a porch was always there, under everything, and tonight it was close to the top.

“I’m going to want the next part,” he said. “When you’re ready. Not before.”

She went still beside him.

“A home that’s ours, not just mine. A name for it that other people have to use.” He kept his eyes on the sky. “A ring. I’m not asking. I said it once. I’m not going to push it on you again. I just want you to know it hasn’t gone anywhere. It’s still there. I can wait. One day at a time. That’s what we said.”

She didn’t answer.

He felt her turn on her side and look at him. Then she put her hand on his face and turned it towards her, and her face in the dark was serious, and frightened, and not running.

“Don’t stop wanting it,” she said.

“I won’t.”

“I’m not ready. Not yet. But I’m not—” She stopped. “I’m not scared of you wanting it any more. I used to be. I’m not now. Keep wanting it. Promise.”

He promised.

She kissed him then, slowly, on the warm roof, with her hand on his face. There was nothing of the party left in it. It went on, and her hand went from his face down into the collar of his shirt and undid a button, and another, and he caught her wrist and laughed.

“Here?”

“Who’s going to see?” said Eliana. “The birds?”

From across the yard, on the far side of the Lin house, as if he’d heard, the old man’s birds started up in the dark.

They went down in the end, because the concrete was hard and the birds wouldn’t stop. But they didn’t go down quickly, and he didn’t sleep much, and in the morning, before she was awake, he went down to the jar in the garden wall under the persimmon branch, the way he did every night and every morning, and checked it, and it was empty.

He didn’t mind. He went back in and made the tea.

chapters.title: Three Flats and a Porch
chapters.desc: They look at three new flats with harbour views and buy none of them. Instead they rebuild the old Song house as theirs, keep the porch, and take down the little wall between the two porches, which needs her father’s permission and costs him more than he lets show.
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t want a view. I want the porch. It has to have the porch.” — Eliana Lin
chapters.content:
The first flat was on the thirty-first floor and the whole of one wall was glass.

“The harbour,” said the agent, sweeping his arm at it, as if he’d put it there. “Both bridges. On a clear day you can see the islands.”

Eliana stood in the middle of the empty white room in her hoodie and looked at the harbour. It was blue and bright. There were boats on it. Everything in the room was white or grey or a kind of pale wood that had never been a tree, and it smelled of new paint and nothing else, and the floor was so clean her socks squeaked.

“The study,” said the agent, to Yu Chen, opening a door. “For you, sir. North light.”

“It’s for her,” said Yu Chen.

The agent looked at Eliana, small and hooded by the window, and then back at Yu Chen, and smiled the smile people smiled at her when they thought she was someone’s little sister.

“Of course. And for the lady, there’s a lovely—”

“Ask her,” said Yu Chen. He didn’t raise his voice. He never did. He just said it slower, so that the agent heard the floor go out from under the smile. “It’s her flat. If she wants it. Ask her what she wants it for.”

The agent turned round.

“What would you use the study for, Miss—”

“Lin,” said Eliana. “Five screens. Two on the wall. And I’d need to drill through that.” She pointed at the glass. “For the cables.”

The agent didn’t show them the bathroom.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second flat was a penthouse on the hill with a terrace and a pool the size of a car. The third was a whole floor of an old building on Harbour Road that someone had made new on the inside, with high ceilings and a kitchen like a hospital. Yu Chen walked through all three with his hands in his pockets and his face polite and pleasant and blank, the way it was with everyone who wasn’t her, and said almost nothing, and watched her.

It had been his idea. He’d said it in May on the roof, a home that’s ours, not just mine, and she’d thought about it for two weeks and then said yes, all right, show me, and he’d found three, because that was how many PLANs he could make in an evening. He’d have bought any of them. She knew that. He’d have bought all three, if she’d said, and not thought about it again.

They sat in the Volvo outside the third with the engine off.

“No,” she said.

“No to that one?”

“No to all of them.” She was looking at her hands. “They’re beautiful. I know they’re beautiful. I hated them.”

He didn’t say anything. He waited.

“There’s nothing in them,” she said. “Nothing’s happened. Nobody’s ever sat on a step in them at two in the morning. There’s no tree. There’s no jar. There’s no wall with a—” She stopped. “I don’t want a view. I don’t care about the islands. I want the porch. It has to have the porch.”

He looked at her across the car, and she couldn’t read his face, and then she could.

“Okay,” said Yu Chen.

She looked up.

“Then we’ll make the porch ours.” He started the engine. “I’ll ring Raiden.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden came on the Saturday with a roll of drawing paper under his arm and walked round the old Song house for an hour, touching walls, knocking on them, lying on his back on the floor of the front room looking at the ceiling, and Jinx came with him and said almost nothing and measured everything twice.

“I can make the two front rooms one,” said Raiden, on his back. “Take that wall out. Put a beam in. You’d have a long room, all the way from the street to the garden. Your two desks at that end, facing.” He sat up. “I could put a safe room under the stairs.”

“No safe room.”

“Everyone needs a safe room.”

“I’m a safe room,” said Eliana. “Do the long room.”

Jinx was standing on the porch, looking at it. The old Song porch, three steps and a little tiled roof, the same as the Lin one next door, and between them the knee-high wall with the iron rail on top that Yu Chen had been stepping over for as long as she’d been sitting on the other side of it.

“Wider,” said Jinx. “And a bench. Steel and wood. I’ll make it.” She looked at the little wall. “If that came down, it’d be one porch. Both houses. The whole front.”

Everybody looked at the wall.

“It’s on the line,” said Raiden. “The Lin line. It’s Baba’s.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She asked him herself.

She went across the little wall on the Sunday after lunch and knocked on the study door, which she’d done perhaps twice in her life, and went in when he said to, and stood in front of his desk. He looked up from his papers. He’d got better at looking up.

“I want to take down the wall,” she said. “On the porch. The little one. Between us and next door.”

Her father put his pen down.

She’d thought about what to say for three days and none of it came out. She stood there in her hoodie with her hands in the pocket and waited, and he looked at her, and she watched him understand what she was asking, and it wasn’t the wall.

He didn’t answer. He got up from the desk, slowly, the way he got up from everything now, and went past her, out of the study and down the stairs and out of the red door, and she followed him. He stood on his own porch and looked at the knee-high wall, and the iron rail on top of it, rusty in places and smooth in one place where a hand had gone over it a thousand times.

He put his own hand on the rail.

“Your mother had this put on,” he said.

It was the first thing he’d ever told her about her mother without being asked. She stood behind him and didn’t breathe. Next door, Yu Chen’s front window had a shape in it that she knew was him, pretending not to watch.

“Take it down,” said Baba.

She opened her mouth and nothing came.

“Take it down,” he said again. “It’s an old wall. It was never any use.” He took his hand off the rail. “Give me the rail. When it comes off. I’ll have it.”

“Yes, Baba.”

He nodded. He looked at the wall a moment longer. Then he turned round and looked at her, and his face was the face from the grave in February, and he said, “It’ll be one porch,” and went back inside before she could see what it did to him.

✦ ✦ ✦

The builders came the week after. Auntie Dai went to stay with her sister for six weeks and said she’d never been so glad of anything. Yu Chen and Eliana lived in two rooms upstairs with the screens in the bedroom and a kettle on the landing and dust on everything, and every night he came home from the hospital to find the house a little more taken apart.

The front wall came out on a Tuesday. The beam went in on a Thursday. On the Saturday, at dusk, the builders took the little wall down.

It took them twenty minutes. She’d thought it would take longer. Two men with hammers and a barrow, and it came apart brick by brick into a pile of rubble and dust on the porch, and the iron rail came off whole, and one of the men carried it next door and laid it on the Lin step, carefully, the way she’d asked him to. The red door opened a little way. A big hand came out and took the rail in. The door shut.

And then there was no wall. There was one long porch, both houses, three steps at each end and the tiled roofs side by side and all that dust in the middle where the line had been.

She stood in it. She stood exactly where the wall had been, in the dust, with sawdust in her hair from the beam and her hoodie grey with plaster, and looked down at her own feet on the line that wasn’t a line any more.

He came up the Song steps behind her in his work clothes, straight from a shift, with his bag over his shoulder.

“It’s gone,” she said. “He kept the rail.”

“I know.” He put his bag down. “I was at the end of the lane when the door opened.”

She turned round. He was looking at her, at her face with plaster on it and the sawdust in her hair, and he reached out and brushed a curl of sawdust off the end of her nose with his thumb. Then he didn’t take his hand away. He left it there, along her cheek, and looked at her, on the porch in the last of the light with the lane full of people coming home and the noodle man ladling soup at the end and the old man next door singing to his birds, and he kissed her.

On the step. In the open, in front of the whole Walled City coming home on a Saturday evening, with dust on both of them. He did it the way he’d done it at the gates of the university, slowly, on purpose, not asking. He kissed her where the wall had been as if he’d been waiting to do it from the other side for years, and she put her arms round his neck and kissed him back and didn’t think about the lane at all.

The noodle man banged his ladle on the pot. Three times. Somebody’s window opened. The old man’s birds went mad.

“Everyone’s watching,” she said, into his mouth, not letting go.

“Yes,” said Yu Chen. “Good.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the last Thursday in July her father rang her.

He’d never rung her. In twenty-three years he’d never once phoned her; he had Mok do it, or Ah Sim, or Elowen. Her phone said BABA on the screen and she sat at her desk in the bedroom with plaster dust on the keyboard and stared at it through three rings before she picked it up.

“There’s a room,” said her father. “Under the rope store, by Raiden’s. Someone may need a phone in it. And a camera on the door.” A pause, and then, as if it hurt: “Can you do it?”

He’d asked. Not told. She sat with the phone against her ear.

“Yes,” she said.

She went that afternoon, on her own, with a bag of cables. She didn’t ask what the room was for. She put a phone on the wall by the door, the old kind with a cord, and a small camera over the steel door outside, pointing at the street, with a screen by the phone so you could see who was on the step before you opened it. It took two hours. When it was done she looked round the room once, at the long table and the light over it and the steel sink, and then at her sister, who was standing by the wall, and she understood whose room it was and didn’t say so.

“It’ll ring from Baba’s number,” said Eliana. “Or from one of Mok’s. Nobody else can get through.”

“Thank you,” said Elara.

“I didn’t do anything,” said Eliana, and left.

She told Yu Chen that night that she’d done a job for Baba, and he looked at her face, and didn’t ask, and made the tea.

✦ ✦ ✦

The house was finished on the first of August.

Not finished. Raiden said a house was never finished. But the long room was there, all the way from the street windows to the garden doors, with the two desks at the garden end facing each other, his and hers, the same height, and her screens on the wall behind hers and his books on the wall behind his. The porch ran the whole width of both houses now. Jinx had brought the bench on the Thursday in her van, steel and old dark wood, long enough for two people to lie on end to end, and bolted it to the Song half of the porch, and sat on it once to test it, and said “It’ll do,” which from Jinx was a speech.

And upstairs there was a bath.

It was the only thing in the whole house he’d asked for himself. Everything else he’d let her choose, the desks and the floor and where the screens went and which wall came out. But he’d come home one evening in June with a picture of a bath, deep, old-fashioned, the kind you could lie down in properly, and said, “This. Please.”

“For you?” she’d said.

He’d gone red. “For you. You never get warm.”

On the Saturday night, the first night, Auntie Dai still at her sister’s, the builders gone, the dust swept, he ran it for her.

She came in to find him kneeling by it with his sleeves pushed up, testing the water with the inside of his wrist, frowning at it, the way he tested everything.

“It’s too hot,” he said. “Wait a minute.”

She didn’t wait. She took hold of his wrist where it was in the water and pulled.

He went in sideways, shirt and all, with a noise like a shout and a wave that went over the side onto the new floor, and came up spluttering with his hair in his eyes and his shirt stuck to him and the water slopping, and stared at her.

“Yu-er.”

“You said it was too hot,” said Eliana. “Show me how hot.” And she got in on top of him.

It was too hot. It didn’t matter. There was water everywhere, on the floor and the walls and in the doorway, and his shirt was impossible to get off wet and they laughed until they couldn’t breathe, and then he got it off and threw it on the floor with a slap, and pulled her down against him in the deep old bath with the water up to their shoulders. She was never warm all the way through, not her hands, not her feet, and she lay in the water against him with his arms round her and his mouth on her neck and was warm to the bone, and it made her shake.

“Too hot?” he said, into her neck.

“No,” she said. “No. Don’t move.”

He didn’t move. Then he did, slowly, and the water moved with them, and she turned round in his arms and kissed him with her wet hands on his face, and the bath went on slopping over onto the new floor and neither of them cared. He held her like she was something that might go down the drain, and she held on to him with her knees and her hands and her mouth, and in the end there was more water on the floor than in the bath, and they lay in what was left of it, laughing, and didn’t get out until it was cold.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday the third of August he started emergency training.

She got up before him for once, at half past five, and went down the stairs of the house that was theirs now, and made the tea in the new kitchen, chrysanthemum and dried pear and too much rock sugar, the way he made it for her, because she still didn’t know how much was right. She filled his dented flask. She took it out onto the long porch in the grey morning and sat on Jinx’s bench where the wall had been and waited for him to come out.

He came out at ten past six in his new navy scrubs with his bag over his shoulder, and stopped, and looked at her on the bench with his flask in her hands.

“You made the tea,” he said.

“It’s too sweet.”

He took it from her and drank some, standing on the porch, and made a face, and drank some more.

“It’s perfect,” said Yu Chen, and kissed the top of her head, and went down the three steps and along the lane on his father’s green bicycle with the camera on the back of the seat that nobody had asked for, and she sat on the bench and watched him go until he turned at the noodle stall.

chapters.title: Nainai
chapters.desc: Yu Chen takes Eliana north to meet the grandmother he has written to every month for years. Nainai has kept every letter, has known Eliana’s name since the summer of 2021, and before they leave she gives him his mother’s ring.
chapters.epigraph: “You’re the girl from the letters. Sit down. He’s been boring me about you for five years.” — Grandmother Wang
chapters.content:
She tried to get off the train before it left.

They were in their seats by the window at a quarter to seven on Saturday morning, with her laptop bag on her knees and his flask between them, and the doors were still open, and she stood up.

“I can’t,” she said.

He looked up at her.

“I can’t do it. She’s going to look at me. She’s going to ask me things. I’ve got nothing. I looked her up and there’s nothing, there’s not even a photograph, she’s like your cousin, she doesn’t exist.” Her voice was going high. “What if she doesn’t like me? What if she’s like Baba? What if I say the wrong thing and you have to watch?”

He didn’t take her hand. He didn’t pull her back down. Two years ago he’d have done both. He sat in the seat by the window and looked up at her standing in the aisle with her hood up and her bag clutched to her chest, and he thought about what she’d said to her father at a table, and to a man in a grey jacket at a market, and to a detective on a phone.

“Then get off,” he said. “I’ll ring her from the platform. She’ll understand.”

She stared at him.

“You’d let me. You’ve been planning this for a month.”

“Since July,” he said. “I’d still let you.”

The doors beeped. She stood in the aisle with the man behind her trying to get past with a suitcase, and looked at the platform, and at him, and at the platform.

She sat down.

“I hate you,” she said.

“I know.”

“I’m not talking to you till the tunnel.”

“All right,” said Yu Chen, and poured her some tea, and the doors closed, and the train pulled out, and she drank the tea with her face against the window, and she started talking to him again about ten minutes before the tunnel, which he didn’t point out.

✦ ✦ ✦

The north was dry and gold and wide, and by noon the hills had started.

Nainai’s house was at the end of a long road through trees, old and low and grey, built round a courtyard, with a gate that a man opened before the car had stopped. He came up most New Years, and it was still strange to come into it with her beside him. The courtyard had stone paving and a jujube tree in a raised bed and four doors opening onto it, and in the middle of it, in a padded jacket, on a wooden chair someone had carried out for her, with a black lacquered stick across her knees, was his grandmother.

She was small now. She’d shrunk every year. Her face had gone brown and creased like a walnut and her hair was white and pulled back so tight it looked painted on, and her eyes were the same as they’d always been, which was to say they missed nothing.

She didn’t get up. She pointed the stick at Eliana.

“You,” she said. “Come here.”

Eliana went. He watched her go across the courtyard with her hands in her hoodie pocket and her shoulders up round her ears, the way she walked into rooms full of strangers, and stop in front of the chair. She was the same height as his grandmother sitting down.

Nainai looked at her. She looked at the hoodie and the glasses and the pencil in the knot of hair, and the bitten nails, and the face.

“You’re the girl from the letters,” she said.

Eliana nodded. She didn’t seem able to do anything else.

“Sit down,” said Nainai, and pointed the stick at the stool beside her. “He’s been boring me about you for five years. Every month. Pages. I know what you eat. I know when you don’t sleep. I know you drink that tea he makes out of a tin that has a dent in it, because he wrote me a whole letter about the dent.” She looked up at Yu Chen over Eliana’s head. “You. Go and do something useful. Tell them to bring the soup. I want to talk to her without you standing there turning red.”

He went.

When he came back with the woman who cooked and the soup, Eliana was sitting on the stool beside the chair with the black lacquered box open on her knees, and his grandmother was reading out loud.

“Her light was on at three again. I could see it from my desk. She’d ordered noodles at one and not eaten them, they were still in the bag on the windowsill in the morning. I don’t know how to make her eat without asking her, and I don’t want to ask her, because she’ll say she’s fine.” Nainai put the letter down. “That’s August 2021. He was twenty-one.” She picked up another one. “She did a thing to a fish stall. I’m not supposed to know. I think she’s the cleverest person I’ve ever met and I can’t tell anyone, so I’m telling you.”

He stood in the doorway with the soup tray and wanted the courtyard to open and take him.

Eliana was looking at the letters. She had about forty of them on her knees, all in his handwriting, in order, years of them, the lacquered box half empty beside her. She’d gone still, and he couldn’t see her face.

Then she looked up at him across the courtyard.

He’d thought she might be angry. He’d written his grandmother everything for five years, every night her light stayed on, every order she hadn’t eaten, every grey morning. All the watching. It was all there in the box in his own handwriting, written down, kept. He stood in the doorway and waited for her to see it for what it was.

She was crying a little. She wasn’t angry at all.

“You wrote her about the dent,” she said. “A whole letter.”

“You did it on the third flight,” said Yu Chen. “It seemed important.”

His grandmother looked from one of them to the other with her stick across her knees, and then she laughed, high and cracked and delighted, and said, “Oh, good. Oh, good. She’s as bad as you are,” and banged the stick on the stones.

✦ ✦ ✦

They ate in the courtyard. Nainai made Eliana sit beside her and put things in her bowl without asking, the way Ah Sim did, and Eliana ate them, all of them, without saying she wasn’t hungry, which he’d never seen her do for anyone.

His uncle was away in the east city on business. Nainai said it was the best thing about the weekend.

“He’d ask you about money,” she said to Eliana. “He asks everybody about money. Xing Yue’s bringing his girl at New Year and he’ll ask her too, and from what I hear she’ll tell him to mind his own business.” She looked pleased. “I’ve heard she talks. You don’t. That’s good. Between the two of you, you’ll balance.”

“I know Elara,” said Eliana. “She’s my sister.”

Nainai stopped with her chopsticks in the air.

“Your sister.”

“Adopted. We’re all—it’s complicated. She’s my sister.”

Nainai looked at her, and then at Yu Chen, and then she put her chopsticks down and laughed again, so hard she had to hold the table.

“Two of mine,” she said. “Two of mine, and two of yours, from the same house. Next door to each other. And neither of them thought to tell me.” She wiped her eyes. “I’m going to hit them both with this stick.”

It was easy. That was the thing he hadn’t let himself expect. He sat at his grandmother’s table in the courtyard in the gold afternoon and watched Eliana, who couldn’t buy a coffee without practising, talk to an eighty-six-year-old woman about her firm and the dumpling shop and the bank, plainly, in her own voice, while Nainai listened and asked short sharp questions and nodded. Nobody at this table looked over her head. Nobody talked about her to someone else. His grandmother looked straight at her and asked her things and waited for the answers.

The Wangs were rich. Much richer than the Lins; they owned hospitals, and the school that trained the doctors for them, and land, and the port the equipment came through. He’d never told her how much. He’d never really told himself. But they were rich in a house where people talked to each other, and the Lins were rich in a tall house where nobody did, and he watched her see that across the table, and see something about him in it, and look at him differently, and he didn’t know what to do with his face.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nainai called him in at dusk, alone.

Her room was off the courtyard, small and plain, with a bed and a chest and a window onto the jujube tree. Eliana was outside, on the stool by the tree, with the woman who cooked, being taught how to fold something, and he could hear her laughing.

Nainai sat on the edge of the bed with the stick beside her. She had a small box in her lap, red, old, worn white at the corners.

“Sit,” she said.

He sat on the chest.

“Your father gave this to your mother,” said Nainai. “It came back to me with his things. I’ve kept it.” She held the box out. “I wasn’t going to give it to you until I’d seen her. Now I’ve seen her.”

He took it. He didn’t open it. He sat holding it in both hands on his knees.

“Open it, boy.”

He opened it. It was a plain ring, gold, old-fashioned, with a small round stone in it the colour of weak tea, in a setting worn smooth. He looked at it and didn’t know what he was feeling, or rather he did, and there was too much of it for one face.

“She’s small,” said Nainai. “It’ll need making smaller. Your mother had big hands. Like yours.” She folded her own hands on the stick. “Don’t give it to her here. Don’t give it to her on a train or in a restaurant with men in white coats standing round with a cake. Give it to her somewhere that means something. You’ll know where.”

“I know where.”

“Of course you do. You’ve known for five years. It’s in every letter.” She looked at him with her sharp old eyes. “Have you asked her?”

“Once. On a step. She ran inside.”

“And?”

“And then she came back,” said Yu Chen. “Nine days later. She said I could have tomorrow. One at a time.”

His grandmother looked at him. Then she reached out and put her old dry hand on the side of his face, which she’d never done.

“Then ask her again,” she said. “When she tells you to. Not before. You’ve always been good at waiting.” She took her hand away. “Wait for her to tell you. And then don’t wait one minute more.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The night train south left at ten.

The berth was tiny. Two narrow bunks one above the other, a fold-down table, a window with a blind, and a curtain across the end that shut out the corridor. He’d booked it so they could lie down. He hadn’t thought about how small it would be, or about his legs.

“You don’t fit,” said Eliana, from the bottom bunk, watching him try. “Your feet are in the corridor.”

He said they could stay in the corridor, then.

She was sitting cross-legged on the bottom bunk with her shoes off and her hood down, and her face had been different all day, open, as if something in it had been unlocked and not shut again. She’d hugged his grandmother at the gate. She’d done it herself, without being asked, and Nainai had held on and said something in her ear he hadn’t heard, and Eliana had nodded with her eyes wet, and then got in the car and not said a word to the station.

The ring was in the inside pocket of his jacket, in its red box, against his chest. He could feel it every time he moved.

“What did she say to you?” he said. “At the gate.”

“That’s mine.” She pulled her knees up. “What did she say to you? In her room. You were in there half an hour.”

He looked at her. He felt the box against his chest.

He could tell her. He could take it out now, here, on the night train with the lights going past outside, and ask. She was open tonight. She might say yes. She might say yes tonight and not run, and he’d have it, the thing he’d wanted since a June night on a step, and he’d have got it on a train with his feet in the corridor because he couldn’t wait.

Wait for her to tell you.

“She told me to eat more,” he said.

The train went over points and lurched, hard, all at once, and Eliana, who’d been leaning forward to say something, came off the edge of the bunk straight into him.

He caught her. She landed on his chest with her face an inch from his and her glasses knocked crooked and one knee in his stomach, and she started to say “Sorry—” and he didn’t let her finish. He kissed her before the word was out, with one hand flat on her back holding her there and the train still rocking under them, and she made a small surprised sound into his mouth and then laughed into it and kissed him back.

“You did that on purpose,” she said, against him. “You’d have made the train do it if you could.”

“Yes,” said Yu Chen. “I would.”

It was the most ridiculous place they’d ever been. The bunk was too narrow for one person, let alone two, and the bunk above was so low he hit his head on it twice and she laughed so hard she had to hide her face in his neck so the people in the next berth wouldn’t hear. His feet were in the corridor. The curtain kept swinging open on the bends and she kept reaching out to pull it shut and missing. The table folded down on its own and hit him in the knee. They tried twice, and gave up twice, and lay there helpless with laughing, wedged together on the bottom bunk with her hair in his mouth and the lights of a town going past behind the blind in stripes.

And then she stopped laughing and looked at him in the stripes of light, close, and put her hand on his face the way his grandmother had, and kissed him, slowly, and after that the bunk didn’t matter.

They were careful because they had to be. Slow because there was no room to be anything else. He held her on top of him on the narrow bunk with the train going south under them through the dark, and she moved against him with her face in his neck and his hands on her back under her hoodie, and every lurch of the train made her catch her breath and laugh and then not laugh, and she hid her mouth against his shoulder so the next berth wouldn’t hear, and he turned her face up and kissed her anyway. The ring was in his jacket on the hook by his head. He could see the shape of the pocket in the light from the corridor. He looked at it over her shoulder once, and then didn’t look at it again, because she said his name against his throat, the name she only used here, and there wasn’t room in him for anything else.

Afterwards she fell asleep on his chest, wedged against the wall, with his jacket over both of them because the blanket had fallen on the floor. Her ear was right over the inside pocket. Right over the box. If she’d been awake she’d have felt it, hard and square against her cheek.

He lay awake and didn’t move.

The train went south through the night. Somewhere past midnight it stopped at a station he didn’t know, under orange lights, and a man went along the platform outside knocking on the wheels with a hammer, and the train started again. He thought about his grandmother’s hand on his face. He thought about a red box worn white at the corners, and a step, and a jar in a wall.

He didn’t know when. That wasn’t his to know. He’d wait for her to tell him.

But he knew where. He’d always known where.

chapters.title: The Ring in the Jar
chapters.desc: After the hillclimb, and after a night in the emergency department when she nearly loses him, Eliana leaves a note in the jar in the wall: “Ask me again.” He does, at two in the morning, on the porch where it started, with his mother’s ring.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m asking again. One day at a time. Starting now. Will you?” — Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
They drove up to the mountain the night before in four cars, and on Sunday morning they stood at the finish line at the top of the pass in the cold in a row: Baba in his good coat, Elowen in green with Zhao behind her, Evangeline in pale blue with Jun Hyuk explaining sidecar steering to a marshal, Elara with Xing Yue, Jinx’s father with a pigeon in a basket he’d been told not to bring, and Serafina on the wall by the timing hut in a red jumper, with her husband, shouting.

Eliana had a laptop and a camera on a stick. Yu Chen held the laptop.

He kept touching his jacket. She noticed it on the drive up and at breakfast and now, at the finish line, the flat of his hand going to the left side of his chest every few minutes, the way you’d check for a wallet. She thought he’d brought something for luck. She didn’t ask. She had a race to film.

The black outfit came round the last corner flat out with Raiden hanging off the side of it over the road, and crossed the line, and the man from the magazines read the time off his stopwatch twice. Then Raiden was off the chair taking Jinx’s helmet off, and kissing her on the gravel in front of all of them, and they went over against the bike, and Baba laughed, the big rusty laugh, right across the mountain.

Eliana filmed all of it. She’d filmed every kiss in this family for years. When she lowered the camera she found Yu Chen looking at her instead of the race, with his hand flat on his jacket.

“What?” she said.

“Nothing,” said Yu Chen, and kissed her temple, behind the camera, where nobody was looking, and gave her back the laptop.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Friday night three weeks later, at twenty to midnight, her phone rang with a number she’d only ever seen once.

“Eliana. It’s Xing Yue.” His voice was flat and clear and careful. “He’s all right. I want you to hear that first. He’s all right. He’s been hurt at work. I’m with him.”

She was standing up. She didn’t remember standing up.

“Hurt how?”

“A cut on his arm. He hit his head. He’s awake and talking. They’re keeping him in tonight to watch his head.” A pause. “He told them not to ring you. I’m ringing you.”

“I’m coming.”

“I know,” said Xing Yue. “I’ll be at the ambulance doors.”

She didn’t go to hospitals at night. She’d said it to him once, on the end of his bed, with smoke on a screen: people go in at night. Every bad thing in her family’s life had happened at night in a building like that, and she’d sat at home in the dark every time and waited to be told.

She was in a taxi in four minutes, with her laces undone and her hands shaking too hard to hold her phone, watching the hospital come up out of the dark with every window lit. It didn’t feel like a choice. She just went.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xing Yue was at the ambulance doors in his dark coat, as he’d said. He took one look at her face and didn’t say anything, and walked her through the department at a pace she could keep up with, past the cubicles and the noise and a security man standing by a curtain with his arms folded, to a side bay at the end.

He was sitting up on the trolley in his navy scrubs with the top half cut off.

His left forearm was bandaged from wrist to elbow. There was a dressing on the side of his head above his ear, and his hair was stiff with dried blood round it, and his face was grey, and there were splashes of blood, his own, down the front of what was left of his scrubs. Dr. Toh was at the end of the trolley in her cardigan, writing something.

He looked up and saw her, and he looked caught.

“I told them not to ring you,” he said, and looked past her at his cousin. “I asked you not to.”

“I know you did,” said Xing Yue, and stayed exactly where he was.

Dr. Toh looked at Eliana over her glasses.

“You’re the girl from the car park,” she said. “With the noodles.” She closed the notes. “A man came in high on something with a broken bottle and went for Bernie in the corridor. Your doctor got in the way. He got the bottle off him, which is the only reason Bernie isn’t the one on this trolley. The man shoved him into the edge of the resus trolley on the way down.” She looked at Yu Chen. “Eleven stitches. A bang on the head. CT’s clear. He stays in till morning so I can wake him up every hour and ask him what day it is, which he’ll hate.”

Then, to Eliana at the curtain, lower: “He held the man’s wrist and said something to him, and the man dropped the bottle. Bernie heard it. She says she’s never been so frightened of anyone who was on her side.” She went out.

Eliana stood at the end of the trolley.

He was looking at his phone. He had it in his right hand, the good one, with the screen lit. She could see it from where she stood. It was the food app.

“You didn’t eat,” he said, not looking up. “There’s nothing since lunch. Yu-er, you said you’d—”

Something in her went.

“You’re checking my noodles?”

He looked up.

“You’ve got eleven stitches in your arm,” she said. Her voice was coming out high and fast and she couldn’t stop it. “You’ve got a hole in your head. There’s blood in your hair. A man came at you with a bottle and you got in the way, you just got in the way, like it’s a door, like it’s nothing, and you’re sitting there checking whether I’ve had my dinner—”

“Yu-er—”

“No. No. You don’t get to. You told them not to ring me. You were going to let me sleep. You were going to come home in the morning with a bandage and say you’d cut it on a trolley, weren’t you, I know you, you’d have—” She was shaking. “You promised me you’d be next door every day you’re alive. You said it on your step. Every day. And you stood in front of a broken bottle for a nurse, and you didn’t think, you didn’t once think—”

He put the phone down.

He reached out with his good hand and took a fistful of the front of her hoodie and pulled her down to the trolley, and kissed her.

Mid-sentence. He’d never done it. In five years of her talking too fast and too much, he’d never once stopped her mouth with his; he’d always let her finish. He didn’t let her finish now. He held her down by her hoodie with his bandaged arm across his lap and kissed her hard, on a trolley in a side bay in the emergency department, with blood in his hair and her glasses crushed against his face, and the rest of the sentence went out of her into his mouth.

She went scarlet. She felt it go all the way down into the hoodie he was holding.

Behind her, in the gap in the curtain, Xing Yue turned round and looked at the wall.

When he let her go she stayed where she was, bent over the trolley, too close, her face burning, her mouth still open on the word she hadn’t said.

“I did think,” said Yu Chen. His voice was low and not quite steady. “I thought about you the whole time. That’s why I’m on this trolley and not under it.” He held on to her hoodie. “I’m sorry I frightened you. I’m sorry I told them not to ring. I won’t do that again. But you’re not going to stand there and tell me off until you fall over. Sit down. Please.”

She sat down on the plastic chair beside the trolley, because her legs had gone.

She’d come. That was what she kept thinking. Her face was still hot and her mouth still felt it and she sat on the chair by his trolley and thought: it’s night, and I’m in a hospital, and I came. Nobody had to tell me anything. I came.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t go home. Neither did Xing Yue.

At one, Toh’s registrar came and asked him what day it was, and he said Friday, and she said it was Saturday now. At two, he was asleep. Eliana sat on the plastic chair with her hand on the edge of the trolley next to his good one, not holding it, just near, and watched him breathe, and counted, the way he counted her blinks.

Xing Yue sat on the other chair, by the curtain, with his coat on, and read something on his phone, and didn’t talk.

“Thank you,” she said, at some point after three. “For ringing me.”

Xing Yue didn’t look up.

“He told me not to,” he said. “He’s been wrong about almost nothing in his life. He was wrong about that.” He went back to his phone. “Go to sleep. I’ll wake you if anything changes.”

She didn’t sleep. But she put her head down on the edge of the trolley next to Yu Chen’s hand, and some time before it got light his hand moved, in his sleep, and found her hair, and stayed.

✦ ✦ ✦

For two weeks after that she was frightened all the time.

She lay beside him at night and listened to him breathe. She watched the bandage come off and the stitches come out and a long pink line left behind on his forearm, and she looked at it every morning when he reached for the kettle. It was the old thing. People say forever and then they’re in a hospital.

She didn’t run.

That was the difference, and she noticed it, the way you notice a sound that’s stopped. She was frightened, and she stayed. She was frightened, and she made his tea when he went back to work on the Tuesday, too sweet, and filled the flask, and stood on the porch and watched him cycle away to the place where it had happened, and didn’t ask him not to go. She’d never once asked him to stop anything. He’d never once asked her. She wasn’t going to start because of a bottle.

And the fear, she found, didn’t make her want to run. It made her want the opposite. It made her want to hold on to him with both hands, in daylight, out loud, with a word for it that other people had to use.

On the Saturday, the seventh, at nine in the evening, when he was upstairs in the bath, she took a sticky note off her pad and wrote three words on it in pencil, and didn’t draw anything at all.

She went out into the garden in her socks with it folded in her hand. The persimmons were ripe on the branch over the wall, orange in the light from the kitchen. She took the loose brick out and put the note in the jar, and stood there with her hand on the brick.

She nearly took it out again. She stood under the persimmon branch for ten minutes with her hand on the jar.

Then she put the brick back, and went inside, because that was the rule: you don’t read a note until the writer has gone in.

✦ ✦ ✦

He checked the jar every night. He always had. He’d never once gone to bed without walking down the garden and taking the brick out, even the nights there was nothing. That was why she’d chosen the jar.

She lay in bed with her back to the door and pretended to be asleep, and heard him go down at eleven. Heard the back door. Then nothing.

He didn’t come back up.

At two her light was off, because she was in his bed, and the house was dark, and she heard the front door open and close.

She got up. She went down the stairs on the edges, the way she’d taught him, in his T-shirt, and opened the front door onto the porch.

The long porch ran the width of both houses now, with Jinx’s bench on the Song half and the place in the middle where the wall had been. He wasn’t on the bench. He’d gone along to the Lin end and sat down on the third step of the tall house, her step, the one with the crack in it, under the faded charm on the red door. He had the blue checked blanket round his shoulders. He was looking at the lane.

She went along the porch and sat down beside him.

He put half the blanket round her. She let him. Neither of them said anything. The lamp at the end of the lane, the noodle stall shuttered, the persimmon branch black against the sky over the wall. It was cold. Her feet were bare and she put them under his leg, and he let her.

“You read it,” she said.

He held up the sticky note between two fingers. In the light from the lamp she could see her own pencil. Ask me again.

“I read it at eleven,” he said. “I’ve been sitting in the garden for three hours. I didn’t want to do it in the garden. I wanted to do it here.”

“Why here?”

“Because this is where you were sitting,” said Yu Chen. “The night I knew.”

He put the note in his pocket. He took something else out. A small box, red, old, worn white at the corners. He didn’t open it straight away. He held it on his knee and looked at the lane.

“Nainai gave me this,” he said. “In September. It was my mother’s. Aurelia made it smaller. She swore she wouldn’t tell Elowen, and then she told me she’d tell Elowen the second you said yes, because it’s a point.” He was quiet. “I’ve had it in my jacket since the station. At the hillclimb. On the trolley. I nearly asked you on the train and I nearly asked you on the mountain, and I didn’t, because I said I’d wait till you told me. And you’ve told me.”

He opened the box.

It was a plain old gold ring with a small round stone in it the colour of weak tea. She looked at it in the lamplight and couldn’t breathe.

“I asked you once, on this step, and you said I could have tomorrow,” he said. “So I’m not asking for forever.” His voice was steady and his hands weren’t. “I’m asking again. One day at a time. Starting now. Will you?”

She tried to say it.

She opened her mouth and nothing came out. Not a sound. She’d said no to her father at a table and her own name to a detective and his daughter’s school to a man in a grey jacket, and she sat on her own front step at two in the morning with the only boy she’d ever loved holding out his mother’s ring, and she couldn’t make a single word.

So she did the only thing she could think of.

She took the edge of the blue blanket and pulled it all the way round both of them, so they were inside it together, the way they’d been on this step the night she’d finished school. And then she held up her left hand, between them, in the lamplight, shaking.

He looked at her hand. Then at her face.

He took the ring out of the box and put it on her finger. It went on first time. Aurelia had made it exactly right.

She looked at it on her hand.

“Yes,” said Eliana.

It came out cracked and small. She said it again, louder.

“Yes. Yes.”

And then she couldn’t stop. She kissed him, inside the blanket, on the third step, and said it against his mouth, and kissed him again, and said it again, yes, between every one, laughing and crying at once, with her cold hands on his face and the ring cold on her finger against his cheek. He was crying too. He wasn’t doing anything about it. He held on to her inside the blanket and kissed her back every time and every time she said it he said “I know” into her mouth, like he’d said it on this step once when she’d said the other thing, and she kept saying it anyway, because for so long she hadn’t been able to say it, and now she could, and she wanted the whole lane to hear.

Somewhere behind them, in the tall house, a light came on. Then another, on the floor above. Then her father’s study.

Neither of them looked round.

chapters.title: A Wedding Between Two Gardens
chapters.desc: They marry where they both lived for years, across both back gardens, under the persimmon tree, through a gate cut in the wall. She means to walk to him on her own. At the gate her father is waiting, and for the first time in her life he asks her something.
chapters.epigraph: “Can I walk you? I never asked you anything. Let me ask you this.” — Lin Jian
chapters.content:
The gate had gone in on Tuesday.

Raiden had drawn it and Jinx had made it, out of the same dark wood as the porch bench, with iron hinges she’d forged herself, and two men had cut the opening in the old garden wall between the Lin yard and the Song one, right under the persimmon branch. They’d left the loose brick. Eliana had stood over them the whole time to make sure. The jar was still behind it, a hand’s width from the new gatepost, with nothing in it now but the two notes he’d put back after the porch: hers, Ask me again, and under it his, from the March of the nine days, I’M NOT GOING ANYWHERE. EAT SOMETHING.

On Saturday morning she stood in the Lin yard in her socks at seven and looked through the open gate into the Song garden, at the persimmon tree hung with ripe orange fruit, at the chairs, at the long tables going in.

She hadn’t slept much. She’d been on the third step at two in the morning, and so, for part of it, had her father, and that was hers to keep and she wasn’t going to think about it now, or she’d cry before she’d even had breakfast.

Ah Sim came out of the back door with a bowl.

“Eat,” she said.

“I’m not hungry.”

“I didn’t ask,” said Ah Sim, and stood there until she’d eaten all of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The lights were her own.

She’d strung them all week, on a ladder, with him holding it. Along the porch, both halves, all the way from the red door to the Song door, under the tiled roofs. Through the branches of the persimmon tree. Over the gate. Along the top of the garden wall on both sides, and across the Lin yard to their mother’s empty pots, and across the Song garden to the tables. Thousands of small warm lights, more than she’d put in Elowen’s shop four years ago, and none of them on yet.

“When do they come on?” said Elowen, at eleven, in Eliana’s old room at the top of the tall house, with a comb in her teeth. “What time?”

“I’m not telling you.”

Elowen took the comb out of her teeth and the pencil out of Eliana’s hair, which she’d been trying to do for twenty minutes. “And you’re not wearing a pencil. It’s your wedding.”

Eliana took it back and put it in the knot, and Elowen looked at her in the mirror and gave up and laughed and had to fix her own eyes.

The dress was white and plain and came to her ankles, and it had pockets, deep ones, because she’d said she wouldn’t wear anything without them. Aurelia had made it. She’d come to the Song house in August with a tape measure and pins in her mouth and said nothing for forty minutes except numbers, and at the end she’d said, “Pockets. Fine. But you’re not putting a phone in them.” Eliana had told her she’d be putting two in them, and Aurelia had looked at her over the pins and nearly smiled. She’d also made the ring smaller, the autumn before, and told Elowen the morning after he asked that it was a point. Elowen still disputed it. The score, depending which of them you asked, was forty-four to forty-three either way.

Her sisters came up one by one. Evangeline in pale blue, as always, who sat on the end of the bed and said nothing and held Eliana’s hand while Elowen did her face. Elara, married five months, crying already, who said “I’m not crying, I’m not, I’m just so—” and then cried. Elowen in green with a white camellia. The four of them in the dark room at the top of the stairs that wasn’t dark now, with the curtains open and the pale squares still on the wall where the monitors had been.

“Are you frightened?” said Elara.

Eliana thought about it.

“Yes,” she said. “Not of him.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They came all afternoon, through the red door and along the porch and down through the Lin yard and the new gate, or straight in at the Song door and out through the long room into the garden. More people than had ever been in either house.

Nainai had come south on the Thursday, with her stick, and had been put in the best chair under the persimmon tree, and pointed the stick at everyone who came through the gate to make sure she knew who they were. Wei Long in his plain dark coat, with fruit. The triplets, Si-Jie in pink and already crying, Si-Yuan in sunglasses, Si-Wei in cream with a black coffee she’d brought from somewhere. Ren Hao in a suit the colour of persimmons, on purpose, who hugged everybody including Zhao, which nobody had ever seen happen and which Zhao bore for four seconds without moving. Serafina and Haozhen, who’d driven Nobody up the lane and parked it at the end by the noodle stall. Chen Si and Aurelia, who stood at the edge of everything and looked at the lights in the tree. He Si-Mei, in a hoodie, with headphones, who gave Eliana a small wrapped box and said “Don’t open it near a network” and went and stood by the wall. Dr. Toh, in a cardigan. Bernie from the department, who’d brought a cake.

Mrs. Choi from the flower market, with her stick, and her daughter, and a pot of yellow chrysanthemums so big two men had to carry it in, who looked at Yu Chen across the garden and said loudly, to everyone, “Still too tall.”

Jinx’s father had brought the pigeon. This time nobody had bothered telling him not to.

Baba was nowhere.

Eliana looked for him from the window of her old room at four. The Lin yard was full of people. The Song garden was full of people. The porch was full of people. Her father wasn’t anywhere in any of it.

“He’s downstairs,” said Elowen, behind her. “In the front room. He’s been in there since two. Mok’s with him.”

“Is he all right?”

“No,” said Elowen. “He’s never been less all right in his life. He’ll be there.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d meant to walk on her own.

She’d decided it in the summer, and told nobody but Yu Chen. Not because of Baba. Because she’d done everything that mattered on her own, the fence and the hunt and the hill and the phone call, and this mattered more than any of them, and she wanted to walk to him on her own feet, by herself, from her side of the wall to his, the way he’d crossed it to her every day for years. Elowen had said once, under the persimmon branch, that she didn’t have to do the hard things alone. She knew. She was choosing to.

At five, when the light was going gold, she went down the stairs of the tall house, past the study, past the front room with its door shut, and out of the back door into the Lin yard.
