Everyone was through the gate on the Song side now, in the chairs, under the tree. She could see them through the opening in the wall. She could see Nainai’s stick. She could see the celebrant, a small brisk woman from the registry with a folder. She could see him, under the persimmon tree, in a dark suit, not moving, with his hands at his sides. Xing Yue was beside him. Wei Long was beside Xing Yue.

The Lin yard was empty. It was twenty steps from the back door to the gate. She’d counted.

She started walking.

She’d done about ten when she saw him.

He was standing by the gate, on her side of the wall, in the shadow under the persimmon branch, by the loose brick. In his funeral suit, the only suit he had. With his big hands at his sides and his face grey and his eyes on her, coming across the yard in a white dress with a pencil in her hair.

She stopped.

He didn’t move towards her. He waited until she was close enough that he didn’t have to raise his voice, and then he spoke, to her, not to anyone else, not to the yard, not to the people on the other side of the wall who’d all turned round in their chairs.

“Yu-er,” said her father.

She couldn’t say anything.

“Can I walk you?” he said. His voice was rough. “I never asked you anything. Not when it mattered. Not what you were studying, not what you wanted.” He swallowed. “Let me ask you this.”

She’d meant to walk on her own. She’d decided it. She stood in the Lin yard in front of the gate with the lights unlit in the tree above them and looked at her father, who’d boiled her an egg at four in the morning every year of her life and left it where she’d find it, and stood outside her door and couldn’t knock, and kept the iron rail off the porch wall in his study by the window, and said nothing at New Year when Ah Sim put the boy next door in a chair at the long table, and been on the step with her at two that morning, and she understood that walking on her own and saying yes to this weren’t different things. They were both hers to choose.

“Yes,” she said. “Please.”

He held out his arm. Not his hand. His arm, crooked, the old-fashioned way, the way he must have held it out once a long time ago for someone else. She put her hand through it.

He looked at her. All the way through the gate and across the Song garden, ten steps, past Nainai and the triplets and Ren Hao and her sisters, with everyone watching, he looked at her and not at where he was going, and didn’t look away once, and she had to steer him round a chair.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yu Chen couldn’t speak.

She saw it when she got to him. Her father let go of her arm, and put her hand into Yu Chen’s, and held both their hands in his, briefly, and then let go and went and sat down in the front row beside Nainai, who patted his knee with her stick. And Yu Chen stood under the persimmon tree holding her hand and looked down at her, and his ears were scarlet and his eyes were wet and his mouth opened, and nothing came out of it.

“Yu-er,” he said at last. That was all he could manage.

The celebrant was brisk and kind and didn’t take long, because Eliana had asked her not to. She read the parts that had to be read. Then she looked at Yu Chen over her folder.

“You said you’d each say something short.”

He’d written it down. She’d seen him do it, at his desk across from hers, over and over for a week, and tear it up. He had a folded square of paper in his jacket pocket now; she could see the corner of it. He didn’t take it out.

“I’ll come out,” said Yu Chen. “Every night. Whatever time it is. Every day I’m alive.” He stopped. “That’s it. That’s all of it.”

There was no speech in it. It was the plainest thing she’d ever heard him say, and from the front row she heard Elara make a noise like a burst pipe.

The celebrant looked at her.

Eliana had nothing written down. She’d decided on the stairs.

“Tomorrow,” she said. Her voice came out small. She made it bigger. “And the one after. I’ll say it every day. I’m saying it now.”

The celebrant opened her mouth to say the next part, the part about the kiss, and she’d got as far as “You may now—” when he let go of Eliana’s hand and took her face in both of his and kissed her.

He didn’t wait for the rest of it. Behind them the whole garden laughed, and then cheered, and Ren Hao shouted something that was certainly I love you, and she stood on her toes on the grass under the persimmon tree in front of everyone she’d ever known and kissed him back, with her hands on his wrists and the pencil coming out of her hair. A year ago she’d have wanted the ground to open. Years ago she’d have made him promise never to do this where anyone could see. She held on to him in front of all of them and let them see all of it, the whole of it, and didn’t hide one bit.

Behind them, by the gate, Raiden had her laptop open on his knees, with one key to press when she gave the sign. She lifted one hand off Yu Chen’s wrist without looking and gave it.

The lights came on.

All of them, all at once. The porch, both halves. The tree above them, through every branch, so the persimmons glowed orange among them like lamps. The gate. The tops of both walls. The Lin yard and the Song garden and the long tables and their mother’s empty pots, all of it gold in the dusk, both houses lit up at once, as if there had never been a wall there at all.

“What time is it?” said Elowen, from the front row, into the noise. “Why now? Yu-er, what time—”

“It’s not a time,” said Eliana, against his mouth. “It’s when I said yes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They ate at the long tables across both gardens until the lights were the only light. Ah Sim and Auntie Dai had cooked together for three days and stopped speaking on the second, and the food was the best anyone had eaten. Ren Hao made a speech nobody had asked for. Raiden showed everyone the DRAW (OFFICIAL) video from April, again, and contested it, again, and was removed from the table by Jinx. Nainai hit Yu Chen on the shin with her stick and said “Five years,” and then hit him again and said “Good,” and then asked Eliana if she’d eaten.

Baba didn’t make a speech. He sat in the front row under the tree with Nainai and drank one glass of something, slowly, and watched. Once, when Eliana went past, he reached out and touched her elbow, just that, and let her go.

At midnight, when the last of them had gone along the porch and down the lane, she found Yu Chen on the long bench, on their half of the porch, with his jacket off and his tie undone and the folded square of paper in his hand.

“What did it say?” she said, sitting down beside him. “The one you didn’t read.”

He gave it to her.

It said, in his capitals, PLAN (VOWS). 1. Don’t read this. Just say it.

She laughed until she had to lean on him. Then she stopped, and looked at him in the lights, her husband, on the porch where the wall had been, and kissed him slowly with the lights still on in the tree behind them, and his hands came up into her hair and took the pencil out at last and put it in his pocket.

“Upstairs,” she said, against his mouth.

“The lights.”

“Leave them,” said Eliana. “Let the whole lane see.”

He carried her in through the long room and up the stairs, the middle of every one, loud.

Aurelia had put thirty small buttons down the back of the dress, and he stood behind her in the gold light coming through the curtains and undid every one of them himself, slowly, with his big careful hands, kissing the back of her neck at each one, and she stood there and laughed and shook and told him to hurry, and he didn’t. When the dress went down at last she turned round in his arms and he looked at her as if he’d never seen her before, and said “Wife,” once, as if he were trying the word.

“Don’t make it a thing,” said Eliana.

“It’s a thing,” he said, and kissed her. He laid her down on their bed with the ring on her hand against his shoulder and the lights from both gardens moving on the ceiling. They’d done this a hundred times. It wasn’t the same. She held his face and kept her eyes open the whole time, because she wanted to see him, and he let her see everything, and said her name, and then the other one, the one that was only for here, and tomorrow, once, into her hair, and she said it back.

The lights stayed on all night across both gardens. In the tall house next door one window stayed lit late too, and then went dark, and its owner, for the first time in years, slept.

chapters.title: 2 A.M., The Porch
chapters.desc: Epilogue. On the night she turns twenty-five, Eliana sits on the porch at two in the morning, not because the house is too quiet but because it’s exactly quiet enough. She has something to ask. The boy next door comes out and sits down beside her.
chapters.epigraph: “You came out.” / “I live here now. I’ll always come out.” — Eliana Lin and Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
She went out at two because she wanted to, which was new.

Not because she couldn’t sleep. She slept now. She’d slept most nights for two years, in the bed upstairs in the house that was theirs, with the bath down the landing and the blue blanket on top of everything, and some mornings she woke up after he’d gone and didn’t know what time it was, which had never happened to her once in the tall house. Tonight she’d woken at a quarter to two with a thought in her head, and lain there with it, and then got up and taken the blanket off the end of the bed and gone down the stairs on the edges and out of the front door.

The porch was cold and long and dark. Both halves. She went past Jinx’s bench to the Lin end and sat down on the third step of the tall house, the one with the crack, under the red paper charm on the door that Ah Sim had changed at New Year and that was already going pink.

She put the blanket round her shoulders. It was thin now, worn soft at the edges, with a darn in one corner where she’d caught it on a nail during the building. He’d darned it. He’d sat at his desk with a needle for an hour, frowning, and not let her watch.

The lane was empty. The noodle stall was shuttered. The lamp at the end was on.

She looked at the lane and thought about the thing in her head, and waited, because she knew.

✦ ✦ ✦

It had been a good birthday. She hadn’t known birthdays could be that.

They’d gone to the grave at dawn, all of them, the way they always would. Baba first up the path, slow now, with Mok’s arm under his elbow on the steep bit. Elowen with the flowers. Raiden, Jinx, Evangeline and Jun Hyuk, Elara with Xing Yue; and Zhao and Yu Chen waiting at the gate together the way they’d waited for three years now, saying nothing, which Zhao had told Elowen was his favourite part of February.

At the stone, when the incense was lit, her father had turned round to her the way he had two years ago, and said it. Happy birthday, Yu-er. To her face. He didn’t have to work himself up to it now. He just said it, and looked at her, and then he’d done the thing he’d learned to do with her at last, which was to ask.

“Is it good? The firm?”

She said it was good. He asked if they were paying her enough, and she said Si-Wei thought they were paying her too much.

“Then she’s wrong,” said her father, and turned back to the stone, and she’d seen Elowen’s shoulders start to shake with laughing.

At lunch there’d been a cake at the long table in the tall house, a small one, with her name on it in Ah Sim’s terrible icing, and twenty-five candles that Raiden had counted out loud. Nobody had made a speech. Jun Hyuk had talked. She’d blown the candles out in one breath, and her father had clapped, three times, slowly, the way the noodle man clapped, and then looked embarrassed and passed her the vinegar.

And in the morning, before any of it, there’d been two eggs.

One on the top step of the Song half of the porch at a quarter to five, red, warm, in a white saucer, where a big old man still came along the porch in the dark every year to leave it because he’d never once missed and wasn’t going to start. And one outside their bedroom door, on the landing, in a teacup, a bit lopsided, because the person who’d boiled it at four had never got the dye right.

“You don’t have to,” she’d said, sitting up in bed with it in her hand.

“You did mine,” said Yu Chen. “In January.”

Hers had come out green. He’d eaten all of it anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

FENCE had four people in it now, and two floors of the building over the dumpling shop, and a real sign at last, small and metal and plain, with the sticky note framed behind glass on the wall inside the door where every client saw it on the way up. Legal. Mostly. Si-Wei had wanted to take the mostly off the metal one. Eliana had won.

Ren Hao sent them a new client every month and came to visit twice a month to tell them he loved them. The dumpling woman had stopped asking whether the landlord was coming and started asking whether the landlord was eating. Professor Ou had sent two of his best students to be interviewed and one of them was so frightened of her she’d hired him on the spot because he reminded her of herself.

The family’s things she still did, sometimes, from the back room behind the door that locked. Not upstairs at four in the morning any more. When Baba rang, or Chen Si, or one of her sisters. Not often. Enough.

He was in his second year of emergency training. He’d stopped being frightened of the department sometime last summer and started being the person the frightened ones went to find. Dr. Toh had started calling him by his first name, which Bernie said she’d never once done in twenty years for anybody. He still came home on his father’s green bicycle with the camera on the seat. He still waited for her on kerbs, outside FENCE, outside the hospital, outside the tall house on Sundays, with his elbows on his knees, and she still went red when she came out and saw him, every single time, which he said was the best thing about any day.

✦ ✦ ✦

She heard the front door open behind her just after two.

She didn’t turn round. She heard him come along the porch in his socks, past the bench, past the place in the middle where the wall had been and where the boards were newer and paler, and stop beside her. Then he sat down on the third step of the tall house next to her, the way he’d sat down there the first time, and put half the blanket round himself, and she let him.

“You came out,” she said.

“I live here now,” said Yu Chen. “I’ll always come out.”

He’d brought the flask. Of course he had. He unscrewed the top and poured some and gave it to her, and she drank it, and it was too sweet, and it was the only tea she’d ever liked.

“Your light wasn’t on,” he said. “I woke up and you weren’t there, and the light wasn’t on in the long room, and I thought—” He stopped. “I knew where you’d be.”

She’d known he’d look. He looked every night, at two, and she’d stopped wanting him not to a long time ago.

She put her feet under his leg. They were freezing. He let her. “I want to ask you something.”

He went still beside her. She felt it. She’d asked him things before, but not like this, not out loud on a step at two in the morning in the voice she used when it mattered, and he knew the voice.

“There’s a job,” she said. “Not here. A long way. A firm across the sea wants me for three months, to look at everything they’ve got and tell them what’s wrong. Ren Hao sent them. They’re paying a lot. Si-Wei says I have to.” She looked at the lane. “I’ve never been anywhere. Not really. Not without a laptop and a reason to come home in two days. I want to go. I want to go and see it and be somewhere nobody’s ever heard of the Lins.”

He didn’t say anything.

“And I want you to come,” said Eliana. “For some of it. As much as you can. I know you can’t come for all of it, I know you’ve got the department, I’m not asking you to—I just want you there. Some of it. On a different step.” She swallowed. “That’s what I wanted to ask. I didn’t want to put it in the jar. I wanted to say it.”

She’d said it. Out loud, to his face, the thing she wanted, without making it smaller first. She sat on the step with her heart going and waited.

“You’ve ordered noodles at two in the morning every night this week,” said Yu Chen.

She turned and stared at him.

“Since Monday,” he said. “From the place that does the beef. And not eaten them till morning, because they’ve been in the fridge. You only do that when you’re trying to decide something and you can’t sleep for it.” His ears were going in the lamplight. “I put in for leave on Wednesday.”

“You what?”

“Four weeks. In the summer. Toh owes me. I’ve done every Christmas since I started.” He looked at the lane. “I didn’t know what it was for. I didn’t know where. I didn’t ask. I just knew you were going to ask me something, and that it was going to be big, because of the noodles, and I wanted to be able to say yes before you’d finished.”

She sat there with the tea in her hands.

“You read my food orders,” she said. “Still.”

“Every night. It’s on my card.” He didn’t look sorry at all. “Yes. To all of it. Wherever it is. I’ll come for every day they’ll give me.” He took the tea out of her hands and put it down on the step. “Ask me again, if you want. I’ll still say yes.”

She started to laugh. She couldn’t help it. She put her face in his shoulder in the blanket and laughed until her eyes ran, at him, at herself, at four portions of beef noodles in the fridge and a man who’d watched them pile up and gone and put in for leave without a word, because that was who he was and she’d never once in nearly seven years wanted him to be anybody else.

“Four weeks,” she said, into his jumper.

“For now. I’ll get more,” said Yu Chen. “We’ll go everywhere. And then we’ll come back here. To this step.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She kissed him first. She’d started doing that a lot, these last two years. She’d decided somewhere along the way that she didn’t need to wait for him to break a rule, because there weren’t any rules left except the ones they wanted, and she wanted this one.

She did it slowly. There was no hurry in it at all. She turned his face to her with her cold hand and kissed him on the third step of her father’s house at two in the morning, under the faded charm, with the blanket slipping off both of them and the flask on the step and the lamp on at the end of the lane, the way you kiss someone you’re going to kiss every day for the rest of your life and don’t need to prove anything to. He made a low sound against her mouth and put his hand in her hair and kissed her back exactly the same way, unhurried, married, as if they had all night, which they did, and all the nights after.

It didn’t stay slow. It never did with them. His hand went from her hair to the back of her neck, warm, and hers went into the front of his jumper, and she was half in his lap on the step with the blanket gone altogether and the cold not mattering.

“We’re on your father’s step,” he said against her throat.

“He’s asleep. He’s always asleep at two now.”

She laughed into his mouth and kissed him harder.

“Inside,” he said, at last. “It’s February. Your feet are ice.”

“In a minute,” said Eliana. “I want to say something first.”

He waited. He always waited.

She looked up past him at the tall house. Her father’s study window, on the second floor, was dark. It had been dark at two every night for months; he slept now too. She looked along the porch at the Song house, their house, with its long room and its two desks and its bath, and the bench where the wall had been. Over the garden wall the persimmon tree was bare, black branches against the orange sky of the city, waiting for October. Somewhere behind its roots, behind a loose brick, there was a jar with notes in it that nobody read until the writer had gone in.

For years she hadn’t been able to say one word. She’d been afraid of it the way some people are afraid of water. People say it and then they’re in a hospital. People say it and then they don’t come home. It had been the most frightening word she knew, and she’d run from it inside a red door and bolted it, and come back nine days later and asked him to teach her, and he had, one day at a time, by never once not being there.

She wasn’t afraid of it any more. She found that out sitting on the step, the way you find a coin in a pocket.

“Forever,” she said.

She said it out loud, plainly, to his face, in the lamplight at the end of the lane: just the word, said by someone who wasn’t scared of it.

He looked at her. His eyes had gone wet. He didn’t do anything about it.

“Forever,” said Yu Chen.

Then he picked up the blanket off the step and put it round her, and stood up, and pulled her up after him, and took her in along the porch past the bench and through their own front door, and she didn’t look back at the lane, or the lamp, or the step, because she knew they’d all be there tomorrow, and the night after, and every night after that, and so would he.

The front door shut. The lane was quiet. The lamp stayed on at the end of it.

Across the porch, on the third step of the tall house, the flask sat where they’d left it, still warm, until the morning.

chapters.title: A History of Untangled Headphones
chapters.desc: Six years of Yu Chen untangling Eliana’s wired headphones, mending the ones she breaks, and buying the last forty pairs in the city when the make is stopped. He has never once complained. Then she finds the one pair she untangled for him.
chapters.epigraph: “Pair twenty-six. She’d tied it in a reef knot and a bowline. I was almost impressed.” — Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
On the last Sunday in November she went looking for a pen in his desk and came back with a pair of headphones.

She held them up by one earpiece. They hung in a coil the size of a fist, wound the wrong way round, with a strip of tape round the middle. On the tape, in her own small handwriting that sloped backwards, it said DONE (SORT OF).

“Why is this in your drawer?”

“It’s mine,” said Yu Chen.

“They’re my headphones. They’re all my headphones.” She turned the coil over in her fingers. It was raining on the garden and the long room was grey, and she was in his jumper over her hoodie, married five weeks, with her feet bare on the cold boards. “I did this. I remember doing it. It’s awful.”

“I know. That’s why it’s in the drawer.”

She sat on the edge of his desk, on the textbook he’d been reading, and waited.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first ones came over the wall in a shoebox in July 2021, with a skull drawn on the lid.

She’d been clearing her desk for another screen. She said she couldn’t throw them out and couldn’t look at them, and would he keep them, and went back over the wall before he could answer. Nearly twenty pairs, all the same make, all white, all wired, because wireless ones could be listened to by anyone who cared to, and she would know.

He didn’t open the box for months. She’d said she couldn’t look at them, and it felt like hers to open. When he did, one Friday in October, he sat on his bedroom floor for two hours and untangled every pair, slowly, the way he’d been shown to tie off stitches in the skills lab: find the end, follow it back, don’t pull. He coiled each one round three fingers and taped it, and wrote on the tape how long it was now, because the ones she’d mended herself had all come out different.

That was the night she opened the red door before he knocked.

In August he’d found the shop that sold them, in the arcade under the flyover, and bought ten. The man behind the counter asked if he was starting a business. Yu Chen said no and paid. He gave her the ten on the second Thursday of term, at the bottom of the library stairs, and told her not to argue, because she went through them like socks.

She’d dropped his flask down the middle of those same stairs a week and a half before, on her first day. It had hit every flight to the bottom. He’d gone down and got it and drunk from it with the dent facing her, and he’d never had it fixed. It was the one thing he never mended, because the dent was hers.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You remember all of them,” she said.

“Not all of them.”

“You do. You’re doing the face.” She pushed her glasses up. “Go on.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In January 2022 the man in the arcade told him the make was stopping. The factory had closed. He had forty left in the back.

“Your girlfriend’s?” said the man, when Yu Chen asked for all of them.

“My neighbour’s.”

It was a lie by then, and the first one he told about her to a stranger. But she had a rule for it, the morning after his roof: if anyone asks, we’re neighbours. So he stood in the arcade and said neighbour, politely, and carried forty boxes home in two bags on the handlebars of his father’s bicycle in the rain.

He wrote a number on each box with a marker, one to forty, and put them on top of his wardrobe. When a pair died, he left a new one beside the flask on her third step, or in the jar, and said nothing. She never once said thank you, and never once ran out.

He knew her months by them. That was the part he didn’t tell anyone. A pair lasted six or seven weeks if things were all right. When things were bad it lasted ten days. He could read a winter by how fast the numbers went down, the same way he read the orders on his card, and he never said so out loud until much later, because said out loud it sounded like what it was.

✦ ✦ ✦

Pair seven came back in two pieces.

It was a Monday in March, three days after a stranger called He Si-Mei had fixed Eliana’s mistake and sent Chen Si an invoice. He found it in the jar at seven in the morning, behind the loose brick: both halves, cut clean through in the middle with kitchen scissors. No note.

He didn’t ask. He bought a small soldering iron and some heat-shrink from the arcade, where the man had started nodding at him, and sat at Auntie Dai’s kitchen table that night with a magnifying lamp and joined every one of the tiny wires inside, colour to colour. It took him three hours and he burned his thumb twice. The left side came out a finger’s width shorter than the right.

He put them back in the jar.

She wore pair seven for the next four years whenever she wanted to win something. She never told him that either. He’d seen it on the bus, and at her talk about the bank in the raked hall, and round her neck on the morning she went to meet He Si-Mei at last.

✦ ✦ ✦

Pair twelve she wound round a pencil so tight the pencil snapped. Pair fifteen went through Ah Sim’s washing machine in the pocket of a hoodie and came out working, which neither of them could explain. Pair nineteen she lent to Jun Hyuk at New Year, who gave it back to her a week later in a box with a ribbon on it, apologising, because he’d sat on it.

Pair twenty-six was the breach.

Thirty-six hours, in September, the year they graduated. She’d sat at her screens through two nights with her hands going and her face white, and he’d brought tea and food and stood at the door, and never once asked her how. When it was over and Wei Long had come and gone, he found pair twenty-six on the floor under her chair.

She’d knotted it without noticing, the way she always did. But in the middle of the usual mess there were two knots he’d never seen her tie: a reef knot, flat and neat, and next to it a bowline.

He sat on the floor of her room with it while she slept on the camp bed, and worked out that Jinx must have taught her, in June, in the burnt-out shop, tying off cables. She’d learned two real knots in nine days and then used them, at three in the morning, on her own headphones, while she was saving her family.

He was almost impressed. He untangled it anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I don’t remember tying a bowline,” said Eliana.

“You tied two. One of them was upside down. I looked it up.”

She told him that wasn’t possible, and then that he was making it up, and then she looked down at the coil in her lap, at her own writing on the tape, and her face changed, because she’d got to the part she remembered.

✦ ✦ ✦

Pair thirty-three was the October he got in the way of a broken bottle.

Eleven stitches up his left forearm. For a week he couldn’t close his left hand properly, and on the Sunday she found him at the kitchen table trying to untangle pair thirty-three with one hand and his teeth.

She took it off him without a word.

She sat down across the table and did it herself. It took her forty minutes. She swore at it the whole time, in a low steady voice, and pulled when you shouldn’t pull, and lost the end twice, and once put her forehead down on the table and stayed there. He didn’t help. He drank his tea with his good hand and watched her, and didn’t say anything, because she’d never done it before. In five years of him doing it, she’d never once tried.

When she’d finished she wound it round her fingers, the wrong way, and taped it, and wrote on the tape, and pushed it across the table at him and wouldn’t look at him.

He gave her pair thirty-four that night and put thirty-three in his drawer, the coil and the tape and the wrong way round, and never undid it.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You could have used them,” she said. “They work.”

He said he knew they worked.

“You kept a broken coil in your desk for a year because I did it badly.”

“You did it,” he said. “That’s the whole reason.”

She sat on his book with the coil in her hands and looked at him, and he watched her try to be annoyed and not manage it.

She asked how many were left. He told her six, and she sat up as if he’d said the kitchen was on fire.

“What happens after six?”

“I mend them,” said Yu Chen. “I’m good at it. I’ve had practice.”

She stared at him. He looked back, and didn’t make it into a joke, because it wasn’t one, and she knew him well enough by now to see that. He’d mend them when they were old. He’d mend them when his eyes went and he needed the lamp. He’d sit at whichever kitchen table they had and find the end and follow it back, and not pull.

She started to unwind the coil.

He watched her do it. She took the tape off, and shook the wire loose, and it came out as tangled as the day she’d done it, because she’d never really done it at all. Then she got up on her knees on his desk, so she was taller than him for once, and put the wire round the back of his neck like a scarf, and took an end in each hand.

“This is the first time,” she said, “I’ve ever tangled anything on purpose.”

She pulled him in by both ends.

He let her. She kissed him over his own desk with the headphones round his neck and the rain on the garden glass, slowly, with her cold hands holding the wire tight so he couldn’t have gone anywhere if he’d wanted to. He didn’t want to. He put his hands on her waist under the jumper to keep her from falling off the desk, and she said against his mouth that she wasn’t going to fall, and he said he knew, and kept them there.

After a while the earpieces were somewhere under his collar, and his chair had rolled back half a metre and taken her with it off the desk into his lap, and she was laughing into his hair.

“You’re going to untangle that,” she said.

“Later,” said Yu Chen.

He did it at midnight, when she was asleep upstairs. He sat at his desk with the lamp on and took the wire off the arm of the chair where she’d left it, and found the end, and followed it back. Then he coiled it round three fingers the wrong way, the way she had, and put the tape back on with her writing still on it, and put it in the drawer.

chapters.title: Eliana Hacks the Library Booking System
chapters.desc: Study room 4B has been booked to “Wang Y.C.” every weekday morning since the March of his first year, and nobody has ever beaten him to it. The librarian who has watched it for four years has her suspicions. She never finds out how.
chapters.epigraph: “The system’s never wrong, dear. Which is how I knew something was very wrong.” — Mrs. Cai, librarian
chapters.content:
On my last day the new girl asked me what she needed to know, and I gave her four pages.

The heating on the third floor. The man who comes in on Tuesdays to read the newspapers and falls asleep, and must be woken before five because his wife worries. Which of the professors return their books and which have to be visited. And at the bottom of the fourth page, underlined, one line.

4B: leave it.

She read it and looked up. She’s twenty-six and clever, and she thinks I’m sweet, because of the cardigans and the glasses on a chain.

“Is it broken?”

“No,” I said. “It works perfectly. That’s the trouble.”

✦ ✦ ✦

4B is the last of the small study rooms at the end of the fourth floor, past the pillar, where you can’t see in from the stairs. The library is built into the side of the hill, so on that side the fourth floor is level with the path to the computer science building, and 4B’s one window looks straight out onto people’s knees. It’s the quietest room we have. Students used to fight over it.

You can book any room for two hours at a time, up to two weeks ahead. That was the rule for twenty years.

On a Monday morning in March, four years before I retired, I opened the bookings at eight and 4B said Wang Y.C., every weekday morning, nine till one, to the last day of term. Somebody had put it there on the Friday evening, all at once.

I tried to move one, because an external examiner was coming on the Thursday and wanted somewhere quiet to read scripts. The screen told me the room was taken. I tried again. It told me again, politely. I gave the examiner the room next door and she complained about the radiator.

So I rang down for the young man who looks after the computers.

He came up and sat at my desk for the whole afternoon, frowning, eating my biscuits. At five he said the bookings were valid, the student was real and in good standing, and the system was working exactly as it should. He said, “The system’s never wrong, Mrs. Cai,” and patted my desk, and went home.

The system has never been wrong in my experience either. Which was how I knew something was very wrong.

✦ ✦ ✦

I watched.

At ten to nine every morning a tall boy came up the stairs with a bag of books and a steel flask with a dent in the bottom, and said, “Morning, Mrs. Cai,” and went into 4B and shut the door. Graduate-entry medicine; I looked him up. Older than the others. Ears that went red. He was the politest boy I’d ever had on the fourth floor, and after a fortnight I realised I didn’t like it. There was nobody in it. He said good morning to me the way you’d hold a door: properly, and without looking to see who’d gone through.

So I thought it was him. He seemed the type. The clean ones always are.

At ten past nine a small girl came up after him in a hood, with a laptop held against her chest, and went into 4B without knocking. She never once looked at my desk. When she had to ask me for anything, which was twice in four years, she’d stand at the counter for a minute first with her lips moving, practising.

I never suspected her for a second. Not then.

✦ ✦ ✦

It happened every term after that. The night before term began, 4B would fill itself up with Wang Y.C. to the last day. I rang the young man four more times. He started bringing his own biscuits.

The summer after their second year, the university bought a new booking system. It cost a great deal of money and came with a brochure, and a woman from the company came and showed us how nobody could ever book anything more than two weeks ahead again. I asked her particularly about the end room on the fourth floor. She said it was impossible.

On the first Monday of term I opened the screen at eight.

4B — Wang Y.C.

I sat back in my chair and laughed out loud, in a library, for the first time in all my years there.

✦ ✦ ✦

I saw him lose his manners once.

It was a wet morning in their third year. A law student had got up to 4B early, a big confident boy with a good watch, and was sitting in it with his feet on the table when the girl came at ten past nine. I was on the floor with the trolley. I heard him tell her the room was his now, that he’d been waiting all term to get it, and that she could find somewhere else to hide.

She stood in the doorway with the laptop against her chest and didn’t say anything at all.

The tall boy came along the corridor from the stairs with his flask. He’d gone down for something. He saw her in the doorway, and the law student’s feet, and he stopped.

I’d thought there was nobody in him. I’d been wrong about that. Somebody came out, and I didn’t care for him much.

“Get up,” he said. He didn’t raise his voice. He said it slowly, as if he had all morning and the law student didn’t. “You’re in her chair. Get up and go downstairs. I won’t say it again.”

The law student looked at him for a second. Then he took his feet off the table and got his things and went, and didn’t look back, and I don’t think he ever came up to the fourth floor again.

The tall boy held the door for the girl. When she’d gone in, he turned round and saw me with the trolley.

“Sorry, Mrs. Cai,” he said, and he was polite again, all the way through, and went in and shut the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

I saw the other thing once too.

It was later that year, after six, when the fourth floor empties. They’d left the flask on my counter downstairs. I don’t run after students with their belongings. I took it up anyway.

There’s a narrow window in the door of each room. I didn’t mean to look.

She was sitting on the table, on his books, facing him, with her feet on his chair either side of him. She’d been talking; her hands were in the air. He reached up and took her glasses off. He folded them, carefully, and put them down on top of his notes, square to the edge of the book, the way you’d put down something you meant to keep. Then he stood up and kissed her.

She stopped talking. Her hands came down into his hair.

I put the flask on the floor outside the door and went back down the stairs, slowly, on the edge of every step, so they wouldn’t creak. I have grandchildren. My face was hot all the way to the ground floor.

In the morning the flask had gone, and there was a yellow sticky note on my counter with a drawing on it in black pen: a steel flask with a dent in it, and a small heart above it. No name.

I kept it. It’s in my desk drawer, under the stapler.

✦ ✦ ✦

In their last spring, for a week and a half, he sat in 4B on his own.

Every morning at ten to nine. “Morning, Mrs. Cai.” He’d sit at the table with his books open and his pen in his hand, and not write anything, and look at the door. At ten past nine it didn’t open. He kept looking at it.

On the fourth or fifth morning I went to the window at the end of the corridor and saw her outside on the path, in her hood, with her laptop against her chest. She was standing by 4B’s window, looking in at him. He didn’t see her. He was looking at the door.

I nearly went out. I had my cardigan on and everything. Then I thought about the trolley, and the law student, and the flask on the floor, and went back to my desk, because some things aren’t the library’s business.

Then one Thursday the door of 4B opened at ten past nine.

A few weeks after that, on a Saturday in April, they came up the stairs together holding hands. She was the colour of a post box, and he was carrying both their bags and grinning like a fool. He said, “Morning, Mrs. Cai,” and for once I could see who he was saying it to.

✦ ✦ ✦

They graduated that July. I saw the gowns go past the windows.

On the first Monday of the new term 4B said Wang Y.C., nine till one, every weekday, to Christmas.

Nobody came.

It stayed empty all year. The quietest room we had, with nobody in it. The students complained. One of them, a girl in her first week, stood at my counter and told me there must be a mistake, because the room was always booked and always empty.

“The system’s never wrong, dear,” I said.

She found somewhere else. I didn’t ring the young man.

✦ ✦ ✦

On my last day, the Friday, I opened the bookings at eight for the last time.

4B said Wang Y.C., nine till one. And then, under it, from two till four, a name I’d never once seen on that screen in thirty-one years, because I’d never once booked a room for myself.

Cai M.

I went up at two.

On the table there was a steel flask, a new one, with no dent, and a cup beside it. The tea was chrysanthemum, with something sweet in it, still hot. Next to the cup was a yellow sticky note with a drawing on it in black pen: an old woman in glasses on a chain, sitting in a chair, with a cat asleep on her lap and a book open on the cat.

I looked out of the window onto the path. There was nobody there.

I sat in 4B for two hours. I drank all the tea. I read a book I’d been meaning to read for twenty years, and it was the quietest two hours I’d ever had in my life.

I don’t know how. I never did find out. I never knew her name, and I’m not going to ask.

At four I washed the cup in the staff kitchen and put the note in my handbag, and went down and wrote the last line on the fourth page for the new girl, and underlined it twice.

chapters.title: The Sticky Note Drawer
chapters.desc: Every note Eliana was ever too shy to say out loud, kept in order in a drawer in Yu Chen’s desk, from a smiling dumpling in her first fortnight on the hill to the one that just said “Official”. The week before the wedding, she catches him reading them.
chapters.epigraph: “She can’t say it. So she draws it. I keep every one.” — Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
On the Sunday before the wedding he gave up on the vows at eleven at night and opened the drawer instead.

He’d been writing them all week. He sat at his desk at the garden end of the long room with a pad of the small squares he wrote his plans on, and wrote, and read it, and tore it off and folded it and put it in his pocket. There were six in his pocket now. Across from him, at the desk that faced his, she had her screens on and her headphones in and was pretending not to watch him tear them up.

The drawer was the left one. It stuck if you pulled it straight, so he lifted it a little as he pulled, the way he’d done every night in the old room upstairs before the builders came.

They were in order. Six years of them, in stacks held with rubber bands, and a few loose at the front.

He took out the first stack and put it on the desk.

Across the two desks Eliana took one earphone out.

“What are you doing?”

“Reading.”

“Don’t read them in front of me.” She’d gone pink already. “Read them when I’m asleep, like a normal person.”

“I do read them when you’re asleep.”

She put the earphone back in and glared at her screen, and he took the rubber band off.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first one had come stuck to the lid of a plastic box, not in a book at all.

In her second week on the hill he’d had Auntie Dai make pork and chive dumplings, the ones that kept, and taken them round to the back gate of the tall house, where Ah Sim took them off him without a word, the way she’d taken things off him all summer. On the Wednesday the box had come back over the wall, empty and washed, with a yellow square on the lid. A dumpling with a smile on it. Black biro. That was all.

He’d looked at it on the kitchen counter for a while. Then he’d peeled it off carefully, so as not to bend the sticky edge, and taken it upstairs, and put it in the drawer, because he didn’t know where else to put it.

The next day there’d been one in his anatomy textbook, on the page about the bones of the hand. Two people on a step under a little tiled roof, side by side, one big checked blanket round both of them. The smaller one had a pencil in her hair and a flask that wasn’t hers.

He’d sat in a lecture theatre and looked at the crack in the ceiling until his face went back to normal.

On the back of each one, in pencil, small, he’d written the date. He’d done it from the start. He hadn’t thought about why. It was what you did with something you meant to keep for good.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You dated them,” said Eliana.

She’d come round. He hadn’t heard her; she still did the stairs and the floors on the edges, even in their own house, even when there was nobody to wake. She was standing at his shoulder in her socks with one earphone hanging.

“Yes.”

She asked if he’d done every one, and he said he had. She picked up the dumpling and turned it over and read his pencil, and went red, and then went on being red while she frowned at it.

“You’re unbelievable,” she said. Then she sat down on the arm of his chair, so she could see.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first term was mostly food. A bowl of noodles with steam coming off it. A persimmon with a face. A cat in glasses eating a dumpling bigger than the cat. She left them in his books when he wasn’t looking, and he never once caught her doing it, and he looked.

Then the drawing, in October. That one wasn’t a sticky note; it was a whole page torn from a sketchbook, folded once. The porch of the tall house, the three steps, the crack in the third one, the faded charm on the red door, and the two of them on the step under the blanket with her head on his shoulder. And under it, in her small handwriting that sloped backwards, don’t go anywhere.

He kept it at the back of the drawer, flat, because it was too big for the stacks. He took it out and put it on the desk in front of her.

She looked at it and didn’t say anything.

“You were so frightened I’d read it on the bus,” he said.

“You go red on buses.” She put her hand flat on the drawing, on the two people on the step. “I remember drawing it. I did it at four in the morning and I nearly put it in the bin twice.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The rest of that first year had a cat in a hard hat in it, for the week the boiler broke, and three planets and a small star with a label, after the planetarium, which she must have drawn the morning after, because the date on the back was her birthday. The second year had a kidney with a face and a tiny stethoscope, the week before his renal exam.

Then a gap.

There were always gaps. He knew what they were without reading his own pencil: the weeks when her light was on till five and the food orders stopped and she came out grey. She didn’t draw then. She did her work and came back up out of it, and the first note after a gap was always small, and always food.

In October of his third year there was one that wasn’t food.

It was in his clinical handbook, the morning after the porch. A heart, drawn in black biro, and scribbled out so hard the pen had nearly gone through. Then, next to it, drawn again. Smaller. Not scribbled out.

He’d found it on the ward at eight in the morning, in front of a consultant, and had to go and stand in the sluice for a minute.

She took it out of his hand now and looked at it.

“I tried to say it in a note first,” she said. “Before the porch. I’d done it in the afternoon and I couldn’t. So I said it out loud instead. And then in the morning I didn’t know what to do, and I’d already drawn it, so I put it in your book anyway.” She gave it back to him. “I can’t believe you kept the scribbled one.”

“You put it in my book,” said Yu Chen.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next stack began in February, with a drawing in his emergency handbook of the east stairwell at the hospital, the concrete steps and the rail and the door with the wired glass. Two people on a step, one of them with his head in his hands, and a takeaway box between them. No words. She’d put it in the week after the night the delivery rider died under his hands, and he hadn’t been able to look at it for a month. Then he had, and it was the one he looked at most.

She didn’t touch that one. She put her hand on the back of his neck instead, and left it there.

Then the tomorrows.

They were in their own stack with their own rubber band, and there were a lot of them. After the nine days, after she’d knocked on his door at two in the morning and asked him to teach her forever, there’d been one in his revision book every morning until his finals were over. Every one said tomorrow, in her backward pencil, and had a different small drawing next to it: a flask, a bicycle, a pair of headphones in a knot, a skeleton waving, the noodle man, a cat asleep on a stack of books. Every morning for weeks. He’d sat his written papers with one of them in his shirt pocket.

He took the band off and spread them across the desk, and they covered it.

She looked at them for a while.

“I’d forgotten I did that many,” she said.

“I hadn’t.”

“No.” She pushed her glasses up. “You wouldn’t have.”

The last stack was small. Two gowns on a hanger, with a cat’s ear at the neck of one. A shoebox with a skull on the lid, the week she moved next door. And at the front, loose, on top of everything, a yellow square in pencil, with no drawing at all.

Official. — Yu-er

There were a few after it, a building with a sticky note in its window, a bath, a train the size of her thumb. He kept them behind it. That one stayed at the front.

✦ ✦ ✦

“There aren’t many after that,” she said.

“No.”

“Because I say things now.” She sounded almost sorry about it. “Mostly. I say them out loud.”

“I know,” said Yu Chen. “I still check the drawer.”

She laughed, and then stopped, and looked at the six folded squares sticking out of his shirt pocket.

“Is that why you’re reading them? The vows?”

He didn’t answer straight away.

“You can’t say it,” he said. “So you draw it. Six years of it, and I never once had to wonder.” He looked at the tomorrows spread over his desk. “I’ve been trying to write mine down all week. Every one I write sounds like somebody else.”

She took the six squares out of his pocket without asking, and unfolded the top one, and read it. Then the next. Then she folded them all back up together and put them in her own pocket, and went back round to her own desk, and sat down, and took a sticky note off her pad.

He watched her draw.

She did it the way she always did, fast and careful at once, with her head down so her hair fell over her face. He could see it upside down across the two desks. A wall. A gate in the wall, under a branch with fruit on it.

“Don’t read it,” she said, without looking up. “You don’t read it till I’ve gone in. That’s the rule.”

He’d kept that rule for six years.

He leaned across both desks, over his own and over hers, past her screens and her keyboard and her cold tea, and kissed her while she was still drawing.

The pencil skidded right across the note. She made a noise into his mouth, half a laugh and half a protest, and didn’t let go of the pencil, and didn’t pull back either. She kissed him back over the gap between the desks with her free hand in the front of his jumper, holding him there, so he had to brace himself on the edge of her desk between her keyboard and her tea. The tea slopped. Neither of them looked. She tasted of the cold tea. When he stopped she was pink to the ears and he was half lying across two desks with his elbow in her pencil tin.

“You ruined it,” she said.

He looked down. There was a long black line through the gate. He said he’d keep it anyway, and she said she wasn’t finished.

“Finish it, then,” said Yu Chen. “I’ll wait.”

He sat back down in his own chair and waited, and she finished it with her face hot, line by line, over the top of the skid. Two people going through the gate, one tall and one small, with the black line running straight through both of them as if they were walking through rain.

She peeled it off and held it out across the desks.

He took it and turned it over and wrote the date on the back in pencil. Then he put it at the front of the drawer with Official, the two of them together, and shut the drawer, lifting it a little so it wouldn’t stick.

He didn’t write any more vows that night. On Thursday, at his desk, he wrote one line on one of the small squares, and folded it, and put it in his jacket for Saturday, and didn’t read it to anyone.

chapters.title: Eliana Checks Out Si-Wei’s Boyfriend
chapters.desc: When her best friend says, in four words, that she’s seeing a man who runs a crew in the grey market, Eliana does the only thing a good friend can: a thorough, unasked-for background check. She finds nothing bad, which annoys her more than anything else could.
chapters.epigraph: “He’s clean. Annoyingly clean. I ran it three times. Tell Si-Wei he passed.” — Eliana Lin
chapters.content:
Si-Wei said it over dumplings, on a Tuesday, in four words.

“I’m seeing someone. Don’t.”

They were in the front room at FENCE with the window open and the steam coming up from the shop below. Si-Wei had her black coffee and her cream coat and the folder of the month’s numbers, and she said it the way she said everything, looking at the folder, as if it were a line in the accounts.

Eliana put her chopsticks down.

“Don’t what?”

“Whatever you’re going to do,” said Si-Wei, and turned a page.

That was all she said. Not who, or how long. Eliana waited, because Si-Wei always said a second thing if you waited long enough, and Si-Wei drank her coffee and went through the folder line by line and told her she was spending too much on drives, and then went home.

✦ ✦ ✦

Si-Jie said a lot more, at eleven that night, in TRIPLETS + 1.

Si-Jie: SHE TOLD YOU?? SHE TOLD YOU FIRST??

Si-Jie: she told me by ACCIDENT. I saw him. outside her building. he was waiting by the door like a BODYGUARD

Si-Yuan: what does he look like

Si-Jie: like he could lift a car. like he’d lift it for her and then put it back where he found it

Si-Jie: he runs a crew. in the grey market. Si-Wei says it’s “not like that”. what is it like then Si-Wei

Si-Yuan: she’s muted us. I can feel it

Si-Jie: SHE CAN’T MUTE US WE SHARED A WOMB

Eliana read it in bed, upstairs in the Song house, with her knees up and the blue blanket round her and Yu Chen asleep beside her with his arm over his eyes, home from a late shift. She read it twice. Then she sat in the dark with her phone lit in her hand and thought about Si-Wei.

Two quiet people who never make each other talk. That was what they were. Si-Wei had sat beside her on a bench once in the worst week of her life and not asked her anything, and said the one true thing, and gone. Si-Wei had written forty pages for FENCE in the evenings and put her own fifteen per cent in small print near the back. Si-Wei collected nobody. She’d let Eliana in, and as far as Eliana knew she’d never let anyone else in at all, and now there was a man who waited by her door like a bodyguard.

At half past two Eliana got up, put his jumper on over her hoodie, and went down the stairs on the edges.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t do it at FENCE. That was her rule; FENCE was legal, mostly, and this wasn’t anybody’s business but hers. She did it at her own desk in the long room, in the dark, with the garden black behind the glass and her screens the only light.

At the counter of the dumpling shop that morning she’d needed two goes to ask for soy milk. The woman had smiled at her kindly, the way she always did, and Eliana had gone red and said thank you twice. At her desk at three in the morning she wasn’t anybody who needed two goes at anything. Her hands knew where to go, and her face went still.

By five she had everything there was to have about him.

None of it was what she’d wanted.

She’d wanted something. A woman somewhere with his name in her phone and a reason to be afraid of it. Money that came from the wrong kind of place. A man in a hospital who’d done nothing to deserve it. She’d wanted one thing she could take to Si-Wei and put down on the table next to the coffee, so that Si-Wei would know Eliana had been looking out for her the way Si-Wei had once looked out for Eliana.

There wasn’t anything. Nobody he’d ever hurt who hadn’t hurt somebody smaller first, and nothing else at all. The grey market was grey; she’d never pretended otherwise about anyone, least of all her own family. But there wasn’t a single thing in it she could hold against him, and she’d tried. She went back to the start and did it all again, slower, in case she’d missed something because she was tired. Then a third time, out of spite.

He was clean. It was the most annoying thing she’d found all year.

She sat back in her chair with her knees up and glared at the screens.

✦ ✦ ✦

The tea came at six.

She didn’t hear him on the stairs. She never did, now; she’d taught him the edges, and then the house had been rebuilt round both of them, and he’d learned the new edges by himself. He put the flask lid down on the corner of her desk, on the coaster, not touching anything else, the way he’d put it down for five years, and stood behind her chair.

He didn’t look at the screens. He looked at her.

“You’ve been down here since half past two.”

“How do you know that?”

“The bed went cold.” He poured more tea into the lid. “Whose life is that?”

She thought about lying. She’d never managed it with him.

“Si-Wei’s boyfriend.”

He was quiet. Behind her she could feel him not saying the thing, and it was worse than if he’d said it.

“Does she know you’re doing it?”

“She told me not to.”

“Yu-er,” he said.

That was all. He didn’t tell her off. He’d never told her off about the screens in his life and he wasn’t going to start over a man he’d never met. He stood behind her chair with the flask in his hand and said her name, the way he said it when he wanted her to look at something properly.

She spun the chair round to argue with him.

“She’d do it,” she said. “If it was the other way round. You know she would. She checks everybody. She checked Ren Hao’s whole firm before she’d let me take the meeting, and she’s known Ren Hao since a premiere, and she didn’t tell him either. So don’t look at me like that.”

He caught the arms of the chair.

It stopped dead, half-turned, with her in it. He held it there with one hand on each arm and bent down and kissed her, still holding the chair, so she couldn’t spin away, and she didn’t want to. His mouth was warm from the tea. She’d been cold for three hours and she hadn’t noticed till now. She made a sound against him and took hold of his collar and pulled him down further, and the chair tipped back on its wheels, and he held it, and kept kissing her until she’d forgotten they were arguing.

When he let go of the chair she was flushed and out of breath and he’d somehow ended up on his knees on the floor in front of her.

“I wasn’t going to tell you to stop,” he said.

“You were.”

“I was going to ask you to come back to bed. It’s different.” He looked up at her. “She’s the one person who never makes you talk. That’s what you said. You don’t want to be the one who makes her.”

She sat there in his jumper with her hands still in his collar and her mouth stinging, and hated that he was right.

Her phone rang on the desk.

It was Si-Jie. At six in the morning. Eliana answered because Si-Jie would only ring again.

“Did you check him?” said Si-Jie, without hello. “You checked him. I know you did. I’ve been awake all night, I couldn’t sleep, I kept thinking you’d find out he’s got a wife in another country. Has he got a wife in another country?”

Eliana looked at the screens over Yu Chen’s head. Everything there was to have about a man she’d never met, and not one thing wrong with him.

“He’s clean,” she said. “Annoyingly clean. I ran it three times. Tell Si-Wei he passed.”

“You tell her—”

“I can’t tell her. She told me not to.” She rang off.

✦ ✦ ✦

She shut it down before she could change her mind. Everything she’d found, gone. She didn’t keep a copy. She didn’t put him on the Spreadsheet. Yu Chen watched her do it from the floor and didn’t say anything, which was the right thing.

Then she drank the tea.

It was too sweet. It always was.

Four minutes later her phone buzzed on the desk.

Si-Wei: Stop it.

Si-Wei: He’s fine. I checked him myself. Before.

Eliana stared at it. Then another one came.

Si-Wei: I checked yours too. The first month we met. He passed. Barely. He looks at you too much.

She started to laugh. She couldn’t help it. She put her face down on her knees and laughed until Yu Chen got up off the floor to see what was wrong, and she held the phone up so he could read it, and watched his ears go red from the bottom up.

“Barely,” he said. She told him Si-Wei wasn’t wrong, and he didn’t argue.

She typed back one word, sorry, and then deleted it, because that wasn’t what you said to Si-Wei. She drew a coffee cup instead, with a small heart above it, and sent that.

Si-Wei: Dumplings on Tuesday. Same time.

Si-Wei: Go to bed.

“How does she know I haven’t been to bed?”

“Everybody knows that,” said Yu Chen, and picked her up out of the chair, jumper and blanket and all, and carried her back upstairs to the bed that had gone cold.

chapters.title: The Security Flaw Rematch
chapters.desc: Four years after He Si-Mei fixed her mistake and sent a bill, Eliana finally gets her in the same room: a legal contest in Ren Hao’s boardroom, with signed rules and Professor Ou keeping score. Eleven hours later the board says draw. Neither of them believes it.
chapters.epigraph: “Draw. For now. I want a rematch.” / “Obviously.” — Eliana Lin and He Si-Mei
chapters.content:
She wore pair seven.

Yu Chen noticed at the kitchen table at seven in the morning, and didn’t say anything, but she saw him notice. The left side was a finger’s width shorter than the right, because of where he’d joined it four years ago at Auntie Dai’s table with a magnifying lamp. She’d worn it for every exam she’d ever sat and for her talk about the bank. She’d never told him why.

She told him he’d want two flasks. He said he’d made two.

“One’s not for me.”

“I know,” said Yu Chen. “It’s the same tea.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was Ren Hao’s idea, which meant it was loud.

He’d come to FENCE in June with a job too big for one person: all his offices across the sea at once. He’d heard there was only one other person in the city as good as Eliana. He wanted to hire both of them. First, though, he’d like to watch them try to beat each other, legally, in his boardroom, on a Saturday, for money.

“Not real,” Si-Wei had said, reading his letter. “Nothing real. Nothing outside the room.”

“Nothing real!” said Ren Hao. “Two new laptops. I’ll buy them. You each set one up however you like, and hide ten things in it, and then you swap, and whoever finds more of the other one’s in a day wins. And then you’re both hired anyway, because I’m not an idiot.” He beamed. “I love this. I love you both. I haven’t met her.”

Si-Wei had written the rules on one page. Both of them had signed it, Eliana at her desk and He Si-Mei somewhere else, by return, with no message. Eliana had insisted on one thing: a referee who could follow it and didn’t care about the money.

So at a quarter to nine on Saturday, on the top floor of a tower on Harbour Road, Professor Ou was standing at a whiteboard in his weekend cardigan with a marker in each hand, looking as if he’d been given Christmas.

✦ ✦ ✦

He Si-Mei arrived at five to nine.

Eliana had never seen her. In four years she’d never found a photograph, which was the first thing she’d ever admired about her. She was small and pale and about Eliana’s age, in a black hoodie with the hood down and a pair of big headphones round her neck, the expensive kind that sat over your ears, the kind anyone could listen to if they cared to. She had a bag on one shoulder and nothing in her hands.

She looked round the boardroom once: the long table, the glass wall, the harbour, Ren Hao coming at her with his arms open. She stepped to one side. Ren Hao, without stopping, hugged Professor Ou instead.

Then she looked at Eliana.

“You’re smaller than I thought,” said He Si-Mei.

Eliana had practised a sentence for four years. It went out of her head completely.

“You sent a bill,” she said.

Si-Mei looked at her for a second longer, and something happened at the side of her mouth that might, on a different face, have been the start of a smile. Then she sat down at the far end of the table, opposite, put her headphones on, and opened her bag.

✦ ✦ ✦

At nine Professor Ou said “Begin,” and nothing happened for an hour that anyone else could see.

That was the thing about it. Ren Hao had wanted a show. What he got was two women in hoodies at either end of a long table, not moving. Si-Mei sat absolutely still except for her hands. Eliana sat with her knees up on the chair and frowned. Professor Ou stood at the whiteboard with his markers and didn’t write anything. The harbour went on outside the glass. Ren Hao lasted forty minutes and then went out to make phone calls in the corridor, where they could hear him telling someone in another country that he loved them.

Yu Chen sat in a chair by the glass wall with a book and didn’t turn a page.

At ten past eleven Si-Mei lifted one hand.

Professor Ou went down and looked at her screen, and nodded, and went back to the board and wrote a 1 under her name.

Eliana didn’t look up. Her frown got deeper. She’d known that was coming; she’d left that one where somebody good would find it in two hours, and Si-Mei had found it in two. That was information, not losing.

At half past eleven a flask lid came down on the table by her elbow, on a folded napkin, not touching anything else. She didn’t look at it. She drank it.

At the other end of the table, a second flask lid came down beside He Si-Mei.

Si-Mei took one headphone off and looked at it. Then at the tall man walking away from her back to the glass wall. Then, down the whole length of the table, at Eliana.

“So it’s fair,” said Eliana, without looking up.

Si-Mei looked at the tea a moment longer. She didn’t say thank you. She drank all of it.

At twenty past twelve Eliana lifted her hand for the first time, for an ordinary one, and Professor Ou wrote a 1 under her name and looked relieved.

✦ ✦ ✦

The thing in hour four was the best thing Eliana had ever done.

She couldn’t have told anyone about it afterwards, and didn’t, not even him. She’d seen something at the start, a small habit in the way Si-Mei worked, the kind you only have if you’ve worked alone for years and never once had to explain yourself to anyone. Eliana knew it because she had it too. She’d spent two hours waiting to see if she was right.

She was right.

She lifted her hand at five to one. Professor Ou came and looked, and stopped, and looked again, and then he did what he’d done in the raked hall the spring before last, in the second row, during her talk. He put his head in his hands.

He went back to the board and wrote a 2 under her name, and then rubbed it out and wrote a 3, because she’d got two at once.

At the other end of the table He Si-Mei took both headphones off and put them down.

She didn’t say anything. She looked at Eliana down the table, flat and steady, and Eliana looked back, and for the first time in four years she felt the thing she’d told Yu Chen about on the bench behind the observatory when she was nineteen: that there was somebody else in the room who could see the holes.

Then Si-Mei put her headphones back on and went to work as if she’d been insulted.

✦ ✦ ✦

By five Eliana was losing.

Five to three. Si-Mei had found four more since lunch, two of them in one hour, one after the other, and Eliana hadn’t found anything since hour four. Ren Hao had come back in and sat on the edge of the table eating a sandwich and saying “Oh no” every time Professor Ou picked up a marker, until Professor Ou asked him to leave, and he went and stood outside the glass door with his face nearly on it.

She went out to the stairwell.

She didn’t tell anyone. She just stood up and went, the way she used to go out of the red door at two in the morning when the house got too quiet, and sat down on the concrete steps between floors with her hands in her sleeves.

He came out after a minute. He didn’t sit down straight away. He stood at the window on the landing, the one that looked down the side of the tower to the harbour, and waited.

“I can’t help with the inside,” he said. “You know that.”

“I know.”

“Come and stand here for two minutes.”

She came and stood at the window. That was Dr. Toh’s trick, the one he’d brought home from the department and used on her during the breach: two minutes looking at something far away, so your eyes remembered they could. The harbour was full of ferries. She looked at them. He didn’t say anything else, and didn’t touch her, and at the end of two minutes she found she’d stopped shaking.

“She’s better than me,” she said.

“She’s as good as you. You found out in hour four.” He was looking at the ferries too. “You’ve wanted somebody as good as you since the invoice. Now she’s in there drinking my tea.”

Eliana laughed. It came out wet. She wiped her face on her sleeve and went back in.

✦ ✦ ✦

She found three in the next hour, and Si-Mei found one, and then nobody found anything for two hours, and the light went gold on the harbour and then orange.

At ten to eight it was six all.

At four minutes to eight Si-Mei lifted her hand, and Professor Ou wrote 7.

Eliana didn’t lift her head. She had something. She’d had it since six; she’d been walking all the way round it the way you walk round a house at night checking the windows, and she was nearly round. Ren Hao was standing behind Professor Ou with both hands over his mouth. Yu Chen had put his book down.

At a minute to eight she lifted her hand.

Professor Ou came and looked. He looked for a while. Then he went back to the board, and wrote a 7 under her name, and pressed the stopwatch, and said, “Time.”

Nobody said anything.

Seven, seven. Two columns, the same.

“Draw,” said Professor Ou.

Eliana looked at the board. At the other end of the table Si-Mei looked at the board. Then they looked at each other.

“Draw,” said Eliana. “For now. I want a rematch.”

“Obviously,” said He Si-Mei.

Ren Hao burst into tears.

✦ ✦ ✦

Si-Mei packed her bag in about a minute. Her phone buzzed while she was doing it, and she looked at it and turned it face down and put it in her pocket.

Eliana didn’t try to see who it was. She found, to her horror, that she had rules about Si-Mei now, the way she had rules about people she liked.

At the door Si-Mei stopped beside Yu Chen and looked up at him, and then back at Eliana down the table.

“Hour four,” she said. “Nobody’s ever done that to me.”

She went before Eliana could think of anything to say.

✦ ✦ ✦

The car park under the tower was nearly empty and smelled of hot concrete. The Volvo was at the far end by the ramp. He was walking ahead of her with both flasks and her bag, and she watched his back, his long legs, the jumper she’d put on him that morning, and something went up through her that had been building for eleven hours and had nowhere to go.

She ran.

He heard her and turned round, and she jumped, and he caught her. He dropped both flasks to do it; they hit the concrete and rolled. She had her arms round his neck and her legs round his waist and she was kissing him before he’d got his balance, hard, with her glasses crushed against his face and her hands in his hair, in the middle of an empty car park under a tower on Harbour Road. He staggered one step and got his back against the side of the Volvo and held her up and kissed her back the way he never did in public, with his whole mouth, until she was making small sounds against him that echoed off the concrete.

“It was a draw,” he said, at some point, against her jaw, and she said she knew.

“People don’t kiss like this over a draw.”

“I’ve never drawn with anyone,” said Eliana, and kissed him again, and he gave up arguing and opened the car door behind him without looking and nearly dropped her into the back seat, and she laughed so hard she was no help at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

The invoice came at eight the next morning, through the same channel as the first one, four years ago.

Rematch. Date to be agreed. Fee: none.

She read it in bed with pair seven still round her neck. Then she put it on the Spreadsheet, under the old one, in its own row.

chapters.title: Neither of Them Can Cook
chapters.desc: Two clever people who live on instant noodles and whatever Auntie Dai leaves decide to make dumplings from scratch for the whole family’s Sunday lunch. By eleven o’clock they have a plan, a spreadsheet and something that has to be hidden in the oven and later buried in the garden.
chapters.epigraph: “We have two degrees. We cannot fold a dumpling. The data is conclusive.” — Eliana Lin
chapters.content:
Ah Sim went to the country for her brother’s ninetieth birthday, and Sunday lunch had nowhere to go.

Elowen said she’d do it at the house on the hill. Raiden said he’d do it at the garage, which nobody answered. And Eliana, at the end of the long table in the tall house the Sunday before, with her chopsticks in the air, said, “We’ll do it. Next door. In the long room,” and the whole table went quiet and looked at her.

“Who’ll cook?” said Elowen.

“Us.”

Raiden laughed so hard Jinx had to hit him on the back.

Yu Chen, beside Eliana, kept his face perfectly still. Baba, at the head of the table, looked at his youngest daughter and then at Yu Chen, and then went back to his soup, and Yu Chen understood that he’d just been told he was responsible.

✦ ✦ ✦

He made a plan.

PLAN (DUMPLINGS), in capitals, on four of the small squares. He researched it all week, after shifts, the way he researched everything: three cookbooks from the library on the hill, two videos of old women in kitchens who folded faster than he could watch, a set of kitchen scales, a bag of flour the size of a pillow. Pork and chive, because that was what Auntie Dai made, and what he’d taken round to the back gate of the tall house in her second week on the hill, five years ago. Thirty for the family, plus ten in case.

“Thirty’s not enough,” said Eliana, reading the plan over his shoulder at midnight. “Jun Hyuk eats eleven.”

“I’ve put him down for eleven.”

“Zhao eats more than he lets anyone see. Raiden eats off everyone’s plate. Baba will eat exactly six and then watch everyone else.” She took the pen out of his hand. “Sixty.”

She also made a spreadsheet. Of course she did. Time per fold, folds per minute, two people folding, how long the water took to boil on the new hob. By her numbers they’d be finished by half past eleven with time for a nap.

“That’s not how cooking works,” he said.

“Everything’s how spreadsheets work,” said Eliana.

✦ ✦ ✦

They started at eight on Sunday morning. Auntie Dai didn’t come on Sundays. It was the first time he’d ever wished she did.

The dough went wrong first.

The recipe said a cup of water. He measured a cup of water. Eliana, beside him in her hoodie with the sleeves pushed up, decided the dough looked dry and added more from the tap while he was reading the next line, and by the time he looked up she was standing over the bowl with both hands in something that wasn’t dough but a kind of white paste that had got up her wrists.

“It’s fine,” she said.

“It’s soup.”

“It’s wet dough. You add flour.” She added flour. She added a lot of flour. A cloud of it went up and settled on both of them, on the counter and the new floor and the cookbooks, and on his PLAN, which went white.

He added more water to fix the flour. She added more flour to fix the water. By nine they had enough dough for about four hundred dumplings and it was the texture of a car tyre.

“We’ll use some of it,” said Yu Chen.

Eliana looked at the rest of it and didn’t answer.

✦ ✦ ✦

The filling was worse, because they both salted it.

Neither of them told the other. He salted it at nine when she was rolling. She salted it at twenty past when he’d gone to wash his hands. He tasted it at half past and his whole face closed up, and she watched him and tasted it herself and had to drink a glass of water standing at the sink.

They did it again. Fresh pork, from the shop at the end of the lane, where the butcher looked at the flour in Yu Chen’s hair and didn’t ask. They agreed out loud, this time, who was doing the salt.

Then they folded.

The old women in the videos had made it look like nothing. A spoon of filling, a fold, six or seven little pleats along one side, pinched shut, done, next. He watched one of them three times on his phone, propped against the flour bag. He could stitch a cut without looking. He’d closed a scalp wound in the department at four in the morning with a drunk man singing at him. He could not get a dumpling to stay shut.

Eliana’s came out round. All of them. She didn’t pleat; she folded hers in half and pressed the edges with a fork and they came out like little moons, and she sat at the long table with her tongue between her teeth doing them faster than him, one after another, flat on the tray.

“Those aren’t dumplings,” he said.

“They’re more efficient dumplings.”

She looked up at him with flour on her glasses.

“We have two degrees,” said Eliana. “We cannot fold a dumpling. The data is conclusive.”

He laughed, which was a mistake, because she threw a moon at him.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eleven they cooked the first batch, and everything that had gone wrong all morning came out at once.

He steamed his. They opened in the steamer like flowers, every one, and the filling fell out into the water underneath. She boiled hers, because she said boiling was faster, and the moons stayed shut for about a minute and then came apart in the pan with a small sad noise one after another and turned the water grey. He tried frying the rest of his, because the recipe had a picture of fried ones. They stuck to the pan and burned on the bottom and stayed raw on top, and the kitchen filled with smoke, and both their phones went off at once.

SMOKE. KITCHEN. CAM 1.

She’d put the camera there in August. Nobody had asked for it.

They stood in the smoke in the long room with the back door open and the tea towel going and looked at it all: the burned pan, the grey water, the steamer full of opened flowers, the tray of raw moons, the flour on everything. It was twenty past eleven. Eight people were coming at one.

“Okay,” said Eliana. “Okay.”

She got her phone out. He watched her look at it, and then go pink, because she was going to have to ring somebody and speak.

“Terrace Road,” she said. “The woman under FENCE. She does them on Sundays.” She swallowed. “I’ll have to talk to her.”

“I’ll do it.”

“No.” She pushed her glasses up and left a white mark on her nose. “I’ll do it. You hide the evidence.”

She went out onto the porch to ring, and he heard her through the door practising the words twice under her breath before she pressed the number, and then saying them, in a small steady voice, all the way through. Sixty. Pork and chive. To the Song house, the Walled City. Yes, the girl from upstairs. Yes, the landlord’s. No, he can’t cook either.

He put everything that had gone wrong into the big roasting tin, and the roasting tin into the oven, and shut the oven door, and opened every window in the house.

✦ ✦ ✦

The dumpling woman’s son brought them at a quarter to one on his moped, in four big foil trays. He looked at Yu Chen in the doorway, at the flour still in his hair, and said, “Mum says if anyone asks, she’s never heard of you,” and rode off.

They tipped them onto Auntie Dai’s best plates.

At one the family came along the porch in a line, past the bench, through the place where the wall had been, and into the long room for the first time: Baba in his cardigan, slow and enormous, looking at everything; Elowen in green with Zhao behind her; Raiden and Jinx; Evangeline in pale blue with Jun Hyuk carrying a cake nobody had asked him to bring. Wei Long last, with fruit.

They ate at the long table between the two desks.

It was good. That was the trouble. Jun Hyuk ate eleven and said they were the best dumplings he’d had in his life and asked for the recipe, and Eliana said “Spreadsheet,” and he nodded as if that was a recipe. Raiden ate off everyone’s plate. Wei Long ate without a word and looked at the pleats.
