Zhao picked one up with his chopsticks and looked at it for four seconds.

“Hm,” he said.

Elowen looked at Zhao. Then at the dumpling. Then at her sister, who was concentrating hard on the soy sauce. Then she got up, smiling, and said she’d just warm the rest of the cake, and walked to the oven.

Yu Chen got there first.

He didn’t know he could move that fast in his own kitchen. He was standing in front of the oven door before she’d got round the end of the table, with his back to it, being polite.

“It’s not working,” he said. “The oven. Since this morning.”

Elowen looked up at him. He looked back. She was the eldest Lin daughter, and she’d known about him since a dented flask on her shop counter, and she’d said nothing for two years. He didn’t move.

“Is it,” she said.

“Yes.”

Elowen smiled, slowly, and went back to her seat without the cake, and said nothing at all, which was worse.

Baba ate exactly six.

At the end, at the door, with Mok waiting on the porch to walk him the ten steps home, he stopped beside Yu Chen and looked down at him.

“Terrace Road,” said Lin Jian.

He went home along the porch. Yu Chen stood in his own doorway with his ears burning, and behind him in the long room Eliana put her face in her hands.

✦ ✦ ✦

They buried them at dusk.

He dug the hole at the far end of the garden, under the persimmon tree, by the wall, where the fruit was going orange on the branch over the Lin side. She brought the roasting tin out of the oven. It was all still in there: the flowers, the moons, the burned ones, the grey water gone cold, set like glue. They tipped it in. It made a sound he didn’t want to think about.

She crouched at the edge of the hole in her hoodie and looked down at it.

“Two degrees,” she said. “You can close a head wound.”

He said he couldn’t close a dumpling, and she started to laugh. She crouched there in the dirt under the persimmon tree with her hands over her face and flour still in her hair from the morning, laughing. He got down beside her on his knees. This was the best Sunday he’d had in his life, he thought, and nobody would ever believe him.

He put one knuckle under her chin, the only bit of his hand that wasn’t covered in earth, and tipped her face up.

She stopped laughing. He kissed her, slow and light, kneeling in the dirt over the grave of their dumplings, with the fruit going orange above them and the first lights coming on in the tall house over the wall. She tasted of soy sauce. When he moved back there was a white mark on her chin from his knuckle, where the flour had been, and she put her hand on the back of his neck and pulled him in again and kissed him back, longer, until he’d forgotten about the dumplings altogether.

“We’re never telling Auntie Dai,” she said against his mouth.

“She’ll know anyway,” said Yu Chen.

On Monday morning Auntie Dai came at eight, and stood in the long room, and looked at the flour still in the cracks of the new floor and the cookbooks on the counter and the roasting tin, scrubbed, drying on the rack upside down.

She put her bag down. She didn’t say anything. She went and got the big bowl out of the cupboard, and the flour, and at lunchtime there were dumplings on the table, pork and chive, pleated, perfect, a whole tray of them, and a note in her handwriting under the plate that said Watch.

chapters.title: The Lin Sisters’ Group Chat
chapters.desc: Eliana is the admin, which means she runs the sisters’ group chat with an iron hand, adds Haozhen once for a joke, adds Raiden for a worse one, and removes Raiden whenever he gets back in. Three years of a family, told one message at a time.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m the admin. Raiden is removed. Raiden has been re-added by Raiden. Raiden is removed.” — Eliana Lin
chapters.content:
The chat was called LIN SISTERS, and it had been since she made it, and it was going to stay that way whatever anyone else called it.

It had started with four of them. Then Raiden married Jinx, and Elowen said Jinx was a sister now and that was the end of it, so Eliana added her. Then Aurelia found out it existed and was furious that it existed without her. Elowen said absolutely not. Aurelia said she’d been in a chat with Elowen since school and could be in one again. By the end of a long weekend in which nobody could work out who’d added whom, Aurelia was in it, and so was her sister Serafina, who didn’t mind either way.

By the summer of 2024 the rest of the family called it the wives’ chat. Eliana pointed out every time that she wasn’t a wife, Elara wasn’t a wife, and Evangeline and Serafina weren’t wives yet. Nobody listened.

She had two rules for it. No husbands. No Baba.

And no Raiden, ever, which was the same rule as the first one but needed saying separately.

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden came to find her at Sunday lunch in July, in the kitchen of the tall house, while Ah Sim was in the garden.

“Add me,” he said.

“No.”

“One message. One. Then I’ll leave on my own. I promise.” He had the face on, the sunny one, the one Elowen said meant he’d already decided. “Jinx and Serafina have been arguing about the bike and the car since New Year. I’ve found a date and a track. I need to put it to them all at once, and they’re all in there, and they won’t read it if I send it to each of them.”

“Send it to Jinx.”

“Jinx won’t pass it on. She says if she organises it she’s admitting she might lose.” He leaned on the counter. “Yu-er.”

“Don’t Yu-er me.”

He looked at her, and then at what she was wearing, and lowered his voice. “That’s not your jumper. It comes down to your knees.”

She went hot from her neck up. They’d had a pact since a birthday lunch two years before, in this house. He didn’t tell anyone about the boy next door. She didn’t tell anyone she’d known about Jinx since February 2022, which by now was a moot point, but he still kept his side.

“That’s blackmail,” she said.

“It’s a favour between siblings,” said Raiden. “Same thing.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She added him at ten that night, from Yu Chen’s bed, with her laptop on her knees and her phone in her hand and a stopwatch running on the laptop.

He’d fallen asleep with his arm round her. He woke up when she started laughing.

“What?”

“Watch,” said Eliana, and turned the phone so he could see.

Raiden: Good evening ladies!!! Proposal: second Saturday in August, the circuit in the north, Gilded vs the black bike, settle it forever. I’ll hold the money

Aurelia: Who let him in

Jinx: babe no

Serafina: absolutely not

Aurelia: Elowen. Do something.

Then a small grey line across the chat: Elowen had removed Raiden.

Eliana stopped the stopwatch. It said thirty-eight seconds.

Elowen: No husbands.

Eliana: he’s not my husband

Elowen: He’s somebody’s. Who added him?

Eliana: no idea

Evangeline: Eliana.

It was the first word Evangeline had written in the chat in a month. Eliana put her face in Yu Chen’s shoulder and laughed until she couldn’t breathe.

“Why did you add him,” he said, “if you knew she’d do that?”

She wiped her eyes. “I wanted to know how long. I’ve been wondering for two years.”

Her phone buzzed again. Not the chat. Raiden, on his own.

Raiden: worth it. they’ll do it. I’m holding the money

He was right. They did it in August, with Raiden holding the money, which went the way anyone in the family could have told them it would.

She was still laughing when Yu Chen moved behind her and put his mouth on the back of her neck.

She’d been typing. She was going to tell Elowen she had no idea who’d added him, again, at more length. He kissed the back of her neck, slow, under the knot of her hair where the pencil was, then the side of it, then the place under her ear. She typed no ide and stopped. Her thumbs stayed on the screen and didn’t do anything else.

“I’m busy,” she said. “I’m lying to my sister.”

“I know,” said Yu Chen against her ear, and didn’t stop.

She put the phone face down on the blanket. She turned over into him and he kissed her properly, his hand in her hair, the pencil coming out somewhere and going under the pillow, and the phone went on buzzing under the blanket where she’d left it, Aurelia, Aurelia, Elowen, Aurelia, and neither of them looked at it again that night.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday Raiden got back in.

> Jinx has added Raiden.

Raiden: I’ve borrowed my wife’s phone. She doesn’t know. Hello again!!

Eliana went into the settings, on the bus, and changed it so only the admins could add anyone. Then she removed him.

Eliana: I’m the admin. Raiden is removed. Raiden has been re-added by Raiden. Raiden is removed.

Aurelia: Thank you.

Elowen: Thank you.

Aurelia: Don’t agree with me.

Elowen: I said it first. That’s a point.

Serafina: you said it at the same time

Eliana muted them both for an hour and went back to work.

✦ ✦ ✦

He tried again about twice a week for the rest of the year. Once through Jinx’s phone again, after she’d changed the settings, which didn’t work. Once through Baba, who had no idea what a group chat was, and told Ah Sim at breakfast to tell Eliana to give her brother whatever he wanted. Ah Sim told her. Eliana said no. Ah Sim told Baba, and Baba said, “Good,” and went back to his paper.

She removed him every time. She started to enjoy it.

✦ ✦ ✦

In April the next year, a month after a day in a grey car with a man who didn’t say much, she added Haozhen.

It was a joke. Mostly. She’d had his phone open that day in under four minutes and put a ringtone on it he still hadn’t found how to change, and she wanted to see what he’d do in a room full of Lin women and Aurelia.

He did nothing. For three hours the chat talked round him, about a wedding cake and a man at the flower market and the paint on Jinx’s new tank, and Haozhen’s name sat at the bottom of the list and said nothing.

Then, at midnight:

Haozhen: Noted.

And he left.

Serafina: he says thank you for having him

Eliana didn’t add him again. She’d seen what she wanted, which was that he’d read every message for three hours before he went.

✦ ✦ ✦

The chat wasn’t really jokes. She knew that, even if she’d never have said it.

It was where Elowen posted a photograph of the shop every morning at six, buckets and stems and the light coming in, whether anyone answered or not. It was where Jinx put a photo of her bike every time she changed something, and Serafina told her it was beautiful and would look good in her mirror. It was where Aurelia sent screenshots of reviews and pretended she didn’t care.

It was where Evangeline wrote one word a month, and every time she did, everybody stopped.

The winter after the knife at the red door, Elara’s name went quiet at the bottom of the list. She didn’t leave. She just didn’t write anything, for weeks, and then for months. Nobody mentioned it. Elowen went on posting the shop at six every morning, so that there’d be something to look at without having to answer. Eliana pinned her to the top, and for three weeks sent her a message of her own every night, outside the chat, that said only here.

In February, from Fig Tree Lane, Elara sent a photograph to the chat. Sergeant the cat, asleep on Jun Hyuk’s boots. No words.

Eliana looked at it at her desk next door with her hand over her mouth, and didn’t move. Yu Chen came and stood behind her chair and looked at it with her, and didn’t ask, and after a while put a cup of tea down by her elbow.

Underneath it, one after another:

Elowen: ❤️

Jinx: that cat is the size of a dog

Aurelia: Those boots are a crime

Serafina: LOOK AT HIM

Evangeline: Mine.

✦ ✦ ✦

On a Sunday morning in November, at ten past two, she sent a photograph of her left hand.

It had a ring on it. Plain old gold, a small round stone the colour of weak tea. She’d taken it on the third step of the tall house, inside the blanket, with the lamp from the end of the lane on it, and she was still shaking when she pressed send.

For about ten seconds nothing happened.

Then the chat went, all at once, at two in the morning, every single one of them awake.

Elowen: YU-ER

Elowen: WHO MADE IT SMALLER

Aurelia: I did.

Aurelia: Point.

Elowen: That is NOT a point

Jinx: I’M CRYING. Raiden’s crying. I’ve told him. he’s on the floor

Serafina: CONGRATULATIONS!!!!!! Haozhen says congratulations

Elara: Oh Yu-er. Oh I’m so happy. I’m coming over. I’m putting my shoes on

Elowen: It’s two in the morning

Elara: I’ve got my shoes on

Evangeline: Good.

Eliana read it on the step with her head on his shoulder and his arm round her inside the blanket, and the tall house lighting up window by window behind them.

She didn’t add Raiden that night. But in the morning, at six, she added him for one hour, on purpose, so he could see it.

Raiden: I’ve known since 2022

Raiden: I was right about the boy next door

Raiden: I’m leaving now. I love you all. Even Aurelia

Aurelia: Get out.

He removed himself. Eliana didn’t start the stopwatch.

chapters.title: A Notebook of Teas, All for Her
chapters.desc: Yu Chen keeps a notebook of teas, every one worked out for one of Eliana’s bad nights: can’t sleep, won’t eat, nine hours at a screen. It’s a love letter he’d never call one. One page near the back isn’t in his handwriting.
chapters.epigraph: “Page nine: for the nights she won’t say are bad. Chrysanthemum, dried pear, a little rock sugar.” — Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
She came home on the Thursday night in March after two days at FENCE with her voice gone and her hood up, and said she was fine, and went straight to her desk.

He didn’t argue. He went to the kitchen end of the long room and got the notebook out of the drawer by the cooker and opened it at the back, where the clean pages were, and wrote the date at the top and then, under it, in capitals: TWO DAYS AT IT. PRETENDING SHE HASN’T.

Then he stood with the pen over the page and thought about what to put under that.

The notebook was black, with squared paper, from the stationer at the bottom of the hill. He’d bought it on her first day of university, the evening of the day she’d dropped his flask down the middle of the library stairs. He’d come home that night with the dented flask in his bag and a feeling that he was going to have to do this properly, and on the way past the stationer he’d gone in.

The first eight pages were failures.

✦ ✦ ✦

Page one was plain chrysanthemum, because he’d read that it was good for tired eyes and thought he could do better than what was already in her flask. He still didn’t know if the eyes part was true. She’d said it tasted like the inside of a cupboard.

Page two was green tea. Keeps her awake, he’d written underneath, and then, in different ink, a day later, She’s awake anyway.

Page three was jasmine. Smelled like a hotel. Page four was barley, which she drank and said nothing about, which he’d learned by then meant she didn’t like it. Page five was something Auntie Dai recommended that he couldn’t now remember the name of and that Eliana had poured into the flowerbed under the persimmon tree when she thought he wasn’t looking. Pages six, seven and eight were variations on page five, which had been a mistake.

Page nine was the one he’d been making all along.

That was the thing it had taken him eight pages to see. The tea in his flask on the steps that June night, the one she’d taken off him and said was too sweet and gone on drinking, had been his own, the one he made himself every night that summer: chrysanthemum, a pinch of dried pear, a little rock sugar. He’d been making it for her every morning since. Then he’d gone looking for something cleverer, for her eyes and her sleep and her not eating, and what she’d wanted all along was the one she already had.

So he’d written it out, on page nine, in full. How much of each. Water off the boil for a minute. Five minutes, no more. Then, at the top, the heading, which had taken him longer than the recipe.

For the nights she won’t say are bad.

✦ ✦ ✦

The pages after that were for particular things.

For nine hours at a screen: chrysanthemum and goji berries, because Auntie Dai said goji was for the eyes. Eliana picked the berries out and lined them up along the edge of her desk in rows, and sometimes in shapes, and once, during his second-year exams, in the shape of a kidney. He’d written that down too.

For when she wasn’t eating: dried hawthorn and a little honey. He didn’t know if hawthorn did what people said. But it was sour enough that she wanted something salty after, and he always had the noodles ready for when she did. That was the point of that page. It said so, in brackets.

For February: longan and red dates, from a letter of Nainai’s, in the first winter. For people who don’t sleep, Nainai had written. I don’t know if it works. Your grandfather drank it for fifty years and slept like a stone, so either it works or he did. He made it every February in the week before her birthday. She’d slept, the first year, the night after the planetarium. He’d written that down with a question mark, because he was training to be a doctor.

For a cold: ginger and brown sugar. She hated it. He made it anyway and she drank it holding her nose, which wasn’t the point either, but it got the ginger in.

He’d never once made any of it for anybody else. Kenny had asked, on placement, what was in the flask, and Yu Chen had said it was for someone. Bernie, in the department, had asked once at four in the morning if there was any going. He’d given her the hospital’s teabags, politely, with milk, and gone back to his patient.

✦ ✦ ✦

Some of the pages weren’t recipes.

October, the year she was twenty: Plain hot water. Hold the cup for her. That was all he’d written the day the fence found the photograph. He hadn’t been able to think of anything a tea could do. She’d sat on the floor of the front room in the tall house all day and he’d held the cup, and she’d drunk it, a sip at a time, out of his hands.

March, the nine days: Page nine. Every morning. Leave it on the step. Don’t stop. He’d written it on the first morning, in the dark, at half past six, because he needed to see it somewhere. He’d made page nine every day and left it on her third step and gone to the ward, and every day it had gone in.

September, the breach: Strong. Every hour. Make her stand at the window for two minutes. The second part wasn’t tea. It had gone on the page anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Is that the tea book?”

She’d come down the long room in her socks without a sound. She had his jumper on over the hoodie and her voice was a croak.

He didn’t close it. He’d never hidden it. It had lived in the drawer by the cooker with the chopsticks and the rubber bands and the takeaway menus, where anyone could have found it. She’d opened it once, in October, at a clean page at the back, and told him afterwards she hadn’t read any of the rest, because it was his. He’d believed her. She never lied to him about not looking; she only ever told him when she had.

She stood beside him and looked down at the page he’d just started. At the date, and the heading in capitals.

TWO DAYS AT IT. PRETENDING SHE HASN’T.

“I’m not pretending,” she said.

He pointed out that she’d lost her voice. She said that was the air conditioning at FENCE.

“The air conditioning at FENCE is a window,” said Yu Chen.

She opened her mouth and then closed it again. Then she took the notebook out of his hands and turned back through it, page by page: goji, hawthorn, Nainai’s red dates, hold the cup for her, don’t stop. He stood there and let her, with his ears going hot.

“You’ve been writing me down,” she said, “since the first day.”

“Yes.”

“I’m on a spreadsheet.” She sounded strange. “You put me on a spreadsheet.”

“It’s the only one I keep,” he said.

She didn’t say anything to that. She turned another page, and another, and stopped near the back, at the one page in the whole notebook that wasn’t in his handwriting.

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d written it in October, the week after the trolley.

He’d come home from the hospital on the Saturday morning with eleven stitches in his left arm and a dressing on his head, and for three days she hadn’t let him near the kettle. On the Monday, when he came down, the notebook had been open on the counter at a clean page. He hadn’t known she’d ever opened it.

In her small handwriting that sloped backwards, in pencil, she’d written a heading.

FOR WHEN HE GETS IN THE WAY OF THINGS.

And underneath, a recipe. Chrysanthemum, boiled hard for ten minutes, which was wrong. Four spoons of rock sugar, which was worse. Half a lemon. A slice of ginger, and beside it, in brackets, (ginger is for everything). And at the bottom, underlined: Drink all of it.

It had been the worst tea he’d ever tasted. Bitter and sour and sweet all at once, scalding, with a lemon pip in it. She’d stood in the kitchen with her arms folded and watched him drink all of it, the whole mug, with the dressing still on his head. He said it was good. She said he was a liar. He said yes, and asked for another.

She’d made him one the time before, too, the night the delivery rider died, with too much sugar, and brought it up to him in bed. He’d written that one in himself, afterwards, on its own page: Her version. Too sweet. Best one. But this was the only page she’d ever written in his book.

She looked at it now, with her finger on the underlining.

“It was disgusting,” she said. “You had two.”

“I’d have had ten,” said Yu Chen.

✦ ✦ ✦

He made page nine.

She sat on the counter while he did it, in his jumper, with her knees up and the notebook on her lap, and watched him do it the way he’d done it every morning for six years: the water off the boil, the chrysanthemum, the pinch of pear, the rock sugar, five minutes by the clock on the cooker, not by his phone. He poured it into a cup, not the flask, because she was home.

He held it out. She didn’t take it.

She took his own cup instead, the one by the sink with his tea gone half cold in it, and drank from that, and made a face. “That’s too sweet.”

“It’s mine. It’s the same.”

“I know,” said Eliana. She put the cup down and took hold of his jumper and pulled him in between her knees against the counter, and kissed him so that he’d taste it.

She tasted of the tea. His tea, chrysanthemum and pear and too much sugar, warm on her mouth. He made a sound he hadn’t meant to, with one hand flat on the counter beside her and the other in her hair. She kissed him slow and stubborn, with her cold hands under his collar, as if she’d been saving it for two days at FENCE and wasn’t going to be talked out of any of it. He forgot the cup on the counter. He forgot the notebook, which slid off her lap and fell open on the floor.

“You’re ill,” he said against her mouth.

“Then stop making me talk,” said Eliana, and pulled him back.

He carried her upstairs in the end, because she wouldn’t get down off the counter otherwise, with her face in his neck and her cup of page nine going cold in the kitchen. He went back down for it at midnight. He warmed it up and took it up to her, and she drank it in bed, all of it, without complaining once, and fell asleep with the empty cup in her hand.

He took it off her before it fell.

Then he went back down and picked the notebook up off the floor, and found his page, and wrote under the heading, under TWO DAYS AT IT. PRETENDING SHE HASN’T, the only thing that had worked.

Page nine. Carry her up. Bring it to her in bed.

chapters.title: The Monitor Wall
chapters.desc: On the night they graduate, Eliana takes Yu Chen up to her room to show him what she does all night, and he tries, once, to understand her five screens so he can help. He doesn’t. But he learns which chair, and which hour, and that turns out to be the help.
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t understand the wall. I understand her. That’s enough wall for me.” — Wang Yu Chen
chapters.content:
Her father’s light went off at twenty past eleven.

Yu Chen saw it from his kitchen, where he’d been standing in the dark in his good shirt for an hour. The study window on the second floor of the tall house went yellow to black. A minute later, his phone.

Eliana: he’s asleep. door’s open

It was. The red door was standing an inch open with the bolt already drawn back, so it wouldn’t stick and carry. He went in and closed it behind him, holding the handle down.

The hall was dark. The house smelled of Ah Sim’s soup and furniture polish. Somewhere on the second floor a big man was snoring, steadily, through a closed door, and Yu Chen stood at the foot of the stairs and listened to it for a while, because that afternoon the same man had watched his daughter kiss the boy next door on the steps of the Great Hall and turned his back and walked away.

Then he went up on the edges of the stairs, the way she’d taught him four years ago, and didn’t make a sound.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was waiting at the top with her door open.

She still had the cat hoodie on. The gown was on a hanger on the back of the door and her cap was on the real bed on top of a stack of hard drives. She looked nervous. He’d seen her look a lot of things in this room, but not that.

“Come in,” she said. “Sit there.”

She was pointing at her own chair, the good black one with arms, the one thing in the room that had cost real money apart from what was on the desk.

“That’s yours.”

“I know. Sit in it.”

He sat in it.

It was like sitting in the front of a ship at night: three screens on the desk in a curve and two more on the wall above them, filling his whole sight. The blackout curtains were shut. The cables ran along the skirting in their colour-coded bundles, taped down every hand’s width. The camp bed was against the wall with his blanket on it, the blue checked one, folded. Everything in the room was lit blue and white and grey from the screens.

He put his hands under his thighs on the seat.

She saw him do it, and something in her face eased.

“You can put your hands on the arms,” she said.

“I’m fine.”

Two rules, from the first winter: he didn’t ask what she found, and he never went near her computers, ever. He’d kept both of them for four years. He wasn’t going to start breaking them on the night she’d let him up here.

✦ ✦ ✦

She stood beside the chair and showed him.

“That one’s the fence.” The left screen on the wall. It didn’t look like anything to him: a dark page with lines of pale text coming up from the bottom, slowly, and going off the top. “It watches for us. Our names, the house, the shop, everyone’s faces. If anyone anywhere puts any of us next to a price, it wakes me up. Wherever I am. Two short buzzes, that’s family.” She touched the edge of the screen with one finger, not the glass, the frame. “I built it the week after Ev.”

He understood that much. He’d known there was something since that October, when she’d gone grey for a week and then stopped.

“That one’s cameras.” The right one on the wall. A grid of small grey squares, pictures, most of them still: the lane outside, the gate, the back garden of the tall house with his own persimmon tree in the corner of it, the front of Elowen’s shop with its shutter down, a dark street near the Docks, a shop floor with fresh black walls and nothing on them yet.

“Jinx’s,” he said.

“Two more since June.” She didn’t look pleased about it. “Nobody asked for them.”

The three on the desk were work. She said that plainly, and didn’t explain, and he didn’t ask. One was busy, windows on top of windows. One was nearly dark. The third, on the right, was the weather.

He looked at it. Clouds over the harbour, and rain tomorrow.

“Why’s that one the weather?”

“Because I never go outside,” said Eliana. “I like to know what I’m missing.”

He laughed, and she nearly did, and then she went on.

She told him about the middle one. She told it the way she’d have told it to someone who could follow, fast, with her hands, leaning past him to point at things without touching anything, and her voice went from small to quick to excited in about a minute, the way it did when she forgot to be shy. He listened with everything he had. He’d learned every nerve in the body in four years, and he sat in her chair and tried to hold on to what she was telling him, and felt it go past him like water past a stone.

She stopped.

“You didn’t get any of that.”

“I got some of it.”

“How much?”

He thought about it honestly.

“About a third,” said Yu Chen.

She stared at him. Then she put both hands over her face and laughed into them, a real laugh, high and helpless, and had to sit down on the edge of the desk.

“That’s what Jun Hyuk said,” she said through her fingers. “At New Year, when I showed him the fence under the table. I was so happy I showed him more. And the man who drove me in March said it too.”

She took her hands away. “A third’s what people say when they’re not pretending. Everybody else pretends. Elowen nods. Baba doesn’t know it’s here.” She looked at the screens. “I wanted you to see it working. Today. I don’t know why. I thought maybe if I showed you properly you’d—”

She stopped again. She looked disappointed. Not with him; he could see that. With the thing she’d hoped would happen, that hadn’t.

He hated it. He’d got a degree in medicine at three o’clock that afternoon and couldn’t follow one window of the life she lived every night, the part she was proudest of. He wasn’t going to pretend he could. He’d never once pretended with her.

So he asked her something else.

✦ ✦ ✦

“When’s it worst?”

She looked at him.

“Not what it does,” he said. “When. What time does it get bad? When do you sleep, and where, and how long?” He looked round the dark room, at the camp bed, the blanket. “Which hour, if I came up, would I be in the way, and which hour would I not?”

She didn’t answer straight away. She sat on the edge of the desk in the light of five screens and looked at him as if he’d said something in a language she’d thought only she knew.

“Three,” she said at last. “Three’s worst. Everything’s quiet and I’m tired and that’s when I make mistakes. Two’s fine. Four’s fine, if I’ve got through three.” She pushed her glasses up. “I sleep on the camp bed, not the bed. Forty minutes. The bed’s got the drives on it. I forget to eat from about ten. If it’s going well I don’t want to talk. If it’s going badly I want someone in the room and I don’t want them to say anything.”

“How do I tell which?”

“I frown when it’s going well,” said Eliana. “When it’s going badly my face goes flat.”

“I know that one,” said Yu Chen.

She was smiling now, a little, in spite of herself. “If the fence goes, two short, I’m gone. Don’t take it personally. If it ever goes long, three long ones, that’s my own walls. That’s never happened.” She looked at the left screen. “It won’t.”

He nodded. He put it away where he kept everything about her.

Three was the worst hour. She slept on the camp bed, forty minutes at a time, and stopped eating at ten. A frown was good and a flat face was bad. Two short buzzes were family, and three long ones would be hers.

That he understood. All of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came round behind the chair.

He felt her lean on the back of it, and then her chin on the top of his head, and her arms coming down over his shoulders, loose, crossed on his chest. They stayed like that and looked at the screens together, the fence going up and up, the grey squares of other people’s doors, the weather.

“You’re still sitting on your hands,” she said into his hair.

“Yes.”

“You can take them out.”

He took them out. He didn’t put them on the desk. He put them up and over his shoulders and found her wrists where they crossed on his chest and held them there.

Then he tipped his head back against her, all the way, so that he was looking straight up at her face upside down, with the screens’ light on her chin and her glasses sliding.

She bent and kissed him.

Upside down, slowly, from behind the chair, her hair coming down round both their faces like a curtain, her mouth on his the wrong way round. It should have been ridiculous. It was, a little; her glasses fell off onto his chest and she laughed against his mouth and didn’t stop. He held on to her wrists. She kissed him upside down for as long as she liked, gently, in the middle of the thing she loved most, with the fence going past behind her head.

Somewhere below them the snoring stopped.

They both went still. A door, on the second floor. Slow heavy feet on the landing. The bathroom. A long pause, at the foot of her stairs, where her father must have been standing looking up at the line of light under her door. Then the feet again, going back, and the door, and after a minute, the snoring.

She let her breath out into his hair.

“He does that,” she said. “Most nights. He stands there.”

“Does he come up?”

“No,” said Eliana. “Never.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten to three a window opened on the middle screen and she said, “Oh, that’s bad,” with delight, and asked him to get up.

He got up. She sat down in the chair, and frowned, and he went and sat on the camp bed with the blanket behind him and watched her work. She frowned and pushed her glasses up and forgot him completely, and he let her.

At three she pushed her glasses up twice in a minute. At ten past, her face went flat. He went down through the dark house on the edges of the stairs to Ah Sim’s kitchen and made tea, as near to his own as he could with what was there. He brought it up and put it by her elbow on the corner of the desk, where it wouldn’t touch anything, and went back to the camp bed without a word.

She drank it without looking. At twenty past her face came back to frowning.

At four she shut everything down but the fence and turned round in the chair and looked at him, and she was so tired she could barely keep her eyes open.

“You didn’t talk,” she said.

“You told me not to.”

“Once. Hours ago.”

He said once was enough, and she looked at him with her eyes half shut as if she’d like to argue and couldn’t find the energy.

She fell asleep in the chair. She didn’t make it to the camp bed. He got up and took the blue blanket and put it over her, all of it, up to her chin, and took her glasses off her face and folded them and put them on the desk. Then he sat down on the camp bed again, in the light of the fence going up and up and the weather over the harbour, and stayed till the window went grey behind the curtains.

He didn’t understand the wall. He’d never understand the wall. He knew which chair, and which hour, and what her face meant, and where the tea went. At half past five he went down on the edges of the stairs and out of the red door, holding the handle, and went home over the low wall and put the kettle on.

chapters.title: The Boy Who Brought His Blanket
chapters.desc: On their first wedding anniversary Eliana takes the blue checked blanket out of the cupboard and tells Yu Chen what she was thinking on the steps that June night in 2021, the night she finished school, when he sat down beside her and she fell asleep on his arm. Or didn’t.
chapters.epigraph: “I wasn’t asleep. I just didn’t want you to go home.” — Eliana Lin
chapters.content:
The blanket had been in the cupboard on the landing since June, folded in tissue paper, because it was too thin now to take across the sea and she couldn’t stand to see it on the bed without them in it.

On the night of their first anniversary she took it out.

It was a Monday. He’d swapped a shift to have it, and they’d had dinner on Harbour Road at a table Aurelia had booked without asking and paid for without saying so, and walked home up the lane in the dark past the noodle stall, where the noodle man had banged his ladle three times on the pot without looking up. The persimmons were ripe over the gate. They’d come back from the other side of the sea five weeks before with two suitcases, one of her drives and one of his books, and a box of photographs she hadn’t sorted. The house still smelled faintly of being shut up.

She stood on the landing with the blanket over her arm. It was soft as a shirt. The darn he’d put in the corner was the only part of it that still felt new.

He came up the stairs behind her and saw what she was holding, and didn’t ask.

“Come outside,” she said. “I want to tell you something.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They sat on the third step of the tall house, her step, with the crack in it, under the red charm on the door that had gone pink again. The porch ran the width of both houses behind them, and the place where the little wall had been was just pale boards now that you’d only notice if you knew. Her father’s window was dark. It was cold for October.

She put the blanket round both of them herself, before he could.

“You know the night I finished school,” she said.

“Yes.”

“You know your side of it. You’ve told me. You sat on your kitchen floor afterwards.” She looked at the lane. “You’ve never asked me mine.”

He was quiet beside her.

“You told me not to ask about the things you don’t tell me,” he said. “I thought that counted.”

“It counts,” said Eliana. “I’m telling you anyway.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d seen him on his step every evening that week.

She’d come up the lane from her exams and he’d been sitting there in the heat with his phone, reading the same thing over and over and frowning at it. She’d known it was something to do with the end of his degree. Everyone on the lane knew his grandmother wanted him in the north; Auntie Dai had told the noodle man, and the noodle man told everyone. She’d decided it was the north. She’d decided it every evening, coming up the lane, and every evening she’d thought about asking him, and every evening she hadn’t, because if she asked he’d tell her.

On the Friday she came round the corner with the lolly and he was there again, and she lifted it at him, and he said “Well done.”

Nobody else had. She’d stood at the bottom of her steps with green juice running down her wrist and not known what to do with it, so she’d said “Yeah” and gone in, and stood in the dark hall with her back against the red door for a while.

At two in the morning the house was too quiet.

It always was, that summer. Baba was out. Ah Sim’s noodles were in the fridge going stiff. Evangeline was asleep, Elara was on a night placement, Elowen had come in after midnight and gone straight to bed in her old room, and the old man next door had stopped singing to his birds hours ago. Every sound in the tall house went up the stairwell and didn’t come back. She’d sat at her screens and couldn’t do anything with them, and then she’d looked out of her window across the gardens and seen that his light was on.

She went down. She drew the bolt on the red door.

“I knew it stuck,” she said now, on the step. “I knew it carried. Your window was open. I could hear your chair from my room when you leaned back in it. I drew it anyway.”

He turned his head and looked at her.

“I didn’t know why,” she said. “I wasn’t going to admit I’d done it on purpose. I just went out and sat on the step and waited to see if you’d come.”

And he’d come.

She’d heard his door, and his feet, and him stepping over the wall by the rail. She didn’t look round. She’d been terrified he’d say something about the hour, or ask what was wrong, and then she’d have to say, and she didn’t know. He didn’t. He sat down and put half of a blanket round her, and it was warm from his bed, and he said she didn’t have to talk, he’d just sit there, that was allowed.

“I said I wasn’t going to talk,” she said. “And then I talked and talked.”

“You told me off.”

“You were doing the face. The patient face.” She pushed her glasses up. “I was so angry with everyone. And you were the only one there, so you got all of it.”

She’d taken his flask because her hands were cold and it was there. She’d meant to have one mouthful. It was too sweet. It was the first thing she’d tasted properly in a week of exams and toast and energy drinks, and she’d finished one lid and poured another and held it, and she’d told him everyone was leaving. She’d said the thing about the boy who ate paper because she wanted to hear him laugh, and he had, and for half a second she’d been so pleased she forgot to be miserable.

Then she’d told him he was the only one who’d said well done.

“You opened your mouth,” she said. “Right after. I saw you. You were going to tell me something, and I thought, here it is, he’s going to say he’s going north. I was holding the lid so hard I thought it’d crack.”

“I was going to tell you about the hill.”

“I know that now.” She laughed, a little. “And then you didn’t. You went completely still. I said what, and you said my hair was coming down.”

“It was.”

“I wanted you to fix it,” said Eliana. “I didn’t know why. I said leave it.”

He didn’t say anything to that. Under the blanket she felt him go still beside her, the same way, all these years later.

She’d put her feet under his leg because they were cold, and then left them there, and leaned on him. He’d been warm. She’d thought, this is the last time. He’s finished his degree. People who finish go.

So she’d said it.

You’ll go too.

And he hadn’t answered.

“I waited,” she said. “I counted. I got to twenty and you hadn’t said anything, and I knew it was because the answer was yes and you didn’t want to say it to me on my own step at two in the morning. So I shut my eyes.”

The lane was quiet. The lamp at the end of it buzzed.

“I wasn’t asleep,” said Eliana. “I just didn’t want you to go home.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t move. She could feel him not moving, the whole length of her side, under the blanket.

“I made my breathing go slow,” she said. “I let the lid tip, so you’d think. You took it out of my hand before it fell.” She looked down at her own hands. “And then you didn’t go. I kept waiting for you to get up. Your arm went stiff, and then it went dead, I could feel it, and you didn’t move it. The cat came back. A moped went past. A bird started in the tree. The noodle man came and looked at us and I could feel my face go red with my eyes shut and I thought he’d see. And you still didn’t go.”

“I thought you were asleep,” said Yu Chen. His voice had gone rough. “I sat there till five trying not to wake you.”

“I know. I was awake for most of it.” She smiled at the lane. “I fell asleep in the end. When it was going grey. I didn’t mean to. Then Elowen was shaking my knee, and you were still there, and I went in, and I didn’t give you the blanket back. I woke up at noon in my own bed with it round me and no idea how I’d got up the stairs. And in September I found out you’d turned down the north that same morning, about an hour after I went in.”

“All those hours,” he said. “I could have said it.”

“Said what?”

“That I wasn’t going anywhere.” He was looking at her now. “If I’d known you were awake. I’d have said it.”

“You didn’t have to,” said Eliana. “You stayed.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She shut her eyes.

She hadn’t planned it. She just wanted him to see what it had looked like, from the outside, the girl on the step with her eyes shut and her breathing slow, pretending. She sat there under the blanket in the cold with her face turned up to the lamp and her eyes closed, and waited.

He kissed her left eyelid.

Lightly, so lightly she wasn’t sure for a second. Then the right one. Then, while she was still sitting there with her eyes shut and her heart going, her mouth.

She didn’t open her eyes. She let him kiss her like that, slow, on her father’s step, with her eyes shut, and only when his hand came up to the side of her face, warm, his thumb under her ear, did she open them and find him so close she couldn’t see anything else.

“You’re awake,” he said against her mouth.

She kissed him back instead of answering.

It didn’t stay slow. The blanket went off her shoulders and she didn’t feel the cold. She had her hands inside his coat and her knees up against him on the narrow step. He was kissing her throat, the place under her ear, saying her name into her hair, Yu-er, the way he always had. The persimmons hung over the gate.

She stood up before he could tell her it was cold. She picked up the blanket off the step and put it round his shoulders instead of hers. Then she took his hand and walked him along the porch, past the bench and the pale boards, in through their own front door and up the middle of every stair, loud.

He laid the blanket on the bed. She laid him down on it.

She took her time. She undid his shirt a button at a time, the way he’d once undone thirty of hers, and kissed the long pink line on his forearm and the place over his heart where it was beating hard. He lay on the blanket and let her, with his ears scarlet and his hands open on the bed, as if he still couldn’t believe his luck. She put her cold feet on him on purpose and he flinched and laughed and caught her ankles. When he pulled her down at last she was laughing too, and then she wasn’t. His hands were warm everywhere. It was slow and unhurried, with nothing to prove, his mouth at her ear and her fingers in his hair. Once she shut her eyes, and he stopped, and kissed both lids again until she opened them.

Afterwards she lay on his chest with the blanket over both of them, thin and soft and darned, and his heart going under her ear, and the window open a crack on the dark garden and the persimmon tree.

“You never once left,” she said. “Not that night. Not any night since.”

“Where would I go?” said Yu Chen. He put his hand in her hair. “You’re here.”

She fell asleep like that, for real this time. The last thing she knew was his hand in her hair and his arm under her, under the old blanket, and that he wasn’t going to move it until morning.
